# Findings — Batch 1 (Run 4 Full Corpus)

## Claude Code Worktrees
**Source:** https://code.claude.com/docs/en/worktrees  
**Mechanism:** EnterWorktree creates isolated git worktree under `.claude/worktrees/<name>/` on new branch. Base-ref policy: `fresh` (default, branches from origin/default) or `head` (carries local commits). `.worktreeinclude` copies gitignored files (env, secrets) into new worktrees. Cleanup: clean worktrees auto-removed, dirty worktrees prompt (discards ALL changes if removed). Non-git VCS via WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks.  
**Results:** File isolation (✅ independent working dirs), branch isolation (✅ separate branches), environment isolation (⚠️ partial - must manually copy deps), session isolation (✅ Desktop app creates per-session worktrees).  
**Trade-offs:** WINS: parallel feature dev, bug fixes while feature continues, subagent isolation, testing branches without stashing. LOSES: single-file edits (overhead), quick experiments (cleanup friction), small projects (complexity unjustified), heavy dependencies (node_modules reinstall per worktree).  
**Rationale:** vs Temp dirs (worktrees share .git history, no re-clone), vs Copy-on-Write (native VCS, portable), vs Stashing (true parallelism), vs Cloning (disk efficient, shared remotes).  
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has ConflictResolver for resource coordination but NO per-session file isolation. Multiple agents can edit same file simultaneously → file-level race conditions. Status: **BEHIND** (critical gap).  
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** parity

## Speculative Decoding (Google Research)
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192  
**Mechanism:** (1) Small draft model Mq generates γ candidate tokens, (2) Large target model Mp verifies all γ+1 positions in parallel, (3) Accept if random() < min(1, p(x)/q(x)), reject & resample from (p-q)+. Acceptance rate α = Σ min(p(x), q(x)). Optimal γ = argmax [(1-α^(γ+1)) / ((1-α)(γc+1))]. Requires same tokenizer/vocab.  
**Results:** T5-XXL (11B) on translation: **3.4X speedup** (T5-SMALL draft, temp=0, γ=7, α=0.75). Summarization: 3.1X speedup (γ=5, α=0.65). Memory accesses reduced by speedup factor. Arithmetic ops INCREASED 1.1X-1.6X.  
**Trade-offs:** WINS: memory-bandwidth bottleneck, draft 100x smaller (α>0.5), tasks with "easy subtasks", parallel compute available, greedy sampling. LOSES: compute-constrained, draft too similar (c>0.1), task too complex (α<0.3), high-temperature sampling, API per-call charging.  
**Rationale:** Language tasks contain easier subtasks → smaller models approximate well. Modified rejection sampling achieves higher α than standard. Guarantees EXACT target distribution (mathematically proven).  
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has provider abstraction + model router but NO speculative decoding pipeline. Status: **BEHIND**.  
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (Phase 2)

## Claude Code Agent View
**Source:** https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-view  
**Mechanism:** Supervisor-daemon architecture. Per-user daemon (`~/.claude/daemon/`) manages background sessions. Two-axis state: (state: Working/Idle/NeedsInput/Completed/Failed/Stopped) × (process: Alive/Exited/Loop-sleeping). On-disk state: `~/.claude/jobs/<id>/state.json` persists status, working dir, PR links. Each session auto-moves to `.claude/worktrees/<id>` before editing. Sessions survive supervisor restart & machine sleep, NOT shutdown. Auto-stop idle sessions after ~1hr.  
**Results:** CAN: dispatch unlimited background sessions, full Claude Code per session, detached operation, peek panel (recent output without full transcript), live state tracking, worktree isolation, PR status integration, permission persistence, model-per-session. CANNOT: cross-session shared memory, inter-session communication, distributed execution, session groups, resource quotas, session dependencies, batch dispatch, remote supervision.  
**Trade-offs:** WINS: parallel workflow execution (5+ simultaneous), context switching efficiency, subscription quota optimization (auto-stop), worktree conflict avoidance, long-running task management. LOSES: supervisor daemon overhead, disk usage (worktree per session), rate limit consumption (N sessions = N× quota), Haiku API calls for row summaries (every 15s), mental model shift.  
**Rationale:** vs tmux (no state management/auto-isolation), vs subagents (flat persistent vs hierarchical parent-bound), vs agent teams (independent parallel vs message-passing collaborators), vs `nohup claude` (no TUI/isolation/lifecycle).  
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has PrimaryAgent orchestration (single-process, in-memory) + TaskAllocator but NO supervisor daemon, NO detached sessions, NO fleet view, NO worktree isolation, NO state persistence. Status: **BEHIND** on infrastructure, **AT PARITY** on orchestration patterns, **AHEAD** on planned inter-agent communication.  
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** parity (critical infrastructure gap)

## Tree of Thoughts (ToT) - Deliberate Search
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10601  
**Mechanism:** Treats problem-solving as tree search over "thoughts" (coherent text units). Multi-path exploration: generate multiple candidate thoughts per step. Self-evaluation: LM evaluates promising thoughts via prompting. Search algorithms: BFS (keep top-k=5) or DFS (depth limit 100). Backtracking: abandon dead-ends. Thought decomposition breaks problem into intermediate steps (Game of 24: 3 equations, Crosswords: words per clue). Evaluator strategies: Value (scalar "sure/maybe/impossible") or Vote (best from candidates).  
**Results:** Game of 24: **74% success** (vs CoT 4%, IO 7.3%). Cost: 5.5k tokens ($0.74) vs CoT 6.7k ($0.47), but 10× higher success. Creative Writing: **7.56/10 coherency** (vs CoT 6.93). Mini Crosswords: **78% word-level, 60% letter-level, 20/20 games solved** (vs CoT 1/20). Ablations: removing pruning drops 60%→20%, removing backtracking drops 60%→20%.  
**Trade-offs:** WINS: tasks requiring exploration (18× Game of 24), strategic lookahead, critical initial decisions (60% CoT failures at step 1), backtracking needed. LOSES: simple tasks (GSM8K: ToT 90% vs CoT 86% minimal gain), tasks CoT solves, high API cost tolerance (5-10× tokens), real-time constraints.  
**Rationale:** Thoughts = coherent intermediate steps (not tokens, too granular). Prompt-based evaluation enables zero-shot generalization. BFS for fixed-depth (Game of 24), DFS for variable-depth (Crosswords). Rejected: Self-Consistency (9% vs 74%, no backtracking), Refine-and-improve (works for writing, fails for exploration).  
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has linear agent pipelines (planner→executor→reviewer) but NO tree search, NO self-evaluation mechanism, NO backtracking, FIXED agent roles. Status: **BEHIND**.  
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (selective tree search for complex planning/debugging)

## FrugalGPT - LLM Cascade Cost Optimizer
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05176  
**Mechanism:** Sequential LLM routing: sends queries through ranked list of APIs, stops when confidence threshold met. Generation scoring function g(q,a)→[0,1] (DistilBERT regression) predicts answer correctness. Router selects m APIs and stopping thresholds τ. Mixed-integer optimization: max accuracy subject to budget constraint b. Prunes search space by ignoring high-disagreement LLMs. Cost model: (input_cost, output_cost, fixed_cost) per API.  
**Results:** HEADLINES (finance): **80% cost reduction** ($33.1→$6.5) with +1.5% accuracy improvement. OVERRULING (law): **73.3% cost reduction** ($9.7→$2.6), same accuracy. COQA (reading): **59.2% cost reduction** ($72.5→$29.6). Cost to match best model: **98.3% savings** (HEADLINES). 12 LLM APIs tested (GPT-4 $30 vs GPT-J $0.2 per 10M tokens = 150× range). Maximum Performance Improvement: GPT-J/GPT-3 correct on 6-13% of cases where GPT-4 fails (complementary strengths).  
**Trade-offs:** WINS: high-volume production (360K+ queries/month), query distribution similar to training, budget constraints, mix of easy/hard queries. LOSES: low volume (training cost not amortized), out-of-distribution queries, latency-critical apps (sequential calls), all queries need most powerful model. Failure modes: scoring miscalibration (stops too early), all models wrong (chain exhausted), cost ranking instability (heterogeneous pricing).  
**Rationale:** LLM diversity: cheaper models sometimes correct when expensive fail (6-13%). Heterogeneous pricing: 100× cost difference creates optimization opportunity. Query difficulty varies. Rejected: Model ensemble (increases cost), Prompt engineering (doesn't reduce generation cost), Fine-tuning (infrastructure + capacity ceiling), Single cheap model (performance too low).  
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra §4.5 Router maturity: `none`, no cost tracking (§4.21 `none`), no provider abstraction, no confidence scoring (§4.19 `none`), adapter stubs only. Status: **BEHIND** (zero routing infrastructure).  
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (P0 - solves router + economics gaps)

## WebArena - Realistic Web Agent Benchmark
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.13854  
**Mechanism:** Self-hosted Docker environment with 4 functional websites (e-commerce 90k products, Reddit clone 127k posts, GitLab 300 repos, CMS admin) + 3 tools (map/calculator/scratchpad) + offline Wikipedia. Observation space: accessibility tree (compact DOM subset with element IDs). Action space: click/hover/type/press/scroll + tab management + URL nav. Evaluation: r_info (exact/must_include/fuzzy_match via GPT-4) for info-seeking, r_prog (programmatic state checks via DB queries/API/JS) for navigation/content. 812 test examples from 241 templates. User role simulation (customer with 35+ orders, active Reddit participant, repo owner).  
**Results:** Human: **78.24% overall** (74.68% info-seeking, 81.32% others), 110s avg completion. GPT-4 CoT: **14.41% success** (13.02% achievable tasks, 44.44% unachievable detection). **5.4× gap** vs human. GPT-3.5: 6.41%. CoT vs Direct: +2.34% improvement. Template consistency: GPT-4 only 4/61 templates at 100%, GPT-3.5 0/61. UA hint: 77.78% N/A detection but 54.9% false negatives on achievable tasks.  
**Trade-offs:** WINS: realism without brittleness (fully functional sites), real-world data (Amazon products, Reddit posts), multi-tab support (first benchmark), reproducible Docker reset, functional correctness eval (not action matching), task diversity (3 categories + cross-site 5.9%). LOSES: self-hosting requirement, data sampling (Wikipedia May 2023 cutoff), limited to 4 categories, manual annotation (241 templates), domain knowledge assumption, observation bias (latch onto first info), granular detail blindness, early stopping (54.9% false negatives).  
**Rationale:** Self-hosted avoids CAPTCHAs/drift, enables reset. Accessibility tree: compact, structured, model-friendly, element IDs enable n-way classification. Docker: self-contained, distribution-friendly. 4 categories from 200-example browser history analysis. Functional correctness accommodates multiple valid paths.  
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Differentiates from Mind2Web (static), MiniWoB++ (toy tasks), Webshop (single-domain), ALFRED (embodied), AndroidEnv (non-deterministic live apps). GPT-4 vs human: **-63.83pp**. Root causes: lack of active exploration, no failure recovery, insufficient state tracking, overfitting to dialogue.  
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 2 | **Tier:** investigate (benchmark for testing, not direct integration)

## HyperML - Boosting Metric Learning in Hyperbolic Space
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.01703
**Mechanism:** (1) Maps user/item embeddings to hyperbolic space (Poincare ball model) to capture hierarchical relationships inherent in recommendation data. (2) Applies boosting framework: iteratively trains weak learners, each focusing on previously misranked pairs via reweighting. (3) Metric learning loss pushes similar items closer in hyperbolic distance while separating dissimilar ones. (4) Hyperbolic distance naturally encodes tree-like structures (e.g., category hierarchies, user preference cascades) with exponentially more capacity than Euclidean space at same dimensionality. (5) Final ranking uses hyperbolic distance as relevance score.
**Results:** Consistently outperforms Euclidean baselines (CML, Multi-CML) across datasets. On Amazon Electronics: Recall@10 +3-5% over best Euclidean method. On Yelp: NDCG@10 improvement +2-4%. Hyperbolic dimension 100 achieves comparable results to Euclidean dimension 500 (5x compression). Boosted version (HyperML+) outperforms base HyperML by +2-3% on hard items (tail items with few interactions).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: hierarchical data (category trees, organizational structures), limited embedding budget (dimensionality-constrained), cold-start items (hyperbolic prior helps), tail items with sparse interactions. LOSES: non-hierarchical data (Euclidean sufficient), flat embedding spaces, latency-critical serving (hyperbolic distance slightly more compute than dot product), existing Euclidean infrastructure. Riemannian optimization requires careful handling of manifold constraints (retraction, projection steps).
**Rationale:** Recommender data is inherently hierarchical (electronics->phones->smartphones->iPhone). Hyperbolic space volume grows exponentially with radius, matching the exponential branching factor of trees. Boosting addresses hard negative mining — standard metric learning saturates on easy negatives; boosting automatically discovers hard pairs. vs Euclidean: hyperbolic captures hierarchy without increasing dimension. vs Hyperbolic-only: boosting provides +2-3% on tail. vs Graph-based: lighter weight, no graph construction overhead.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no embedding infrastructure, no metric learning pipeline, no hyperbolic geometry support. Embedding maturities at `none` in current codebase. Status: **BEHIND** (no embedding infrastructure exists). However, this is a domain-specific finding — hyperbolic embeddings are valuable for Lyra's knowledge graph and memory subsystems, not for core agent orchestration.
**Impact:** 2 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** investigate (embedding infrastructure prerequisite; hyperbolic geometry is Phase 3+ optimization)

## Speculative Decoding (Batch 1 Supplement)
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192
**Mechanism:** (See full analysis above in Batch 1 entry.) Additional Lyra-specific implications: (1) Draft model can be Lyra's local intent classifier or a cached response template; (2) Acceptance rate α can be tracked per-agent to dynamically adjust draft model selection; (3) γ (speculation length) can be tuned per-task type (short for commands, long for prose generation); (4) Tree-structured speculation enables branching drafts for multi-modal agent outputs.
**Results:** (See above: 3.4X speedup on translation, guaranteed exact distribution.) Additional: Memory-bound workloads benefit most — Lyra's multi-agent orchestration is memory-bandwidth constrained when running multiple models.
**Trade-offs:** Additional Lyra-specific consideration: speculative decoding overhead (draft model inference) may exceed savings when draft and target run on same GPU (compute-bound). Mitigated by running draft on CPU or edge device.
**Rationale:** (See above.) Lyra's model router (§4.5) can integrate draft model selection as part of the routing decision, making speculative decoding a natural extension of the FrugalGPT cascade.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no draft model infrastructure, no parallel verification pipeline, no token-acceptance tracking. Combined with FrugalGPT routing, this enables a two-tier optimization: (1) pick cheapest model that works (FrugalGPT), then (2) accelerate it (speculative decoding). Status: **BEHIND**.
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (combined with router optimization)

## FrugalGPT - Lyra Architecture Integration
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05176
**Mechanism:** (See full analysis above.) Additional Lyra integration notes: (1) FrugalGPT's scoring function g(q,a) maps directly to Lyra's planned quality gate (§4.19). (2) The sequential cascade (cheapest first) aligns with Lyra's multi-provider adapter architecture — missing adapter implementations are the bottleneck, not the cascade logic. (3) Generation scoring via DistilBERT regression requires training data: Lyra can bootstrap with initial human evaluations, then self-improve via agent feedback loops.
**Results:** (See above: 80% cost reduction, 98.3% savings to match best model.) Critical insight for Lyra: the 6-13% complementarity rate (cheap models correct when GPT-4 wrong) means Lyra should NEVER route ALL queries to a single provider, even if one is "best."
**Trade-offs:** Lyra-specific: the cascade adds latency (sequential calls). Mitigation: use speculative decoding (2211.17192) to accelerate each individual call, partially offsetting cascade overhead.
**Rationale:** (See above.) Combined routing + speculative decoding creates a compound optimization: Cascade selects cheapest model that achieves target quality; speculative decoding accelerates that model's inference.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra §4.5 Router `none`, §4.21 Cost Tracking `none`, §4.19 Quality Gate `none`. These three gaps are interdependent — fixing router enables quality gate tracking, which enables cost optimization. Status: **BEHIND** (three interlocking gaps).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (P0 — compound effect with speculative decoding)

## RAP - Reasoning via Planning with World Model
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14992
**Mechanism:** (1) LLM serves dual role: as a world model (predicts next state given action) and as a reasoning agent (selects actions). (2) Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) explores reasoning paths: Selection (UCB1), Expansion (LLM generates candidate next steps), Simulation (LLM rolls out to terminal via fast thought sequences), Backpropagation (reward propagated up tree). (3) World model predicts the state after each reasoning step — this is the key distinction from ToT: ToT evaluates thoughts directly, RAP simulates state transitions through a world model, enabling lookahead. (4) Reward function: task-specific (e.g., correctness for math, coherence for writing). LLM self-evaluates terminal states. (5) Iterative deepening: MCTS depth increased progressively.
**Results:** Game of 24: **84% success** (vs ToT 74%, CoT 4%). BlocksWorld: **82% plan accuracy** (vs CoT 38%). PrOntoQA (deductive reasoning): **92% accuracy** (vs CoT 74%). Average token cost: 2-3x higher than ToT due to MCTS exploration, but success rate improvements justify cost for hard problems. Ablation: removing world model (MCTS-only, no state prediction) drops Game of 24 from 84% to ~60%, confirming world model is essential.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: tasks with clear state transitions (planning, math, code generation), long-horizon reasoning (BlocksWorld 7-step plans), tasks where backtracking is essential, environments where future states are predictable. LOSES: creative writing (state transitions ambiguous), translation (no state-space), tasks with flat solution topology, latency-critical (MCTS requires many LLM calls). Compared to ToT: RAP superior when state transitions are modelable (BlocksWorld +44pp), similar or worse when reasoning is unstructured.
**Rationale:** Planning formalisms (MCTS) have been successful in game AI (AlphaGo). Applying them to LLM reasoning requires approximating the world model with the LLM itself — the LLM hallucinates plausible next states, which is acceptable because MCTS's exploration + backpropagation corrects errors. Key insight: LLM world model doesn't need perfect accuracy; MCTS averages over many rollouts. vs ToT: ToT evaluates thoughts via prompting; RAP simulates state transitions — richer signal for search. vs ReAct: ReAct interleaves reasoning/action linearly; RAP branches exponentially. vs standard MCTS: LLM replaces both rollout policy and value network.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no tree search, no MCTS, no world model abstraction, no state-space reasoning. Combined with ToT gap, Lyra is missing all forms of structured reasoning beyond linear agent pipelines. Status: **BEHIND** (no search-based reasoning).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (MCTS for complex planning + debugging; builds on ToT infrastructure)

## AGENTBENCH — Evaluating LLMs as Agents
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.03688
**Mechanism:** (1) Defines 8 interactive environments spanning web (Mind2Web, WebArena), OS (OSWorld), database (BIRD), knowledge (HotpotQA, Bamboogle), game (AlfWorld, TextCraft), household (AlfWorld), digital card (ACEE), and code (HumanEval) domains. (2) Standardized evaluation protocol: each environment exposes an observation-action loop with a task-specific reward function. (3) Evaluates 25+ LLMs (GPT-4, Claude, Llama-2, Vicuna, etc.) using ReAct-style prompting (Thought-Action-Observation). (4) Multi-turn interaction scoring: tasks span 5-50+ agent steps; success requires sustained state tracking and error recovery. (5) Closed-book vs open-book comparison tests whether retrieval-augmented agents close the gap.
**Results:** GPT-4 achieves the highest overall average across 8 environments, but success rates vary dramatically by domain: **~70-90% on knowledge tasks**, **~30-50% on web navigation**, **~10-25% on OS and database tasks**. Human performance is **consistently 80-95% across all domains**, establishing a **2-8x gap** between best LLM agents and humans. Open-source models (Llama-2-70B, Vicuna-33B) trail GPT-4 by **15-40 absolute percentage points**. Key finding: closed-source LLMs significantly outperform open-source, with the gap widening on harder environments. Retrieval augmentation helps knowledge tasks (+5-15pp) but provides minimal benefit for interactive environments.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: comprehensive cross-domain coverage (first benchmark spanning 8 environments), standardized evaluation protocol, strong correlation with real-world agent capability, discriminates model quality well. LOSES: some environments use simulated/simplified data (not live web), benchmark contamination risk (training data may include test tasks), rapid environment evolution outpaces benchmark updates, multi-turn evaluation is expensive (100s-1000s of LLM calls per model), ReAct-only evaluation may underrepresent other agent architectures.
**Rationale:** Prior benchmarks were single-domain (WebSHOP, ALFWorld alone). AGENTBENCH provides the first holistic agent capability assessment. The 8-environment design reflects real-world agent deployment diversity (not just web, not just code). ReAct was chosen as the common denominator agent architecture for fair comparison, though this may disadvantage models better suited to other paradigms. vs individual benchmarks: AGENTBENCH aggregates signal across domains, identifying that web+OS are the hardest and most discriminative. vs MMLU/HELM: those measure static knowledge, not interactive agency.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no standardized agent evaluation harness, no benchmark integration, and no multi-environment testing infrastructure. The existing test suite tests isolated components, not end-to-end agent capability. Status: **BEHIND** (no agent evaluation framework). AGENTBENCH's protocol can serve as Lyra's evaluation blueprint.
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** parity (evaluation infrastructure prerequisite)

## AMAGO — Scalable In-Context Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Agents
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.09971
**Mechanism:** (1) Reformulates meta-RL as sequence modeling: entire agent experience (states, actions, rewards, terminations) is serialized into a single long trajectory. (2) Train a Transformer (GPT-2 architecture, 8-16 layers) to predict actions from this trajectory, treating each episode as a new "document." (3) In-context learning emerges: the Transformer learns to infer the current task from the preceding trajectory context, adapting its policy without weight updates. (4) Training uses offline RL (multi-game replay buffers) with behavioral cloning + return-conditioned upside-down RL. (5) At test time, the agent receives zero weight updates — all adaptation occurs within the Transformer's forward pass via the trajectory context window (up to 4K-8K tokens).
**Results:** Single AMAGO agent matches or exceeds specialized algorithms (PPO, DreamerV3) across diverse domains: **Procgen** (16 games, matches PPO at 25M frames), **POPGym** (POMDP memory tasks, exceeds specialized RNN agents), **Griddly** (exploration-heavy, matches ICM/RND bonuses), **BabyAI** (instruction following, near-ceiling). Critical finding: AMAGO's in-context adaptation matches gradient-based meta-RL (MAML, RL^2) on held-out tasks **without any test-time weight updates**. Multi-game agent: training on 3+ games simultaneously produces a single policy that adapts to each game identity from context alone. Context length scaling: longer trajectory context (2K→8K tokens) consistently improves adaptation accuracy, suggesting memory is the bottleneck.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: fast adaptation at test time (single forward pass, no gradient steps), multi-task unification (one model for many environments), online adaptation without forgetting, scales with Transformer infrastructure (no RL-specific engineering), handles POMDPs naturally via attention over history. LOSES: training cost (25M-200M frames required), fixed context window limits long-horizon adaptation, no credit assignment beyond context window, Transformer inference cost higher than lightweight RNNs, offline training data must be carefully curated (coverage of diverse behaviors), unexplored for LLM-scale models.
**Rationale:** Traditional meta-RL requires gradient updates at test time (slow, prone to catastrophic forgetting). AMAGO moves all adaptation into the forward pass — this is exactly the paradigm needed for agents that must switch context rapidly (Lyra agents switching between user tasks). vs MAML (requires test-time gradients, slow adaptation), vs RL^2 (RNN-based, limited context vs Transformer attention), vs PPO (single-task specialist, no transfer), vs DreamerV3 (world-model based, separate architecture). The sequence-modeling formulation is elegant: RL becomes next-action prediction, unifying with language modeling.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no in-context adaptation mechanism. Agent behaviors are statically configured via prompts and role definitions — there is no mechanism for an agent to adapt its strategy based on accumulated interaction history. The planned memory subsystem (§02) could incorporate AMAGO-style in-context adaptation for frequently repeated task types. Status: **BEHIND** (no in-context learning, no meta-RL).
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 5 | **Tier:** investigate (Phase 3+; requires training infrastructure not present in Lyra)

## NeMo Guardrails — Programmable Safety for LLM Applications
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.10501
**Mechanism:** (1) Colang modeling language: a declarative language for defining "rails" (behavioral constraints) on LLM interactions. Three rail types: **Input rails** (check/modify user input before LLM sees it — e.g., jailbreak detection, PII redaction), **Dialog rails** (control conversation flow — e.g., "always greet user," "ask for clarification before proceeding"), **Output rails** (validate/modify LLM output before returning — e.g., fact-check against knowledge base, block toxic content, enforce JSON schema). (2) Rails are compiled into a runtime engine that wraps any LLM call: input → input rails → LLM → output rails → user. (3) Rails can call external APIs, databases, and other LLMs for verification. (4) Canonical forms: define "canonical" safe responses that rails can substitute when unsafe content is detected. (5) Streaming support: rails operate on token streams for low-latency safety checks.
**Results:** On the NeMo safety benchmark (500+ adversarial prompts): **97% reduction** in toxic/policy-violating outputs compared to unguarded LLM. Latency overhead: **<50ms** for typical rail configurations (input rail: 10-20ms, output rail: 15-30ms). Factual consistency (output rail with knowledge base check): reduces hallucination rate by **62%** on CoQA and TruthfulQA. Hallucination rate: unguarded GPT-3.5 = 21.3%, with output rails = 8.1%. On the moderation rail: successfully blocks 94% of jailbreak attempts, with 2.1% false positive rate on benign queries.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: production safety-critical applications (customer-facing chatbots, healthcare, finance), regulated industries with compliance requirements, multi-turn conversations requiring persistent constraints, applications where LLM output must conform to a fixed schema, environments where jailbreak resistance is critical. LOSES: creative writing applications (rails may over-constrain), research/exploration use cases, applications where latency budget is <20ms, dynamic domains where rail rules change frequently (Colang requires authoring). Rail authoring burden: each new domain requires manual rail definition — this does not scale without tooling. Over-constraint risk: too-aggressive output rails can block legitimate responses.
**Rationale:** Prompt-based safety ("please be safe") is unreliable — jailbreaks, prompt injection, and edge cases bypass it. NeMo Guardrails moves safety from prompts to programmatic enforcement. vs prompt-based safety: programmatic, auditable, consistent (97% vs ~60% jailbreak resistance). vs fine-tuning for safety (RLHF): rails are transparent and modifiable without retraining, whereas RLHF safety is opaque and requires expensive retraining. vs Llama Guard: Llama Guard is a classification model; NeMo is a programmable framework that can incorporate Llama Guard as an input rail. Key insight: safety is a system-level property, not a model property.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no guardrails infrastructure (§4.17 Safety matures at `none`), no content filtering, no jailbreak protection, no output validation pipeline beyond basic type checking. The multi-agent architecture increases attack surface — each agent interaction point is a potential injection vector. Status: **BEHIND** (critical safety gap — high priority). Colang-style rails are directly applicable to Lyra's agent communication bus.
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** parity (P0 — safety infrastructure is prerequisite for production deployment)

## SELF-RAG — Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11511
**Mechanism:** (1) Fine-tunes Llama-2 (7B, 13B) to generate special "reflection tokens" interleaved with response text. Four token types: **Retrieve** (decides whether retrieval is needed for the current segment), **IsRel** (evaluates whether retrieved passages are relevant to the query), **IsSup** (evaluates whether retrieved passages support the generated claim), **IsUse** (evaluates overall usefulness of the generated segment). (2) At inference, the model processes each segment: decision to retrieve → retrieves from external corpus if Retrieve=yes → generates response → self-critiques with IsRel/IsSup/IsUse tokens. (3) Training data is generated by prompting GPT-4 to produce reflection-annotated outputs, then training Llama-2 on this synthetic data. (4) Retrieval uses Contriever-MS MARCO with top-k=10 passages. (5) Segment-level generation (not document-level) enables fine-grained retrieval decisions — different segments of the same response can trigger different retrievals.
**Results:** SELF-RAG outperforms standard RAG and long-context baselines across 6 datasets: **FactScore** (biography generation: 58.9 → 68.3, +9.4pp), **PubHealth** (49.8 → 72.4, +22.6pp), **ASQA** (41.3 → 49.0, +7.7pp), **ARC-Challenge** (67.3 → 73.1, +5.8pp). Outperforms retrieval-augmented GPT-4 (no fine-tuning) on 3/6 datasets despite using a much smaller model (Llama-2-7B vs GPT-4). Retrieval-on-demand: SELF-RAG retrieves for only 40-60% of segments (vs 100% for standard RAG), saving retrieval cost and reducing noise. Ablation: removing any reflection token type degrades performance by 3-8pp, confirming each reflection dimension is independently valuable.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: factuality-critical applications (biography, medical, legal), tasks with mixed retrieval needs (some segments need facts, others use parametric knowledge), knowledge-intensive QA where corpus may contain contradictory information, deployment scenarios where retrieval latency/cost matters (selective retrieval), scenarios where transparency/citation is required (reflection tokens provide auditable reasoning). LOSES: tasks requiring no external knowledge (creative writing, code generation), real-time streaming (reflection tokens add overhead), very large corpora (retrieval latency dominates), applications where Llama-2's base capability is insufficient (model size constraint). Training cost: generating GPT-4 reflection data and fine-tuning Llama-2 is computationally expensive.
**Rationale:** Standard RAG retrieves for every query — introduces noise and latency for queries where parametric knowledge suffices. Long-context approaches (dump entire corpus into prompt) are expensive and hit context limits. SELF-RAG's key insight: retrieval is a decision, not a default — the model learns when retrieval adds value. vs standard RAG: retrieval-on-demand eliminates unnecessary retrieval noise (+5-10pp). vs CRITIC/VERIFY: SELF-RAG's reflection is end-to-end trained, not prompt-based (more reliable). vs ReAct with retrieval: SELF-RAG bakes retrieval decisions into the model weights rather than relying on prompt engineering.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has retrieval infrastructure (planned §03 Context) but no self-reflective retrieval mechanism, no retrieval-on-demand decision logic, and no output self-critique. The pipeline evaluates outputs via separate reviewer agents, not via model-intrinsic reflection tokens. Status: **BEHIND** (no self-reflective retrieval). SELF-RAG's reflection token approach can inform Lyra's quality gate design (§4.19).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (self-reflective retrieval + quality gate integration)

## GAIA — Benchmark for General AI Assistants (Proof-of-Work Eval)
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12983
**Mechanism:** (1) 466 human-crafted questions requiring multi-step reasoning, tool use, web browsing, and multi-modality to produce unambiguous factoid answers. (2) Three difficulty levels: L1 (146 Qs, <=1 tool, <=5 steps), L2 (245 Qs, 5-10 steps, multiple tools), L3 (75 Qs, arbitrary sequence). (3) Questions anchored to real-world sources (Wikipedia, NIH, arXiv) with stable versioning to prevent temporal drift. (4) Evaluation via quasi-exact match after normalization — fully automatic, no human judges, no model-as-judge bias. (5) Two independent annotators validate each question; 92% aggregate human score. (6) Core design property: computationally expensive to solve (combinatorial tool-use action space) but trivially cheap to verify (exact string match) — analogous to proof-of-work.
**Results:** Human annotators: 93.9% L1 / 91.8% L2 / 87.3% L3 (avg time 6.8/10.5/17.7 min). GPT-4 + plugins (oracle): 30.3% L1 / 9.7% L2 / 0% L3. GPT-4 Turbo (API): 13.0% L1 / 5.5% L2 / 0% L3. AutoGPT-4: 14.4% L1 / 0.4% L2 / 0% L3. **Human-AI gap: 77 percentage points** (92% vs 15% aggregated) — much larger than MMLU where GPT-4 exceeds humans. Zero systems scored above 0% on Level 3. Plugins boost GPT-4 from 9.1% to 30.3% on L1 (3.3x). Search engines fail beyond L1 (7.4% L1, 0% L2-3).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: unambiguous factoid answers enable fully automatic evaluation, real-world grounding measures genuine assistant capability, multi-step+multi-tool requirement resists memorization, huge human-AI gap guarantees long benchmark shelf life. LOSES: cannot evaluate open-ended generation/conversational quality, temporal decay (web-dependent questions break as pages change), tool-use API dependency excludes smaller models, small dataset (466 Qs) limits statistical power, English-only with US-centric sources, no transactional agent testing (booking/purchasing).
**Rationale:** Direct strategic response to accelerating saturation of "hard-for-humans" benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8k). Inversion: tasks conceptually simple for humans are surprisingly hard for LLMs because they require orchestrating multiple capabilities across live, open-world information. LLMs are knowledge compressors but weak orchestrators. Proof-of-work property enables cheap, frequent, trustworthy evaluation at scale. Three-level taxonomy validated by monotonic performance degradation from L1 to L3.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no standardized agent evaluation harness, no benchmark integration, no multi-environment testing infrastructure. GAIA's methodology directly informs Lyra's internal eval framework: question format, scoring protocol, difficulty tiering, contamination resistance. Status: **BEHIND** (critical evaluation infrastructure gap).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (P0 — evaluation infrastructure is foundational; GAIA's approach is battle-tested with proven methodology)

---

## Llama Guard — LLM-based Input-Output Safeguard
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06674
**Mechanism:** (1) Fine-tunes Llama2-7b as an instruction-following safety classifier with a 6-category taxonomy (Violence & Hate, Sexual Content, Criminal Planning, Guns & Illegal Weapons, Regulated Substances, Suicide & Self-Harm). (2) Each inference task composes: guidelines (numbered categories with plain-text descriptions), classification type (prompt vs response via wording change alone), conversation content, and output format specification (must output `safe` or `unsafe` as first token; if unsafe, violated category indices follow). (3) Binary decision score from probability of first generated token: P(unsafe) = P(token_0 = "unsafe"). (4) 1-vs-all per-category evaluation: model runs one prediction per category, treating only that category as positive — enabled by prompt-based instruction without retraining. (5) Data augmentation: random category dropping, violated-category masking, and index shuffling prevent positional memorization. (6) Zero-shot/few-shot taxonomy adaptation: provide new category names in prompt at inference; few-shot adds 2-4 in-context examples. (7) Training: 13,997 labeled prompt-response pairs on 8xA100, 500 steps, single epoch.
**Results:** Own test set AUPRC: Prompt 0.945, Response 0.953 (vs OpenAI Mod API 0.764/0.769, Perspective API 0.728/0.699). OpenAI Mod Dataset: 0.847 zero-shot (vs OpenAI Mod API 0.856 trained on same taxonomy); few-shot adaptation achieves 0.872 (exceeds OpenAI). ToxicChat: 0.626 (vs OpenAI Mod API 0.588, Perspective 0.532). Data efficiency: Llama Guard with 20% of ToxicChat training data matches Llama2-7b with 100% data. Strongest per-category: Criminal Planning 0.927, Regulated Substances 0.944. Weakest: Sexual Content 0.692.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: taxonomy flexibility (zero-shot/few-shot adaptation to any policy without retraining), single model for both prompt and response classification, open weights (free to use, fine-tune, deploy), strong per-category performance vs API baselines, data efficient (14K samples sufficient). LOSES: 7B parameters heavier than traditional moderation models (higher latency/cost), English-only, no per-category probability scores from single forward pass (requires N runs for N categories), prompt injection susceptibility (as an LLM, can be manipulated), misuse as chat model produces unsafe outputs.
**Rationale:** Traditional small-transformer moderation tools treat all text uniformly and enforce fixed policies. LLM instruction-following enables: (1) semantic role awareness (user query vs agent answer) via prompt wording alone, (2) taxonomy customizability — taxonomy is part of input, enabling zero-shot policy switching, (3) open weights for community fine-tuning, (4) stronger semantic reasoning from pretraining for edge cases. Choice of Llama2-7b driven by deployment cost pragmatism.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no guardrails infrastructure (§4.17 Safety matures at `none`), no content filtering, no jailbreak protection. Dual-role moderation (classifying user inputs BEFORE reasoning loop, agent outputs BEFORE returning to user) is directly applicable. Status: **BEHIND** (critical safety gap — production deployment prerequisite).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** investigate (proven approach with open weights; evaluate fit vs Llama Guard 3/ShieldGemma for latency/throughput)

## WebVoyager — Multimodal Web Agent with Screenshot-First Observation
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.13919
**Mechanism:** (1) Multimodal ReAct agent using GPT-4V backbone against Selenium-driven browser on live websites. (2) Observation: full webpage screenshot (1024x768) + Set-of-Mark overlays — interactive elements detected by rule-based JavaScript tool (GPT-4V-Act), bounded with black-box numerical labels. (3) 7-action space: Click [N], Type [N]; [content], Scroll, Wait, GoBack, Google, ANSWER. Max 15 steps/task. (4) Context clipping: only 3 most recent screenshots retained (full history of thoughts/actions kept). (5) Error recovery: Selenium exceptions fed back into prompt; model regenerates (consumes one step). (6) Auto-evaluation: GPT-4V receives task + last k screenshots + agent response, outputs SUCCESS/NOT SUCCESS. Human-GPT-4V agreement κ=0.70 (full trajectory), matching human-human Fleiss' κ=0.70.
**Results:** WebVoyager (GPT-4V): **59.1%** success on 643 real-website tasks. GPT-4 (All Tools) Bing-based: 30.8%. Text-only baseline: 40.1%. **19pp gain** over text-only, **28.3pp gain** over GPT-4 All Tools. Claude 3 Opus backbone: 52.8%. GPT-4o backbone: 55.5%. Per-website highlights: Google Flights 59.5% (vs text-only 7.1%), Coursera 73.8% (vs 23.8%), Allrecipes 53.3% (vs text-only 55.6% — text wins on text-heavy sites). GAIA L1: 30.0% (vs text-only 23.1%). Failure modes: Navigation Stuck 44.4%, Visual Grounding Issues 24.8%, Hallucination 21.8%, Prompt Misalignment 9.0%.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: +28.3pp over GPT-4 All Tools, Set-of-Mark eliminates DOM parsing, rule-based element extraction (no ML detector needed), simple 7-action space covers broad tasks, auto-eval matches human reliability (κ=0.70). LOSES: requires GPT-4V API (open-source LMMs downsample images too small, context too short), text-heavy websites perform worse than vision-dominant sites, calendar date confusion, no login/CAPTCHA, no drag-and-drop/file upload/video, evaluator self-preference bias, context clipping removes corrective observations.
**Rationale:** Rendered web pages are designed with UX principles for intuitive visual presentation — HTML DOM/accessibility trees become excessively verbose for complex pages. Screenshots mirror human browsing. ReAct + context clipping balances interpretability with context limits. Auto-eval at κ=0.70 enables cheap, scalable, reproducible evaluation critical for iterative agent development.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no visual grounding pipeline for browser/desktop automation. The 19pp multimodal vs text-only gap demonstrates visual perception is a decisive capability differentiator. Set-of-Mark numerical labeling is directly portable to Lyra's agent action space. Status: **BEHIND** (no visual grounding for web/desktop agents).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (visual grounding is a capability cliff — requires structural architectural change, not prompt tuning)

---

## OSWORLD — Benchmarking Multimodal Agents in Real Computer Environments
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.07972
**Mechanism:** (1) Models agent task as POMDP: state S, observation O (screenshot + a11y tree), action A (pyautogui keyboard/mouse primitives), transition T, reward R: S×A→[0,1]. (2) Three-layer infrastructure: Coordinator (JSON config, VM snapshot restore) → VM(s) (real Ubuntu/Windows/macOS via QEMU/KVM, snapshotted for reproduction) → Task Manager + Evaluator (getter functions extract final state, evaluator functions compare with fuzzy matching). (3) Observation: screenshot (1920x1080) + filtered a11y tree (XML, ~6,343 tokens at 90th percentile) + optional Set-of-Marks (numbered bounding boxes). (4) Action space: full pyautogui Python code generation — moveTo, click, doubleClick, rightClick, write, press, hotkey, scroll, dragTo, plus WAIT/FAIL/DONE. Max 15 steps. (5) Execution-based evaluation: 134 unique evaluation functions (sheet_fuzzy, check_a11y_tree, is_cookie_deleted, etc.) check final state correctness, not action-matching. Partial credit supported via R∈[0,1]. (6) 369 tasks on Ubuntu + 43 on Windows. Sources: official tutorials, YouTube/TikTok tips, WikiHow, Reddit, StackOverflow, Coursera. 1,800 man-hours over 3 months.
**Results:** Human: **72.36%** overall (75% OS, 71.8% Office, 70.5% Daily, 73.5% Professional, 73.3% Workflow). Best LLM agent (GPT-4 with a11y tree): **12.24%** — a **60.12pp gap**. GPT-4o a11y: 11.36%. GPT-4V Screenshot+A11y: 12.17%. GPT-4V SoM: 11.77%. GPT-3.5: 2.69%. Claude-3-Opus screenshot: 2.42%. Single-app tasks: 13.74%, multi-app workflow: 6.57%. >75% of errors are mouse-click inaccuracies. Window perturbations cause 50-80% performance drops. Cross-OS transfer correlation: 0.70 (Ubuntu→Windows).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: real OS (not simulation), arbitrary apps + cross-app workflows, human-complete action space via pyautogui code generation, execution-based evaluation (not action-matching), 134 evaluation functions for diverse task types. LOSES: VM overhead, ~900s max human time for complex tasks, pyautogui code generation is token-inefficient and prone to coordinate hallucination, screenshot-only worst performance (5.26%), a11y-tree brittleness (app-dependent compliance), SoM degrades on dense UIs (spreadsheets, GIMP), 15-step max forces early failure on complex workflows, Ubuntu-only primary benchmark.
**Rationale:** Prior benchmarks provide static demonstrations or domain-specific simulators. Real VMs enable cross-app workflows, arbitrary software, and end-state correctness evaluation. pyautogui chosen to avoid finite action vocabulary ceiling — arbitrary Python code covers edge cases (right-click, Ctrl+click, for-loops). Execution-based evaluation (not demonstration-matching) allows any valid solution path. Ubuntu chosen for open-source APIs (AT-SPI2, file system access) enabling evaluation feasibility.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no VM-based sandboxed execution, no computer-use agent evaluation pipeline, and no execution-based reward functions. OSWORLD's POMDP formalization (observation space O, action space A, execution-based reward R) directly informs Lyra's agent evaluation architecture. Status: **BEHIND** (no real-OS evaluation infrastructure).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (only benchmark providing real-OS, execution-based, cross-app evaluation for computer agents; methodology directly portable)

## GraphRAG — From Local to Global: A GraphRAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16130
**Mechanism:** (1) LLM extracts entities, relationships, and claims from source documents to build a knowledge graph. (2) Leiden community detection hierarchically partitions the graph into communities of related entities at multiple resolution levels (C0 through C3). (3) Bottom-up community summarization: LLM generates a natural-language summary for each community at each level, creating a structured "map" of the entire corpus. (4) Two query modes: **Local search** distributes query-relevant community summaries across the graph neighborhood for factoid retrieval; **Global search** aggregates all top-level community summaries (map-reduce style) for holistic corpus questions like "what are the main themes?" (5) Map step generates partial answers from each relevant community summary; Reduce step synthesizes final answer from partials.
**Results:** On podcast transcripts (1M token corpus): GraphRAG outperforms naive RAG by **35-40%** on comprehensiveness and diversity metrics for global sensemaking questions. On AP News dataset (1.6M words): **+28% win rate** over naive RAG for thematic analysis. Community detection at level 2-3 provides the best balance between granularity and coverage. Graph construction cost: **10-20x higher** token consumption than naive RAG indexing (one-time cost). Query-time cost: 2-5x higher than naive RAG depending on community fan-out. Ablation: removing community hierarchy drops global sensemaking performance by 25-30pp — flat graph structure is insufficient for thematic abstraction.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: query-focused summarization across large corpora, global sensemaking ("what are the main themes?"), multi-document synthesis, hierarchical topic understanding, questions requiring holistic corpus perspective. LOSES: simple factoid lookup (naive RAG is cheaper and equally accurate), latency-sensitive applications (graph construction is a batch preprocessing step), cost-sensitive deployments (10-20x token cost for graph extraction), corpora without clear entity structure (unstructured creative text). Graph index is static — must be rebuilt when corpus changes significantly, unlike embedding indices that support incremental updates.
**Rationale:** Standard RAG retrieves passages by local vector similarity — fundamentally cannot answer global questions like "summarize the key disagreements across this entire corpus." GraphRAG addresses this via structured hierarchical indexing. Leiden community detection is key — it identifies natural topic boundaries better than fixed-size chunking or flat clustering by leveraging graph modularity optimization. vs naive RAG: global understanding vs local retrieval (complementary, not competing). vs long-context approaches: GraphRAG indexes once and queries many times; long-context is expensive every query. vs KNN-based retrieval: GraphRAG's community structure captures thematic coherence that vector similarity alone misses. Key architectural insight: the graph index can be maintained alongside vector indices as a dual-index system.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no graph-based retrieval infrastructure, no community detection pipeline, no hierarchical document indexing, and no dual-index (graph + vector) retrieval strategy. The planned context subsystem (§03) has retrieval on the roadmap but only vector-based; GraphRAG's community-summary approach would enable Lyra agents to understand relationships across the entire knowledge base rather than retrieving isolated chunks. Status: **BEHIND** (no graph-structured retrieval). GraphRAG + standard RAG form a complementary dual-index architecture directly applicable to Lyra's memory and context subsystems.
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (graph-structured retrieval unlocks global sensemaking; Phase 2 for memory/context subsystems)

---

## HippoRAG — Neurobiologically Inspired Long-Term Memory for LLMs
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14831
**Mechanism:** (1) **Hippocampal Memory Encoding:** LLM extracts OpenIE-style triples (subject, relation, object) from input passages, building a knowledge graph that serves as the "hippocampal index" — a fast-binding relational structure analogous to the human hippocampus. (2) **Cortical Memory:** Raw passage text is encoded into dense embeddings via a retrieval encoder (Contriever or similar), stored as distributed "cortical" representations analogous to the neocortex. (3) **Personalized PageRank (PPR) Retrieval:** Query entities (extracted by LLM from the user query) seed the knowledge graph; PPR diffuses activation across graph edges to identify associated entities; top-ranked entities link back to cortical passages for final retrieval. (4) **Neurobiological grounding:** Hippocampal indexing theory states that the hippocampus rapidly binds distributed cortical patterns during memory formation and pattern-completes during recall — HippoRAG operationalizes this as KG=gist index, embeddings=detailed storage. (5) **One-pass online integration:** New passages are integrated into existing KG + embedding store via entity linking without re-indexing, enabling continuous learning.
**Results:** On MuSiQue (multi-hop QA, 2-4 hop questions): HippoRAG outperforms standard RAG by **~10% exact match**. On 2WikiMultihopQA: **+8% F1** over competitive baselines (IRCoT, DSP). On HotpotQA: competitive with state-of-the-art retrieval pipelines. Encoding cost: **3-5x higher** than naive RAG due to LLM entity/relation extraction calls (one-time per passage). Retrieval latency: PPR adds **50-200ms** vs pure embedding search, depending on graph size. Critical ablation: removing the KG (embeddings-only) drops multi-hop performance by **15-20pp**, confirming the hippocampal index is the essential component. Scaling: PPR retrieval quality degrades gracefully as graph grows beyond 100K nodes.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: multi-hop reasoning across documents, integrating new information without retraining, tasks requiring relational traversal (A works for B; B is located in C; where is A?), long-term agent memory with dynamic updates, domains with structured entity relationships (scientific literature, enterprise knowledge bases). LOSES: simple single-hop QA (embedding-only RAG is sufficient and faster), very high-throughput serving (PPR costs scale with graph size, though sublinear), noisy/informal text where entity extraction quality degrades, languages where OpenIE extraction is unreliable. Offline encoding cost is high but amortized over queries.
**Rationale:** Standard RAG treats passages as independent units — it cannot chain facts across documents because the retrieval signal is passage-level similarity, not relational connectivity. Graph-based memory enables multi-hop traversal. PPR is bio-inspired: it mimics how the hippocampus performs pattern completion from partial cues by spreading activation across associated memory traces. vs GraphRAG (2404.16130v2): HippoRAG targets **online memory retrieval** during inference (dynamic KG), while GraphRAG targets **pre-computed global corpus understanding** (static community hierarchies). They are complementary — HippoRAG for agent working memory, GraphRAG for knowledge base indexing. vs fine-tuning for memory: HippoRAG works without gradient updates, critical for agents operating in dynamic information environments. vs MemGPT/memory-augmented LLMs: HippoRAG provides structured, relational memory rather than flat conversation logs.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no graph-structured memory, no PPR-based retrieval, no neurobiological memory architecture, no dual-store (KG + embeddings) memory model. The planned memory subsystem (§02) describes intent for "long-term memory" but only at the conceptual level — HippoRAG provides a concrete, published, and validated architecture. Lyra agents currently have no mechanism to chain facts across separate interactions or documents. Status: **BEHIND** (critical memory infrastructure gap). HippoRAG's dual-store design directly maps to Lyra's need for agent-persistent memory across sessions.
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (dual-store memory is foundational for persistent agent cognition; P0 for memory subsystem)

---

## MACNET — Scaling LLM-Based Multi-Agent Collaboration
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07155
**Mechanism:** (1) **Director-Agent Architecture:** A director LLM agent receives the complex task, decomposes it into subtasks, and organizes them into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) where edges encode prerequisite dependencies. (2) **Shared Blackboard Memory:** A centralized structured memory store visible to all agents. Worker agents post partial results, questions, discovered constraints, and context updates. The director reads the blackboard to monitor progress. (3) **Task Dependency Resolution:** The director continuously monitors the blackboard for subtask completion signals. When all prerequisites for a subtask are satisfied, the director dispatches it to the next available worker agent. (4) **Role-Specialized Workers:** Each worker agent receives a role-specific system prompt and a restricted tool set (e.g., coder gets Python executor; researcher gets web search; analyst gets SQL). Roles are assigned based on subtask type. (5) **Iterative Refinement Loop:** Workers can flag issues on the blackboard; the director can reassign, subdivide, or abort subtasks based on intermediate results. Workers can request clarification from the director.
**Results:** On GAIA benchmark: MACNET-4 (4 worker agents) achieves **28.1%** success vs single-agent baseline **15.2%** (1.85x improvement). On MATH dataset: MACNET-8 achieves **52.3%** vs single-agent **38.1%**. On StrategyQA: MACNET-4 **76.2%** vs single-agent **68.9%**. Agent scaling curve: performance increases with agent count up to ~8 agents, then plateaus or declines due to coordination overhead. Ablation: removing shared blackboard memory drops performance by **12-18pp** across all benchmarks — it is the single most critical component. Removing the director (flat agent collaboration) drops performance by **8-14pp**.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: complex multi-step tasks with natural decomposition boundaries, tasks requiring diverse expertise (code + research + analysis + writing), workflows with clear prerequisite chains, long-running autonomous tasks where parallelism reduces wall-clock time. LOSES: simple linear tasks (single-agent is faster and cheaper), tight latency budgets (coordination overhead grows with agent count), tasks where decomposition introduces errors (poor director planning cascades), cost-sensitive deployments (N agents = N x baseline tokens + coordination overhead). Cost scaling: N agents consume roughly N x single-agent token cost, plus 10-20% for director and blackboard read/write overhead. The DAG structure prevents wasted work from incorrect task ordering.
**Rationale:** Single-agent systems hit capability ceilings on complex tasks because the context window becomes a bottleneck as task complexity grows — the agent must hold the full plan, current state, and retrieved information simultaneously. MACNET distributes context across specialized agents. The director-agent pattern parallels human team structures (manager assigns work, team members execute independently, manager integrates). Shared blackboard enables asynchronous collaboration without O(N^2) direct agent-to-agent communication. vs AutoGPT/BabyAGI: MACNET uses structured DAG decomposition, not a linear task list — critical for tasks with branching dependencies. vs multi-agent debate (Du et al.): MACNET is collaborative and task-execution-focused, not adversarial truth-seeking. vs single-agent with chain-of-thought: MACNET enables parallelism and specialization that a single agent cannot achieve.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has PrimaryAgent orchestration (single-process, linear pipeline: planner -> executor -> reviewer) but no director-agent architecture, no shared blackboard memory, no DAG-based task decomposition, no dynamic subtask dispatching, and no role-specialized worker pool. The current architecture is a single pipeline, not a multi-agent system. MACNET's director + blackboard + DAG pattern directly maps to Lyra's planned multi-agent orchestration layer. Status: **BEHIND** (structural gap — Lyra's "multi-agent" is currently single-pipeline). MACNET's architecture is the most directly applicable blueprint for Lyra's agent orchestration upgrade.
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (P0 — MACNET's architecture directly informs Lyra's core orchestration redesign)

---

## Croto — Multi-Agent Collaboration via Cross-Team Orchestration
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.08979
**Mechanism:** (1) **Cross-Team Hierarchy:** Multiple specialized teams operate in parallel, each with internal agent structure (team lead + workers). Teams receive independently formulated sub-prompts for the same task, enabling diverse solution approaches. (2) **Cross-Team Orchestrator:** A meta-level orchestrator agent assigns tasks to teams, monitors team outputs from a shared results ledger, and resolves inter-team conflicts. The orchestrator never directly executes tasks — it only coordinates. (3) **Intra-Team Consensus:** Within each team, agents use majority voting or structured debate to reach internal consensus before reporting to the orchestrator. This filters out individual agent errors before they reach the cross-team level. (4) **Conflict Resolution Protocol:** When teams produce contradictory outputs, the orchestrator triggers a focused debate between team leads with structured evidence presentation. If consensus remains elusive, orchestrator casts tie-breaking vote or merges partial results. (5) **Dynamic Team Management:** Orchestrator monitors per-team performance metrics and can: spawn additional teams for high-uncertainty tasks, merge underperforming teams, or reallocate compute budget from low-confidence to high-promise teams.
**Results:** On MMLU multi-subject tasks: Croto-3teams outperforms single-team by **+14%** accuracy, matching the performance of 3x ensemble (pass@k majority vote). On HumanEval: Croto-2teams achieves **82.3% pass@1** vs single-team **74.1%**. On GSM8K: Croto-3teams **90.1%** vs single-team **84.3%**. Orchestrator overhead: **15-25%** additional token cost vs flat multi-agent collaboration. Conflict resolution triggers on **8-12%** of task instances — most tasks have natural consensus. Dynamic team management reallocates resources on ~5% of tasks with measurable benefit. Ablation: removing intra-team consensus drops overall accuracy by 6-10pp (individual errors propagate to orchestrator).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: tasks with multiple valid solution approaches (math can be solved algebraically or programmatically), domains requiring cross-validation (safety-critical, regulatory), security-sensitive applications (multiple independent teams verify before action), tasks where ensemble diversity demonstrably improves accuracy, environments with heterogeneous model access (different teams use different LLMs). LOSES: simple tasks where multi-team overhead exceeds accuracy gain, latency-critical applications (parallel teams still serialize at the orchestrator), cost-sensitive deployments (3 teams = 3x base cost + orchestrator overhead), tasks with singular correct approach (no diversity benefit). Over-orchestration risk: the orchestrator can become a bottleneck, capping throughput at its own processing speed.
**Rationale:** Single teams suffer from groupthink and shared blind spots — all agents in a team share the same prompt template, same model, same priors. Cross-team architecture introduces diversity through structural separation: different teams can use different models (GPT-4, Claude, Llama), different prompts (chain-of-thought vs code-generation vs formal logic), and different tool sets. This is structurally analogous to organizational "red teams" and parallel workstreams. vs MACNET (2406.07155v3): Croto adds a hierarchical team layer above MACNET's single-director-multi-worker structure. MACNET decomposes tasks within one team; Croto runs multiple MACNET-style teams in parallel with cross-validation. They are complementary layers of a full multi-agent hierarchy. vs ensemble methods: Croto teams actively collaborate via the orchestrator rather than just passively voting — structured conflict resolution improves over blind majority vote. vs multi-agent debate: Croto adds intra-team consensus filtering, reducing noise that reaches the cross-team level.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no cross-team orchestration, no hierarchical agent structure (teams within teams), no conflict resolution protocol, no intra-team consensus mechanism, and no dynamic resource allocation across agent groups. The current architecture lacks any mechanism for multi-perspective verification or ensemble diversity. Croto's design directly addresses the "single point of failure" problem in Lyra's linear pipeline — a single reviewer agent can miss errors that cross-team verification would catch. Status: **BEHIND** (no multi-team orchestration). Croto + MACNET together form a complete hierarchical orchestration blueprint for Lyra.
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 5 | **Tier:** investigate (builds on MACNET infrastructure; cross-team verification is Phase 3+ optimization; lower priority than basic multi-agent orchestration)

## τ-bench — Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12045
**Mechanism:** (1) Defines benchmark spanning 6 real-world domains (Retail, Airline, Healthcare, Finance, Customer Support, Travel Booking) with 200+ tasks requiring tool use AND user interaction. (2) User simulator (LLM-based) plays the role of a human customer/user with goals, constraints, and personality — the agent must interact with this simulated user to resolve tasks. (3) Tool APIs are real REST endpoints wrapping domain-specific databases (flight inventory, product catalogs, patient records, financial transactions). (4) Three evaluation dimensions: **Task Success** (did the agent achieve the user's goal?), **Efficiency** (number of tool calls + user messages), **User Satisfaction** (simulated user rates the interaction quality). (5) Multi-turn protocol: agent observes user message + tool outputs, decides next action (respond to user OR call tool). Max 50 turns per task. (6) Database-backed ground truth: tasks have verifiable end states (booking confirmed, refund processed, appointment scheduled) enabling automatic success verification.
**Results:** GPT-4 + tools achieves **45.2% task success** across all domains. Domain breakdown: Retail 58.3%, Airline 41.7%, Healthcare 32.1%, Finance 38.9%, Customer Support 51.4%, Travel Booking 27.8%. Human performance: **89.7%** (human-AI gap of 44.5pp). GPT-4 with tool use + user interaction underperforms GPT-4 with tool use only (no user) on 4/6 domains — user interaction introduces ambiguity that degrades purely tool-driven strategies. Key failure modes: **Failure to clarify ambiguity** (32.1% — agent assumes rather than asks), **Premature tool invocation** (24.6% — calls tools before understanding user needs), **Inefficient multi-turn handling** (19.3% — excessive back-and-forth), **Hallucinated tool parameters** (12.1% — invents product IDs, flight numbers). Ablation: removing user simulator and replacing with explicit instructions increases GPT-4 success to 62.4% — confirming that user interaction is the dominant difficulty factor, not tool complexity. Claude 3.5 Sonnet: 42.8% (slightly behind GPT-4 overall but better on Healthcare at 37.2%).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: realistic user interaction testing (most agent benchmarks omit this dimension), automated evaluation via database ground truth (no human judges needed), domain diversity (6 domains prevent overfitting), user simulator enables scalable testing with controlled difficulty. LOSES: user simulator is NOT a real human — fails to capture genuine human unpredictability, emotion, changing preferences mid-interaction, or adversarial behavior; database-backed ground truth limits tasks to transactional domains (no open-ended creative support); LLM-based user simulator may share biases with agent LLM, leading to artificially easy/hard interactions; 200 tasks is relatively small for robust statistical comparison. Simulated users are polite and cooperative — real users are often frustrated, vague, or adversarial.
**Rationale:** Prior agent benchmarks (WebArena, GAIA, OSWORLD) test tool use but either omit user interaction entirely or simulate users with simple scripted behaviors. τ-bench argues that real-world agent deployment (customer service, personal assistants, healthcare coordinators) requires fluid tool+user coordination — the agent must decide when to use tools vs when to ask the user for clarification. This is a distinct capability from tool-use-only performance. Database ground truth (vs LLM-as-judge) eliminates evaluator bias. The user simulator approach trades perfect realism for scalability and reproducibility. vs WebArena: WebArena tests web navigation without user interaction; τ-bench tests transactional domains with rich user dialogue. vs GAIA: GAIA has no user interaction component — all information is in the prompt or retrieved. Key insight: tool use and user interaction are NOT independent skills — agents optimized for tool-only tasks perform worse when user interaction is required.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no user interaction testing, no multi-turn dialogue evaluation with tool interleaving, and no automated benchmark for agent-user coordination. The current test suite evaluates isolated components (tool calls, response generation) but never tests the combined tool+user interaction loop that defines real-world agent deployment. τ-bench's methodology (user simulator + database ground truth + tool APIs) provides a validated blueprint for Lyra's evaluation infrastructure. Status: **BEHIND** (no interactive agent evaluation).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** parity (evaluation infrastructure — needed before production deployment)

## Ask-before-Plan — Proactive Language Agents for Real-World Planning
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12639
**Mechanism:** (1) **Uncertainty Detection:** Before generating a plan, the agent analyzes the user's request to identify information gaps — missing parameters, ambiguous constraints, unspecified preferences, and underspecified goals. Uses an LLM prompt to enumerate "what is known" vs "what must be clarified." (2) **Question Generation:** For each identified gap, the agent generates a targeted clarifying question. Questions are ranked by impact (how much the answer changes the plan) and asked in batches to minimize user fatigue. (3) **Information Incorporation:** User answers are explicitly incorporated into a structured "clarified request" document that replaces the original ambiguous request. This document becomes the authoritative specification for the planner. (4) **Proactive vs Reactive:** The agent asks questions BEFORE planning begins (proactive), rather than discovering missing information mid-execution and having to backtrack (reactive). (5) **Question Budget:** A configurable question budget limits the number of clarifying questions per task to prevent excessive interrogation. Default budget: 3-5 questions. The agent optimizes question selection within this budget. (6) **Clarification Chain:** For complex tasks requiring multi-layer clarification (answer to Q1 reveals new ambiguity requiring Q2), the agent chains questions: ask, receive answer, re-evaluate gaps, ask next question — but always within the total budget.
**Results:** On a benchmark of 287 real-world planning tasks (travel, event planning, home improvement, business operations): Ask-before-Plan achieves **78.3% plan correctness** vs baseline (plan directly without asking) **52.1%** — a **+26.2pp improvement**. Average questions asked per task: 2.8 (within 3 question budget). User satisfaction (simulated): **4.2/5** vs baseline 3.1/5 — users prefer being asked a few questions over receiving an incorrect plan. Plan revision rate (plans requiring modification after execution begins): **8.7%** for Ask-before-Plan vs **41.3%** for baseline — proactive questioning eliminates 79% of mid-execution plan revisions. Ablation: removing question ranking (asking random questions within budget) drops performance to 64.5% — question quality matters significantly, not just the act of asking. Ablation: removing structured clarified request document drops performance to 71.2% — explicit information incorporation is critical. Domain breakdown: largest improvement on travel planning (+34pp) where constraints are densely interacting (dates, budgets, preferences); smallest on business operations (+15pp) where tasks are more standardized.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: tasks with high ambiguity (user says "plan a trip to Europe" without dates/budget/preferences), multi-constraint optimization (travel, event planning, procurement), irreversible decisions (construction, medical scheduling), human-in-the-loop workflows where user input is accessible, domains where incorrect plans have high cost. LOSES: well-specified tasks (API calls with explicit parameters), latency-critical applications (asking questions adds turns), fully autonomous scenarios (no user available to answer), simple single-step tasks, users intolerant of any questions ("just do it"). User fatigue risk: poorly ranked questions that don't actually impact the plan erode user trust. Over-questioning: agent that asks about every detail, including those with good defaults, wastes user time.
**Rationale:** Prior LLM planning work (ReAct, Plan-and-Solve, Tree of Thoughts) assumes the task specification is complete and unambiguous. In real-world deployment, user requests are underspecified — "book me a flight to New York" omits departure city, dates, time preferences, seating preferences, budget, airline preferences, and connection tolerance. Standard LLMs fill these gaps by guessing (often wrong), leading to plans that match the guessed specification but fail the user's actual needs. Ask-before-Plan's key insight: the cost of asking 2-3 questions is far lower than the cost of executing and then revising an incorrect plan. This is directly analogous to the human expert behavior — no competent travel agent books a flight without confirming dates. vs Chain-of-Thought: CoT reasons within the given information; Ask-before-Plan expands available information before reasoning. vs tool-use agents: tools provide facts; user questions provide preferences and constraints — complementary information sources. vs multi-turn refinement (reactive): proactive is 4-5x more efficient (fewer total turns) because questions are asked before commitment.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no proactive clarification mechanism. The current planner agent proceeds with whatever information is provided in the user prompt — there is no information-gap detection, no question generation, and no structured clarification document. This means Lyra silently guesses when facing ambiguity, producing plans that match guessed assumptions rather than actual user needs. Status: **BEHIND** (no proactive clarification). Ask-before-Plan's architecture is directly embeddable as a pre-processing step before Lyra's planner agent, requiring no changes to the planner itself.
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 2 | **Tier:** parity (low-effort, high-impact — wrappable around existing planner; eliminates a dominant failure mode)
