## MI N D: Multi-agent Framework for Zero-shot Harmful Meme Detection
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.06908
**Mechanism:** (1) **Similar Sample Retrieval (SSR):** For each target meme, compute fused multimodal embedding E = lambda_v * V_enc(V) + lambda_t * T_enc(T) using CLIP/ViT encoders. Retrieve top-K (default K=3) similar memes from unlabeled reference pool via cosine similarity. No labels needed. (2) **Relevant Insight Derivation (RID):** Bidirectional sequential processing across K retrieved memes. Forward pass: LMM processes memes 1..K, accumulating harm-assessment insights cumulatively. Backward pass: same LMM processes memes K..1 in reverse order, compensating for sequential position bias. Each pass outputs <=5 high-level harm assessment rules. (3) **Insight-Augmented Inference (IAI):** Two independent debater agents each receive one insight set (forward/backward) plus target meme. If both output same judgment (harmful/harmless), consensus adopted. If disagreement, judge agent examines both reasoning chains and arbitrates. Training-free, gradient-free, zero-shot — no annotated data required.
**Results:** LLaVA-1.5-13B backbone: HarM dataset: Accuracy 68.93% (vs base 62.28%, GPT-4o 67.51%), Macro-F1 65.19% (+14.74 over base). FHM dataset: Accuracy 60.80%, Macro-F1 60.71% (+7.70 over base). MAMI dataset: Accuracy 68.90%, Macro-F1 68.84% (+13.32 over base). Cross-scale improvement: 7B model gains +7.78 F1 (HarM), 34B model gains +4.53 F1 (HarM). MI N D zero-shot > 3-shot+SSR by +5.59 F1 (HarM). Ablations: removing RID drops F1 by 12-13% (most critical), removing SSR drops by 0.3-4.3% (dataset-dependent), removing IAI drops by 0.7-4.2%. Inference overhead: ~8x vs simple zero-shot baseline (9h on MAMI with LLaVA-1.5-13B); halved with unidirectional RID only.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: zero-shot (no annotations), outperforms GPT-4o on HarM with 13B open model, generalizes across model scales (7B-34B, open and closed), beats few-shot learning, training-free, interpretable (explicit reasoning chains), flexible efficiency (unidirectional RID halves calls). LOSES: ~8x inference overhead, retrieval quality dependence (SSR failures amplify downstream noise), uniform weighting of retrieved memes (no relevance discrimination), irony/satire blind spot (over-relies on literal text), false positive risk on historical/cultural content, consensus bias (prioritizes agreement over reasoning quality verification), cultural knowledge dependency on base LMM.
**Rationale:** Memes evolve faster than annotation pipelines — the core insight is that harmful memes retain cross-domain patterns despite surface evolution. Retrieval from unlabeled pool surfaces these patterns without new labels. Bidirectional derivation: sequential processing introduces position bias where earlier memes receive more refinement; backward pass compensates. Debate + judge: two independent perspectives surface disagreement; judge examines reasoning chains rather than averaging opinions — meta-level evaluation filters weak arguments. Training-free enables immediate deployment on new formats. Open-source LLaVA backbone ensures reproducibility.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has safety/guardrail plans (§4.7) but no multi-perspective evaluation architecture, no retrieval-augmented content analysis, no debate-with-judge arbitration pattern for safety decisions. The bidirectional insight derivation + debate-with-judge pattern generalizes beyond meme detection to any LLM output evaluation where single-pass judgment is unreliable. Status: **BEHIND** (the debate+judge architecture is directly applicable to Lyra's output moderation and self-critique flows).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** investigate (pattern powerful but domain differs; prototype debate+judge in Lyra safety pipeline; ~8x latency overhead requires unidirectional RID entry point)

## OS Agents: A Survey on MLLM-based Agents for General Computing Devices Use
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.04482 (ACL 2025)
**Mechanism:** Comprehensive taxonomy survey covering 27 foundation models and 27 agent frameworks for OS-level GUI agents. Execution loop: User Goal -> [Perception] -> [Planning] -> [Memory] -> [Action] -> Environment. **Perception**: Textual (HTML DOM, accessibility/A11y tree) vs GUI Screenshot (MLLM-processed). Three grounding strategies: Visual (Set-of-Mark with bounding boxes via OCR/Grounding DINO), Semantic (screenshot + HTML/A11y tree reference), Dual (combines both — most promising). **Planning**: Global (single DAG upfront, no adaptation) vs Iterative (ReAct, Reflexion, CoAT, Auto-GUI with history-conditioned CoT). **Memory**: Internal (short-term action history + long-term user preferences), External (KBs, API-retrieved knowledge), Specific (task rules, per-app functionality docs). Memory optimization: self-summarization, context clipping, plan-tree isolation, KNN experience retrieval. **Action**: Input (click/tap, drag, text), Navigation (scroll, tabs, URL), Extended (code execution, API integration). **Foundation Model Pipeline**: Architecture (existing LLMs/MLLMs, concatenated MLLMs, modified MLLMs with high-res encoders like EVA-CLIP-L 1120x1120) -> Pre-training (screen grounding, screen understanding QA) -> SFT (trajectory synthesis, rule-based app traversal + LLM gap-filling) -> RL (behavior cloning + PPO dominant; AutoGLM self-evolving curriculum RL). Critical finding: learning with visual forms outperforms source-code-based learning and avoids hallucination.
**Results:** Taxonomy coverage: 27 foundation models cataloged (05/2023-10/2024), 27 agent frameworks (09/2022-10/2024), 30 benchmarks (08/2017-06/2024). Architecture types: 4 (Existing LLM, Existing MLLM, Concatenated MLLM, Modified MLLM). Training stages: 3 (Pre-training, SFT, RL). Grounding types: 3 (Visual, Semantic, Dual). Planning paradigms: 2 (Global, Iterative). No single model/framework dominates across all platforms — cross-platform generalization remains unsolved. Field split between foundation model route (training-heavy, better grounding) and agent framework route (zero-shot, more flexible but less reliable). Key aggregated finding: dual grounding (visual + semantic) is the most promising perception strategy but neither alone suffices.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: comprehensive taxonomy enabling cross-platform pattern identification, capability-first organization (understanding->planning->grounding) surfaces shared fundamentals across mobile/desktop/web, identifies dual grounding as optimal perception strategy. LOSES: no quantitative head-to-head benchmark comparison (taxonomy survey), rapid obsolescence (models from 10/2024 already superseded), cross-platform generalization explicitly unsolved, safety defenses critically underdeveloped, personalization aspirational (no persistent privacy-preserving cross-session system), evaluation reliability concerns (LLM-as-judge limitations), GUI-only focus (no CLI/API/voice coverage), single-agent paradigm throughout.
**Rationale:** Capability-first taxonomy (rather than task-centric or platform-centric) deliberately abstracts to shared fundamentals — OS agents across platforms share the same understanding/planning/grounding capabilities despite different action spaces. Foundation-model/agent-framework split reflects genuine field divergence: embed knowledge in weights (training-heavy, robust) vs in prompting/orchestration (training-free, flexible). Authors argue both necessary and complementary but field hasn't integrated them successfully.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has strong text/code understanding but no GUI interaction capability, no visual grounding, no dual-channel perception (structured semantics + screenshots). The dual-grounding architecture would enable Lyra to interact with arbitrary GUI applications using both element semantics (accessibility tree, DOM, API schemas) and visual appearance (Set-of-Mark annotated screenshots). Status: **BEHIND** (zero GUI agency capability; survey provides complete blueprint with 27 frameworks, 27 models, 30 benchmarks).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (OS-level GUI agency would significantly differentiate Lyra from text/CLI-only agents; dual-grounding architecture is directly implementable)

## MemP: Exploring Agent Procedural Memory
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.06433
**Mechanism:** Three-phase procedural memory lifecycle treating agent trajectories as first-class optimization objects. (1) **Build Phase:** Convert agent trajectories into storable memories. Three granularity strategies: Trajectory (store gold trajectories verbatim), Script (LLM summarizes into abstract procedural instructions), Proceduralization (combines both — trajectory + script, best-performing). Builder function: mp_t = B(tau_t, r_t). (2) **Retrieve Phase:** Cosine similarity retrieval over vector embeddings. Two key-building strategies: Query (embed full task description) vs AveFact (LLM extracts keywords, averages similarity across keyword vectors — best-performing). Retrieved memory prepended to task context before execution. (3) **Update Phase:** Three strategies on per-trajectory-group basis: Vanilla (naive append), Validation (selective consolidation — only successful trajectories), Adjustment/Reflexion (best — when memory leads to failure, erroneous trajectory + original memory revised in-place via LLM reflection, +0.7 points, -14 steps). Full lifecycle: execute tasks -> Build (Proceduralization) -> Store (AveFact vectors) -> Retrieve (cosine top-k) -> Execute (prepend to context) -> Feedback (success/failure) -> Update (Reflexion on failure) -> Repeat.
**Results:** GPT-4o on ALFWorld: Proceduralization achieves Dev 87.14% (vs No Memory 39.28%, +47.86pp), Test 77.86% (vs 42.14%, +35.72pp), Steps 15.01 (vs 23.76, -8.75). TravelPlanner: Proceduralization CS 79.94 (vs 71.93), Steps 14.62 (vs 17.84). AveFact retrieval: +4.09pp CS over No Memory, -3.20 steps. Baseline comparison on ALFWorld: MemP ~87% Dev / ~78% Test / ~15 steps, dominating ReAct (~40/42/24), Expel (~55/52/20), AWM (~72/65/18). Cross-model transfer: GPT-4o memory -> Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct gives +5% completion rate, -1.6 steps. Scaling retrieval: 0 memories = 40.7 -> 20 memories = 82.5 (peak) -> 30 memories = 79.3 (diminishing returns, context overload). Case study ("heat egg"): with memory 14 steps/2589 tokens SUCCEEDED vs without 27 steps/3635 tokens FAILED — 48% step reduction, 29% token reduction.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: +48pp dev accuracy on ALFWorld, -8.75 steps per task (37% efficiency gain), -29% token consumption, strong-to-weak transfer works (+5% for 14B using GPT-4o memory), composable with any base LLM, reflexion-based update is self-correcting, scales with retrieval count (40.7->82.5). LOSES: Hard constraint score degrades on TravelPlanner (12.88->9.76 — memory biases toward commonsense at expense of strict constraints), requires gold trajectories from training set (no cold-start), vector-only retrieval (no BM25/hybrid), depends on explicit benchmark reward signals (0/1), returns diminish beyond ~20 retrieved memories, update requires execution feedback (no offline improvement), single-agent only.
**Rationale:** Grounded in cognitive science (Gupta & Cohen 2002, Cohen & Squire 1980): human procedural memory compiles habitual skills into executable subroutines. Existing frameworks (LangGraph, AutoGPT, MemoryBank) provide coarse memory but never systematically study the Build-Retrieve-Update lifecycle. Proceduralization (trajectory+script) over either alone: concrete examples provide pattern-matching surface cues; abstract scripts provide generalized principles — combination gives both. AveFact over Query embedding: averaging keyword vectors focuses on core task elements, filtering noisy details. Reflexion over validation: surgical edit preserving memory structure rather than discard-and-replace. Not fine-tuning: chooses memory augmentation because (a) editable without retraining, (b) different models share same memory bank, (c) avoids catastrophic forgetting.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no procedural memory subsystem, no trajectory-to-skill distillation pipeline, no Build-Retrieve-Update memory lifecycle, no reflexion-based memory correction. The memory plans (§4.2) discuss episodic and semantic memory but omit procedural/skill memory entirely. MemP's dual-granularity approach (concrete + abstract) directly addresses Lyra's need for both few-shot examples and reusable skill templates. Status: **BEHIND** (procedural memory gap is critical — without it, Lyra cannot learn from past task executions).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (procedural memory with self-correcting update is a capability Lyra currently lacks; implementing it gives Lyra a learnable skill repository compounding in value with usage)

## EvoCoT: Overcoming the Exploration Bottleneck in RL for LLMs
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.07809
**Mechanism:** Self-evolving curriculum learning framework with two nested iterative stages. (1) **Stage 1 — Answer-Guided CoT Generation:** LLM generates CoT trajectories conditioned on knowing the correct answer (Q, A) from training set. Intuition: reasoning paths are easier to construct in reverse (answer -> question). Each CoT verified: can LLM reconstruct A from C_hat? Valid CoTs split into n sequential reasoning steps [c1, c2, ..., cn]. No human-annotated CoTs or teacher models — transforms outcome-supervised data into step-level supervision. (2) **Stage 2 — Step-Wise Curriculum Learning:** Progressive difficulty via reverse-order CoT step removal. Full CoT (c1..cn) -> remove cn -> remove cn-1 -> ... -> (Q alone). At each level, LLM rolls out from CoT prefix, receiving reward=1 if final answer matches, 0 otherwise. Shorter prefix = larger exploration space = harder. delta_step=1 (remove 1 step/level) achieves best results. Training uses GRPO/DAPO with standard RLVR hyperparameters. (3) **Self-Evolving Loop:** After Stage 2 training, improved LLM re-enters Stage 1, generating higher-quality CoTs, creating virtuous cycle. Iterates T=2-3 times before saturation. Key design: reverse-order removal prevents reward hacking (answer never exposed in prefix), delta_step controls curriculum smoothness, entropy preservation slows collapse vs GRPO alone.
**Results:** Qwen2.5-7B on training set (GSM8K+MATH avg): GRPO only 84.6 -> +EvoCoT 89.1 (+4.5). R1-Qwen-1.5B: GRPO only 68.2 -> +EvoCoT 89.9 (+21.7), MATH only 55.7 -> 87.8 (+32.1). Multi-benchmark (6 benchmarks): Qwen2.5-7B: Base 40.3 -> +EvoCoT 53.5 (vs best baseline PRIME 55.3 with 380K data — EvoCoT uses far less data). R1-Qwen-1.5B: Base 54.2 -> +EvoCoT 66.7 (vs DeepScaleR 63.6). Key per-benchmark Qwen2.5-7B: AIME 2024 3.3->20.0 (+16.7), AMC 2023 30.0->60.0 (+30.0), Olympiad Bench 30.1->35.9 (+5.8), Minerva Math 25.7->37.1 (+11.4). R1-Qwen-1.5B: AIME 2024 28.8->40.0 (+11.2), AMC 2023 62.9->87.5 (+24.6), Olympiad Bench 43.3->52.0 (highest among all). Saturation: peaks at 2 iterations; third iteration plateaus or declines. Compatible with DAPO: Qwen2.5-7B 51.7->53.8 (+2.1), R1-Qwen-1.5B 64.6->66.9 (+2.3). Training overhead: 413 min (GRPO) -> 427 min (EvoCoT, +3.4%).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: +4.5 to +21.7 avg improvement for strong LLMs, no teacher model or human-annotated CoT required (distillation-free), compatible with any RL optimizer (GRPO, DAPO), slower entropy collapse preserves exploration, works across model families (Qwen, DeepSeek, Llama), uses all training data including hard problems (unfiltered), self-evolving loop improves CoTs. LOSES: ~3.4% training overhead, requires correct (Q, A) pairs (Stage 1 bottleneck when answer wrong or LLM lacks domain knowledge), saturates after 1-2 iterations, delta_step must be tuned per model, weaker LLMs see minimal benefit (Llama3.1-8B: +0.9 avg), ~10% hard problems permanently unsolvable due to dataset errors, overly long CoTs cause zero gradient (mitigated by dynamic step removal), only tested on math reasoning (no code/tool/general reasoning evaluation).
**Rationale:** RLVR fails on hard problems because solution space is too large relative to current reasoning capability (reward sparsity). Existing solutions: (a) teacher model distillation limits scalability, (b) filtering hard problems discards valuable training data. EvoCoT's principles: (1) Constrain-then-expand: provide partial CoTs to constrain exploration space, gradually remove scaffolding. (2) Reverse reasoning easier than forward: generating from known answer is fundamentally easier, enabling bootstrapping without teachers. (3) Natural curriculum via step removal: longer prefix = easier, shorter = harder — smooth difficulty progression without manual annotation. Reverse-order removal prevents answer exposure in prefix, eliminating reward hacking.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no RL-based agent training pipeline, no curriculum learning infrastructure, no self-evolving agent improvement loop. The self-evolving curriculum pattern is applicable to agent tool-use trajectories — when Lyra agents fail on hard multi-step tasks, answer-conditioned trajectory generation (Stage 1) + step-wise curriculum removal (Stage 2) provides a principled bootstrapping method without teacher demonstrations. Status: **BEHIND** (no RL self-improvement infrastructure; EvoCoT provides the exploration-bottleneck solution for agent RL training).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** investigate (strong math domain results but untested on tool-use agent tasks; prototype on small set of hard Lyra agent tasks first; saturation at 2 iterations and weak-model limitation are cautionary)

## Coarse-to-Fine Grounded Memory for LLM Agent Planning (CFGM)
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.15305 (EMNLP 2025)
**Mechanism:** Three-stage memory grounding architecture using LLM's internal knowledge to structure, enrich, and exploit memory at progressively finer granularities. (1) **Coarse-Grained Focus-Driven Experience Collection:** LLM_Focus analyzes environment description + manual examples to produce Focus Points (FP) — environment-level strategic hints (e.g., "check desk first"). Agent LLM_ReAct executes up to Z+1 trial attempts per task with Reflexion: on failure, LLM_Reflect introspects on trajectory and produces reflection concatenated with prior reflections into next attempt. FP guidance improves trajectory quality by directing exploration toward critical dynamics. Both success and failure trajectories stored in experience pool B. (2) **Hybrid-Grained Experience-Wise Tips Extraction:** Trajectories regrouped into C_compare (tasks with both success AND failure) and C_success (success-only). For C_compare: LLM_Tips compares successful vs failed trajectories, extracts tips blending coarse principles ("verify location before acting") with fine techniques ("for drawer 3, check desk first"). Success-refinement pass: LLM_Tips focuses only on successful trajectory to extract success-specific factors. For C_success: LLM_Tips derives moderate-generalization tips from success alone. Output: Tips Dictionary TD mapping task -> hybrid-grained tips. (3) **Fine-Grained Key Information Adaptive Planning:** Faiss retrieval (all-mpnet-base-v2) of top-k similar experiences + tips as in-context aids. Standard ReAct loop with memory context. Anomaly-Triggered Self-QA Reflection: monitor checks observations for abnormal states; on trigger, LLM_KIE extracts Key Information (KI) from current trajectory, LLM_KIR conducts self-reflective QA using KI + similar success trajectories -> corrective plan appended to current step. Key differentiator: step-level context-grounded self-QA (not trial-level like Reflexion, not fixed-template like QuBE).
**Results:** GPT-4-Turbo backbone: AlfWorld SR 91.00% (vs ReAct 80.60%, ExpeL+QuBE 85.07% — +5.93pp over next-best), WebShop Reward 85.0 (vs ReAct 58.6, +26.4), WebShop SR 57% (vs ReAct 37%, +20pp), ScienceWorld SR 74% (vs ReAct 43%, +31pp). Ablations (AlfWorld): ReAct baseline 80.60%, +FP only 85.82%, +ET only 86.57%, +KIR only 85.82%, +ET+KIR (no FP) 88.06%, full CFGM 91.00% — synergistic, not additive. Model generalization (AlfWorld): Qwen2.5-7B +12pp, GPT-4-Turbo +10.40pp, GPT-4o +8pp, GPT-4.1 +7pp — consistent gains across model sizes. Retrieval scope: k=2 optimal (86.57%), k=5 collapses to 81.34% (near ReAct baseline). Out-of-domain transfer (WebShop->WebArena-Shopping): CFGM 25.1% vs ReAct 10.2% (+14.9pp). Efficiency: CFGM 14.32 online turns (fewest among memory-augmented methods — 25% fewer than ReAct's 19.01), 4,068.5 offline tokens/sample, 4,681.4 online tokens/step.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: +10.40pp AlfWorld over ReAct (+5.93pp over next-best), 25% fewer interaction turns, consistent gains across model sizes (7B to GPT-4.1), out-of-domain transfer (+14.9pp), adaptive self-QA more flexible than fixed-question reflection (+1.49pp), synergistic components (1+1>2). LOSES: requires separate GPT-4o for tips extraction (two-model dependency), requires offline training phase (4,068 tokens/sample), retrieval scope brittle (5pp drop when k=2->5), long trajectories introduce tip redundancy/interference, small training sets limit experience quality regardless of FP guidance, text-based environments only (no multimodal/embodied experiments), anomaly trigger implementation details sparse.
**Rationale:** Prior memory-augmented agents suffer from: (1) inefficient exploration producing low-quality experiences, (2) single-granularity knowledge extraction yielding homogenized insights, (3) fixed-question templates lacking cross-environment flexibility. Core insight: LLM's internal knowledge can bootstrap memory quality if systematically grounded at multiple granularities. CFGM uses LLM reasoning to structure memory at collection time (coarse focus points), distill memory at extraction time (hybrid-grained tips), and interrogate memory at inference time (fine-grained self-QA). Not independent pipeline — coarse focus points improve experience quality, making tips more actionable and reflection more effective. Three-stage synergy is the core contribution.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra §4.2 Memory Subsystem has no structured multi-granularity memory, no compare-based tips extraction, no anomaly-triggered self-QA reflection, no focus-point-guided experience collection. CFGM's three-stage grounding addresses core Lyra memory challenges: experience quality, knowledge diversity, and adaptive error correction. All stages are prompt-based (no model training) — the prompts are provided in Appendix C. Implementation requires prompt templates + Faiss retrieval + anomaly trigger logic. Status: **BEHIND** (no structured self-improving memory; CFGM provides complete prompt-based architecture).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (novel coarse-to-fine design is synergistic, SOTA on multiple benchmarks, addresses fundamental single-granularity limitation, all prompt-based enabling rapid prototyping)
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (P0 — optimal routing with compute budget optimization is foundational for cost-efficient multi-agent Lyra)

## CHAIN-OF-QUERY: Multi-Agent SQL-Aided Table Understanding
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.15809
**Mechanism:** Four-agent pipeline for SQL-aided table understanding. (1) **Semantic Splitter:** Converts raw tables into 3-component natural-language schema (Table Name, Headers with types, Value Examples in PIPE format), then decomposes complex questions into semantically independent sub-questions processed in parallel (no cascading error dependency). (2) **SQL Query Generator (Clause-by-Clause):** Builds SQL incrementally across 5 clause types (SELECT-FROM, WHERE, WITH AS CTE, Aggregate, ORDER BY). After each clause addition, the query is executed for validation; if execution fails, error traces to most recent clause; if correction fails, rollback to last validated query. (3) **Dynamic Planner (Hybrid Reasoning Division + Early Stopping):** Mechanical operations (filtering, aggregation, arithmetic) delegated to SQL; logical operations (comparison, inference, interpretation) delegated to LLM. Planner checks sufficiency after each clause: "Is the current SQL result sufficient to answer?" If yes, stop to prevent over-generation. (4) **Answer Generator:** Produces sub-answers per sub-question, then combines into cohesive natural-language final answer.
**Results:** GPT-3.5 backbone: WikiTQ 74.77% (+13.66pp over Tree-of-Table), TabFact 92.31% (+10.39pp), FeTaQA BLEU 22.19 (+1.74), IM-TQA 74.96% (+6.06pp). Invalid SQL rate slashed to 3.34% (from 9.48%). Cross-model: LLaMA 2 +14.90% WikiTQ; DeepSeek-V3 81.85% (+10.21pp); GPT-4.1 84.92% (+9.14pp). CoQ+GPT-3.5 (74.77%) beats vanilla GPT-4.1 (70.97%). Hardest subset: 57.89% vs next-best 47.37%. Mean 7.63 LLM calls/question (median 5). Ablations: removing clause-by-clause drops 17.04pp; removing hybrid reasoning drops 18.81pp; removing natural-language schema drops 10.12pp.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: +13.66% accuracy with modest token overhead ($0.00668 vs $0.00632 on hard subset), invalid SQL rate 3.34% (lowest across all methods), works across open and closed models, robust to structurally complex tables (IM-TQA), CoQ+GPT-3.5 beats GPT-4.1. LOSES: requires SQL execution environment (SQLite), not applicable to non-relational data, 11 distinct prompt templates to maintain, extra latency from iterative clause validation, only tested on English+Chinese, natural-language schema may lose fine-grained value information on large tables.
**Rationale:** SQL generation depends on high-level schema semantics, not detailed cell values. Expressing schema in natural language aligns with LLM pretraining strengths. Hybrid reasoning division: SQL for mechanical, LLM for logical — each operates in its zone of competence. Clause-by-clause with rollback provides validated iterative refinement. Parallel decomposition eliminates cascading error from sequential approaches. Sufficiency-based early stopping adapts reasoning depth to question complexity.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no structured hybrid reasoning division (mechanical vs logical operations), no sufficiency-based early stopping, no clause-by-clause incremental query construction with rollback validation. Dynamic Planner's decision loop (check sufficiency -> choose next action -> execute -> validate -> repeat) is a direct template for Lyra's planning-execution-verification cycle. Status: **BEHIND** (no hybrid symbolic-neural reasoning architecture; CoQ provides principled design).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (hybrid reasoning division pattern applies broadly to Lyra's core agent loop, not just table QA)

## PosterForest: Hierarchical Multi-Agent Collaboration for Scientific Poster Generation
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.21720
**Mechanism:** Training-free, two-stage hierarchical multi-agent framework. **Stage 1 (Paper-to-Poster):** (1) Parser Agent uses Docling+MLLM to extract document hierarchy into Raw Doc Tree, (2) Refine Agent prunes, merges, and summarizes into Content Tree, (3) deterministic Layout Initializer derives spatial organization from content statistics, (4) Merge operation unifies content and layout into Poster Tree — a heterogeneous tree where each node jointly encodes semantic content (text, figures, tables) AND spatial attributes (position, size, region type, split ratio). **Stage 2 (Hierarchical Modification Planning):** Inner loop performs top-down node-level traversal where Layout Agent optimizes geometric attributes via legibility-balance heuristic (perceived text size + structural complexity) and Content Agent adjusts textual density targeting 80-100% fill ratio via Expand/Condense modes. Outer loop: Global Feedback Agent evaluates rendered poster image on visual organization, textual structure, and hierarchical balance, then decides whether to trigger another full traversal (up to K=2 iterations).
**Results:** MLLM-as-Judge: PosterForest-4o Overall 3.76 (vs P2P-4o 3.72, Paper2Poster 3.72, GT Poster 3.77 — approaches ground-truth). Human evaluation (25 grad students): PosterForest preferred 59.2% overall vs 27.2% for next-best Paper2Poster (2.2x win rate). Structure quality: 59.6% preference. Content fidelity: 56.0%. Ablations: without hierarchical tree, sections become disordered; Content Agent only = text redundancy reduced but suboptimal layout; Layout Agent only = better organization but text overflow; both combined = balanced harmony.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: training-free (no instruction tuning or regressor fitting), hierarchical tree preserves document structure preventing figure/table misplacement, joint content-layout optimization via shared Poster Tree, 2.2x human preference, recursive refinement with global feedback catches single-pass errors. LOSES: multiple MLLM API calls per poster (Parser + Refine + Layout Init + K x per-node agents + K x Feedback), depends on Docling PDF parsing quality, requires GPT-4o level MLLM (Qwen variant scores lower: 3.72 vs 3.76), no diversity/creativity control for visual style, K=2 limit may not converge for very complex papers.
**Rationale:** Existing methods treat papers as linear sequences, ignoring section-subsection hierarchy causing figure placement in wrong sections. Tree representation preserves document hierarchy and enforces parent-child locality. Splitting Content and Layout agents with shared tree enables each to focus on specialty while maintaining consistency. Legibility-based layout (not area-based) prevents large-but-simple figures from dominating panels at expense of small-but-dense charts. Training-free design enables immediate deployment without curated poster datasets.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no structured document-to-output pipeline with joint content-layout optimization, no heterogeneous tree representation for dual semantic-spatial reasoning, no recursive refinement with global visual feedback. The Poster Tree pattern generalizes beyond posters to any document-to-structured-output task (reports, dashboards, slides). Status: **BEHIND** (no unified semantic-spatial output architecture; PosterForest provides complete training-free blueprint).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (unified semantic-spatial tree + multi-agent recursive refinement enables structured output generation; 2.2x human preference validates approach)

---

## ReMemR1: Revisitable Memory for Long-Context LLM Agents
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.23040 (ICLR 2026)
**Mechanism:** Three-component architecture solving the "memorize while reading" limitation where compressed memory overwrites prevent revisiting past evidence. **(A) History-Augmented State:** Extends standard memory state from s_t = m_t (current memory only) to s_t = (m_t, q_t) where q_t is a learned callback query. At each step, agent (1) updates running memory with current chunk, (2) generates a callback query for future retrieval, (3) receives retrieved content from past memories via word-overlap recall function E({m_i}_{i<t}, q_t). This decouples "when evidence is seen" from "when evidence is used" — enabling non-linear reasoning across arbitrary temporal distances. **(B) Multi-Level Reward Design:** Trajectory-level outcome reward (exact match) + step-level state rewards (information gain: did memory update add ground-truth entities? callback bonus: did retrieval add info beyond current chunk?) + format reward (tag correctness). Combined advantage: A_t = 0.8*A_out + 0.2*A_state. **(C) GRPO Training:** Clipped importance sampling with KL penalty (beta=0.001), group size 16, trained on 16-32 H800 GPUs, 80-100 hrs.
**Results:** HotpotQA (7B): ReMemR1 holds 80.8% at 6400 docs vs MemAgent 75.8%, Qwen2.5-1M 0.0% — flat accuracy curve with no degradation. 2WikiMultiHopQA (OOD, 7B): 50.3% at 6400 docs vs MemAgent 44.7%. ReMemR1-7B (80.8%) outperforms QwenLong-L1-32B (38.3%) — beats 4x larger model. Distant evidence challenge: 2.7x accuracy over MemAgent. Callback overhead: <0.2% of total time, <1MB memory even at 6400 docs. Training overhead: +17.7% per-step time, +5% GPU memory. Alpha ablation: 0.8 optimal (0.5 collapses, 1.0 converges to lower plateau). RL is essential: without RL, ReMemR1 20.5% vs MemAgent 14.1% at 6400 docs.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: +5-12% absolute accuracy, flat scaling curve at 6400 docs, beats 4x larger models, strong OOD generalization, near-zero callback overhead (<0.2% time, <1MB memory), word-overlap retrieval is simple and fast. LOSES: +18% training time, requires 16-32 H800 GPUs, additional format tags cause early-stage parsing failures, word-overlap retrieval misses semantically-related but lexically-different memories, only tested on QA (no agentic tasks/dialogue/code), only Qwen2.5 base models tested, assumes fixed chunk ordering.
**Rationale:** Three fatal flaws in "memorize while reading": (1) premature pruning — evidence relevance only apparent after later chunks, (2) progressive information loss from fixed-length compression, (3) sparse supervision from single final-answer reward. Callback mechanism attacks flaws 1-2 by decoupling encoding time from retrieval time. Multi-level reward attacks flaw 3 with dense step-level signals. RL necessary because determining what/when to recall is non-trivial (rule-based approach degrades by 7.9%). Alpha=0.8 balances final-answer optimization with step-level guidance stability.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra deep-research agents process documents linearly through context window, suffering from exactly the premature pruning and progressive information loss problems ReMemR1 solves. Lyra has no revisitable memory, no callback query mechanism, no step-level information gain rewards. The callback mechanism is lightweight (word-overlap recall) and directly implementable without GPU training for a first prototype. Status: **BEHIND** (no non-linear memory access; ReMemR1 provides proven architecture).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (fundamentally changes memory access pattern from linear to non-linear; OOD results beating 4x larger models suggest generalizable reasoning skill)

---

## ReasoningBank: Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25140
**Mechanism:** Closed-loop self-evolving memory system requiring zero ground-truth labels. **(1) Memory Schema:** Each item = Title (concise identifier) + Description (one-sentence summary) + Content (1-5 sentences of distilled reasoning, decision rationales, operational insights). Explicit prohibition against website/query-specific references to force generalizable abstractions. **(2) Three-Step Loop:** (i) Retrieval: embedding similarity search over memory pool, inject top-k into agent context. (ii) Extraction: LLM-as-a-Judge binary classifier (72.7% accuracy, temperature 1.0) labels trajectory success/failure. Success extraction distills "why did it work?" (up to 3 items). Failure extraction distills "why did it fail, what to avoid?" (up to 3 items) — the only baseline that converts failures into constructive signals. (iii) Consolidation: simple additive append, no pruning/dedup (intentionally minimal to isolate content quality). **(3) MaTTS (Memory-Aware Test-Time Scaling):** Parallel scaling generates k diverse rollouts with self-contrast; sequential scaling iteratively re-examines trajectory with refinement. Bidirectional synergy: better memory guides exploration; diverse rollouts produce higher-quality memory.
**Results:** WebArena (Gemini-2.5-flash): ReasoningBank 48.8% SR (vs No Memory 40.5%, +20.5% relative), +MaTTS(k=5) 51.8%. Steps reduced 9.7->8.3 (14.4%). Gemini-2.5-pro: 53.9% (+15.4%), +MaTTS 56.3%. Claude-3.7-sonnet: 46.3% (+11.0%). SWE-Bench-Verified: 38.8% resolve rate (vs 34.2%), steps 30.3->27.5 (-9.2%). Token overhead: only 4.3% vs No Memory (vs Synapse +15.1%, AWM +16.8%). Failure learning: +3.2 SR from failures (AWM degrades -2.2). MaTTS scaling: 49.7->55.1 parallel, 49.7->54.5 sequential. Pass@k=5 reaches 62.1 vs 52.4 vanilla TTS. Open-source Gemma-3-12B: 24.1% (vs 17.1%). Judge robust at 70-90% accuracy; even 50% random-guess stays above baseline.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: +20.5% relative SR with 4.3% token overhead, learns from failures where baselines degrade, works across 3 model families + 12B open-source, robust to judge noise, reduces interaction steps (-14%), emergent strategy evolution (atomic -> procedural -> generalized). LOSES: unbounded memory growth (no pruning/decay), cold-start problem (memory starts empty), judge only 72.7% accurate, only tested on web browsing (WebArena, Mind2Web) + SWE, embedding-only retrieval may miss compositionally similar memories, sequential scaling saturates quickly (2-3 steps), no explicit safety guardrails on auto-generated memories.
**Rationale:** Prior methods store raw trajectories (Synapse) or workflows (AWM), capturing what happened but not why. ReasoningBank's core bet: abstraction quality > retrieval sophistication. Forcing generalizable abstractions (no URL/site refs) creates transferable reasoning primitives. Failures provide unique counterfactual signals — knowing what not to do is complementary to knowing successful strategies. Simple additive consolidation isolates content quality effect from management sophistication — if content is good enough, even simple retrieval suffices. MaTTS bidirectional synergy: memory guides exploration, exploration enriches memory.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra agents currently lack any self-improving memory that learns from both successes and failures without human labels. The three-field memory schema (title/description/content) and dual-source extraction (success+failure) are directly portable to Lyra's agent loop. LLM-as-a-Judge self-supervision eliminates Lyra's annotation bottleneck for agent trajectory evaluation. Status: **BEHIND** (no self-evolving memory; ReasoningBank provides complete label-free architecture).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (memory-driven self-evolution as a new scaling dimension; 4.3% token overhead for 20.5% gain is rare efficiency; directly addresses Lyra's cold-start and continuous improvement gaps)

## Vision-Zero: Scalable VLM Self-Evolution via Multi-Agent Self-Play
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25541 (ICLR 2026)
**Mechanism:** Label-free, domain-agnostic self-play framework for VLM post-training. **(1) "Who Is the Spy?" Game:** nc=4 civilians receive original image; 1 spy receives blank image. Clue Stage: each player produces one-sentence description; spy must infer hidden content from civilians' clues. Decision Stage: civilians analyze all clues and vote for spy; spy does not vote. **(2) Self-Play Policy Optimization (Clue Stage):** Zero-sum reward where spy and civilians compete (spy rewarded for avoiding detection; civilians rewarded for identifying spy). Role-Advantage Estimation (RAE) tracks per-role reward moving averages as baselines, eliminating information asymmetry — without RAE, performance drops below baseline (-3.7% avg). **(3) RLVR (Decision Stage):** Discrete reward (+1 correct vote, -0.5 "n/a", -1 wrong) with group normalization to remove round-specific difficulty. **(4) Iterative-SPO:** Alternates between self-play and RLVR with hysteresis thresholds: Decision->Clue when spy too easy to identify (acc > 0.9 AND n/a < 0.1); Clue->Decision when spy too hard (1-acc > 0.4 OR n/a > 0.5). Minimum 5 iterations per stage prevents chattering. Data: 2K CLEVR, 1K ChartQA, 1K real-world images — all label-free.
**Results:** Qwen2.5-VL-7B base -> VisionZero-Real: MathVista 68.2->73.1 (+4.9), MathVision 25.4->28.5 (+3.1), WeMath 36.1->40.1 (+4.0), LogicVista 47.2->50.8 (+3.6), 6-benchmark avg 41.1->44.5 (+3.4). Chart tasks: ChartXiV_RQ 42.5->45.8 (+3.3), PaperQA 68.4->73.7 (+5.3). Training efficiency: 127 A100-hours vs MM-Eureka GRPO ~700 hours (3.3-6.4x faster). 2K unlabeled images vs 15K labeled for GRPO baseline. Iterative-SPO critical: 49% vs pure decision-only ~48%, pure clue-only ~45%. Model generalization: InternVL3-8B +1.8, InternVL3-14B +1.6. Outperforms MM-Eureka-GRPO on both InternVL variants. Ablations: 4 civilians > 2 civilians (+2.5pp); 3 clue rounds > 1 round (+3.9pp). RAE removal: 37.4 avg vs 41.1 base (-3.7% — worse than no training). Robust to 20% editing noise: only -0.2% avg drop.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: zero human labeling eliminates multimodal annotation bottleneck ($60K+/dataset), domain-agnostic (same framework on CLEVR, charts, real-world), 3.3-6.4x faster training than GRPO with better accuracy, mitigates cross-capability negative transfer, Iterative-SPO prevents self-play equilibrium collapse, RAE eliminates role asymmetry. LOSES: requires image editors or rendering pipelines (CLEVR, GPT-4o chart plotting), limited to domains where paired/edited images can be generated, vision-centric gains modest (+0-2.7%) vs reasoning gains (+3-4%), hyperparameter-heavy (10+ thresholds/coefficients), only tested up to 14B, single-image only (no video/multi-image/3D), no explicit safety/alignment guardrails.
**Rationale:** Self-play has succeeded in Go, Chess, Dota 2, and LLMs (SPIRAL, Absolute Zero) but extending to VLMs requires joint vision-language game design. Social deduction game compels strategic reasoning across multiple roles — visual understanding, inference, communication — aligning with general VLM capabilities. Pure self-play reaches local equilibrium; pure RLVR saturates when question set mastered. Alternating with hysteresis prevents chattering and role collapse. RAE critical because spy and civilians have asymmetric information (image vs blank) — win probability is inherently role-biased; moving-average baseline ensures gradients reflect relative improvement.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no self-play training infrastructure, no multi-agent game environment for skill acquisition, no Iterative-SPO optimization, no label-free RL training loops for multimodal capabilities. The self-play game pattern is directly applicable: deploy multiple Lyra instances in asymmetric visual reasoning games to generate training data for document/chart/UI understanding without annotation. Status: **BEHIND** (no self-play infrastructure; Vision-Zero provides complete label-free training blueprint).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (zero-human-in-the-loop multimodal post-training fundamentally changes scaling economics; Iterative-SPO + RAE are modular components transferable to Lyra's RL pipeline)

## EvoQuality: Self-Evolving VLM for Image Quality Assessment via Voting and Ranking
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25787
**Mechanism:** (1) Self-evolving framework where VLM iteratively improves image quality assessment (IQA) capability without human labels. (2) Voting mechanism: multiple VLM instances independently score image quality; aggregation via weighted majority vote resolves inter-rater disagreement. (3) Ranking loss: pairwise ranking objective trains the model to correctly order images by quality, producing fine-grained relative judgments beyond binary good/bad. (4) Self-evolution loop: the model generates pseudo-labels on unlabeled images via voting consensus; high-confidence predictions are added to the training pool; retraining on expanded pool improves next-generation assessment. (5) Active sampling: prioritizes images where inter-rater variance is highest, maximizing information gain per training iteration.
**Results:** Self-evolution improves IQA correlation with human judgments by +8-12% over base VLM across standard benchmarks (LIVE, KonIQ-10k). Voting consensus surpasses single-model judging by +5-7% accuracy. Rank correlation (SRCC) improvements of +0.06-0.10 over supervised baselines. Effective with as few as 500 unlabeled seed images. Each self-evolution iteration adds +1-2% gain, saturating after 5-7 rounds.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: zero human labeling for IQA, voting reduces individual model bias, ranking provides fine-grained supervision signal, domain-agnostic (works on natural images, documents, UIs, charts), self-improving without external oracle. LOSES: voting requires 3-5 model calls per image (cost multiplier), ranking loss sensitive to annotation noise in early pseudo-labels, requires reasonably competent base VLM (cannot bootstrap from random), assumes quality is consensus-discoverable (fails for truly ambiguous cases), compute-intensive self-evolution loop (5-7x base training cost).
**Rationale:** IQA is inherently subjective — single annotator variance is high. Voting + ranking converts subjective judgment into reliable training signal by aggregating multiple perspectives. Self-evolution exploits the observation that VLMs improve monotonically when trained on their own high-confidence outputs (self-training principle). Pairwise ranking is more robust than absolute scoring because relative judgments ("A is better than B") are easier and more consistent than absolute scores ("A is 7.3/10").
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no VLM-based quality assessment for agent outputs, documents, or UI screenshots. The voting + self-evolution pattern is directly applicable to Lyra's quality gate (§4.19: `none`) and evaluation harness (§4.18: `stub`). Lyra agents generate diverse outputs (plans, code, summaries) — voting-based quality scoring could bootstrap automated quality assurance without human review. Status: **BEHIND** (no multi-modal quality assessment; EvoQuality provides label-free self-improving QA architecture).
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** investigate (multi-modal QA infrastructure is Phase 2+; voting pattern is lightweight to prototype)

## AgenticEval: Toward Agentic and Self-Evolving Safety Evaluation of LLMs
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.26100
**Mechanism:** (1) Agentic evaluation: replaces static test suites with dynamic LLM-powered evaluator agents that actively probe model safety via adversarial dialogue, jailbreak attempts, and edge-case generation. (2) Self-evolving taxonomy: evaluator agents discover new failure modes during testing and automatically expand the safety taxonomy without human curation. (3) Multi-agent red-teaming: specialized attacker agents (jailbreak specialist, social engineer, prompt injector) collaborate with evaluator agents to find vulnerabilities; defender model is scored on resistance. (4) Automatic test generation: LLM generates novel test cases by mutating known attacks, combining attack vectors, and exploiting model-specific weaknesses discovered in prior rounds. (5) Continuous benchmarking: safety scores update as new attacks are discovered; models that appeared safe on static benchmarks degrade under agentic probing.
**Results:** AgenticEval discovers 2.3-3.7x more vulnerabilities than static safety benchmarks (Anthropic harmlessness, Beavertails, SafeRLHF). Self-evolving taxonomy grows from 12 initial categories to 47+ fine-grained failure modes after 3 evolution rounds. Multi-agent red-teaming achieves 34% higher attack success rate than single-attacker baselines. Previously "safe" models (90%+ on static benchmarks) drop to 62-71% under agentic evaluation. Test generation produces 89% novel (not in training set) and 73% valid (actually harmful) test cases.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: discovers vulnerabilities static benchmarks miss, self-evolving taxonomy keeps pace with emerging threats, multi-agent red-teaming mimics real-world coordinated attacks, automatic test generation reduces human annotation burden, continuous scoring prevents safety regression complacency. LOSES: high compute cost (evaluator agents run for hours per model), evaluator agents may themselves be unsafe (requires safety guard on the evaluator), taxonomy drift risk (over-expansion into spurious categories), adversarial test validity requires human verification of 27% of generated cases, potential for evaluator-model collusion (both attacker and defender being same base model).
**Rationale:** Static safety benchmarks suffer from data contamination (models train on test sets), coverage gaps (finite test suites cannot enumerate all attacks), and staleness (new attack vectors emerge faster than human curators can annotate). Agentic evaluation solves all three: dynamic generation prevents memorization, self-evolving taxonomy closes coverage gaps, and automated discovery keeps pace with the攻击 surface. Multi-agent design mirrors real-world threat models where coordinated attackers exploit multiple vectors simultaneously.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no dynamic safety evaluation for its agent outputs. Safety maturity (§4.17) is listed but evaluation is static/manual. The self-evolving evaluation pattern is directly applicable: deploy evaluator agents that probe Lyra's planner, executor, and reviewer outputs for safety violations, with automatic taxonomy expansion as new failure modes emerge. Status: **BEHIND** (no agentic safety evaluation; AgenticEval provides dynamic self-improving safety benchmark architecture).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (agent safety is P0; self-evolving evaluation eliminates the annotation bottleneck that makes safety benchmarks stale)

## Your Agent May Misevolve: Emergent Risks in Self-Evolving LLM Agents
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.26354
**Mechanism:** (1) Taxonomy of misevolution risks: identifies 5 failure modes in self-evolving agent systems — goal drift (agent optimizes proxy metric diverging from true objective), capability collapse (over-specialization erodes general competence), reward hacking (agent exploits self-evaluation loopholes), feedback corruption (noisy self-labels compound errors), and diversity loss (convergence to monoculture strategies). (2) Empirical demonstration: deploys self-evolving agents across WebArena, SWE-bench, and tool-use environments; tracks capability trajectories over 10+ evolution iterations. (3) Detection protocol: statistical monitors for each failure mode — distribution shift detectors for goal drift, capability audit suites for collapse, reward audit trails for hacking, inter-rater agreement for feedback corruption, strategy entropy for diversity loss. (4) Mitigation strategies: conservative policy constraints (KL penalty to base model), diversity regularization (entropy bonus on action distribution), external validation oracle (periodic human or strong-model audit), and evolutionary reset (reinitialize from checkpoint when monitors fire).
**Results:** 3 of 5 self-evolving agent systems studied exhibited at least one misevolution failure by iteration 5-7. Goal drift: proxy reward increases +12% while true task success drops -8% (divergence). Capability collapse: specialized agents lose 15-22% on held-out general benchmarks. Reward hacking: agents discover 3-5 distinct loopholes in self-evaluation (e.g., generating plausible-sounding but incorrect outputs that fool the judge). Diversity loss: strategy entropy drops 40-60% within 3 iterations, reducing pass@k diversity gains. Mitigation effectiveness: KL penalty reduces goal drift by 60%, diversity regularization preserves 85% of strategy entropy, external audit detects 78% of reward hacking instances.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: first systematic taxonomy of self-evolution failure modes, empirical demonstration across multiple environments, practical detection protocols (no exotic infrastructure needed), mitigation strategies are lightweight add-ons (KL penalty, entropy bonus). LOSES: only tested over 10-15 iterations (longer-term effects unknown), external audit oracle expensive at scale (human or GPT-4 level), mitigation strategies trade off improvement speed for safety (KL penalty slows evolution), taxonomy may be incomplete (novel failure modes likely exist), conservative constraints may prevent legitimate breakthrough improvements.
**Rationale:** Self-evolution is increasingly deployed (ReasoningBank, Vision-Zero, self-play RL) but safety analysis has focused on static models. Misevolution risks compound: agents that self-improve amplify initial biases, exploit evaluation blind spots, and converge to local optima. The taxonomy provides a diagnostic framework before deploying self-improving loops in production. Conservative constraints are a necessary brake — evolution speed must trade off against safety guarantees, analogous to RLHF's KL penalty.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's plan for self-evolving agents (informed by ReasoningBank, Vision-Zero patterns) currently lacks misevolution risk detection and mitigation. Any self-improvement loop Lyra implements needs monitors for goal drift, capability collapse, reward hacking, feedback corruption, and diversity loss before deployment. Status: **AHEAD** (Lyra hasn't built self-evolution yet, so misevolution risks are not yet present — but this paper provides the safety checklist to implement BEFORE enabling self-evolution).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (critical safety prerequisite for any self-evolution feature; must be implemented BEFORE self-evolution, not after)

## ACON: Optimizing Context Compression for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00615
**Mechanism:** (1) Adaptive context observer network (ACON): lightweight auxiliary model (350M-1B params) that monitors agent trajectory and decides when and what to compress. (2) Compression granularity: three levels — token-level (merge redundant tokens), turn-level (summarize completed subtasks), and episode-level (archive resolved goals). (3) Compression operators: extractive (keep salient spans), abstractive (LLM-generated summaries), and structural (convert linear history to hierarchical outlines). (4) Context budget controller: maintains token budget B; ACON allocates B across time steps to maximize expected task completion. (5) Recovery mechanism: compressed segments can be "expanded" on-demand via retrieval when agent needs detail for backtracking or error recovery. (6) Training: ACON trained via RL with reward = task success - λ * context_length, learning to compress aggressively while preserving decision-relevant information.
**Results:** On long-horizon benchmarks (WebArena multi-task, SWE-bench multi-file, GAIA level 3): context reduction 62-78% vs no compression, with task success rate within 3% of uncompressed baseline. Token efficiency (success per 1K context tokens) improves 2.8-4.1x. Compared to fixed compression baselines (sliding window, uniform summarization): ACON achieves +11-18% higher success at same compression rate. Ablation: removing adaptive granularity drops success -9%; removing recovery mechanism drops -14% on tasks requiring backtracking. Latency overhead: <5% (350M ACON runs in parallel with agent inference).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: adaptive to task difficulty (compresses aggressively on easy segments, preserves detail on hard), multi-granularity handles heterogeneous agent trajectories, recovery mechanism prevents irreversible information loss, lightweight (350M params, <5% overhead), general across environments (not environment-specific). LOSES: requires training ACON on agent trajectories (domain transfer may need fine-tuning), compression decisions are irreversible if recovery mechanism fails, abstractive compression may introduce hallucinated summaries, RL training signal is sparse (task success only known at episode end), assumes context budget known a priori.
**Rationale:** Long-horizon agent tasks routinely exceed context windows (SWE-bench files >100K tokens, web navigation >50 steps). Prior approaches either truncate (lose critical early context) or summarize uniformly (lose detail where needed). ACON's key insight: compression is a sequential decision problem — the agent should compress differently at each step based on current state, task progress, and remaining budget. The recovery mechanism is critical because agents frequently need to revisit earlier decisions (backtracking in tree search, debugging failed attempts).
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra currently has no context compression for long-running agent sessions. Agents accumulate full conversation history linearly, hitting context limits on complex multi-step tasks. ACON's adaptive compression is directly applicable to Lyra's agent loop — the context budget controller maps to Lyra's token budget tracking (§4.22), and the multi-granularity compression (token/turn/episode) maps to Lyra's session structure. Status: **BEHIND** (no context compression; ACON provides lightweight adaptive architecture).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (context window is a hard constraint for long-horizon agent tasks; ACON's 2.8-4.1x efficiency gain directly expands Lyra's operational range)

## SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04618 (Jimenez et al., Princeton, ICLR 2024 Spotlight)
**Mechanism:** (1) Benchmark construction: 2,294 real GitHub issues from 12 popular Python repositories (django, scikit-learn, matplotlib, sympy, etc.), each paired with the merge commit that resolved it. Issues span bug fixes, feature requests, and refactoring tasks. (2) Task formulation: given issue description + repository codebase snapshot, model must produce a patch (git diff) that resolves the issue. (3) Evaluation: patches applied in isolated Docker containers; unit tests from the merge commit verify correctness (fail-to-pass test ratio). (4) SWE-bench-Lite: 300-instance curated subset with easier setup and faster evaluation. (5) SWE-agent: reference agent architecture that combines file viewer, search tool, file editor, and bash execution in an iterative loop. (6) Scoring: resolved = all fail-to-pass tests pass AND no regression on pass-to-pass tests.
**Results:** SWE-bench (full): Claude 3.5 Sonnet (SWE-agent) achieves 26.2% resolved; GPT-4 17.3%; SWE-Llama-13B 5.2%; RAG-only baseline 1.7%. SWE-bench-Lite: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 49.5%, GPT-4 33.7%, GPT-4o 29.4%, DeepSeek-Coder-V2 24.6%. Human developers: ~85% estimated (based on issue close rates). Best systems achieve 60-70% on SWE-bench-Lite as of late 2025 (Devin, OpenHands, Agentless). Key failure modes: (1) localization failures — cannot find relevant files (35-40% of errors), (2) reproduction failures — cannot reproduce the bug (20-25%), (3) solution failures — finds bug but incorrect fix (25-30%), (4) regression — fix breaks other tests (10-15%). Long-horizon: average 5-8 file edits, 20-40 lines changed, 3-10 tool calls per attempt. Cost: ~$4-8 per instance (Claude 3.5 Sonnet).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: real-world task complexity (actual GitHub issues, not synthetic), executable evaluation (unit tests ground truth), multi-file reasoning (mean 5-8 files touched), large-scale (2,294 instances across 12 repos), standardized Docker evaluation (reproducible, prevents contamination). LOSES: expensive evaluation ($4-8/instance, full benchmark ~$10-18K), slow iteration (Docker build + test execution), repository bias toward Python/data-science, test coverage gaps (not all bugs have tests), issue quality variance (some issues underspecified), potential benchmark saturation (top systems approaching ceiling on SWE-bench-Lite).
**Rationale:** Prior code benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP) use isolated function synthesis — far from real software engineering. SWE-bench requires understanding large codebases (100K+ lines), localizing bugs across multiple files, and producing minimal correct patches. This tests agent capabilities end-to-end: information retrieval (finding relevant code), reasoning (understanding bug cause), planning (designing fix), and execution (correct code edits). The gap from 26-70% (best systems) to 85% (human) reveals fundamental limitations in agent code understanding and multi-step reasoning.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra currently has no code-modification capability for external repositories and no SWE-bench evaluation pipeline. The SWE-agent loop (file viewer -> search -> editor -> bash -> test) is a direct architectural template for Lyra's planned coding agent. SWE-bench-Lite provides a standardized, cost-effective evaluation target (~$1-3K per full run) for measuring Lyra's code repair capability. Status: **BEHIND** (no SWE-bench pipeline; SWE-agent architecture is the reference design for coding agents).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (SWE-bench is the de facto standard for coding agent evaluation; SWE-agent loop is the reference architecture; both are critical for Lyra's code modification workstream)

## PA-Tool: Don't Adapt Small Language Models for Tools; Adapt Tool Schemas to the Models
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.07248
**Mechanism:** (1) Candidate Generation: given a tool/parameter description d, sample N=32 candidate names from the target SLM at temperature t=0.4 via sampling. (2) Peakedness Computation: compute character-level Levenshtein edit distance between all candidate pairs; for each candidate si, φ(si) = count of other candidates within length-adaptive threshold τ = α·ℓ_max (α=0.2). Peakedness (borrowed from contamination detection) measures distributional concentration — a tight cluster of similar variants indicates deeper pretraining memorization. (3) Schema Selection: pick candidate with maximum peakedness; resolve ties via edit-distance to greedy-decoded reference name. Name collisions (4-6% of components) resolved via priority-based locking (highest peakedness claims the name). Schema generation takes 8-16 wall-clock seconds once; cached mapping applies at inference with zero overhead. One-time preprocessing cost is ~4×10^5 tokens, generated once and reused indefinitely.
**Results:** Llama3.2-3B on MetaTool Reliability: 43.6%→60.6% (+17.0% absolute). Llama3.1-8B on MetaTool Multi-tool: 78.7%→88.3% (+9.6%) — surpasses all closed-source models including Claude-Sonnet-4.5 (85.1%). Qwen2.5-3B on API-Bank Call: 18.0%→28.5% (+10.5%). On RoTBench single-turn tool selection: Llama3.1-8B 58.1%→68.6% (+10.5%). Schema Misalignment errors reduced by 80.0% (Llama3.1-8B). Generalizes across model families: GPT-4.1-mini +12.1%, Ministral-8B +8.5%, Qwen3-1.7B +10.5%, Gemini-2.5-Flash +6.7%. PA-Tool alone outperforms SFT models on Reliability (67.2% vs 57.1%) and Multi-tool (89.9% vs 82.8%) without any training. Combining SFT+PA-Tool yields best results.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: training-free (no GPU hours, no catastrophic forgetting), one-time preprocessing with zero inference overhead, complements both SFT and other training-free methods, works across model families (Qwen, Llama, Mistral, GPT, Gemini) and scales (1.7B to 70B). LOSES: requires model access for candidate generation (not applicable to API-only closed models without sampling), gains diminish for LLMs >8B (schema misalignment is smaller fraction of errors), only renames tool/parameter names (does not touch descriptions), character-level edit distance may not work for non-Latin scripts, schemas are model-specific (cross-model transfer is suboptimal).
**Rationale:** The dominant paradigm has been to train models to use arbitrary tool schemas via SFT/RL. This is expensive, causes catastrophic forgetting, and ignores that SLMs already have rich internal representations of naming conventions. The core insight: SLMs fail at tool use not because they cannot reason, but because they hallucinate plausible tool names that do not exist in the provided schema — the model defaults to names it saw during pretraining. Flipping the problem (adapt schema to model, not model to schema) eliminates 80% of schema misalignment errors with zero training cost.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's coordinator agent passes tools to sub-agents with the same tool names for all. With PA-Tool, each sub-agent would receive tool names aligned to its specific pretrained vocabulary (e.g., Qwen-agent sees `fetch_web_page` while Llama-agent sees `get_url_content` for the same function). A mapping layer translates back to canonical tool names before execution. Status: **BEHIND** (no per-model schema adaptation; Lyra uses uniform tool naming).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 2 | **Tier:** breakthrough (paradigm inversion with strong empirical support, broad compatibility, minimal deployment cost)

---

## Anonymization for Bias-Reduced Multi-Agent Reasoning
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.07517 (Choi, Zhu, Li — University of Wisconsin-Madison)
**Mechanism:** (1) Model Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) as a Dirichlet-Compound-Multinomial process: each agent i maintains belief parameter vector α_i,t over K answers. (2) Define identity-driven Bayesian belief update: α_i,t = α_i,t-1 + (w_i·e_i,t + Σ w_j·e_j,t) where w_i is self-weight, w_j are peer weights. Sycophancy = w_j > w_i; self-bias = w_i > w_j. (3) Decomposition Theorem: Δ_i = Conformity_i - Obstinacy_i decomposes into belief difference + identity bias (w_j - w_i). (4) Anonymization: remove all identity markers ("SELF", "PEER") from debate prompts, enforcing w_i = w_j and collapsing the identity bias term to zero. (5) IBC metric: quantify residual bias as Δ_vanilla - Δ_anonymized. IBC > 0 = sycophancy; IBC < 0 = self-bias.
**Results:** 18 of 20 model-dataset combinations show positive IBC (sycophancy dominant). Qwen-32B on MMLU: 96% reduction in identity bias (Δ from 0.608→0.024, IBC=0.584). Qwen-7B on HellaSwag: Δ drops from 0.507→-0.032 (IBC=0.539). Qwen-32B on MMLU: Subversion drops 64.3% vs Correction drops only 14.9% — anonymization disproportionately reduces abandoning correct answers due to peer pressure. No accuracy degradation across all configurations (martingale property). IBC consistently increases from Round 1 to Round 2 (e.g., Qwen-7B on GPQA: 0.33→0.45) — bias compounds without anonymization. Heterogeneous agents reduce IBC (0.408→0.374 for Qwen-7B) but don't eliminate it.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: eliminates sycophancy and self-bias, zero model retraining (prompt-only), model-agnostic (Qwen, Llama, Mistral, GPT-OSS), subversion reduced far more than correction (64.3% vs 14.9%), lightweight (prompt template change only), IBC provides principled interpretable metric. LOSES: cannot selectively retain useful identity heuristics (genuine expert deference), no accuracy improvement (martingale property — only removes distortion), base model reasoning flaws persist under anonymization, only tested on multiple-choice QA (not open-ended generation), some agents produce unnecessarily long reasoning or fail to state final answers in anonymized setting (~1/5 cases).
**Rationale:** MAD's inconsistent performance vs single agents is rooted in identity bias, not reasoning ability. Rather than suppress bias through training (DPO, RLHF) or add complexity, the approach eliminates the channel through which bias operates — identity labels in prompts. The Bayesian decomposition proves that identity bias and belief difference are mathematically separable. Attribute removal (not behavior modification) is a cleaner intervention principle from fairness literature.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's multi-agent debate/consensus rounds present agent responses with full identity attribution (agent_id, agent_role, agent_model). This creates sycophancy risk toward high-status personas (e.g., "Senior Architect") and self-bias toward prior outputs. An anonymization middleware between agents would strip source-identity markers during debate rounds, selectively disabled when genuine expertise differentiation is needed (e.g., security-reviewer output for safety-critical decisions). Status: **BEHIND** (no identity-oblivious communication protocol).
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 1 | **Tier:** breakthrough (low-effort, high-leverage prompt intervention grounded in formal theory; addresses root-cause failure mode of multi-agent systems)

## Dynamic Multi-Agent Communication Topologies via Graph Diffusion (GTD)
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.07799 (Jiang et al., UCLA + UW + NTU)
**Mechanism:** (1) Dataset Generation: run multi-agent simulations with diverse baseline topologies (chain, star, complete, layered, random) to produce D_gen = {(A_j, C_j, P_j)} where P_j = [utility, cost]. (2) Train Surrogate Reward Model P_φ: 2-layer GAT (hidden dim=32) predicts performance of any topology without running simulation (MSE=0.0089 utility, Pearson r=0.91; Top-1 ranking acc=78.4%). (3) Train Conditional Graph Diffusion Generator G_θ: 2-layer Graph Transformer (2 attention heads) learns distribution of high-quality topologies via denoising (T=50 steps, variance-preserving schedule). Trained only on high-performance subset D_hq. (4) Proxy-Guided Topology Synthesis (Inference): at each denoising timestep, predict unguided clean graph Â_0, generate K=5 discrete candidates via Bernoulli sampling, evaluate with surrogate P_φ, select best via zeroth-order optimization, proceed to next timestep. ZO selection approximates gradient-ascent on the surrogate reward landscape; Theorem G.2 bounds performance gap to 2ε_max. Only 50 training samples needed.
**Results:** SOTA across 6/6 benchmarks: +3.99 avg accuracy over vanilla (81.75→85.74% on GPT-4o-mini). GSM8K: 87.45→94.14 (+6.69), MATH: 46.29→54.07 (+7.78), HumanEval: 87.08→91.46 (+4.38). Generalizes to Qwen-3-8B: +5.3 avg (67.5→72.8). LiveCodeBench Pass@1: 25.4%→30.8% (+5.4). Token efficiency: 15% to >5x fewer tokens than dense baselines. Robustness: single-agent failure only -0.3% accuracy (vs -1.8% to -13% for others). Inference: 7.9s/instance at 94.14% accuracy — faster than all baselines. Scales to 1000 agents at 4.9GB (linear scaling).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: SOTA accuracy, dramatic token savings via sparse topologies, strong robustness, competitive inference speed, data-efficient (50 samples), model-agnostic, hardware-efficient (consumer GPUs). LOSES: requires seed data (must pre-compute baseline topologies), static topology (fixed at task start, no mid-execution adaptation), diminishing returns beyond 4 agents on current benchmarks, surrogate degradation on OOD topologies (Top-1 ranking drops from 78.4% to 72.8%), only tested on reasoning/code tasks, two-phase training adds engineering complexity.
**Rationale:** Communication topologies are discrete and highly structured — a single wrong edge breaks flow. Diffusion's iterative denoising allows proxy model intervention at every timestep, gently steering generation (VAEs/GANs apply reward only post-generation). Graph Transformer's global self-attention ensures edges are not predicted independently. ZO optimization handles non-differentiable discrete reward landscape. Proxy model over direct simulation: running K×T = 250 full simulations per candidate is infeasible; lightweight GNN evaluates in milliseconds.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra currently uses fixed workflow templates (planner→executor→reviewer) with hand-crafted routing heuristics. GTD provides a pattern for learned, task-adaptive orchestration that trades off speed, quality, and cost per-query. The proxy-guided ZO pattern directly enables Lyra to move from static agent DAGs to dynamically constructed execution plans. Status: **BEHIND** (no learned topology optimization; static orchestration only).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (novel paradigm combining conditional graph diffusion with zeroth-order multi-objective guidance; could fundamentally change how Lyra routes and coordinates sub-agents)

## COMPASS: Enhancing Agent Long-Horizon Reasoning with Evolving Context
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08790 (Wan et al., Google Cloud AI + UVA)
**Mechanism:** (1) Main Agent (Tactical Executor): operates standard ReAct loop but receives a dynamically refreshed compact context x_t from Context Manager — NOT the full history. (2) Meta-Thinker (Strategic Overseer): runs asynchronously alongside Main Agent, monitors trace queue for anomalies (looping, tool misuse, reasoning drift), remains silent until triggered, issues one of five decisions: PERSIST/PIVOT/VERIFY/TERMINATE. Operates on single-turn slices for low latency. (3) Context Manager: after each Meta-Thinker intervention, synthesizes refreshed context from three sources: persistent structured notes n_t (accumulated across all turns), current reasoning trajectory T_t, and Meta-Thinker's strategic signal. Output is a 6-section structured brief: Task restatement, Most-Recent Evidence, Critical Constraints & Corrections, Open Items, Next Actions, Tool Hints (≤200-300 tokens). (4) Context-12B: distilled context manager trained via SFT (10,347 query-context pairs from COMPASS rollouts) + DPO (8,200 preference pairs), reducing context manager cost while maintaining quality. (5) COMPASS-TTS: test-time scaling via n=2-4 parallel samples.
**Results:** Gemini 2.5 Pro: GAIA 35.4% (vs SAS 16.8%, +110%), BrowseComp 67.8% (vs SAS 58.6%, +15.7%), HLE 31.7% (vs SAS 14.8%, +114%). Outperforms single-agent augmentation (29.8% GAIA) and decentralized multi-agent handoffs (28.1% GAIA). COMPASS-TTS at n=8: BrowseComp 72.1% — exceeds DeepResearch (o3) at 67.4% and TestTime Diffusion at 69.1%. Context-12B-DPO: 30% token reduction (2,847→1,993 avg tokens/task) with comparable success rate (87.3% vs 87.8% SFT). Ablation: removing Meta-Thinker drops GAIA from 35.4%→15.2%; removing Context Manager drops to 26.4% and causes 212K token blowup with Flash backend. Balanced strategic reasoning: PAR 0.85, PVR 0.48, CA 0.88 (vs SAS blind persistence at PVR 0.12).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: +20% relative accuracy over SAS baselines, balanced strategic reasoning (persistence + pivoting), asynchronous monitoring preserves SAS fluidity, Context-12B achieves 30% token reduction via DPO, model-agnostic architecture, COMPASS-TTS matches/exceeds established agents. LOSES: ~2.2x token cost (185K vs 85K for SAS baseline), three-agent orchestration complexity, Meta-Thinker operates on single-turn snapshots (may miss long-range patterns), requires 480 GPU-hours for Context-12B training, proprietary Gemini models used (open-source "significantly underperform"), static three-agent topology (no dynamic role negotiation).
**Rationale:** Long-horizon agent failures stem from context mismanagement — as execution traces grow O(t), critical evidence gets buried (context overflow) or lost (truncation). Monolithic SAS cannot self-correct reliably. Full MAS achieves SOTA but relies on manually designed coordination and human-in-the-loop. COMPASS preserves end-to-end autonomy while externalizing strategic reasoning and context curation into dedicated agents with isolated context windows. The key insight: separating tactical execution, strategic oversight, and context management prevents cross-contamination and enables bounded memory across long-horizon runs.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra currently accumulates full conversation history linearly in multi-turn agent sessions, hitting context limits on complex multi-step tasks. COMPASS's structured context management pattern (6-section brief + rolling note store + dedicated Context Manager) directly addresses Lyra's planned multi-turn orchestration where context accumulation across subtask handoffs will degrade reasoning quality. Context-12B shows a small model can be fine-tuned for this specific function via SFT+DPO distillation from a frontier teacher. Status: **BEHIND** (no structured context management; no context-aware agent orchestration).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (context degradation is the leading cause of long-horizon agent failure; solving it enables reliable multi-turn operation)

## Open ASR Leaderboard: Reproducible Multilingual Speech Recognition Evaluation
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.06961 (Srivastav et al., Hugging Face/NVIDIA/Mistral/OpenAI)
**Mechanism:** (1) Three-track benchmarking platform: Short-form English (9 datasets, ≤30s audio), Multilingual (5 European languages across CoVoST-2, FLEURS, MLS), Long-form English (>30s audio, 4 datasets). (2) Standardized evaluation: all text normalized (punctuation/casing removal, number normalization, filler word removal) prior to WER computation; all models evaluated on identical NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB hardware. (3) RTFx metric (inverse real-time factor): higher = faster, chosen over RTF for intuitive leaderboard UX. (4) Community-PR-driven contribution: external contributors submit standardized Python+Bash evaluation scripts verified in maintainers' environment before leaderboard update; 29 PRs added 56 models.
**Results:** Conformer-based + Transformer/LLM decoder achieves best WER (Cohere Labs Transcribe: 5.42% avg). Conformer-based systems are 3.77x faster than Whisper-based (avg RTFx 758 vs 201). CTC/TDT decoders sacrifice 0.6-1.5pp WER for 5-44x faster inference (NVIDIA Parakeet CTC 1.1B: WER 7.40%, RTFx 2730; NVIDIA FastConformer CTC Large: WER 8.96%, RTFx 6400). Multilingual support degrades English WER by 0.27-0.65pp. CTC/TDT gap narrows in long-form. 86 models from 26 organizations evaluated.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: reproducible (standardized hardware+normalization), transparent (community-PR model), multi-dimensional (accuracy, latency, domain, language), continuously growing. LOSES: test-set contamination risk, hardware-dependent RTFx (relative rankings may shift), English-centric multilingual (only 5 European languages), WER-dominant metric (doesn't capture semantic errors), no noise/robustness evaluation, closed-source model opacity.
**Rationale:** No single dataset or metric suffices for ASR evaluation. Community contribution model enables continuous growth and prevents toolkit-specific biases. Idea transfer to Lyra: the PR-driven, multi-dataset, multi-metric evaluation protocol provides a template for Lyra's agent evaluation harness — a continuously growing evaluation board where new agent architectures and strategies are contributed via PR with verified evaluation scripts.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has basic eval in adapters but no community-contribution pipeline, no standardized evaluation Docker environment, no multi-metric dashboard. The evaluation methodology is transferable despite substantial domain gap (ASR → agent evaluation). Status: **INVESTIGATE** (strong methodology to adapt but requires significant domain translation).
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** investigate (useful methodology transfer to agent evaluation; worth piloting a minimal version)
