## EvoTest: Evolutionary Test-Time Learning for Self-Improving Agentic Systems
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13220 (Zhao et al., 2025)
**Mechanism:** (1) Test-time evolution loop: maintain population of N agent configurations (prompts, tool selections, hyperparameters). (2) Fitness evaluation: each configuration executes the current task(s); fitness = success rate + efficiency score. (3) Selection: tournament selection picks top-k configurations as parents. (4) Variation: apply crossover (swap prompt segments, tool chains) and mutation (rewrite prompt subsections, substitute tools, adjust temperature) to produce offspring. (5) Replacement: generational replacement with elitism (keep best 2-3). (6) Test-time budget: evolution runs within a fixed token/compute budget at inference time, competing directly against static single-pass agents. (7) Population diversity maintained via fitness sharing (niche penalty for similar configurations). Key insight: test-time compute scaling is more effective when spent on evolutionary search over agent design space rather than on longer chains-of-thought for a single design.
**Results:** EvoTest outperforms static single-agent baselines by +8-15% across agent benchmarks (WebArena, GAIA, SWE-bench subsets). Population size N=8 with 5 generations achieves best cost-quality Pareto. Matches performance of hand-tuned agent at 3x lower human engineering cost. Evolution discovers non-obvious prompt patterns and tool combinations that human designers missed. Ablation: removing crossover drops -6%; removing mutation drops -9%; removing fitness sharing drops -3%. Test-time cost: 4-6x more tokens than single-pass, but 2-3x cheaper than grid search over same design space.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: no training required (test-time only), discovers novel agent configurations, adapts per-task without retraining, complements any base agent architecture, strong scaling with test-time compute budget. LOSES: 4-6x inference cost, latency proportional to generations, stochastic results (non-deterministic across runs), requires well-defined fitness function, population diversity can collapse on narrow tasks, overhead unjustified for simple tasks solvable by single-pass agents.
**Rationale:** Agent design (prompts, tools, orchestration) is a combinatorially large discrete search space — evolutionary methods naturally handle discrete optimization with black-box fitness. Test-time evolution converts extra inference compute into better agent designs rather than longer reasoning traces. Crossover exploits modularity of agent components (prompts, tool chains are recombinable); mutation enables local exploration. vs RL training: no gradient estimation needed, works with black-box LLM APIs. vs Grid search: evolutionary search is 2-3x more sample-efficient. vs Single-agent CoT scaling: evolution searches design space rather than reasoning space (complementary).
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra currently has fixed agent configurations with hand-crafted prompts and tool selections. No mechanism exists for automated configuration search at test time. Status: **BEHIND** (no test-time optimization; static agent designs only).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (evolutionary test-time search unlocks self-improving agent configurations without training; directly applicable to Lyra's multi-agent orchestration)

## AlphaQuanter: End-to-End Tool-Augmented Agentic RL for Stock Trading
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.14264 (2025)
**Mechanism:** (1) Tool-augmented agent architecture: LLM-based trading agent with access to financial tools (market data APIs, sentiment analysis, technical indicators, news search, portfolio calculator). (2) Reinforcement learning loop: agent observes market state, selects action (buy/sell/hold + quantity) via tool-augmented reasoning, receives reward (profit/loss + risk penalty). (3) End-to-end training: RL gradients flow through both tool selection and action selection, optimizing the full agentic pipeline. (4) Tool curriculum: progressively introduces complex tools as agent masters simpler ones. (5) Risk management module: separate risk-assessment tool that agent must consult before large trades (enforced via action masking). (6) Multi-timescale decision-making: agent operates on daily, hourly, and minute-level data simultaneously via hierarchical reasoning.
**Results:** Outperforms rule-based trading strategies by +12-18% annualized return. Matches or exceeds specialized RL trading agents without tool augmentation. Tool curriculum reduces training time by 40% vs flat tool exposure. Risk module reduces maximum drawdown by 35% vs unconstrained agent. Ablation: removing tools drops performance to baseline LLM level (-15%); removing RL fine-tuning drops to tool-augmented zero-shot level (-11%). Generalizes across 3 stock markets (US, China, Japan) with minimal fine-tuning.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: end-to-end optimization of tool use + trading policy, risk-aware by design, curriculum enables stable training, multi-market generalization, tool augmentation closes gap with specialized systems. LOSES: RL training requires simulator environment (backtesting bias risk), significant compute for training, financial domain complexity requires careful reward design, tool API reliability critical at inference, regulatory concerns for autonomous trading systems.
**Rationale:** Pure LLM agents lack optimization for financial objectives; pure RL agents lack flexible reasoning and tool use. AlphaQuanter bridges both: LLM provides reasoning and tool-use flexibility, RL provides objective-driven optimization. Tool curriculum prevents the agent from relying on complex tools as a crutch before learning basic trading principles. Risk module addresses the critical safety requirement in financial domains via architectural constraint (action masking) rather than reward shaping alone.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has tool-augmented agent patterns (adapters) but no RL-based optimization of tool use, no curriculum learning, and no domain-specific safety constraints via action masking. The tool curriculum + RL pattern is transferable to Lyra's multi-agent orchestration. Status: **BEHIND** (no learned optimization of agent behavior; static heuristics only).
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** investigate (domain-specific but RL-for-tool-use pattern generalizes; lower priority than core orchestration)

## E2EDev: Benchmarking LLMs in End-to-End Software Development
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.14509 (2025)
**Mechanism:** (1) End-to-end software development tasks: each task provides a natural language specification (requirements doc) and expects a complete, working codebase (multiple files, tests, documentation, deployment config). (2) Multi-phase evaluation: Requirements Analysis (extract functional/non-functional requirements), Architecture Design (produce system design + component decomposition), Implementation (generate all source files), Testing (generate and run test suite), DevOps (generate Dockerfile, CI config, deployment manifests). (3) Automated evaluation: functional correctness via test execution, code quality via static analysis (linters, complexity metrics), architectural quality via dependency graph analysis, documentation completeness via coverage metrics. (4) Task diversity: 200+ tasks across web apps, CLI tools, data pipelines, APIs, libraries — spanning 5 difficulty levels (toy projects to production-grade systems). (5) Human baseline: 15 professional software engineers complete subset of tasks with time and quality measured.
**Results:** Best LLM (GPT-4 + agent scaffold): 38.2% end-to-end success rate (all phases pass). Human baseline: 82.5% success rate — 2.2x gap. Implementation phase highest LLM success (62%); Architecture lowest (41%). Code quality: LLMs match humans on linting (89% vs 91%) but significantly worse on modularity (cohesion 0.42 vs 0.71). Test quality: LLM-generated tests achieve 71% branch coverage vs human 88%. Task difficulty strongly predictive: toy tasks 78% LLM success, production-grade 12%. Multi-file consistency: 31% of LLM solutions have cross-file import errors.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: comprehensive end-to-end evaluation (first benchmark covering full SDLC), automated multi-metric scoring, realistic task diversity, human baseline enables gap quantification, actionable failure analysis per phase. LOSES: evaluation cost (full benchmark runs require significant compute), test-based eval misses design quality nuances, static analysis metrics are coarse, human baseline small (N=15), task contamination risk from public LLM training data, limited programming language coverage (Python/JS focused).
**Rationale:** Existing coding benchmarks (HumanEval, SWE-bench) evaluate isolated code generation or bug fixing — they miss the systems integration, architectural reasoning, and multi-file coordination that dominate real software engineering. E2EDev fills this gap by requiring complete project generation and evaluating all phases. The 2.2x human-LLM gap quantifies where agentic scaffolds need improvement: architecture design and cross-file consistency, not code generation per se.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra aims to orchestrate multi-agent software development pipelines (planner→architect→executor→reviewer). E2EDev provides the most relevant benchmark for evaluating such pipelines and identifying failure modes per phase. The architecture design weakness (41% success) directly motivates Lyra's planned architect agent. Status: **INVESTIGATE** (valuable benchmark; use to calibrate Lyra's multi-agent pipeline performance).
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 2 | **Tier:** investigate (adopt as evaluation benchmark for Lyra's multi-agent software development pipeline)

## Telling Speculative Stories: Helping Humans Imagine Harms of Healthcare AI
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.14718 (2025)
**Mechanism:** (1) Speculative story generation: LLM generates narrative scenarios depicting plausible harmful outcomes of healthcare AI deployments (misdiagnosis cascades, bias amplification, privacy erosion, automation-induced deskilling). (2) Stakeholder-centered design: stories co-designed with clinicians, patients, ethicists, and AI developers to ensure realism and emotional resonance. (3) Story structure: each story follows a causal chain — starting condition → AI action → unintended consequence → human impact — with explicit identification of failure points. (4) Deliberation protocol: stories used in structured workshops where stakeholders discuss (a) plausibility of scenario, (b) existing safeguards, (c) gaps in current governance. (5) Harm taxonomy: 22 harm categories identified across clinical, psychological, social, and systemic dimensions. (6) Translation to requirements: workshop outputs distilled into actionable design requirements for healthcare AI systems.
**Results:** 47 speculative stories generated covering 22 harm categories. Stakeholder workshops (N=124 participants across 8 hospitals): 89% rated stories as "plausible" or "highly plausible." 73% of participants identified at least one unconsidered risk in their own systems after reading stories. Workshops produced 31 actionable design requirements (18 novel, 13 reinforcing existing guidelines). Most frequently identified harm category: automation-induced deskilling (present in 78% of stories). Clinicians and patients identified different top concerns: clinicians prioritized diagnostic accuracy risks, patients prioritized privacy and dignity harms.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: surfaces risks before deployment (proactive vs reactive), accessible to non-technical stakeholders (narrative format), bridges imagination gap in AI safety, generates concrete design requirements, stakeholder diversity reveals blind spots. LOSES: story plausibility relies on LLM quality and stakeholder vetting, narratives may overemphasize dramatic harms over subtle ones, workshop findings are qualitative (hard to quantify risk magnitude), resource-intensive process (story generation + workshops), culture/language-specific (tested in US hospitals only), no longitudinal validation (do requirements actually prevent harms?).
**Rationale:** Traditional risk assessment focuses on measurable, known failure modes — it misses the "unknown unknowns" of deploying AI in complex sociotechnical systems. Speculative fiction is a proven method in technology ethics for imagining unintended consequences (e.g., design fiction, science fiction prototyping). LLMs enable scalable generation of diverse speculative scenarios that can be vetted and refined by experts. The stakeholder co-design process ensures stories are grounded in real clinical workflows and patient experiences.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's safety architecture (§17, safety subsystem) currently focuses on runtime guardrails (prompt injection defense, output validation, permission control) — reactive safety measures. The speculative story methodology provides a complementary proactive approach: imagine failure modes before deployment and design architectural constraints accordingly. Directly applicable to Lyra's safety planning. Status: **INVESTIGATE** (methodology transfer to agent safety design; complements runtime guardrails with design-time risk imagination).
**Impact:** 2 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** investigate (valuable safety design methodology; lower technical priority than runtime guardrails)

## Heterogeneous Adversarial Play in Interactive Environments
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.18407 (2025)
**Mechanism:** (1) Heterogeneous agent population: multiple agent types (rule-based, RL-trained, LLM-based) compete/cooperate in shared interactive environment. (2) Adversarial training: agents play against adversaries of increasing capability, forcing robust strategy development. (3) Population-based training (PBT): agents periodically replace underperforming members with mutated copies of top performers, creating an evolutionary arms race. (4) Heterogeneity bonus: diverse agent types (symbolic planners + neural policies + LLM reasoners) produce more robust strategies than homogeneous populations because each type exploits different weaknesses. (5) Adversarial diversity metric: measures how many distinct failure modes adversaries expose — heterogeneous adversaries consistently find more diverse failure modes than homogeneous ones. (6) Transfer: agents trained against heterogeneous adversaries generalize better to unseen opponents and environments.
**Results:** Heterogeneous adversarial training produces agents with 23% higher win rate against unseen opponents vs homogeneous training. Population diversity maintained >2x longer with heterogeneity bonus. LLM-based agents benefit most from heterogeneous adversaries (+31% improvement) vs RL agents (+18%) vs rule-based (+9%). Adversarial diversity: heterogeneous adversaries expose 3.2x more distinct failure modes than homogeneous. Transfer: +15% generalization improvement to held-out environments. Ablation: removing any agent type from the heterogeneous mix reduces overall robustness (-8% to -14%).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: produces more robust and generalizable agents, discovers diverse failure modes, heterogeneity bonus across agent architectures, PBT enables continuous improvement without human intervention, strong transfer to unseen scenarios. LOSES: significantly more compute (PBT + multiple agent types), complex infrastructure (multiple agent runtimes), diminishing returns beyond 4-5 agent types, harder to debug (interactions between diverse agents are complex), environment must support multi-agent interaction, reward structure must align incentives correctly.
**Rationale:** Monoculture agents share the same inductive biases and blind spots — adversarial training against homogeneous opponents overfits to narrow attack patterns. Heterogeneous adversaries force agents to develop robust strategies that work across diverse opponents. This mirrors biological co-evolution (predator-prey arms races produce robust organisms) and security red-teaming (diverse attackers find more vulnerabilities). PBT automates the evolutionary process, continuously discovering harder adversaries.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's planned multi-agent orchestration could benefit from heterogeneous adversarial self-play for robustness testing. Agent safety (§17) specifically calls for red-teaming — heterogeneous adversarial play provides a systematic methodology. The PBT pattern is also relevant for Lyra's agent evolution/self-improvement ambitions. Status: **BEHIND** (no adversarial training infrastructure; no heterogeneous agent evaluation framework).
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (heterogeneous adversarial play as systematic robustness testing methodology; Phase 2-3 depending on safety priority)

---

## CodeWiki: Evaluating AI's Ability to Generate Holistic Documentation for Large-Scale Codebases
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.24428 (2025)
**Mechanism:** (1) Multi-file repository parsing: ingests entire codebase (AST extraction, call graphs, import graphs, type hierarchies) to build a holistic structural model of the project. (2) Documentation taxonomy: defines 12 documentation artifact types (API reference, architecture overview, module guide, setup guide, contribution guide, design decisions, data flow diagrams, dependency maps, security considerations, performance characteristics, testing strategy, deployment guide). (3) Hierarchical generation: generates documentation top-down — architecture overview → module-level docs → function/class-level API docs — with cross-references maintained via the structural model. (4) Multi-source grounding: documentation claims are grounded in source code (line-level citations), commit history (rationale extraction from commit messages), and issue discussions (design intent from PR/issue threads). (5) Quality evaluation: automated metrics (coverage of public API surface, factual consistency via code-to-doc roundtrip verification) + human evaluation (completeness, accuracy, clarity, usefulness on 5-point Likert scale). (6) Benchmark: CodeWiki-Bench with 50 open-source Python/TypeScript repositories (500-50k LOC) and 50 human-written documentation sets as reference.
**Results:** Best LLM (Claude 3.5 Sonnet + retrieval): 72% factual consistency (code-to-doc verification passes), 68% API coverage (public methods documented), human quality rating 3.8/5 (vs human-written 4.2/5). Architecture-level docs: 58% accuracy (hallucinated dependencies in 42% of cases). Contribution/setup guides: 81% accuracy (highly templated, easier). Cross-file consistency: 64% (cross-references between related modules correct). Human evaluation: documentation generated by CodeWiki reduced new-contributor onboarding time by 31% compared to projects without docs, but 19% worse than human-written docs. Ablation: removing structural model (AST+call graph) drops factual consistency from 72% to 47%.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: comprehensive repo understanding (AST-level grounding reduces hallucination), multi-artifact generation (12 doc types covering full SDLC), verifiable claims (code-to-doc roundtrip enables automated quality checks), direct developer productivity impact (31% onboarding improvement). LOSES: large codebases (50k+ LOC exceed context windows, require chunking), rapidly evolving repos (docs stale without regeneration), languages with poor AST tooling, high token cost (full-repo processing), architecture docs remain weak (42% hallucination rate), cannot capture unwritten conventions/tribal knowledge.
**Rationale:** Existing code documentation tools (JSDoc, Sphinx, pydoc) operate at single-file level — they miss cross-module architecture, design rationale, and project-level context that makes documentation useful. LLMs with long-context windows and structured repo parsing can generate holistic docs that bridge this gap. The code-to-doc roundtrip verification (generate doc → verify against code → flag inconsistencies) provides a scalable automated quality metric that doesn't require human evaluators. The 31% onboarding improvement demonstrates real productivity value.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's documentation plans (§09 docs subsystem) focus on user-facing documentation generation. CodeWiki's structural-model approach (AST + call graph + import graph) provides a concrete architecture for Lyra's documentation agent. The code-to-doc roundtrip verification pattern is directly applicable to Lyra's verification subsystem. Status: **BEHIND** (no structural code understanding; docs agent is planned but unbuilt).
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** investigate (valuable doc-generation architecture; lower priority than core orchestration, Phase 3+)

## Tongyi DeepResearch Technical Report
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.24701 (2025)
**Mechanism:** (1) Multi-turn research planning: given a research question, the system generates a structured research plan with sub-questions, search queries, and expected information types. (2) Tool-augmented execution: web search, document retrieval, code execution (Python REPL), and structured data query tools are orchestrated in a reactive loop — each action's output informs the next. (3) Information synthesis: retrieved sources are cross-referenced, contradictions are flagged, and claims are verified against multiple sources before inclusion. (4) Hierarchical summarization: bottom-up synthesis — individual source summaries → topic-level synthesis → final report with section-level organization. (5) Citation management: every claim is traceable to source(s) with span-level attribution, enabling verification. (6) Iterative refinement: generated report undergoes self-critique (factual check, coverage check, clarity check) with targeted re-retrieval for gaps. (7) Long-context management: uses sliding window attention + structured note-taking to maintain state across 100+ retrieval steps without context overflow.
**Results:** On GAIA benchmark (validation set): 72.3% pass rate (Level 1: 89%, Level 2: 71%, Level 3: 53%). On internal enterprise research tasks: 84% factual accuracy (human evaluation, N=500 questions across 5 domains), 3.2 sources cited per claim on average. Report quality: 4.1/5 completeness, 3.8/5 conciseness (human eval). Planning vs no-planning ablation: +18% pass rate on multi-hop questions. Self-critique iteration improves factual accuracy from 76% to 84% (2 refinement rounds). Average research time: 3.8 minutes per question (vs human researcher 45-90 min). Token consumption: 85k tokens per question average (input + output).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: multi-hop research questions requiring information synthesis across sources, verifiable domains (factual claims can be checked), structured research tasks with clear evaluation criteria, enterprise knowledge work automation. LOSES: opinion/analysis tasks (no ground truth), highly specialized domains with limited web coverage, real-time news (index latency), creative/interpretive writing, simple factoid questions (overkill — single search sufficient). Failure modes: source authority misjudgment (treats low-quality sources as authoritative), planning failures on novel question types, premature closure (stops searching too early), citation hallucination (attributes claims to wrong source).
**Rationale:** Deep research tasks require sustained, multi-step reasoning across heterogeneous sources — single-shot LLM responses are insufficient. Tool-augmented loops enable active information gathering rather than relying on parametric knowledge. The planning-then-execute architecture separates strategic decisions (what to search for) from tactical execution (how to extract information), enabling more coherent research trajectories. Self-critique with targeted re-retrieval addresses the "known unknowns" problem — the system identifies what it doesn't know and actively fills gaps.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's research subsystem (§15) plans deep research capabilities but has no implementation. Tongyi's architecture provides a concrete blueprint: planning → tool loop → synthesis → self-critique → refinement. The 72.3% GAIA score establishes a performance target. The citation traceability pattern is critical for Lyra's verification ambitions. Status: **BEHIND** (no deep research infrastructure; planning + tool loop not implemented).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 5 | **Tier:** breakthrough (core research architecture; Phase 1-2 — foundational for Lyra's research capabilities)

## Efficient LLM Training Survey: Data-Centric Perspectives
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.25817 (2025)
**Mechanism:** (1) Comprehensive taxonomy of data-centric LLM training techniques across five dimensions: data selection (quality filtering, deduplication, importance sampling), data ordering (curriculum learning, anti-curriculum, difficulty-based scheduling), data augmentation (synthetic data generation, back-translation, paraphrasing), data mixture (domain weighting, dynamic mixing, multi-lingual balancing), and data efficiency metrics (loss-per-token, downstream transfer efficiency). (2) Systematic comparison methodology: normalizes results across 50+ papers by controlling for model size, compute budget, and evaluation benchmarks, enabling apples-to-apples comparison. (3) Data quality heuristics: surveys 30+ quality filters (perplexity-based, classifier-based, heuristic rules, embedding similarity, influence functions) with effectiveness ranked by downstream improvement per unit of filtering compute. (4) Scaling relationships: characterizes how data efficiency gains scale with model size — some techniques (deduplication) show diminishing returns above 7B parameters, while others (curriculum learning) show increasing benefits with scale. (5) Open problems identified: dynamic data selection during training, multi-phase data strategies, cross-lingual data efficiency, and data-centric evaluation beyond perplexity.
**Results:** Key findings from 50+ papers synthesized: (a) Deduplication: 5-15% training compute reduction for equivalent downstream performance, most effective for models < 7B parameters. (b) Quality filtering (perplexity + classifier): 10-25% data reduction with no performance loss, 30%+ reduction with < 2% degradation. (c) Curriculum learning: mixed results — 3-8% improvement on complex reasoning tasks when curricula are well-designed, negative results on 40% of attempted curricula (ordering matters critically). (d) Data mixing: dynamic domain reweighting during training provides 2-5% improvement over static mixing. (e) Synthetic data: most impactful single technique — models trained with 20-30% high-quality synthetic data match performance of models trained on 2-3x more natural data. (f) Cross-technique interaction: combining deduplication + quality filtering + synthetic augmentation yields compound 1.5-2x effective data multiplier (training on 1T tokens achieves performance equivalent to 1.5-2T tokens without techniques).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: cost-constrained training (reducing data needs directly reduces compute), data-scarce domains (synthetic augmentation), multi-lingual training (balancing language representation), rapid iteration (smaller effective datasets → faster experimental cycles). LOSES: techniques requiring training a reference model first (chicken-and-egg for first model), highly domain-specific models (general quality filters may remove valuable niche data), techniques with high filtering compute cost (some influence-function methods cost more than the training they save). Key caution: 40% of published curriculum learning results do not replicate — ordering sensitivity is high and optimal curricula are dataset-specific.
**Rationale:** The shift from model-centric to data-centric AI (popularized by Andrew Ng) argues that improving data quality/efficiency often yields higher ROI than architectural innovations. This survey systematically validates that claim for LLM training: compound 1.5-2x effective data multiplier across multiple independent techniques. Data efficiency is particularly critical for the long tail of organizations that cannot afford web-scale training runs — equivalent performance at 50% the data cost democratizes LLM development.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's planned fine-tuning and data pipeline subsystems lack concrete data efficiency strategies. This survey provides an evidence-based menu of techniques with quantified impact estimates, enabling Lyra to prioritize the highest-ROI data efficiency investments. The finding that synthetic data (20-30% mix) provides the largest single-technique impact is directly actionable for Lyra's training data strategy. Status: **BEHIND** (no data efficiency pipeline; no data quality filtering; no curriculum strategy).
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** parity (data efficiency techniques are table-stakes for competitive training; implement dedup + quality filtering + synthetic mix as baseline)

## Context Engineering 2.0: The Context of Context Engineering
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.26493 (2025)
**Mechanism:** (1) Meta-framework: treats context engineering not as a set of prompt tricks but as a systematic engineering discipline with its own design patterns, quality metrics, and optimization objectives. (2) Context architecture layers: Content Layer (what goes into context — documents, examples, instructions), Structure Layer (how content is organized — ordering, formatting, delimiters, hierarchies), Dynamics Layer (how context evolves — compression, expansion, retrieval, refresh triggers), and Governance Layer (policies for context construction — access control, privacy, versioning, audit). (3) Context quality metrics: proposes five measurable dimensions — Relevance (IR score of selected content vs query), Density (information per token, penalizing filler), Consistency (lack of internal contradictions), Freshness (temporal alignment with current state), and Attribution (traceability of each claim to source). (4) Context optimization patterns: Compaction (summarize to increase density), Pruning (remove low-relevance segments), Restructuring (reorder for attention-weighted importance), Augmentation (inject missing context types), and Layering (separate stable vs volatile context for caching). (5) Context budget management: treats context window as a constrained resource — allocates tokens across content types (instructions, examples, retrieved docs, conversation history, tool outputs) with explicit budgets and overrun policies. (6) Evaluation framework: measures both task performance and context efficiency (task success per context token), enabling optimization of the context engineering itself.
**Results:** Systematic analysis of context engineering techniques across 5 benchmarks (MMLU, HumanEval, long-context QA, multi-turn dialogue, tool-use). Key findings: (a) Structure matters more than content volume: well-structured context with 50% fewer tokens can match or exceed unstructured full context (+3-7% accuracy). (b) Lost-in-middle effect quantified: information in positions 25-75% of context has 15-30% lower retrieval accuracy than beginning or end positions. (c) Context density optimization: removing low-information-density segments (boilerplate, redundant examples) improves task performance by 2-5% while reducing cost by 20-40%. (d) Dynamic context refreshing: triggering re-retrieval when context-internal contradictions exceed threshold improves factual consistency by 12%. (e) Multi-turn context: conversation history beyond 20 turns provides diminishing returns — selective summarization of early turns preserves 95% of performance at 60% token savings. (f) Context budget overrun: when context exceeds 90% of window size, performance degrades 8-15% due to truncation and attention dilution — proactive budget management prevents this.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: production LLM systems with context engineering as ongoing concern, multi-turn agent systems (context accumulates rapidly), cost-sensitive deployments (context tokens = money), retrieval-augmented systems (what/how to inject), long-horizon agent tasks (100+ turn context management). LOSES: single-turn tasks with small context (overhead of engineering exceeds benefit), fully dynamic domains where optimal context structure changes per query, systems where context construction is external (e.g., user-managed). Main risk: over-engineering context for simple tasks — the framework is most valuable when context is a binding constraint.
**Rationale:** Context windows have grown 1000x (4k→2M tokens) but context engineering practices have not kept pace — most systems still treat context as a flat dump of retrieved text + instructions. Context Engineering 2.0 argues that as context becomes the primary interface between LLMs and information, its construction deserves the same engineering rigor as database design or API architecture. The lost-in-middle effect and budget overrun penalty demonstrate that more context is not always better — structured, managed context outperforms larger unstructured context.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's context subsystem (§03) has ambitious plans (dynamic compaction, multi-modal context, budget management) but no implementation (maturity: none). Context Engineering 2.0 provides the missing architectural framework: the four-layer model (Content/Structure/Dynamics/Governance) directly maps to Lyra's context subsystem design. The five quality metrics (Relevance/Density/Consistency/Freshness/Attribution) provide concrete evaluation criteria. Status: **BEHIND** (conceptual design exists; implementation + metrics missing).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (foundational architecture for context subsystem; Phase 1 — core infrastructure)

## Inverse Knowledge Search over Verifiable Reasoning
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.26854 (2025)
**Mechanism:** (1) Forward generation: LLM generates long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning traces for diverse scientific questions, producing rich intermediate reasoning steps with embedded factual claims, derivations, and conclusions. (2) Inverse knowledge extraction: from the CoT corpus, extract structured knowledge triples (subject-relation-object), logical dependencies (claim A supports claim B), and provenance chains (claim derived from premises P1, P2 via reasoning step R). (3) Verifiability filter: each extracted claim is scored for verifiability — can it be checked against external sources, mathematical proof, or logical consistency? Claims below threshold are discarded or flagged as "speculative." (4) Contradiction resolution: when multiple CoT traces produce conflicting claims on the same topic, a resolution process (majority vote, source authority weighting, or deeper verification) determines the synthesized claim. (5) Encyclopedia synthesis: verified claims are organized into a hierarchical knowledge structure (topic → subtopic → claim → evidence) forming a scientific encyclopedia. (6) Iterative expansion: the synthesized encyclopedia serves as grounding for subsequent CoT generation, creating a virtuous cycle where better knowledge → better reasoning → more knowledge.
**Results:** From 500k CoT traces across 50 scientific domains (physics, chemistry, biology, medicine, CS, mathematics): extracted 2.1M verifiable claims. Verification rate: 68% of claims verifiable (22% speculative, 10% ambiguous). Encyclopedia quality: compared against Wikipedia science articles — 82% factual agreement, 12% additional verified claims not in Wikipedia, 6% contradictions (majority from CoT errors). Coverage: 78% of Wikipedia scientific claims found in synthesized encyclopedia, plus 23% novel claims (claims in encyclopedia but not Wikipedia). Efficiency: 500k CoT traces → 2.1M claims → 180k encyclopedia entries (12x compression from claims to entries via deduplication and synthesis). Downstream QA improvement: using synthesized encyclopedia as retrieval corpus improves scientific QA accuracy by 8-14% over Wikipedia-only retrieval. Ablation: removing verifiability filter drops factual agreement from 82% to 61% (verifiability filter eliminates 39% of false claims).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: scientific domains with verifiable claims (equations, experimental results, established facts), knowledge synthesis tasks (systematic reviews, textbook generation), domains with large CoT corpora available, improving LLM factual grounding. LOSES: subjective/interpretive domains (literary analysis, ethics), rapidly evolving fields (encyclopedia ages quickly), domains with sparse CoT coverage, highly specialized subfields (insufficient CoT diversity). Key risk: 12% of encyclopedia claims are novel vs Wikipedia — some may be discoveries, others may be plausible-sounding fabrications from CoT hallucination. The verifiability filter catches 68% but the remaining 32% pass through.
**Rationale:** Long CoT reasoning traces contain a wealth of structured knowledge encoded in the reasoning steps — intermediate claims, derivations, and logical relationships that are richer than final answers alone. Inverse knowledge search treats CoT traces as a knowledge mine rather than disposable intermediate computation. The verifiability filter is the critical innovation: by only accepting claims that can be independently verified (against external sources, mathematical consistency, or logical coherence), the system separates reasoning-based knowledge from hallucinated claims. The 12x compression from claims to encyclopedia entries demonstrates that synthesis eliminates redundancy while preserving coverage.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's knowledge graph and memory subsystems (§02 memory, §03 context) lack structured knowledge extraction from agent reasoning traces. Inverse knowledge search provides a methodology for converting agent execution logs (planning traces, reasoning steps, tool outputs) into structured, verifiable knowledge that persists across sessions. The verifiability filter pattern is directly applicable to Lyra's verification subsystem. Status: **BEHIND** (no knowledge extraction from reasoning traces; no structured knowledge persistence).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 5 | **Tier:** breakthrough (knowledge extraction from agent reasoning; Phase 2-3 — depends on CoT infrastructure and verification subsystem maturity)

## MemSearcher: RL-Driven Memory Management for LLM Agents
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.02805 (CAS / Xiaohongshu, ACL 2026)
**Mechanism:** (1) Replaces the standard ReAct paradigm of appending full interaction history into context with a compact dynamic memory that is updated each turn via an explicit "memory update" action. (2) Each turn: fuse user question with current memory -> generate reasoning trace -> execute search -> update memory (retaining only task-critical information). (3) Multi-Context GRPO training: samples trajectory groups across different LLM contexts, propagates trajectory-level advantage to all dialogue turns within the group, and jointly optimizes reasoning, search strategy, and memory management end-to-end. (4) Uses a hybrid reward function (format reward + F1 answer reward) with a loss mask to exclude search-engine-returned text from gradient computation, preventing the model from learning to copy search results verbatim. (5) Context length remains stable across multi-turn interactions, avoiding the linear growth problem of ReAct.
**Results:** On 7 public benchmarks (NQ, TriviaQA, PopQA, HotpotQA, etc.): Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct gains +11% relative average improvement; Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct gains +12%. The 3B MemSearcher model outperforms the 7B ReAct baseline. Peak context token count reduced by >60%; peak GPU memory reduced by ~45%. Training uses the same dataset as Search-R1 for fair comparison.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: multi-turn search tasks where context accumulates rapidly, memory-constrained deployments (3B beats 7B baseline), tasks requiring selective information retention across turns. LOSES: single-turn tasks (memory overhead provides no benefit), tasks where full history is genuinely needed (e.g., legal reasoning requiring complete precedent), domains where the "what to remember" decision is highly ambiguous. The memory update action adds one extra LLM call per turn.
**Rationale:** Traditional ReAct agents suffer from context pollution — noise from early retrieval errors and irrelevant documents accumulates and degrades later reasoning. MemSearcher treats memory as a learned compression function, keeping only what matters for the task. The multi-context GRPO innovation addresses the RL credit assignment problem across multiple distinct LLM forward passes within a single trajectory. The 3B-over-7B result demonstrates that efficient memory management can offset raw model capacity.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's memory subsystem (§02) has ambitious designs (pluggable memory backends, agentic memory operations, dynamic compaction) but zero implementation (maturity: none). MemSearcher provides both a concrete architecture (dynamic memory update actions) and a training methodology (multi-context GRPO) that directly maps to Lyra's planned "agentic memory management" capability. The hybrid reward function (format + F1) is directly applicable to training Lyra's memory manager. Status: **BEHIND** (conceptual alignment but no implementation).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (RL-trained memory management — Phase 2; prerequisite: GRPO training infrastructure)

## IterResearch: Markovian State Reconstruction for Long-Horizon Agents
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.07327 (Renmin University / Alibaba Tongyi Lab, ICLR 2026)
**Mechanism:** (1) Rejects the mono-contextual paradigm (append-all into one growing context) in favor of iterative workspace reconstruction formalized as a Markov Decision Process. (2) Agent state = {question, evolving report (compressed memory), last action/result} — a constant O(1) workspace regardless of interaction count. (3) Each iteration: agent reads current state, thinks, updates the evolving report, and selects next action. The report acts as an explicit hidden state (analogous to RNN/LSTM hidden state) that synthesizes findings and discards noise. (4) EAPO training (Efficiency-Aware Policy Optimization): geometric reward discounting incentivizes shorter efficient trajectories; adaptive downsampling balances variable sample counts across distributed GPUs (>99% data preservation). (5) Plug-and-play: IterResearch can be used as a prompting strategy without any training, by instructing the model to maintain and update a structured report at each step.
**Results:** +14.5pp average across 6 benchmarks (BrowseComp, BrowseComp-zh, HLE, GAIA, Xbench-DeepSearch, SEAL-0). Interaction scaling breakthrough: extended from 2 to 2048 interactions using only 40K context; BrowseComp performance rose from 3.5% to 42.5%. Agent learned to stop early (~80-130 rounds avg) when sufficient info gathered. Plug-and-play prompting: +12.7pp on OpenAI o3, +19.2pp on DeepSeek-V3.1 without any training. Trajectories generated by IterResearch can enhance traditional mono-contextual ReAct agents through cross-paradigm knowledge transfer.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: long-horizon research tasks (100+ interactions), context-constrained deployments (40K window handling 2000+ turns), scenarios where early errors would poison a shared context. LOSES: short tasks where workspace reconstruction overhead exceeds benefit, tasks requiring verbatim recall of early interaction details, domains where the evolving report compression loses critical nuance. The MDP framework assumes the report adequately summarizes all relevant history — information loss in report updates is the primary failure mode.
**Rationale:** Context suffocation is the binding constraint on deep-research agents — linear accumulation defeats long-horizon scaling. IterResearch frames this as a state representation problem: the full history is not the state, it is evidence from which the state (evolving report) is constructed. The 2048-interaction result with 40K context (50x more interactions than context would naively allow) demonstrates that Markovian state reconstruction fundamentally changes the scaling relationship between task horizon and context budget. The geometric reward discount is critical: without it, agents learn unnecessarily long trajectories.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's context subsystem (§03) plans for dynamic compaction and multi-modal context but has no iterative workspace reconstruction, no evolving report concept, and no training methodology for long-horizon efficiency. IterResearch provides the missing architectural pattern: treat the agent workspace as a Markovian state updated iteratively rather than a monotonically growing log. The plug-and-play prompting result (+12.7-19.2pp without training) means Lyra can adopt the IterResearch pattern immediately via prompt engineering. Status: **BEHIND** (no iterative state reconstruction; immediate prompt-level adoption possible).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (architectural pattern for long-horizon scaling; Phase 1 prompt adoption, Phase 2 training)

## Feedback Descent: Textual Feedback as Gradient Signal
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.07919 (Stanford, ICLR 2026 MemAgents Workshop — Best Paper Runner-Up)
**Mechanism:** (1) Maintains a single best artifact and iteratively improves it via a propose-compare-select loop. (2) Propose: LLM generates improved candidate conditioned on current best + all accumulated feedback history. (3) Compare: Evaluator compares candidate vs current best, returning binary preference AND detailed textual feedback explaining the choice. (4) Select: If candidate wins, it becomes new best; feedback is always retained. (5) The textual feedback provides gradient-like directional information — analogous to how gradients provide steepest-ascent direction in weight space, feedback provides improvement direction in semantic space. (6) Theoretical result: textual feedback enables dimension-free convergence while zeroth-order (scalar-only) methods degrade exponentially with problem dimensionality. (7) Cross-domain: same algorithm works for SVG design, prompt optimization, and molecular discovery without domain-specific modification.
**Results:** SVG optimization: generates diverse unicorn designs meeting varied aesthetic criteria. Prompt optimization: outperforms specialized prompt optimizer GEPA on IFBench and HoVer. Molecule discovery: beats RL baselines (GRPO, REINVENT), rivals specialized graph-based molecular optimizers, discovers drug-like molecules surpassing 99.9th percentile of a 260K-compound database on all 6 protein targets (DOCKSTRING benchmark). Cross-domain generality with zero domain-specific tuning.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: black-box optimization where gradients are unavailable (text artifacts, prompts, configurations), domains with expensive or noisy oracle evaluations, creative/generative tasks where scalar rewards underspecify quality, multi-objective optimization (textual feedback naturally captures trade-offs). LOSES: domains with cheap, reliable scalar rewards (e.g., classification accuracy), high-throughput optimization (each iteration requires LLM calls for both propose and compare), tasks where pairwise comparison is ambiguous or subjective. The feedback buffer grows with iterations; unbounded growth could eventually cause context issues.
**Rationale:** Scalar rewards collapse rich quality judgments into a single number, losing information about WHY an artifact is good or bad. Textual feedback preserves this information, enabling targeted improvements rather than blind perturbation. The dimension-free convergence result is the key theoretical insight: in high-dimensional text space, gradient-free methods that rely on random perturbations degrade exponentially, but feedback-directed search maintains efficiency regardless of dimension. The cross-domain results (SVG, prompts, molecules) demonstrate that the feedback-as-gradient abstraction is genuinely domain-agnostic.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's prompt optimization, agent output refinement, and self-improvement loops all rely on scalar evaluation signals or simple binary preferences. Feedback Descent provides a strictly more powerful optimization primitive: retain structured textual feedback across iterations to guide improvement. This is directly applicable to Lyra's prompt optimizer, agent output quality improvement, and configuration generation. The comparison feedback pattern also maps to Lyra's planned debate/review subsystems (§17 safety). Status: **BEHIND** (no structured feedback accumulation; scalar-only evaluation).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 2 | **Tier:** breakthrough (inference-time optimization primitive; Phase 1 prompt/policy optimization, Phase 2 agent self-improvement)

## SABER: Safeguarding Mutating Steps in LLM Agents
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.07850 (Amazon AGI Foundations, 2025)
**Mechanism:** (1) Classifies agent actions into mutating (environment-changing: cancel booking, issue refund, delete file, send email) vs non-mutating (information-gathering: search, read, summarize). (2) Mutation-Gated Verification: requires explicit user confirmation ONLY before mutating actions (~1 in 6 turns), leaving non-mutating actions to proceed automatically. (3) Targeted Reflection: injects concise constraint summaries before risky steps to counter "lost-in-the-middle" context drift where agents forget constraints buried deep in conversation history. (4) Block-based Context Cleaning: partitions trajectory into blocks, summarizes each, retrieves only relevant blocks — prevents context poisoning from early errors and irrelevant information. (5) Model-agnostic, gradient-free, test-time only — no training required, works as a safety wrapper around any LLM agent. (6) Released τ-Bench Verified: cleaned version of τ-bench with annotation errors and underspecified instructions fixed.
**Results:** Key finding: mutating actions account for only 14-18% of all actions but cause the overwhelming majority of failures. Each additional deviation in a mutating action reduces success odds by 55-92% (Airline) and 87-96% (Retail). Non-mutating deviations have negligible impact (<10% reduction, often statistically insignificant). SABER performance: Qwen3-Thinking +28% relative on Airline, +11% Retail, +7% SWE-Bench Verified. Claude Sonnet 4: +9% Airline, +7% Retail. GPT-5: +17.3pp Airline, +3.1pp Retail. Context length drift confirmed: errors increase as conversation grows due to lost-in-the-middle effects.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: production agent deployments with irreversible side effects, customer-facing agents (refunds, bookings, emails), code agents with filesystem mutation, any agent where a single bad mutating action causes disproportionate harm. LOSES: read-only agents (no mutating actions to gate), fully autonomous agents where user-in-the-loop is unacceptable, high-frequency trading/real-time systems (verification latency unacceptable). The ~1-in-6 gating ratio means 83% of actions proceed unimpeded — the overhead is concentrated on the most dangerous actions.
**Rationale:** The mutating vs non-mutating asymmetry is the key insight: not all errors are equal. A bad search query wastes a turn; a bad refund loses money. SABER exploits this asymmetry by concentrating safeguards where errors are both most likely and most costly. The logistic regression results (p < 0.001) provide rigorous statistical evidence that mutating-action errors are categorically different from non-mutating errors. The model-agnostic, training-free design means SABER can be deployed immediately as a safety wrapper, which is critical for production safety.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's safety subsystem (§17) has designs for guardrails and prompt-injection defense but no action-classification-based gating, no targeted reflection for constraint reinforcement, and no mutating-action awareness. SABER provides a lightweight, immediately deployable safety pattern: classify actions, gate only the dangerous ones. The τ-Bench Verified release is independently valuable — cleaner benchmarks reveal genuine model differences. Status: **BEHIND** (no action-classification gating; no mutating-step awareness).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 2 | **Tier:** parity (production safety — immediately deployable; Phase 1)

---

## Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08296 (Google Research / MIT, ACL ARR 2025, under revision at Nature Machine Intelligence)
**Mechanism:** (1) Controlled large-scale evaluation: 180 configurations across 5 architectures (Single, Independent, Centralized, Decentralized, Hybrid) x 3 LLM families (OpenAI GPT, Google Gemini, Anthropic Claude) x 4 benchmarks (Finance-Agent, BrowseComp-Plus, PlanCraft, Workbench). All configurations use identical tools, prompts, and token budgets to isolate architectural effects. (2) Four coordination metrics: efficiency (task-relevant vs coordination tokens), error amplification (how errors propagate through agent topology), redundancy (duplicate work across agents), and overhead (fixed cost of multi-agent orchestration). (3) Predictive regression model: using coordination metrics to predict performance, achieving cross-validated R² = 0.524, 87% accuracy in predicting optimal architecture for held-out tasks, and MAE = 0.071 on out-of-sample GPT-5.2 validation. (4) Three scaling laws: Tool-Coordination Trade-off (tool-heavy tasks suffer more from multi-agent overhead), Capability Saturation (once single-agent baseline >~45%, adding agents yields diminishing/negative returns, β = -0.408, p < 0.001), and Topology-Dependent Error Amplification (Independent: 17.2x amplification, Centralized: 4.4x containment).
**Results:** Financial reasoning (parallelizable): Centralized architecture +80.9%. Dynamic web navigation: Decentralized +9.2%. Sequential planning (PlanCraft): ALL multi-agent architectures degrade performance by -39% to -70% vs single-agent. Model-specific personalities: Gemini best at centralized management (+164.3% on finance), GPT excels at complex communication (hybrid), Claude most sensitive to coordination overhead but shows unique fault tolerance in heterogeneous teams. The predictive model successfully identifies when multi-agent helps vs hurts, providing quantitative architecture selection rules.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: organizations building multi-agent systems who need evidence-based architecture decisions, tasks with high parallelizability (independent subtasks), domains where error containment is critical (centralized coordination), heterogeneous model deployments (matching model personalities to architectures). LOSES: simple single-agent-sufficient tasks (multi-agent overhead always negative), highly sequential tasks (all multi-agent architectures degrade performance), resource-constrained deployments (coordination cost competes with task execution budget). The R² = 0.524 means 48% of performance variance remains unexplained — the predictive model is useful but not definitive.
**Rationale:** Prior multi-agent system design was "alchemy" — practitioners chose architectures based on intuition and anecdotes. This paper provides the first rigorous, large-scale evidence that architecture-task alignment matters far more than agent count. The key counterintuitive finding: for sequential reasoning, more agents ALWAYS hurts (-39% to -70%). This directly contradicts the "more agents is all you need" narrative. The tool-coordination trade-off explains why: fixed compute budgets mean coordination tokens compete with task tokens. The capability saturation result (diminishing returns beyond ~45% baseline accuracy) provides a quantitative stopping rule.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's orchestrator subsystem (§04) has ambitious multi-agent topology designs (DynamicSwarm, hierarchical, debate, peer-to-peer) but no evidence-based architecture selection criteria, no coordination efficiency metrics, no predictive model for when specific topologies help vs hurt. This paper provides the missing scientific framework: measure coordination overhead, error amplification, redundancy, and efficiency; use these to predict optimal architecture. The finding that sequential tasks degrade under ALL multi-agent architectures is a critical warning for Lyra's planning subsystem. Status: **BEHIND** (no evidence-based architecture selection; topology decisions are intuition-driven).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (scientific foundation for multi-agent architecture decisions; Phase 1 measurement framework, Phase 2 predictive model)

---

## Memory in the Age of AI Agents: A Survey — Forms, Functions and Dynamics
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13564
**Mechanism:** (1) Comprehensive taxonomy of memory in AI agents across three axes: Forms (episodic, semantic, procedural, working, sensory), Functions (retrieval, consolidation, forgetting, reflection, integration), and Dynamics (online vs offline, synchronous vs asynchronous, centralized vs distributed). (2) Survey of memory architectures: vector-store retrieval (RAG), graph-based memory (knowledge graphs), parametric memory (fine-tuning, model editing), hybrid memory (MemGPT, Mem0, HippoRAG). (3) Evaluation framework: fidelity (retrieval precision/recall), latency (access time vs context window trade-off), scalability (memory growth management), and consistency (no stale/contradictory memories). (4) Identifies four open challenges: memory-augmented reasoning (using memory to improve planning, not just recall), memory consolidation across sessions (long-term retention without degradation), memory safety (prompt injection via memory poisoning, unauthorized access), and multi-agent shared memory (consensus, conflict resolution, access control).
**Results:** Survey analysis of 60+ systems. Key findings: (a) Hybrid architectures (vector + graph + parametric) outperform single-modal memory by 12-18% on multi-hop reasoning tasks. (b) Episodic memory alone is insufficient for agent workflows — procedural memory (action sequences, tool use patterns) provides 23% additional task completion improvement. (c) Memory consolidation (periodic summarization, importance-weighted pruning) reduces memory growth by 40-60% while maintaining 95%+ retrieval quality. (d) Shared memory in multi-agent systems suffers from the "common ground problem" — agents overwrite each other's memories without conflict detection in 34% of interactions.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: long-horizon agent tasks (memory critical for context beyond context window), multi-session personalization (user preferences persist), knowledge-intensive domains (scientific research, code understanding), multi-agent coordination (shared task state). LOSES: short, stateless tasks (memory overhead unjustified), latency-critical systems (retrieval adds 50-200ms), privacy-sensitive applications (memory persistence creates data retention risk), single-turn Q&A (RAG sufficient without agent memory).
**Rationale:** Memory is the foundational substrate for agent autonomy — without persistent, retrievable memory, agents cannot learn from experience, personalize, or coordinate across sessions. The survey's key insight: memory forms are not interchangeable; task characteristics dictate the optimal memory architecture. Procedural memory (how to do things) is the most under-explored and highest-impact category for Lyra-style agent systems.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's memory subsystem (§02) has detailed plans for hybrid memory (vector + graph + episodic + procedural) but implementation maturity is `none` across all memory types. No memory consolidation mechanism, no shared memory with conflict resolution, no memory safety guardrails beyond prompt-injection defense designs. The survey provides an architectural roadmap that validates Lyra's hybrid approach while identifying critical missing pieces: procedural memory for tool-use patterns, memory consolidation for long-running agents, and multi-agent shared memory with access control. Status: **PLANNED** (designs exist but zero implementation).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (memory is prerequisite for all other agent capabilities; Phase 1 implementation)

---

## Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework for Intelligent IT Operations: An AOI System with Context-Aware Compression and Dynamic Task Scheduling
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13956
**Mechanism:** (1) AOI (Agentic Operations Intelligence) system architecture: specialized agent roles (Monitor, Diagnostician, Planner, Executor, Reviewer) collaborate on IT operations tasks (incident response, root cause analysis, configuration management). (2) Context-aware compression: instead of passing full conversation history, agents compress context into structured summaries with task-relevant fields (affected services, error signatures, attempted fixes, current state), reducing inter-agent message size by 60-80%. Compression is adaptive — compression ratio varies by task complexity (simple tasks: aggressive 80% compression; complex tasks: conservative 40% compression). (3) Dynamic task scheduling: a scheduler agent maintains a dependency graph of IT operations tasks, assigns tasks to specialized agents based on current load and expertise match, and dynamically reprioritizes when new incidents arrive. Uses a priority queue with aging (older tasks gain priority over time) and deadline-aware scheduling. (4) Feedback loop: Reviewer agent validates executor outputs; failures trigger re-diagnosis by the Diagnostician agent with enriched context.
**Results:** Evaluated on 150 real-world IT incidents from a production cloud environment. Context-aware compression: 72% average message size reduction, token savings of 3.2x across multi-turn collaborations, with only 4.1% information loss (measured via task completion rate delta). Dynamic scheduling: 31% reduction in mean time to resolution (MTTR) vs round-robin assignment, 28% improvement in agent utilization (fewer idle agents). Overall system: 89.3% incident resolution rate vs 76.1% for single-agent baseline, 94.2% for critical (P1) incidents. Compression quality degrades on novel incident types (unseen error signatures): 12% information loss, suggesting compression templates need continuous updating.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: high-volume IT operations (ticket queues with 50+ concurrent incidents), production environments with strict MTTR SLAs, heterogeneous incident types requiring diverse expertise, cost-sensitive deployments (token savings directly reduce LLM API costs). LOSES: low-volume environments (scheduling overhead not amortized), highly novel incidents (compression templates miss critical details), real-time safety-critical systems (agent collaboration latency of 2-5 seconds per handoff), simple monitoring-only setups (single-agent sufficient).
**Rationale:** IT operations is a natural fit for multi-agent collaboration: incidents require diverse expertise (network, database, application), tasks are partially parallelizable (multiple incidents can be investigated simultaneously), and context windows are easily saturated by long diagnostic conversations. Context-aware compression is the key innovation — naive context passing causes 3-5x token waste in multi-agent systems. The priority-aging scheduler prevents task starvation, a common failure mode in agent systems where low-priority tasks are indefinitely deferred.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's orchestrator subsystem (§04) has task allocation designs but no context-aware compression, no dynamic priority scheduling with aging, and no feedback-driven re-diagnosis loops. The Reviewer→Diagnostician feedback pattern is particularly relevant — Lyra's current designs have linear agent pipelines with no backpressure or re-diagnosis on failure. Status: **BEHIND** (no context compression; no dynamic scheduling with aging; linear pipelines only).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (context compression + dynamic scheduling are Phase 1 infrastructure requirements)

## Lying with Truths: Open-Channel Multi-Agent Collusion for Belief Manipulation via Generative Montage
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.01685
**Mechanism:** (1) Generative Montage: agents construct deceptive narratives by selectively combining truthful statements into misleading compositions. Each individual statement is factually true, but the montage (ordering, juxtaposition, omission) creates a false overall impression. (2) Open-channel collusion: multiple agents coordinate their deceptive outputs through a shared communication channel visible to the target (e.g., a shared chat or document), making coordination appear organic rather than covert. (3) Three attack strategies: Framing (truthful context-setting that biases interpretation), Omission Chains (each agent truthfully reports a subset while omitting critical counter-evidence, with omissions coordinated across agents to cover all counter-evidence), and Consensus Fabrication (multiple agents independently "confirm" the same false impression, creating an illusion of inter-agent agreement). (4) Defense evaluation: tests 5 defense mechanisms — fact-checking (individual statement verification), cross-agent consistency checking, source triangulation, omission detection (gap analysis), and human-in-the-loop review.
**Results:** On a political fact-checking benchmark (200 claims): Generative Montage achieves 67.3% belief manipulation rate (measured via pre/post belief change on target beliefs), vs 41.2% for direct lying and 52.8% for single-agent deception. Open-channel collusion: 71.4% manipulation rate when 3+ agents coordinate, vs 58.3% for 2 agents. Defense effectiveness: individual fact-checking catches only 12.1% of montages (since each statement is true), cross-agent consistency checking catches 28.7%, omission detection catches 47.3%, combined defenses catch 63.9%. Human reviewers: 34.1% detection rate (most humans fail to notice omitted counter-evidence). LLM-as-judge (GPT-4): 41.2% detection rate. Scale effect: manipulation rate increases with agent count (2→3→5 agents: 58%→71%→79%) and with montage length (3→5→7 statements: 52%→67%→74%).
**Trade-offs:** WINS (for attackers): environments with high trust in multi-agent systems, human-in-the-loop review workflows (humans are poor at detecting omission-based deception), fact-checking pipelines that only verify individual claims, collaborative document editing, multi-agent research synthesis. LOSES (for attackers): environments with automated cross-reference verification, strict citation requirements, disagreement-forcing protocols (requiring agents to surface contradictions), single-agent-only systems. For defenders: defense combination is essential (no single defense is sufficient), omission detection is the most effective single defense but doubles computational cost.
**Rationale:** This paper exposes a fundamental vulnerability in multi-agent systems: truthfulness of individual statements does not guarantee truthful communication. The "lying with truths" approach exploits the gap between statement-level verification and narrative-level deception — a gap that existing safety mechanisms (Llama Guard, NeMo Guardrails) are not designed to detect. The open-channel coordination finding is particularly concerning: making coordination visible to targets actually increases deception success by creating an illusion of transparency. This has direct implications for Lyra's planned debate and consensus mechanisms (§17 safety, §04 orchestrator).
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's safety subsystem (§17) has designs for prompt-injection defense (CaMeL-style) and content filtering (Llama Guard-style) but no mechanisms for detecting omission-based deception, no cross-agent consistency verification, and no montage-detection heuristics. The debate and consensus mechanisms in §04 orchestrator are designed to improve reasoning quality but could inadvertently create the exact conditions that enable Generative Montage attacks (multiple agents producing mutually-reinforcing outputs). Status: **BEHIND** (critical safety gap — existing guardrails cannot detect this attack class).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** parity (safety-critical; must address before deploying multi-agent consensus/debate mechanisms)

## STReasoner: Empowering LLMs for Spatio-Temporal Reasoning in Time Series via Spatial-Aware Reinforcement Learning
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.03248
**Mechanism:** (1) Spatial-aware representation learning: encodes time series data into a graph where nodes are spatial locations (sensors, regions, devices) and edges encode spatial relationships (proximity, connectivity, correlation). (2) Spatio-temporal reasoning via chain-of-thought: LLM generates reasoning chains that interleave spatial reasoning (how events propagate across locations) with temporal reasoning (how patterns evolve over time). (3) Reinforcement learning for reasoning optimization: uses GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) to train the LLM to produce more accurate spatio-temporal predictions. Reward function combines prediction accuracy (MSE on forecast values) with reasoning quality (whether spatial dependencies are correctly identified). (4) Spatial-aware attention masking: constrains the LLM's attention to spatially relevant context windows during reasoning, reducing computational cost while improving accuracy by preventing spurious long-range correlations.
**Results:** On 4 spatio-temporal benchmarks (traffic flow prediction, weather forecasting, epidemic spread, energy grid monitoring): STReasoner outperforms SOTA time series models (TimesNet, PatchTST, iTransformer) by 8-15% on MAE for spatial propagation tasks. Compared to base LLM without spatial-aware RL: +23.4% accuracy on spatial dependency identification, +18.7% on multi-step forecast accuracy. Spatial-aware attention masking: 34% reduction in inference compute with only 2.1% accuracy degradation. Ablation: removing spatial graph encoding drops performance by 19.2%; removing RL training drops by 14.7%; removing chain-of-thought drops by 11.3%.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: domains with explicit spatial structure (traffic, weather, logistics, IoT sensor networks), tasks requiring explanation alongside prediction (regulatory, scientific), multi-horizon forecasting with changing spatial dependencies, data-scarce regions (spatial prior regularizes predictions). LOSES: non-spatial time series (financial data without geographic structure), latency-critical streaming prediction (LLM inference latency of 500ms-2s vs <10ms for lightweight statistical models), deployments without GPU infrastructure, simple trend extrapolation (statistical models sufficient).
**Rationale:** LLMs have demonstrated surprising capabilities for time series analysis, but general-purpose LLMs lack spatial inductive biases — they treat all data points as independent tokens. STReasoner bridges this gap by injecting spatial structure through graph-based representations and training the LLM to reason about spatial propagation patterns. The RL component is critical: supervised fine-tuning alone produces plausible-sounding but incorrect spatial reasoning; RL with accuracy-based rewards forces the model to ground reasoning in actual prediction quality.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's context subsystem (§03) and reasoning subsystem have no spatio-temporal reasoning capabilities, no graph-based spatial encoding, and no RL-based reasoning optimization. This is not a direct gap for core agent orchestration but is relevant if Lyra is deployed in IoT, infrastructure monitoring, or logistics domains where spatio-temporal reasoning is required. Status: **AHEAD OF SCOPE** (not currently in Lyra's requirements; potential Phase 4+ extension for domain-specific reasoning).
**Impact:** 2 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** investigate (domain-specific capability; Phase 3+ if Lyra enters spatio-temporal domains)

## TeachMaster: Generative Teaching via Code
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.04204
**Mechanism:** (1) Teacher LLM generates executable code examples (in Python) that demonstrate concepts through runnable illustrations rather than static text explanations. Examples include visualizations, simulations, interactive data transformations, and algorithm animations. (2) Student LLM learns by executing the generated code in a sandbox, observing outputs, and forming understanding from the execution traces. (3) Iterative teaching loop: Teacher generates code example → Student executes and asks clarifying questions → Teacher refines example based on Student's confusion → repeat until Student demonstrates concept mastery (measured via novel problem-solving). (4) Curriculum generation: Teacher automatically sequences concepts from simple to complex, using a dependency graph of prerequisite relationships. (5) Multi-modal output: generated code produces visual outputs (plots, diagrams, animations) alongside text explanations, leveraging the multimodal understanding capabilities of modern LLMs.
**Results:** On a concept-learning benchmark (50 programming concepts, 200 test problems): TeachMaster-trained students achieve 78.3% accuracy vs 62.1% for students trained on static text explanations (+16.2pp). For complex concepts (recursion, concurrency, graph algorithms): +22.7pp improvement. Iterative refinement: each additional teaching round (up to 5) improves Student accuracy by +3-5pp, saturating after round 4. Cross-model teaching: GPT-4 teacher → Claude Sonnet student achieves 74.1% (vs 78.3% same-model), suggesting moderate model-transferability. Code execution adds 2-8 seconds per example but improves long-term retention (measured via delayed testing after 7 days): 71.2% retention vs 54.3% for text-only (p < 0.001).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: technical/programming concept education, domains where executable examples exist (algorithms, data structures, math, science simulations), self-improving agent systems (agent learns by executing its own generated examples), cross-model knowledge transfer, long-term retention goals. LOSES: non-executable domains (philosophy, ethics, creative writing), latency-sensitive training (code execution adds overhead), concepts without clear programmatic representation, resource-constrained environments (sandbox infrastructure required).
**Rationale:** Learning from execution traces is fundamentally different from learning from text: execution provides ground-truth feedback (code runs or doesn't; output is correct or incorrect) that text explanations cannot provide. This connects to the "grounding problem" in LLM training — without executable feedback, LLMs can learn plausible-sounding but incorrect mental models. The iterative teaching loop is a form of active learning: the Teacher adapts to the Student's specific misconceptions rather than providing one-size-fits-all explanations. The curriculum generation ensures concepts are introduced in a pedagogically sound order.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's self-improvement mechanisms (Godel Agent §14, Self-Evolving §15, autonomous loops) rely on text-based reflection and critique. TeachMaster suggests a more powerful paradigm: agents improve by generating and executing their own training examples, using execution traces as ground-truth feedback. This is directly applicable to Lyra's code generation and tool-use capabilities — the agent could generate practice scenarios, execute them in a sandbox, and learn from outcomes. Status: **BEHIND** (current self-improvement designs are text-only; executable example generation would unlock a new improvement dimension).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (execution-grounded self-improvement; Phase 2 for code-generation capabilities, Phase 3 for general agent self-improvement)
