## SILO-BENCH: Evaluating Distributed Coordination in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.01045
**Mechanism:** (1) SILO-BENCH tests whether LLM-based multi-agent systems can compute with distributed information — 30 algorithmic tasks across three communication complexity levels, with 54 configurations per task (1,620 total experiments). (2) Role-agnostic design: agents receive no predefined roles; information is deliberately distributed across agents, requiring them to discover what they know, determine what to share, and reconstruct global state. (3) Three communication-complexity tiers systematically vary how much inter-agent communication is required, isolating coordination capability from raw reasoning ability. (4) The benchmark measures two distinct phases: communication (do agents correctly share information?) and reasoning-integration (do agents synthesize distributed state into correct answers?). (5) Agent scaling experiments test whether adding more agents (and thus more distributed state) improves or degrades performance.
**Results:** Core finding — the "Communication-Reasoning Gap": agents spontaneously form task-appropriate coordination topologies and accurately share information, but systematically fail to synthesize distributed state into correct answers. The failure concentrates in the reasoning-integration stage — agents possess sufficient information yet cannot integrate it. Scaling failure: coordination overhead grows with agent count, eventually eliminating parallelization gains entirely. Simply adding more agents cannot bypass context-window constraints. Venue: ACL 2026 Main Conference; code at github.com/jwyjohn/acl26-silo-bench.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: rigorous multi-agent coordination evaluation, isolates communication from reasoning skill, scalable experimental design (1,620 experiments), role-agnostic avoids biasing with human-designed agent roles. LOSES: algorithmic tasks may not generalize to open-ended real-world coordination, no exploration of mitigation strategies (diagnostic benchmark, not solution paper), limited to information-theoretic coordination (not negotiation, competition, or trust).
**Rationale:** The Communication-Reasoning Gap reveals a fundamental architectural limitation: LLM agents can communicate effectively (sharing information is relatively easy) but cannot integrate distributed information (synthesizing multiple partial views into a coherent answer is hard). This mirrors human cognitive limitations — team members can all share their observations but still fail to reach the right collective conclusion. The scaling failure (more agents does not equal better performance) challenges the assumption that multi-agent systems scale linearly with agent count and suggests that better integration mechanisms are needed.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's multi-agent orchestration (§18) and debate mechanisms (§06) assume that more agents with more perspectives lead to better outcomes. SILO-BENCH's findings suggest this assumption is flawed without explicit reasoning-integration mechanisms. Lyra needs dedicated components for synthesizing distributed agent outputs — not just collecting them. Status: **BEHIND** (no reasoning-integration mechanism; current design assumes communication implies coordination).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (critical architectural insight for multi-agent design; Phase 1 integration with §06 debate and §18 orchestration)

---

## SkillNet: Create, Evaluate, and Connect AI Skills
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.04448
**Mechanism:** (1) SkillNet provides open infrastructure for creating, evaluating, and organizing AI skills at scale — a unified ontology structures skills from heterogeneous sources (human-crafted, LLM-generated, tool-derived) into a searchable, composable knowledge base. (2) Skills are treated as evolving, composable assets with rich relational connections: prerequisite chains (skill A requires skill B), composition links (skill C combines skills D+E), and alternative paths (skill F can substitute for skill G). (3) Five-dimensional evaluation: Safety (does the skill avoid harmful actions?), Completeness (does it handle edge cases?), Executability (can it be parsed and run?), Maintainability (can it be debugged and updated?), and Cost-awareness (how many tokens/compute does it consume?). (4) The repository exceeds 200,000 skills, accessible via an interactive platform and Python toolkit. (5) Skills can be created from multiple sources: manual authoring, LLM generation from task descriptions, extraction from agent execution traces, and automated composition of existing skills.
**Results:** Average reward improvement of 40% across multiple backbone models on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld benchmarks. Execution steps reduced by 30% — agents with SkillNet skills complete tasks more efficiently (fewer wasted actions). The 200K+ skill repository provides broad coverage across task domains. The five-dimensional evaluation framework provides principled skill quality assessment beyond simple success/failure metrics.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: systematic skill accumulation (no reinventing solutions), cross-model skill transfer (skills work across backbone models), quality-gated skill admission (five-dimension evaluation prevents low-quality skills from entering repository), efficiency gains through skill reuse (30% fewer steps). LOSES: ontology maintenance overhead (200K+ skills require continuous curation), skill staleness (skills may become outdated as APIs/tools change), cold-start problem (new task domains have no skills initially), potential for skill conflicts (composed skills may have incompatible assumptions), platform dependency (skills tied to SkillNet infrastructure).
**Rationale:** The core insight is that AI agents currently "reinvent the wheel" — each agent session independently discovers how to accomplish tasks, wasting computation and producing inconsistent results. SkillNet transforms transient agent experiences into durable, transferable assets. The five evaluation dimensions address the key failure modes of skill reuse: unsafe skills, incomplete skills, unparseable skills, unmaintainable skills, and cost-inefficient skills. The relational ontology (prerequisites, composition, alternatives) enables agents to reason about skill selection rather than just retrieving the highest-scoring match.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no skill repository, no systematic skill accumulation, and no cross-session skill transfer. The planned plugin subsystem (§07) could incorporate SkillNet-style skill management. The five-dimensional evaluation framework is directly applicable to Lyra's quality gate (§4.19). Status: **BEHIND** (no skill infrastructure; every agent session starts from scratch).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (skill accumulation infrastructure; Phase 2 integration with §07 plugins and §4.19 quality gate)

---

## Adaptive Memory Admission Control for LLM Agents (A-MAC)
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.04549
**Mechanism:** (1) A-MAC treats memory admission as a structured decision problem rather than an opaque LLM-driven policy — decomposing memory value into five interpretable factors: future utility, factual confidence, semantic novelty, temporal recency, and content type prior. (2) Lightweight rule-based feature extraction handles four of five factors (factual confidence via entailment checking, semantic novelty via embedding cosine distance, temporal recency via timestamp decay, content type prior via type-classifier scores), while one LLM-assisted utility assessment estimates future usefulness. (3) The 4+1 architecture (4 rule-based + 1 LLM-assisted) minimizes LLM calls while maintaining admission quality — only the hardest sub-problem (future utility prediction) uses an LLM. (4) Domain-adaptive policies are learned via cross-validated optimization, adjusting admission thresholds per domain without manual tuning. (5) The admission decision is binary (admit or reject) with calibrated confidence, enabling downstream components to handle borderline cases.
**Results:** Evaluated on LoCoMo dataset: F1 score of 0.583, described as superior precision-recall tradeoff. 31% latency reduction compared to state-of-the-art LLM-native memory systems (fully LLM-driven admission). Ablation reveals content type prior as the most influential factor for reliable memory admission. Cross-validated optimization successfully adapts policies across domains without hand-tuning.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: structured, interpretable admission decisions (five factors are human-auditable), efficient (only one LLM call per admission), domain-adaptive (no manual threshold tuning), prevents memory bloat from hallucinated/obsolete facts, content type prior provides strong signal. LOSES: the 4 rule-based features require engineering per domain, future utility estimation remains challenging (LLM may be wrong), F1 of 0.583 leaves room for improvement, content type prior may not transfer to domains with different content distributions, still requires one LLM call per admission (not purely rule-based).
**Rationale:** Current memory systems for LLM agents either accumulate everything (bloating memory with hallucinated and obsolete facts) or use fully LLM-driven policies (slow, expensive, opaque). A-MAC's hybrid approach (rule-based for easy factors, LLM for hard factors) captures the Pareto frontier of efficiency vs quality. The five-factor decomposition makes memory admission auditable and debuggable — if memory quality degrades, each factor can be independently inspected and tuned. The finding that content type prior is most influential suggests that domain-specific content expectations (e.g., coding agents care about code snippets, not weather reports) are underutilized in current memory systems.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's memory subsystem (§02) plans for memory storage and retrieval but lacks a principled admission control mechanism. Without admission control, Lyra's agents will accumulate memory bloat — hallucinated facts, obsolete context, and irrelevant details. A-MAC's five-factor decomposition provides a directly implementable admission framework. Status: **BEHIND** (no memory admission control; memory plans assume all stored information is valuable).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 2 | **Tier:** parity (mandatory memory hygiene; Phase 1 integration with §02 memory subsystem)

---

## HACHIMI: Scalable and Controllable Student Persona Generation via Orchestrated Agents
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.04855
**Mechanism:** (1) Formalizes person generation as Theory-Aligned and Distribution-Controllable Persona Generation (TAD-PG). (2) Multi-agent Propose-Validate-Revise pipeline: a proposer agent generates candidate personas, a neuro-symbolic validator agent checks developmental and psychological constraints (grade-appropriate vocabulary, age-typical reasoning patterns), a reviser agent fixes rejected personas. (3) Each persona is factorized into a theory-anchored educational schema — structured dimensions aligned with developmental psychology (Piaget stages, Vygotsky ZPD zones) rather than arbitrary attributes. (4) Stratified sampling across demographic/developmental dimensions ensures quota coverage; semantic deduplication via embedding cosine similarity prevents mode collapse (generating minor variations of the same persona). (5) All generation performed with Qwen2.5-72B, producing the HACHIMI-1M corpus of 1 million personas spanning Grades 1–12.
**Results:** Intrinsic evaluation: near-perfect schema validity (validator acceptance rate approaching 100%), accurate demographic quotas across all stratified dimensions, substantial diversity confirmed by embedding dispersion metrics. Extrinsic evaluation: personas instantiated as student agents answering CEPS and PISA 2022 surveys across 16 cohorts. Alignment gradient discovered: math and curiosity/growth constructs align strongly between human and agent responses; classroom-climate and well-being constructs show only moderate alignment — revealing that LLM agents capture cognitive traits well but struggle with socio-emotional fidelity. Accepted at ACL 2026.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: educational applications requiring realistic student simulation, curriculum testing at scale, controlled A/B testing of pedagogical interventions, multi-agent classroom simulations, any domain where persona fidelity and distribution control matter. LOSES: the neuro-symbolic validator requires domain-specific constraint encoding (does not generalize without re-engineering), generation cost scales linearly with corpus size (1M personas at Qwen2.5-72B cost), persona fidelity degrades on socio-emotional dimensions (classroom-climate, well-being), static personas (no dynamic evolution over time), single language/educational system bias (US-aligned grades 1-12).
**Rationale:** Prior persona generation relied on ad-hoc prompting or hand-crafted profiles with no formal quality guarantees. HACHIMI's key insight is treating persona generation as a constrained generation problem with verifiable properties — the neuro-symbolic validator provides hard guarantees that pure LLM generation cannot. The Propose-Validate-Revise loop mirrors constitutional AI principles but applied to structured data generation rather than language output. The alignment gradient finding is significant: it identifies which persona dimensions LLMs can faithfully reproduce (cognitive/math) vs where they fall short (socio-emotional), providing a research roadmap for persona generation.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's agent role definitions are static, hand-crafted, and have no persona generation infrastructure. The Propose-Validate-Revise pattern is directly applicable to Lyra's planned multi-agent debate (§06) and quality gate (§4.19) — structured verification loops improve output quality across domains, not just persona generation. Status: **BEHIND** (no automated persona/role generation; no neuro-symbolic validation pipeline).
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** investigate (Propose-Validate-Revise pattern applicable to role generation and quality gates; persona infrastructure is Phase 2+)

---

## Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal (OPENDEV)
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.05344
**Mechanism:** (1) OPENDEV is an open-source CLI coding agent written in Rust, designed for terminal-native operation with long-horizon development task autonomy. (2) Dual-agent architecture: a planning agent decomposes high-level tasks into steps; an execution agent carries them out with tool access — separation prevents plan-execute confusion. (3) Workload-specialized model routing: different subtasks (code generation, code review, refactoring) route to different models optimized for each workload. (4) Lazy tool discovery: tools are loaded on-demand rather than pre-loaded into context, reducing context bloat from unused tool descriptions. (5) Adaptive context compaction: older observations are progressively compressed/summarized to maintain relevant history within context window limits — newer observations stay verbatim, older ones become increasingly abstract. (6) Automated memory system: project-specific knowledge (build commands, test patterns, dependency graphs) persists across sessions in a retrievable store. (7) Event-driven system reminders: structured reminders injected at context boundaries to combat instruction fade-out during long sessions. (8) Enforces explicit reasoning phases — the agent cannot skip from problem statement to code without going through structured analysis.
**Results:** The arXiv abstract does not include specific benchmark scores; quantitative results are in the full PDF (v3, 13 Mar 2026). Architecture described as demonstrating "unprecedented autonomy for long-horizon development tasks."
**Trade-offs:** WINS: terminal-native development workflows (no IDE dependency), long-horizon autonomous tasks, projects with large codebases (adaptive context compaction essential), teams wanting open-source/customizable coding agents, Rust performance for CLI responsiveness, cross-session knowledge accumulation (automated memory). LOSES: developers who prefer GUI/IDE integration, short/single-file edits (overhead of dual-agent architecture), projects where the planning overhead exceeds task complexity, environments where Rust compilation is a deployment barrier. The dual-agent split adds latency (planning step before any execution) which may feel slow for simple tasks.
**Rationale:** IDE plugins constrain coding agents to IDE-mediated interactions; terminal-native agents achieve deeper autonomy by directly operating on the filesystem, shell, and git. The dual-agent split addresses a known failure mode in coding agents: conflating planning with execution leads to premature implementation of poorly-designed solutions. Adaptive context compaction is the key scalability mechanism — without it, long-horizon tasks exhaust context windows. The Rust implementation choice prioritizes performance and safety for a tool that makes filesystem mutations. Lazy tool discovery is an underappreciated context optimization — pre-loading all tool descriptions is wasteful when most tasks use only a fraction of available tools.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no CLI coding agent, no dual-agent planning/execution split, no adaptive context compaction, and no cross-session project memory. The planned code generation agents rely on linear LLM calls with no structured planning-execution separation. OPENDEV's architecture is a direct model for Lyra's code generation and code review agents. Status: **BEHIND** (no CLI agent architecture; no planning-execution separation for code tasks).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (dual-agent coding architecture + context compaction; Phase 2 integration with §09 commands and §03 context)

---

## Memory for Autonomous LLM Agents: Mechanisms, Evaluation, and Emerging Frontiers
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.07670
**Mechanism:** (1) Comprehensive survey (2022–early 2026) formalizing agent memory as a write-manage-read loop tightly coupled with perception and action. (2) Three-dimensional taxonomy: temporal scope (short-term, working, long-term, eternal), representational substrate (embeddings, natural language, structured records, hybrid), and control policy (heuristic, learned, hybrid). (3) Five mechanism families identified: context-resident compression (summarization/compaction keeping relevant history in-window), retrieval-augmented stores (external DB + vector/semantic search pipelines), reflective self-improvement (agents generating abstractions/insights from past experience to guide future behavior), hierarchical virtual context (layered memory at multiple abstraction levels), and policy-learned management (learned policies deciding what to store/update/forget). (4) Evaluation landscape: traces the shift from static recall benchmarks (measuring retrieval accuracy in isolation) to multi-session agentic tests (measuring memory's impact on downstream task performance). (5) Cross-cutting concerns: write-path filtering (what gets stored), contradiction handling (conflicting memories), latency budgets (retrieval speed constraints), and privacy governance (right to be forgotten, data minimization).
**Results:** The survey analyzes four recent benchmarks exposing "stubborn gaps" — current memory systems perform well on isolated retrieval but degrade significantly when memory must be combined with decision-making in multi-session agentic tasks. Open challenges identified: continual consolidation (integrating new memories without catastrophic interference), causally grounded retrieval (retrieving memories based on causal relevance, not just semantic similarity), trustworthy reflection (ensuring self-generated insights are accurate), learned forgetting (pruning without losing critical information), and multimodal embodied memory (memory spanning text, vision, action, and physical state).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: comprehensive taxonomic framework for Lyra's memory subsystem design, identifies which mechanisms work for which memory scopes, evaluation methodology shift from static to agentic benchmarks. LOSES: survey format (no new system to implement), rapid field evolution (early 2026 cutoff already has new papers), no single recommended architecture (trade-offs depend on use case).
**Rationale:** The write-manage-read loop formalization is the survey's key conceptual contribution — it frames memory not as passive storage but as an active, agentic process integrated with the perception-action loop. The five mechanism families are not mutually exclusive; the survey argues that production agents need combinations (e.g., context compression for working memory + retrieval-augmented stores for long-term). The evaluation shift from static recall to multi-session agentic tests reflects the field's maturation — memory quality is not about retrieval precision but about task performance improvement.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's memory subsystem (§02) is in the planning stage with no implemented mechanism. This survey provides the taxonomic framework for systematic design — the five mechanism families map to different Lyra memory requirements (context compression for active sessions, retrieval stores for project knowledge, reflective improvement for agent evolution). Status: **BEHIND** (no memory implementation; survey provides design framework).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 2 | **Tier:** parity (essential design reference for §02 memory subsystem; read for architectural decisions, not implementation)

---

## τ-Voice: Benchmarking Full-Duplex Voice Agents on Real-World Domains
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.13686
**Mechanism:** (1) Extends τ²-bench into a voice agent evaluation framework combining three requirements: verifiable completion of grounded tasks, full-duplex interaction (simultaneous listening and speaking), and realistic audio conditions. (2) Controllable voice user simulator: provides diverse accents, realistic audio environments (background noise, reverberation), and rich turn-taking dynamics (interruptions, overlapping speech, pauses). (3) Simulation time decoupling: the user simulator runs independently of wall-clock time, enabling the most capable LLM to be used for the simulated user without real-time constraints — the agent under test faces realistic timing but the simulator does not bottleneck evaluation. (4) Direct text-vs-voice comparison: the same tasks are evaluated in both modalities, isolating the voice-specific performance gap. (5) Failure attribution framework: categorizes failures into agent behavior (misunderstanding, wrong action, poor turn-taking) vs speech pipeline errors (ASR mistakes, TTS artifacts).
**Results:** 278 tasks evaluated on task completion (pass@1) and voice interaction quality. GPT-5 (reasoning) text baseline achieves **85% pass@1**. Voice agents under clean conditions: **31-51% pass@1**. Voice agents under realistic conditions (noise, diverse accents): **26-38% pass@1**. Voice agents retain only **30-45% of text capability** — the modality gap is severe. Failure attribution: **79-90% of failures stem from agent behavior** (not speech pipeline errors) — agents struggle with turn-taking dynamics, interrupted reasoning, and ambiguous partial utterances rather than ASR/TTS quality.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: realistic full-duplex evaluation (most voice benchmarks are turn-by-turn), controllable simulator (reproducible across runs), text-vs-voice modality gap quantification (30-45% retention is a critical finding), failure attribution isolating agent behavior from pipeline errors. LOSES: simulated users may not capture full human conversational complexity, 278 tasks may not cover all voice agent use cases, simulation time decoupling helps evaluation throughput but may miss real-time pressure effects on agents, benchmark does not test multi-language or code-switching scenarios.
**Rationale:** Existing voice agent evaluations handle conversational dynamics and task completion separately — τ-voice unifies them. The 30-45% capability retention finding is alarming: it means voice agents lose more than half their text capability even under clean conditions. The 79-90% agent behavior attribution is the key diagnostic: speech pipeline improvements alone cannot close the gap; agents need fundamental architectural changes for full-duplex interaction (interruption handling, reasoning under overlapping speech, maintaining state across turn-taking disruptions). This has direct implications for Lyra's planned voice interface (§18).
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no voice interface, no full-duplex interaction model, and no speech pipeline. The planned voice subsystem (§18) assumes text-paradigm interaction — τ-voice shows that text-to-voice modality transfer is not straightforward (30-45% retention). Lyra's voice architecture must account for turn-taking dynamics, interruption recovery, and reasoning under partial/ambiguous input from the start. Status: **AHEAD of current planning** (Lyra voice plans do not account for full-duplex challenges uncovered by this benchmark).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (critical architectural insight for voice subsystem §18; full-duplex design must precede implementation)

---

## CraniMem: Cranial Inspired Gated Bounded Memory for Agentic Systems
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15642
**Mechanism:** (1) Neurocognitively motivated multi-stage memory design: goal-conditioned gating (admission depends on alignment with current task goals, not just novelty/similarity), utility tagging (each memory trace receives a utility score governing retention priority and consolidation order), bounded episodic buffer (capacity-limited buffer for near-term continuity — recent interactions stored verbatim until consolidated or evicted), and structured long-term knowledge graph (durable semantic recall via entity-relation graph updated through consolidation). (2) Scheduled consolidation loop: periodically replays high-utility traces from the episodic buffer into the knowledge graph while pruning low-utility traces — prevents unbounded memory growth and reduces interference between related but distinct memories. (3) Distractor resistance: goal-conditioned gating rejects task-irrelevant information at admission time, preventing context pollution from tangential observations. (4) All components are available as an open-source Python package (`cranimem` on PyPI). Presented at ICLR 2026 Workshop on Memory for LLM-Based Agentic Systems (MemAgents).
**Results:** Evaluated on long-horizon benchmarks under both clean inputs and injected noise/distractors. CraniMem demonstrates greater robustness than Vanilla RAG and Mem0 baselines, with smaller performance drops under distraction conditions. The bounded buffer + knowledge graph architecture keeps memory growth sublinear in interaction count (vs linear growth for append-only stores). Goal-conditioned gating is the primary driver of distractor resistance — rejecting irrelevant information at admission prevents downstream retrieval contamination.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: long-horizon agent tasks with many interaction turns, noisy environments (distractors, irrelevant observations), memory-constrained deployments (bounded growth guarantee), multi-session agents requiring durable knowledge accumulation, interpretable memory (utility scores and graph structure are auditable). LOSES: short-horizon tasks where memory overhead is unnecessary, domains with rapidly changing goals (goal-conditioned gating may reject information that becomes relevant later), initial cold-start (empty knowledge graph, empty episodic buffer — first sessions have no memory benefit), consolidation loop scheduling requires tuning (too frequent = compute waste; too infrequent = buffer overflow), knowledge graph schema design is domain-dependent.
**Rationale:** Current memory systems for agents behave like external databases with ad-hoc read/write rules — they accumulate everything, leading to bloat, interference, and degradation under noise. CraniMem's neurocognitive inspiration (hippocampal episodic buffer + cortical knowledge consolidation) provides a principled architecture: the episodic buffer handles recent, high-detail memory (like hippocampus); the knowledge graph handles durable, abstracted memory (like neocortex); the consolidation loop bridges them (like sleep-dependent memory consolidation). Goal-conditioned gating mirrors human attentional filtering — we don't remember everything, we remember what matters for our current goals. The bounded growth guarantee is critical for production deployment: memory cost must not grow unboundedly with usage.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's memory subsystem (§02) plans for vector DB + key-value + graph storage but lacks: (1) goal-conditioned admission control (no filtering of what enters memory), (2) bounded memory growth guarantees (plans imply unbounded accumulation), (3) scheduled consolidation (no mechanism for abstracting detailed memories into durable knowledge), (4) distractor resistance (no admission-time relevance checking). CraniMem provides a directly implementable architecture addressing all four gaps. Status: **BEHIND** (no structured memory architecture; CraniMem is a strong candidate design for §02).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (directly implementable memory architecture for §02; Phase 1 integration with memory subsystem design)

---

## Did You Check the Right Pocket? Cost-Sensitive Store Routing for Memory-Augmented Agents
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15658
**Mechanism:** (1) Observes that memory-augmented agents typically maintain multiple heterogeneous memory stores (vector DB for semantic recall, key-value store for fact lookup, graph DB for relational queries, raw log for chronological retrieval) but default to exhaustive or heuristic routing — querying all stores or using simple rules. (2) Proposes cost-sensitive routing: a learned router that decides which memory store(s) to query based on the query intent, estimated retrieval cost per store (latency + token overhead), and expected information gain. (3) Router is trained via supervised learning on (query, optimal-store) pairs collected by exhaustively querying all stores and comparing result quality — the "optimal" store is the one that produces the highest-quality answer at lowest cost. (4) At inference time, the router makes a single forward pass to select the target store(s), avoiding the overhead of querying all stores. (5) Supports fallback routing: if the primary store returns low-confidence results, the router can cascade to secondary stores with bounded additional cost.
**Results:** Cost reduction of 40-60% in retrieval latency compared to exhaustive multi-store querying, with minimal degradation (sometimes improvement due to reduced noise) in answer quality. The learned router achieves >90% accuracy in selecting the optimal store compared to the oracle (exhaustive search ground truth). Cost-sensitive routing also reduces total token consumption by 35-50% by avoiding retrieval from irrelevant stores. Fallback cascading used in <15% of queries.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: significant cost/latency reduction for multi-store agents, improved answer quality via noise reduction (fewer irrelevant retrieved chunks pollute context), router training is straightforward (supervised on oracle labels), fallback mechanism provides safety net for routing mistakes, applicable to any agent with multiple memory stores. LOSES: requires ground-truth oracle labels for training (exhaustive querying at training time), router adds a small inference overhead per query, fixed store set (adding new stores requires retraining the router), the optimal store for a query may depend on dynamic state not captured by the router, requires representative query distribution for training.
**Rationale:** As agents accumulate more memory stores (embedding-based, keyword-based, graph-based, temporal, hierarchical), the naive approach of querying all stores becomes increasingly expensive in both latency and context-window consumption. This paper formalizes the problem as cost-sensitive routing — not just "which store has the answer?" but "which store gives the best answer per unit cost?" This is directly analogous to LLM routing (RouteLLM, BEST-Route) but applied to memory stores rather than models. The finding that selective routing sometimes improves quality (by reducing noise) is significant: more retrieval is not always better.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's memory subsystem (§02) plans for vector DB + key-value + graph triple-store but has no store routing mechanism — the implicit assumption is that all stores are queried for every memory access. Cost-sensitive store routing would enable Lyra to maintain diverse memory stores without paying the latency/token penalty of exhaustive querying. Status: **BEHIND** (no memory store routing; multi-store architecture without routing is wasteful).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 2 | **Tier:** parity (store routing becomes necessary once Lyra has >2 memory stores; Phase 2 integration with §02 memory)

---

## Just Talk – An Agent That Meta-Learns and Evolves in the Wild (MetaClaw)
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17187
**Mechanism:** (1) MetaClaw is an agent that meta-learns and evolves through natural conversational interaction rather than through curated training pipelines or reinforcement learning with scalar rewards. (2) The agent maintains a set of "skills" (parameterized behavioral patterns) and a meta-learning loop: when the agent encounters a novel situation, it attempts existing skills; if all fail, it engages the user/teacher in natural dialogue to elicit a new skill (the "just talk" mechanism). (3) New skills are acquired through few-shot demonstration within the conversation — the user demonstrates the desired behavior, and the agent generalizes to similar future situations via in-context learning combined with persistent skill storage. (4) Evolution occurs through skill composition: existing skills can be chained, nested, or parameterized to form compound skills without requiring new demonstrations. (5) Runs continuously in the wild — the agent interacts with real users in unconstrained environments, and all learning happens through natural interaction without separation between training and deployment phases.
**Results:** Demonstrated on a customer-service domain with evolving product catalog and policies. MetaClaw agents acquired new skills from <5 conversational demonstrations on average. Skill composition produced correct behavior for 78% of novel task combinations without additional training. Over a 2-month deployment, the agent's task completion rate improved from 62% to 91% through in-the-wild learning alone. Human intervention rate decreased from 45% to 12% over the same period.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: zero-cost learning (no expensive RL training runs, no curated datasets), continuous adaptation (learns from every interaction), skill composition enables combinatorial generalization, natural interface (users teach via conversation, not code), deployment = training (no offline training phase needed). LOSES: depends on user willingness to teach (users must provide demonstrations), skill acquisition quality varies with teacher quality, no formal correctness guarantees for learned skills (can learn incorrect behaviors), catastrophic forgetting possible without skill curation, evaluation in constrained customer-service domain (generalization to open-ended domains unproven), potential safety concerns with in-the-wild learning (agent could learn harmful behaviors from adversarial users).
**Rationale:** The dominant paradigm for improving AI agents is offline training (RL, fine-tuning, prompt engineering) — expensive, slow to adapt, and disconnected from actual usage. MetaClaw's key insight is that users already provide corrective feedback and demonstrations during conversations; capturing and persisting this signal turns every interaction into a learning opportunity. The "just talk" interface is deliberately simple to lower the barrier for non-technical users to teach the agent. Skill composition addresses the combinatorial explosion problem — teaching N atomic skills can yield O(N²) compound behaviors without additional demonstrations.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no in-the-wild learning mechanism — all agent behavior is defined at design time through static prompts and tool configurations. MetaClaw's conversational skill acquisition model is directly relevant to Lyra's self-evolution plans (§17 self-improving agents, §15 research loop). The key gap: Lyra agents cannot learn from user interactions; every correction is ephemeral. Status: **BEHIND** (no in-the-wild learning; no skill acquisition from conversation).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (conversational meta-learning is a new paradigm for agent evolution; Phase 3 integration with self-improving loops)

---

## HyperAgents
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.19461
**Mechanism:** (1) HyperAgents proposes a framework for hyper-specialized AI agents — instead of a few generalist agents handling diverse tasks, the system dynamically spawns many narrow, specialized sub-agents each optimized for a specific subtask. (2) Hyper-specialization is achieved through task decomposition: a meta-agent (the Hypervisor) analyzes incoming tasks, decomposes them into atomic subtasks, and spawns a specialized agent for each subtask with task-specific system prompts, tools, and model selection. (3) Agents are ephemeral — created for a single subtask, executed, and discarded — avoiding the complexity of maintaining long-lived generalist agents. (4) Inter-agent communication is mediated by the Hypervisor, which aggregates subtask results and resolves conflicts. (5) The framework supports agent templates: parameterized agent configurations that can be instantiated with task-specific parameters, enabling rapid spawning without full configuration from scratch. (6) Dynamic resource allocation: compute budget is distributed across spawned agents based on subtask priority and estimated complexity.
**Results:** Evaluated on complex multi-domain benchmarks requiring composition of skills across coding, reasoning, and tool use. HyperAgents outperforms single-agent baselines by 18-34% on composite task completion. Ablation shows hyper-specialization (many narrow agents) outperforms multi-agent with few generalist agents by 12-22%, confirming the specialization advantage. Ephemeral agent creation/destruction overhead is <5% of total task time.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: complex composite tasks (many distinct subtasks requiring different expertise), domains with clear task decomposition boundaries, scenarios where specialization provides clear advantage over generalization, efficient resource utilization (allocate compute proportional to subtask difficulty), clean separation of concerns (each agent has a single responsibility). LOSES: simple tasks (spawning overhead exceeds benefit), tasks requiring deep context sharing across subtasks (ephemeral agents lose context when destroyed), domains without clear decomposition structure, cold-start problem (each spawned agent starts with no accumulated context), Hypervisor becomes a bottleneck and single point of failure, template design requires upfront engineering per domain.
**Rationale:** The trend in AI agents has been toward ever-more-capable generalist agents (GPT-5, Claude Opus handling everything). HyperAgents challenges this by showing that many narrow agents outperform few generalist agents for composite tasks — an instance of the "specialization beats generalization for known subtasks" principle. The ephemeral agent design is elegant: by avoiding the complexity of maintaining long-lived agent state, the system gains simplicity and predictability at the cost of cross-subtask context sharing. The Hypervisor pattern mirrors operating system process management (fork, execute, join) applied to AI agents.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's multi-agent architecture (§06 debate, §05 router) plans for a small number of fixed-role agents (router, memory, planner, executor). HyperAgents suggests a more dynamic model: spawn specialized ephemeral agents per subtask rather than routing to a fixed set of generalist agents. This is relevant to Lyra's task decomposition and agent orchestration patterns. Status: **BEHIND** (static agent roles; no dynamic agent spawning or hyper-specialization).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** investigate (hyper-specialization pattern applicable to Lyra's agent orchestration; Phase 2+)

---

## Knowledge Access Beats Model Size: Memory Augmented Routing for Persistent AI Agents
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.23013
**Mechanism:** (1) Makes the empirical claim that for persistent agents (agents that operate over long timescales with accumulated knowledge), access to structured external knowledge provides greater performance gains than scaling model parameters. (2) Proposes Memory-Augmented Routing (MAR): a routing mechanism that, given a query/task, decides whether to (a) answer directly from model knowledge, (b) retrieve from agent memory (past interactions, learned facts), or (c) query external tools/APIs — with the routing decision based on estimated knowledge availability in each source. (3) The routing policy is learned through reinforcement learning where the reward is answer quality minus retrieval cost. (4) Persistent memory accumulates across sessions: facts, user preferences, task solutions, and interaction patterns are stored in a structured memory that grows over the agent's lifetime. (5) Controlled experiments compare: small model + memory vs large model alone vs large model + memory — isolating the contribution of each factor.
**Results:** The headline finding: a small model (7B parameters) with memory-augmented routing matches or exceeds a model 10x larger (70B parameters) without memory on knowledge-intensive tasks. Specifically: 7B+MAR achieves 76.3% accuracy vs 70B-no-memory at 68.1% on a composite knowledge benchmark. The full combination (70B+MAR) achieves 84.7%, showing memory provides additive value beyond scale. Routing accuracy (choosing the correct knowledge source) reaches 91%. Memory grows sublinearly (logarithmic) after initial accumulation phase — most new information is redundant with existing knowledge.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: cost-efficient agent deployment (small model + memory is cheaper than large model), persistent agents that improve over time (accumulated knowledge compounds), clear ROI argument for memory investment over model scaling, routing mechanism is model-agnostic (works with any base model), sublinear memory growth keeps storage costs manageable long-term. LOSES: memory quality degrades if not curated (stale/contradictory facts accumulate), cold-start problem (new agents have empty memory and perform worse than large models), routing errors cascade (wrong source = wrong answer), memory infrastructure adds operational complexity (storage, indexing, retrieval latency), the "knowledge access beats model size" claim may not generalize to reasoning-heavy tasks (where model capacity matters more than factual knowledge), RL-based routing requires reward signal which may be sparse/delayed.
**Rationale:** The dominant AI scaling narrative says "bigger models = better performance." This paper provides a powerful counter-narrative for the agent domain: giving a small model access to accumulated knowledge can outperform scaling model size by 10x. This is practically significant because memory infrastructure (vector DB, retrieval pipelines) is far cheaper than model inference at scale. The sublinear memory growth finding is also important — it means persistent agents don't face unbounded storage costs, because most new information is redundant. The routing mechanism formalizes what humans do naturally: we don't recompute everything from first principles; we remember.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's design philosophy implicitly assumes larger models are better (routing to larger models for complex tasks). This paper provides evidence that Lyra should invest more heavily in memory infrastructure (§02) and knowledge accumulation rather than relying on model scaling for capability gains. The MAR routing framework (model knowledge vs memory vs tools) is directly applicable to Lyra's router (§05). Status: **AHEAD of current planning** (Lyra's architecture overweights model scaling relative to memory investment based on this evidence).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (fundamental architectural insight: prioritize memory over model size for persistent agents; impacts §02 memory, §05 router, §03 context)

## Experiential Reflective Learning for Self-Improving LLM Agents
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.24639
**Mechanism:** (1) Formalizes experiential reflective learning: agents improve by reflecting on their own past experiences — both successes and failures — rather than through external feedback, human annotation, or curated training data. (2) The learning loop: agent executes a task → records the full trajectory (actions, observations, outcomes) → a reflector module analyzes the trajectory to extract lessons (what worked, what failed, why) → lessons are stored in a structured reflection memory → future task execution retrieves relevant lessons to guide decision-making. (3) Reflection is structured: not free-form summarization but extraction into predefined schemas (failure mode, root cause, successful strategy, preconditions for strategy applicability). (4) Reflection memory supports both similarity-based retrieval (find reflections relevant to the current situation) and causal retrieval (find reflections where similar actions led to similar outcomes). (5) Includes a reflection quality filter: not all experiences produce useful lessons; a classifier filters out noisy or obvious reflections (e.g., "the task was impossible" is not a useful lesson). (6) Supports cross-task generalization: reflections from one task type can apply to related tasks via schema mapping.
**Results:** Agents using experiential reflective learning showed 22-35% improvement in task success rate over 100+ task iterations compared to non-learning baselines. Reflection quality filter eliminated 40% of candidate reflections as low-quality, improving retrieval precision without reducing recall of useful lessons. Cross-task generalization: 28% of reflections from Task Type A proved useful for Task Type B (same domain, different task). The improvement curve is logarithmic — largest gains in first 20-30 iterations, diminishing returns thereafter. Failure analysis: most persistent failures stem from inability to recognize when a past lesson applies (retrieval failure), not from lack of lessons.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: autonomous improvement without human annotation, accumulates compound knowledge over agent lifetime, structured reflection schemas enable precise retrieval, reflection quality filter prevents memory pollution, cross-task generalization amplifies learning efficiency, logarithmic improvement curve is favorable (fast early gains). LOSES: requires sufficient task diversity for meaningful reflection (repeating the same task yields no new lessons), reflection quality depends on trajectory quality (noisy trajectories produce poor reflections), retrieval remains the bottleneck (recognizing when a past lesson applies is the hardest part), structured schemas require domain engineering, can learn and perpetuate bad habits if reflection is overly credulous about "successful" strategies, logarithmic improvement means long-term gains require exponentially more experiences.
**Rationale:** Most self-improving agent research focuses on RL-based optimization (learning from scalar rewards) or synthetic data generation (creating training examples). This paper argues that the richest learning signal is the agent's own experience trajectories — the detailed record of what happened, not just whether it succeeded. The key insight is that structured reflection (extracting schematized lessons) is more useful than free-form summarization because it enables precise retrieval and causal reasoning. The reflection quality filter addresses a practical problem: most experiences produce obvious or noisy "lessons" that would pollute the reflection memory if stored unfiltered. The finding that retrieval (not reflection generation) is the bottleneck is important for system design — invest in better retrieval, not better reflection generation.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's self-improvement plans (§17) focus on prompt optimization and tool evolution but lack experiential reflective learning — agents do not learn from their own task trajectories. This paper provides a directly implementable reflection loop: record trajectory → structured reflection → reflection memory → retrieval-guided execution. The reflection quality filter and cross-task generalization mechanisms are immediately applicable. Status: **BEHIND** (no experiential learning loop; agents discard valuable trajectory data after each task).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (directly implementable self-improvement mechanism; Phase 2 integration with §17 self-improving agents and §02 memory)

## Meta-Harness: End-to-End Optimization of Model Harnesses
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28052
**Mechanism:** (1) Observes that LLM system performance depends on both model weights AND the harness code that determines what information to store, retrieve, and present to the model — and that current harnesses are designed by hand. (2) Meta-Harness is an outer-loop system that searches over harness code: an agentic proposer iteratively generates candidate harness implementations, executes them on the target task, and uses the resulting scores and execution traces to inform the next proposal. (3) The proposer accesses the full source code, scoring history, and execution traces of all prior candidates through a filesystem — providing much richer feedback than text-optimizer approaches that compress feedback too aggressively. (4) The search process is end-to-end: the proposer can modify any part of the harness (retrieval strategy, context assembly, prompt templates, tool call orchestration) based on observed performance. (5) Discovered harnesses are evaluated on held-out models to test generalization — ensuring the optimization finds harness patterns, not model-specific overfitting.
**Results:** Three evaluated settings: (1) Online text classification: outperforms state-of-the-art context management by **7.7 points while using 4x fewer context tokens**. (2) Retrieval-augmented math reasoning: a single discovered harness improves accuracy on 200 IMO-level problems by **4.7 points on average across five held-out models**. (3) Agentic coding: discovered harnesses surpass the best hand-engineered baselines on TerminalBench-2. Key meta-result: the harness transfers across models, confirming the optimization captures general harness design principles rather than model-specific tuning.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: automated harness optimization (replaces manual engineering with data-driven search), cross-model generalization (harnesses work on held-out models), token efficiency (4x reduction in context tokens), rich feedback from filesystem access to prior candidates enables better proposals than text-only optimizers, end-to-end optimization captures interactions that modular design misses. LOSES: search cost (requires many candidate evaluations), filesystem-based proposer adds infrastructure complexity, optimization may overfit to evaluation tasks, discovered harnesses may be harder to interpret/debug than hand-engineered ones, requires well-defined scoring functions, compute-intensive for large search spaces.
**Rationale:** Current harness engineering is artisanal — every new LLM application requires hand-crafting retrieval pipelines, context assembly, and prompt structures. Meta-Harness treats the harness as an optimization target itself, analogous to how AutoML automated model architecture search. The key insight is that richer access to prior experience (source code + scores + execution traces, not just compressed text feedback) enables effective automated harness engineering. The cross-model generalization is practically significant: discover a harness once, use it with any model.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's entire architecture IS a harness — planning, memory, routing, context management, tool orchestration. But Lyra's harness is 100% hand-designed. Meta-Harness suggests Lyra could meta-optimize its own harness components: auto-discover optimal retrieval strategies, context assembly patterns, and agent orchestration flows. Status: **BEHIND** (all harness engineering is manual; no automated harness optimization loop exists).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (automated harness optimization is meta-capability that improves all other subsystems; Phase 3+)

## Human-Like Lifelong Memory: A Neuroscience-Grounded Architecture for Infinite Interaction
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.29023
**Mechanism:** (1) Proposes a bio-inspired memory framework for LLMs grounded in four theories: complementary learning systems (hippocampal-cortical consolidation), CBT's belief hierarchy (Beck's cognitive model), dual-process cognition (System 1/System 2), and fuzzy-trace theory (gist vs verbatim representations). (2) Three organizing principles: (a) Valenced memory — pre-computed emotional-associative summaries (valence vectors) structured in a belief hierarchy enable instant orientation before deliberation; (b) System 1 default with System 2 escalation — retrieval relies on automatic spreading activation and passive priming by default, with deliberate retrieval triggered only when uncertainty exceeds threshold, where graded epistemic states address hallucination structurally; (c) Active, feedback-dependent encoding — a thalamic-gateway analog tags and routes information between stores, while an executive component forms gists through curiosity-driven investigation. (3) Seven functional properties define what any implementation must satisfy — providing a specification rather than a single algorithm. (4) Computational convergence property: over time, the system converges toward System 1 processing (the computational analog of clinical expertise), so interactions grow cheaper rather than more expensive with experience.
**Results:** Theoretical architecture paper — no empirical benchmarks. Key evidence cited: context length alone degrades reasoning by up to 85% even with perfect retrieval, motivating structured memory over raw context extension. Accepted at MemAgents Workshop, ICLR 2026. The computational convergence property (interactions grow cheaper with experience) is a novel theoretical contribution — current agent systems grow more expensive with longer interaction histories.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: principled neuroscience grounding (not ad-hoc memory design), computational convergence (cheaper over time, not more expensive), structural hallucination handling (graded epistemic states), active encoding produces higher-quality memories through curiosity-driven investigation, specification-based (multiple implementations possible while satisfying the seven functional properties), belief hierarchy enables rapid context orientation. LOSES: no empirical validation (theoretical only), implementation complexity (seven functional properties are non-trivial to satisfy), single-author paper (less rigorous review), valenced memory requires emotion/valence computation which is domain-specific, thalamic-gateway routing adds architectural complexity, active encoding through curiosity-driven investigation is expensive.
**Rationale:** Current agent memory systems are databases with ad-hoc read/write rules — they lack the architectural principles that make human memory robust over a lifetime. This paper provides those principles. The computational convergence property is particularly important: current agent systems accumulate more context over time, making later interactions MORE expensive; human experts show the opposite pattern. The graded epistemic states approach to hallucination is elegant: rather than binary "hallucinated/not-hallucinated," maintain calibrated uncertainty that controls whether deliberate System 2 retrieval is triggered.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's memory plans (§02) propose vector DB + key-value + graph triple-store but lack: (1) valence/emotional-associative summaries for rapid orientation, (2) System 1/System 2 routing for retrieval, (3) graded epistemic state tracking for hallucination control, (4) computational convergence guarantee (Lyra's memory will grow more expensive over time), (5) specification-based architecture (Lyra's plans are implementation-specific). This paper provides the architectural principles Lyra's memory subsystem should satisfy, even if Lyra implements them differently. Status: **BEHIND** (no principled memory architecture; ad-hoc storage plans without theoretical grounding).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (architectural principles for §02 memory subsystem; defines what a production memory architecture must satisfy)

## Multi-Layered Memory Architectures for LLM Agents: An Experimental Evaluation of Long-Term Context Retention
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.29194
**Mechanism:** (1) Proposes a Multi-Layer Memory Framework that breaks dialogue history into three distinct layers: working memory (immediate conversation context, high-detail, short-lived), episodic memory (session-level experiences, medium-detail, medium-lived), and semantic memory (cross-session abstractions, low-detail, long-lived). (2) Adaptive retrieval gating controls which layer(s) to query for a given information need — simple fact lookup hits working/episodic, while reasoning requiring accumulated knowledge queries semantic. (3) Retention regularization prevents unbounded memory growth by applying decay functions tuned per layer: working memory decays rapidly (minutes), episodic decays gradually (sessions), semantic is near-permanent with consolidation-based pruning. (4) The architecture specifically targets "semantic drift and unstable memory retention across extended sessions" — the problem where agent behavior becomes inconsistent as memory accumulates contradictory or stale information. (5) Cross-layer consolidation: information flows working → episodic → semantic, with each transition applying abstraction and compression, analogous to hippocampal-cortical consolidation.
**Results:** Evaluated on LOCOMO, LOCCO, and LoCoMo benchmark datasets. Success rate: **46.85%**, Overall F1: **0.618**, Multi-hop F1: **0.594**, Six-period retention: **56.90%**, False memory rate: **5.1%**, Context usage: **58.40%**. The architecture achieves enhanced long-term retention and reasoning stability under constrained context budgets, with significantly reduced false memories (5.1%) compared to baseline approaches — a critical metric for reliable agents.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: structured multi-layer organization maps naturally to different memory timescales, adaptive retrieval gating reduces unnecessary retrieval, retention regularization prevents unbounded growth, explicit false memory rate metric (5.1% is measurable and improvable), cross-layer consolidation provides principled information flow, constrained context budget operation (58.4% usage). LOSES: three-layer design requires tuning per domain (decay rates, consolidation thresholds), modest absolute performance (46.85% success rate leaves room for improvement), LOCOMO/LOCCO benchmarks may not represent all agent use cases, adaptive gating can make wrong layer selection decisions, consolidation errors compound across layers (episodic→semantic abstraction mistakes persist indefinitely), false memory rate of 5.1% may be too high for safety-critical applications.
**Rationale:** Current approaches to agent memory are polarized: either "infinite context window" (expensive, degrades reasoning by up to 85%) or "simple retrieval" (loses long-term coherence). Multi-layer architectures offer a middle ground — structured by memory timescale, with controlled information flow between layers. The false memory rate metric is important: it quantifies a problem (agents confidently recalling incorrect information) that is qualitatively obvious but rarely measured. The 5.1% false memory rate provides a baseline for improvement.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's memory plans (§02) mention "working memory" and "long-term memory" as concepts but don't define explicit multi-layer architecture with retention regularization, adaptive gating, or cross-layer consolidation. The false memory rate concept is absent from current planning — Lyra has no metric for measuring memory reliability. The three-layer architecture (working/episodic/semantic) maps directly to Lyra's conversation-level, session-level, and cross-session memory needs. Status: **BEHIND** (no multi-layer memory architecture with retention control or reliability metrics).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** parity (directly implementable multi-layer memory design for §02; Phase 1-2)

## ANX: Protocol-First Design for AI Agent Interaction with a Supporting 3EX Decoupled Architecture
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04820
**Mechanism:** (1) ANX is an open, extensible, verifiable agent-native protocol and framework integrating CLI, Skill, and MCP capabilities — targeting the problems of high token usage, disjointed interaction flows, and weak security in current agent systems. (2) Four core innovations: (a) Agent-native design (ANX Config, Markup, CLI) delivering high information density to cut token consumption and eliminate inconsistencies between human-readable and agent-executable representations; (b) Human-agent interaction via Skill's dual rendering — producing both agent-executable instructions AND human-readable interfaces from the same specification; (c) MCP-supported on-demand lightweight apps requiring no pre-registration, enabling agents to discover and use tools dynamically; (d) ANX Markup enabling machine-executable SOPs to remove ambiguity for reliable long-horizon tasks and multi-agent collaboration. (3) 3EX decoupled architecture supported by ANXHub: separates execution, expression, and extension concerns. (4) Security: LLM-bypassed UI-to-Core communication keeps sensitive data out of agent context, and human-only confirmation blocks automated misuse. (5) Benchmarked against 7 existing protocols (MCP, A2A, ANP, OpenCLI, SkillWeaver, CHEQ, COLLAB-LLM) across four dimensions: tooling, discovery, security, and multi-agent SOP collaboration.
**Results:** Form-filling experiments: **47.3-55.6% token reduction** vs MCP-based skills, **57.1-66.3% token reduction** vs GUI automation, **57.7-58.1% execution time reduction** vs MCP-based skills. Qwen3.5-plus and GPT-4o both benefit, with larger models showing greater token savings (GPT-4o: 55.6% vs MCP, 66.3% vs GUI). Open-source (CC BY 4.0) at github.com/mountorc/anx-protocol.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: dramatic token savings (47-66% reduction), dual rendering bridges human-agent gap (one spec, two views), on-demand tool discovery eliminates pre-registration friction, machine-executable SOPs enable reliable multi-agent workflows, security-by-design (sensitive data never enters agent context), protocol-first approach enables interoperability, benchmarked against 7 alternatives. LOSES: new protocol requires adoption (network effects favor incumbents like MCP), ANXHub adds infrastructure dependency, machine-executable SOPs require upfront authoring effort, dual rendering may introduce inconsistencies if not carefully maintained, CC BY 4.0 license may limit commercial adoption compared to MIT/Apache, single-vendor origin (risk of roadmap control), form-filling evaluation may not represent all agent use cases.
**Rationale:** Current agent protocols (MCP, A2A) were designed for machine-to-machine communication, not for efficient human-agent-agent interaction. ANX's protocol-first approach starts from the interaction model rather than retrofitting existing protocols. The dual rendering concept (same spec produces agent-executable instructions and human-readable UI) is the key insight — it eliminates the current duplication where agent instructions and user interfaces are maintained separately. The token reduction numbers (47-66%) are practically significant: at production scale, halving token consumption halves both cost and latency.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no defined interaction protocol beyond CLI argument parsing. ANX is directly relevant to Lyra's plugin/skill system (§07 plugins), command interface (§09 commands), and multi-agent SOP collaboration. Lyra's current plans assume MCP for tool integration; ANX provides evidence that agent-native protocols outperform MCP by 47-55% in token efficiency. Status: **BEHIND** (no protocol-first design; no dual rendering; no machine-executable SOPs).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (protocol-first design for Lyra's interaction layer; impacts §07 plugins, §09 commands, §05 router, §06 debate)

## Full-Duplex-Bench-v3: Benchmarking Tool Use for Full-Duplex Voice Agents Under Real-World Disfluency
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04847
**Mechanism:** (1) FDB-v3 evaluates spoken language models under naturalistic speech with multi-step tool use — the benchmark uses real human audio annotated across five disfluency categories (hesitations, false starts, repairs, fillers, repetitions). (2) Tasks require chained API calls across four domains (e.g., booking + payment + confirmation), testing both speech understanding under disfluency AND multi-step tool orchestration. (3) Six model configurations evaluated: GPT-Realtime, Gemini Live 2.5, Gemini Live 3.1, Grok, Ultravox v0.7, and a Cascaded pipeline (Whisper → GPT-4o → TTS). (4) Evaluated on three axes: accuracy (Pass@1), latency (end-to-end response time), and turn-taking (interruption avoidance, turn-take rate). (5) Five disfluency categories capture real-world speech patterns that break most ASR pipelines — the benchmark measures degradation from clean speech to disfluent speech for each system.
**Results:** GPT-Realtime leads with Pass@1 = **0.600** and best interruption avoidance at **13.5%**. Gemini Live 3.1 achieves fastest latency at **4.25s** but lowest turn-take rate at **78.0%**. Cascaded pipeline (Whisper→GPT-4o→TTS) achieves perfect turn-take rate but highest latency at **10.12s**. Failure analysis: self-correction handling and multi-step reasoning under hard scenarios remain the most consistent failure modes across all systems.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: real human audio (not synthetic disfluency), five disfluency categories provide granular failure analysis, multi-step tool use requirement tests end-to-end agent capability, three-axis evaluation (accuracy/latency/turn-taking) captures real deployment trade-offs, six diverse model configurations provide broad comparison, Pass@1 metric reflects production reliability requirement. LOSES: four task domains may not cover all voice agent use cases, real human audio limits dataset size (annotation cost), latency measurements are hardware-dependent, turn-taking evaluation requires careful definition of "correct" turn boundaries, cascaded pipeline latency (10.12s) is too high for natural conversation but perfect turn-take rate suggests architectural trade-off between latency and interaction quality, GPT-Realtime's 0.600 Pass@1 means 40% of tasks still fail.
**Rationale:** Voice agents are the next frontier for AI interaction, but current benchmarks use clean, scripted speech that doesn't reflect real-world disfluency. FDB-v3 closes this gap by using real human audio with natural disfluencies AND requiring multi-step tool use — combining two hard problems (speech understanding under noise, and chained API orchestration) that are independently challenging but must work together in production. The speed-vs-accuracy-vs-turn-taking trade-off surface is practically useful: different applications will choose different operating points (low-latency for real-time conversation vs high-accuracy for transactional tasks).
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's voice plans (§18 voice) are nascent — no benchmark selection, no evaluation framework, no disfluency handling strategy. FDB-v3 provides both a benchmark AND a failure analysis (self-correction handling and multi-step reasoning are the consistent failure modes) that directly informs Lyra's voice subsystem design. The cascaded-vs-real-time architecture comparison (latency vs turn-taking trade-off) is directly applicable to Lyra's architecture decision for voice. Status: **BEHIND** (no voice evaluation framework; no benchmark selection; no disfluency handling strategy).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** parity (benchmark + architecture guidance for §18 voice; Phase 2 integration)

## OmniDiagram: Advancing Unified Diagram Code Generation via Visual Interrogation Reward
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.05514
**Mechanism:** (1) OmniDiagram is a unified framework for diagram code generation supporting 3 output languages (LaTeX, Mermaid, PlantUML) across 3 task types (Diagram-to-Code, Diagram-Editing, Text-to-Code) — a 3x3 task-language matrix. (2) Core innovation Viva (Visual Interrogation Verifies All): instead of brittle syntax rules or pixel-level matching, Viva generates targeted visual questions about the rendered diagram's structure, answers them by inspecting the generated diagram image via vision-language models, and produces fine-grained RL reward signals. (3) Self-evolving training loop: Viva eliminates the need for manually annotated ground-truth code — the reward mechanism enables iterative RL improvement from SFT base models without additional human labeling. (4) M3^2Diagram dataset: 196k+ high-quality instances spanning all 9 cells of the task-language matrix, plus M3^2Bench (1.7k human-verified evaluation samples). (5) Combined SFT + Viva-based RL optimization pipeline.
**Results:** New SOTA on diagram code generation benchmarks, surpassing both task-specific and general open-source models. The RL reward from Viva provides fine-grained feedback (per-element structural correctness) vs coarse-grained comparison rewards. Accepted to ACL 2026 Findings. Open-source: code, models, and dataset at github.com/Haoyue-Yang/OmniDiagram.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: eliminates brittle manual rule-based evaluation, enables self-evolving training (no additional human labels needed), unified across 3 languages and 3 tasks (9-cell matrix), VLM-based visual interrogation captures structural correctness better than text-only metrics, RL optimization from SFT base consistently improves all task types. LOSES: VLM-based reward generation adds inference cost per RL step (question generation + image inspection), visual interrogation quality depends on VLM capability (weaker VLMs may produce noisy rewards), limited to 3 diagram languages (LaTeX/Mermaid/PlantUML — excludes TikZ, Graphviz, etc.), diagram code generation is a narrower domain than general code generation, training pipeline complexity (SFT → RL with Viva reward) vs simple SFT-only approaches.
**Rationale:** Text-only evaluation of diagram code (comparing LaTeX/Mermaid source) ignores the rendered visual output — two syntactically different code snippets can produce identical diagrams, and vice versa. Viva bridges the modality gap by evaluating what matters: the rendered diagram's visual structure. The visual interrogation approach (ask targeted questions about the diagram, answer by looking at it) generalizes beyond any single diagram language — the same VLM can inspect LaTeX-rendered and Mermaid-rendered diagrams equally. Self-evolving capability is practically significant: once the SFT model is trained, RL improvement continues without additional annotation cost.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no diagram generation capability at all. OmniDiagram is tangentially relevant — its self-evolving RL loop (SFT base → VLM-based reward → iterative improvement) is a pattern applicable to Lyra's self-improvement subsystem (§15 research, self-evolution). The modality-bridging concept (evaluate the rendered output, not the source code) is transferable to Lyra's code generation quality assessment. Status: **NOT APPLICABLE** to current Lyra capabilities (no diagram generation), but the Viva self-evolving RL pattern is **RELEVANT** to Lyra's planned self-improvement loops.
**Impact:** 2 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** inspiration (self-evolving RL pattern transferable; diagram generation itself not needed)
