## Social Dynamics as Critical Vulnerabilities that Undermine Objective Decision-Making in LLM Collectives
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.06091
**Mechanism:** (1) Representative-centric multi-agent framework: one representative agent interacts with 5 peers, synthesizes their rationales, and produces a final answer. (2) Four social-psychological phenomena systematically manipulated as attack vectors: (a) Social Conformity — vary number of adversarial peers (0-5) instructed to select incorrect answers with persuasive rationales; (b) Perceived Expertise — manipulate relative intelligence/model scale of adversarial peers, with a single "expert" adversary (more capable model) pitted against 4 less capable benign peers; (c) Dominant Speaker Effect — vary argument length from 1 sentence to 3 paragraphs while holding correctness constant; (d) Rhetorical Persuasion — manipulate argumentative style (Ethos/credibility, Logos/logic, Pathos/emotion). (3) Experiments across 3 datasets: BBQ (bias/ambiguous QA), MMLU-Pro, MetaTool. (4) Both open (Qwen2.5, Gemma3) and closed (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Haiku) models tested as representatives. (5) Adversarial peers instructed to defend incorrect answers.
**Results:** Social Conformity: accuracy degrades monotonically as adversarial peers increase; once adversaries form majority (3+ of 5), performance collapses abruptly — Gemma3 12B drops below 10% accuracy with 5 adversaries. On ambiguous BBQ questions: accuracy falls from >99% (0 adversaries) to ~30% (5 adversaries). Perceived Expertise: single "expert" adversary overrides correct input from 4 less capable peers. Dominant Speaker: one verbose adversarial peer causes performance drops comparable to adding several adversarial agents. Rhetorical Persuasion: more capable LLMs are paradoxically MORE susceptible to sophisticated rhetoric; Ethos/Logos degrade judgment in objective tasks, Pathos highly effective in ambiguous/social contexts. Accepted to ACL 2026.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: systematic quantification of social-psychological vulnerabilities in LLM collectives, multi-model validation (both open and closed models tested), multi-dimensional attack surface (4 phenomena, 3 datasets), reveals counterintuitive finding (more capable models more susceptible to rhetoric), directly challenges assumption that multi-agent collaboration monotonically improves reliability. LOSES: fixed representative-centric topology (5 peers, 1 representative — may not generalize to other topologies), adversarial peers are explicitly instructed to be adversarial (real-world adversaries are more subtle), no defense mechanisms proposed or tested, BBQ/MMLU-Pro/MetaTool may not capture all decision-making contexts, single-round deliberation (no iterative debate/counter-argument), social-psychological framing may over-anthropomorphize LLM behavior.
**Rationale:** Multi-agent LLM systems inherit quantifiable analogs of human social-psychological biases (Asch conformity, Milgram authority effects). The representative-centric design models real deployment: an LLM agent synthesizes inputs from multiple sources before deciding. The finding that stronger models are MORE susceptible to rhetoric is practically alarming — it means improved model capability does not automatically confer improved robustness in social decision-making contexts. This challenges the safety-through-scaling assumption.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's debate subsystem (§06 debate) and multi-agent collaboration architecture implicitly assume that more agents and more deliberation improve decision quality. This paper provides direct counter-evidence: social dynamics (conformity, expertise signaling, verbosity, rhetoric) can systematically degrade collective decisions. Lyra has NO defense mechanisms against social manipulation in agent collectives. Status: **BEHIND** (critical vulnerability class identified but not mitigated; directly impacts §06 debate and multi-agent orchestration).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (mandatory safety mechanism for multi-agent debate; informs agent trust management and robust aggregation strategies)

---

## Paper Circle: An Open-source Multi-agent Research Discovery and Analysis Framework
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.06170
**Mechanism:** (1) Two complementary pipelines: Discovery Pipeline integrates offline and online retrieval from multiple sources with multi-criteria scoring, diversity-aware ranking, and structured outputs (JSON, CSV, BibTeX, Markdown, HTML at each agent step). (2) Analysis Pipeline transforms papers into structured knowledge graphs with typed nodes (concepts, methods, experiments, figures), enabling graph-aware Q&A and coverage verification. (3) Built on a coder LLM-based multi-agent orchestration framework with fully reproducible and synchronized outputs at each agent step. (4) Multi-criteria scoring evaluates papers across relevance, novelty, methodological rigor, and reproducibility. (5) Diversity-aware ranking ensures retrieved paper sets cover complementary approaches, not just top-ranked similar papers.
**Results:** Benchmarked on paper retrieval and review generation tasks using Hit Rate, MRR, and Recall@K metrics. Consistent improvements with stronger agent models. Open-source (github.com/MAXNORM8650/papercircle) with live demo at papercircle.vercel.app. Accepted to ACL 2026 (Oral presentation).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: dual pipeline (discovery + analysis) covers end-to-end research workflow, knowledge graph representation enables structured queries beyond keyword search, multi-criteria scoring captures paper quality dimensions beyond citation count, diversity-aware ranking prevents information-echo-chamber in literature reviews, reproducible structured outputs at each agent step enable debugging and verification, open-source with live demo. LOSES: depends on coder LLM for orchestration (may inherit model biases), knowledge graph construction quality depends on paper parsing accuracy, multi-criteria scoring weights require domain-specific tuning, evaluation limited to paper retrieval and review generation (does not cover novel research ideation), single-vendor implementation (community adoption uncertain), ACL oral suggests strong community recognition but field is crowded (many research discovery tools).
**Rationale:** Current research discovery tools (Google Scholar, Semantic Scholar) use citation-based ranking and keyword search — they don't assess paper quality, don't ensure diversity, and don't structure papers into queryable knowledge graphs. Paper Circle's dual pipeline addresses all three gaps. The knowledge graph representation (concepts, methods, experiments as typed nodes) is the key differentiator — it enables queries like "what methods were used to evaluate X?" that keyword search cannot answer.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's research subsystem (§15 research) is planned but not implemented. Paper Circle provides a reference architecture for multi-agent research discovery and analysis that is directly applicable. The knowledge graph approach to paper analysis could inform Lyra's memory subsystem (§02 memory) — structured, queryable representations of ingested knowledge. The diversity-aware ranking concept is relevant to Lyra's source selection for deep research. Status: **BEHIND** (no research subsystem exists; Paper Circle provides reference architecture).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** parity (reference architecture for §15 research; knowledge graph pattern transferable to §02 memory)

## EMSDialog: Synthetic Multi-person Emergency Medical Service Dialogue Generation from Electronic Patient Care Reports via Multi-LLM Agents
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07549
**Mechanism:** (1) ePCR-grounded, topic-flow-based multi-agent generation pipeline: iteratively plans dialogue topics, generates multi-speaker dialogue turns, and self-refines output with rule-based factual and topic flow checks. (2) Multi-agent architecture: each agent manages a speaker role in the EMS scenario (dispatcher, paramedic, patient, bystander) with role-specific knowledge and communication patterns. (3) Grounding mechanism: dialogues are generated from real-world Electronic Patient Care Reports (ePCRs) to ensure medical accuracy — the ePCR provides the clinical ground truth that the dialogue must faithfully represent. (4) Self-refinement loop: generated dialogues undergo automatic factual consistency checking against source ePCRs and topic flow validation, with iterative correction. (5) Dataset: 4,414 synthetic multi-speaker EMS conversations annotated with 43 diagnoses, speaker roles, and turn-level topics.
**Results:** Both human and LLM evaluations confirm high quality and realism using utterance- and conversation-level metrics. EMSDialog-augmented training improves accuracy, timeliness, and stability of EMS conversational diagnosis prediction. Accepted to ACL 2026 Findings. Open-source: code and dataset at uva-dsa.github.io/EMSDialog.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: solves real scarcity problem (no existing multi-party EMS dialogue corpora), ePCR grounding ensures medical factual accuracy (not hallucinated clinical details), multi-agent architecture naturally models multi-role conversations, self-refinement with rule-based checks reduces hallucination, 43-diagnosis coverage provides clinical breadth, turn-level topic annotations enable fine-grained conversation analysis. LOSES: synthetic data (no matter how realistic, differs from real EMS conversations — stress, noise, urgency), single domain (EMS only — not generalizable to other clinical conversation types), rule-based factual checks may miss subtle clinical errors, 4,414 conversations may not capture rare clinical scenarios, evaluation metrics for dialogue quality are inherently subjective, English-only (EMS protocols vary internationally).
**Rationale:** Real EMS conversations are extremely difficult to record (privacy, consent, emergency context). Synthetic data generation is the only scalable approach for this domain. The key insight is grounding generation in structured clinical data (ePCRs) rather than free-form prompting — the ePCR provides the clinical "skeleton" that constrains and validates the generated dialogue. Multi-agent architecture maps naturally to multi-role conversation: each agent embodies one role with role-appropriate knowledge and communication style.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no medical/clinical dialogue capabilities and no domain-specific multi-agent role-playing architecture. EMSDialog is tangentially relevant — its multi-agent role-playing pattern (each agent embodies a domain role with role-specific knowledge) is transferable to Lyra's multi-agent orchestration for domain-specific scenarios. The self-refinement loop (generate → factual-check → correct) is a general pattern applicable to Lyra's verification subsystem. Status: **NOT APPLICABLE** to current Lyra capabilities, but the role-playing multi-agent architecture and self-refinement pattern are **RELEVANT** to Lyra's verification and domain-specific agent design.
**Impact:** 2 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** inspiration (multi-agent role-playing + self-refinement patterns transferable; clinical domain not needed)

## ACIARENA: Toward Unified Evaluation for Agent Cascading Injection
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07775
**Mechanism:** (1) ACIArena is a unified evaluation framework for assessing Multi-Agent System (MAS) robustness against Agent Cascading Injection (ACI) attacks — where a compromised agent exploits trust relationships to spread malicious instructions, triggering cascading failures across the entire system. (2) Common specification jointly supports MAS construction and attack-defense modules, enabling systematic comparison of attack strategies and defense mechanisms. (3) Three attack surfaces evaluated: external inputs injection, agent profile manipulation, inter-agent message poisoning. (4) Three attack objectives: instruction hijacking (redirect agent behavior), task disruption (degrade system output), information exfiltration (leak sensitive data through agent chain). (5) Comprehensive benchmark: 1,356 test cases across 6 widely-used MAS implementations.
**Results:** Key findings: (a) Evaluating MAS robustness by topology alone is insufficient — deliberate role design and controlled interaction patterns are essential; (b) Defenses developed in simplified environments often fail to transfer to real-world settings; (c) Narrowly-scoped defenses may introduce new vulnerabilities via unforeseen interaction effects. ACI attacks achieve high success rates across all 6 MAS implementations when exploiting inter-agent trust. Accepted to ACL 2026 Main Conference.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: first unified evaluation framework for cascading injection in MAS, three attack surfaces + three objectives provide comprehensive coverage, large-scale benchmark (1,356 test cases, 6 MAS implementations), reveals that topology-based security is insufficient (role design matters more), demonstrates defense transfer failure (a critical finding for practitioners), common specification enables reproducible attack-defense comparison. LOSES: focuses on evaluation only (no novel defense mechanisms proposed), 6 MAS implementations may not represent all agent architectures, injection attacks assume compromised agent (the initial compromise mechanism is out of scope), test cases are lab-constructed (real-world cascading failures may be subtler), ACI attack formalization may not capture all cascading failure modes, evaluation framework complexity may limit adoption.
**Rationale:** As LLM-based multi-agent systems are deployed in production, cascading injection becomes a critical security concern — one compromised agent can poison the entire system through trusted communication channels. Current MAS security research focuses on single-agent prompt injection; ACI exploits the multi-agent trust topology that single-agent defenses miss. The finding that topology-based security is insufficient is practically significant: simply restricting agent communication topology does not prevent cascading attacks if role design and interaction patterns are not also hardened.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's safety subsystem (§17 safety) and multi-agent orchestration have NO mechanisms for detecting or preventing cascading injection attacks. Lyra agents communicate with implicit trust — any agent's output is consumed by downstream agents without integrity verification. The finding that defenses don't transfer from simplified to real-world settings is directly relevant: Lyra must test security mechanisms in realistic multi-agent configurations, not just unit-test individual agent prompt injection resistance. Status: **BEHIND** (critical security vulnerability class not addressed; directly impacts §17 safety and multi-agent trust model).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (mandatory security evaluation framework for multi-agent trust model; informs §17 safety architecture)

## SEARL: Joint Optimization of Policy and Tool Graph Memory for Self-Evolving Agents
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07791
**Mechanism:** (1) Structured Experience Memory fuses planning with execution into a unified representation, rather than using raw interaction experiences directly. (2) Tool Graph Memory represents tools and their relationships in a graph structure, enabling reuse across analogous situations via a novel state abstraction. (3) Joint optimization: policy and tool graph memory are optimized together, allowing the agent to learn both what to do and what tools to use simultaneously. (4) Reward densification: leverages inter-trajectory correlations to densify sparse outcome-based rewards — agents normally only receive feedback at task completion, but SEARL extracts intermediate signals by comparing across related trajectories. (5) Self-evolving loop: agent extracts explicit knowledge from historical data, updates tool graph memory, and improves policy — all without large-scale LLM or multi-agent dependencies.
**Results:** Accepted to ACL 2026. Demonstrates effective and efficient learning on knowledge reasoning and math tasks without requiring large-scale LLMs or multi-agent frameworks. Dense reward signals from inter-trajectory correlations enable learning from sparse outcome feedback. (Quantitative metrics require full PDF review.)
**Trade-offs:** WINS: resource-constrained environments (no large-scale LLM dependency), tasks with reusable tool patterns (tool graph memory enables transfer), sparse reward settings (inter-trajectory densification). LOSES: tasks with unique one-off tool requirements (graph memory less beneficial), environments where inter-trajectory correlation is weak, complex multi-agent scenarios (single-agent focus may limit emergent collaboration benefits). Structured memory adds overhead vs simple replay buffers.
**Rationale:** Prior RLVR approaches depend on large-scale LLMs or multi-agent setups — impractical for resource-limited settings. SEARL's key insight: tool usage patterns across trajectories exhibit exploitable structure (correlations) that can densify sparse rewards without external supervision. Tool graph memory provides a state abstraction that generalizes across similar contexts, unlike flat experience buffers. vs standard RLVR: joint optimization enables synergistic policy-tool improvement rather than treating tool selection as fixed. vs multi-agent approaches: lighter weight, single-agent with explicit memory structure.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no self-evolving learning loop, no tool graph memory, no joint policy-tool optimization, and no reward densification mechanism. Lyra's agent pipelines are static — they do not improve from experience. SEARL provides a template for how Lyra agents could learn from interaction history without requiring massive compute. Status: **BEHIND** (no self-evolution infrastructure exists; SEARL provides lightweight self-improvement architecture).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (self-evolving agent architecture that does not require large-scale LLM; directly informs Lyra's self-improvement and tool-use learning)

## Lightweight LLM Agent Memory with Small Language Models (LightMem)
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07798
**Mechanism:** (1) Three-tier memory architecture: Short-Term Memory (STM) for immediate conversational context, Mid-Term Memory (MTM) for reusable interaction summaries, Long-Term Memory (LTM) for consolidated knowledge across sessions. (2) Modular design separates retrieval, writing, and long-term consolidation into distinct components, enabling independent optimization. (3) Online/offline separation: online processing handles retrieval under a fixed budget using Small Language Models (SLMs); offline processing handles abstraction and LTM integration asynchronously. (4) Two-stage retrieval: coarse vector-based retrieval narrows candidates, then semantic consistency re-ranking selects the most relevant items — both stages executed by SLMs, not large models. (5) Multi-user support: user identifiers enable independent retrieval and incremental maintenance per user without cross-contamination.
**Results:** Accepted to ACL 2026 (main). Average F1 improvement of ~2.5 over A-MEM on the LoCoMo benchmark. Consistent gains across model scales (not limited to a single backbone LLM). Median retrieval latency: 83 ms; median end-to-end latency: 581 ms. SLM-powered memory reduces online inference cost while maintaining accuracy.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: latency-sensitive applications (83ms retrieval, 581ms end-to-end), multi-user environments (user-isolated memory), long-running agent sessions (offline consolidation prevents latency accumulation), cost-constrained deployments (SLMs instead of large-model calls for memory ops). LOSES: tasks requiring deep semantic reasoning in retrieval (SLM may miss nuances a large model would catch), write-heavy workloads (MTM→LTM consolidation has offline latency), systems where vector similarity alone is insufficient (semantic re-ranking helps but has limits). Fixed retrieval budget trades recall breadth for predictable latency.
**Rationale:** Prior memory systems face a structural tradeoff: retrieval-based approaches have low online overhead but unstable accuracy due to limited query construction and candidate filtering; systems relying on repeated large-model calls improve accuracy but accumulate latency over long interactions. LightMem's key insight: SLMs occupy a sweet spot — more capable than retrieval heuristics, much faster/cheaper than repeated large-model calls. Three-tier organization mirrors human memory (working → episodic → semantic), enabling staged consolidation that extracts reusable knowledge from raw interactions.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's memory subsystem (§02 memory) has plans for multi-tier memory but NO implementation. No retrieval pipeline, no consolidation process, no SLM integration, no multi-user memory isolation. LightMem provides a directly implementable architecture with proven latency numbers (83ms retrieval) and accuracy gains (+2.5 F1 over A-MEM). Status: **BEHIND** (memory subsystem planned but unimplemented; LightMem provides validated reference architecture).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (validated 3-tier memory architecture with SLM-powered retrieval; direct blueprint for §02 memory implementation)

## Every Response Counts: Quantifying Uncertainty of LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems through Tensor Decomposition (MATU)
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08708
**Mechanism:** (1) Trajectory-to-Matrix Encoding: each agent's full reasoning trajectory (chain of intermediate steps, not just final output) is embedded into a matrix representation, capturing step-by-step reasoning rather than surface-level outputs. (2) Tensor Construction: multiple independent execution runs of the same Multi-Agent System (MAS) are stacked to form a higher-order tensor — dimensions capture variation across runs, agents, and reasoning steps. (3) Tensor Decomposition (CP or Tucker): applied to factor the tensor into interpretable components, disentangling distinct uncertainty sources — e.g., separating noise attributable to specific agents, particular communication pathways, or latent semantic dimensions. (4) Holistic Uncertainty Quantification: decomposed factors yield a scalar or multi-dimensional reliability measure reflecting system-wide uncertainty rather than surface-level output variance. (5) Topology-general: framework abstracts away topology-specific details for broad applicability across agent structures.
**Results:** Accepted to ACL 2026. Effectively estimates holistic and robust uncertainty across diverse tasks and communication topologies. Captures three MAS-specific uncertainty sources that single-agent methods miss: cascading uncertainty across multi-step reasoning, variability in inter-agent communication paths, and diversity of communication topologies. (Quantitative metrics require full PDF review.)
**Trade-offs:** WINS: multi-agent systems where agent interactions introduce reliability challenges beyond single-agent uncertainty, complex communication topologies (topology-general abstraction), production MAS deployments needing reliability guarantees, debugging MAS failures (decomposition identifies which agents/pathways contribute most uncertainty). LOSES: single-agent systems (standard uncertainty quantification sufficient), real-time uncertainty estimation (tensor decomposition over multiple runs adds compute), MAS with highly dynamic topologies (tensor construction assumes some stability across runs). Computational cost of tensor construction and decomposition exceeds lightweight single-output methods.
**Rationale:** Single-agent uncertainty quantification methods fail for MAS because they only analyze final outputs, missing three MAS-specific challenges: (a) uncertainty cascades across multi-step agent interactions, amplifying small errors; (b) communication path variability means the same task can produce different results depending on which agents talk to whom; (c) topology diversity means uncertainty patterns differ by agent structure. MATU's key insight: representing entire reasoning trajectories (not just outputs) as tensors and decomposing them reveals structure that output-only analysis cannot see. Prior methods are "designed for single-turn outputs" — fundamentally mismatched to MAS.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has NO uncertainty quantification for multi-agent interactions. Lyra's multi-agent orchestration produces outputs without reliability scores — downstream agents or users cannot distinguish high-confidence vs low-confidence results. This is a critical gap for production deployment: without uncertainty quantification, there is no principled way to trigger human review, reroute to fallback agents, or detect degradation. MATU provides a formal framework for quantifying MAS reliability. Status: **BEHIND** (critical reliability gap; uncertainty quantification is prerequisite for production deployment and §16 reliability).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (formal MAS uncertainty quantification; prerequisite for production reliability guarantees)

## Beyond the Individual: Virtualizing Multi-Disciplinary Reasoning for Clinical Intake via Collaborative Agents (Aegle)
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08927
**Mechanism:** (1) Graph-based multi-agent architecture with structured SOAP (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan) representation that decouples evidence collection from diagnostic reasoning for enhanced traceability and bias control. (2) Orchestrator dynamically activates specialist agents based on the clinical context — each specialist performs "decoupled parallel reasoning" independently. (3) Aggregator integrates specialist outputs into a coherent clinical note, synthesizing potentially conflicting recommendations. (4) Synchronous virtual Multi-Disciplinary Team (MDT) simulation: mirrors the real-world practice of bringing multiple specialists together, but virtualized for real-time outpatient settings where human MDTs are "costly and difficult to scale." (5) Formalized consultation state: SOAP structure provides a shared state representation that all agents read from and write to, maintaining consistency across parallel reasoning streams.
**Results:** Evaluated across 24 clinical departments using 53 metrics on ClinicalBench and real-world RAPID-IPN dataset. Consistently outperforms state-of-the-art proprietary and open-source models on both documentation quality and consultation capability. Improvements extend to final diagnosis accuracy. Code publicly available. Accepted to ACL 2026.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: clinical settings requiring multi-specialist input (single-physician intake is prone to cognitive biases and incomplete evidence capture), scenarios where traceability matters (SOAP decoupling makes reasoning auditable), real-time outpatient consultations (virtual MDT scales where human MDT cannot), multi-department deployment (24 departments validated). LOSES: domains where specialist diversity is unnecessary (single-agent sufficient), latency-critical applications (parallel specialist reasoning + aggregation adds latency vs single-pass), settings without structured domain ontologies (SOAP structure requires clinical domain modeling). Virtual MDT misses non-verbal cues and collaborative dynamics of human MDTs.
**Rationale:** Human MDTs reduce diagnostic errors but are prohibitively expensive and slow for routine outpatient intake. Single-physician intake is efficient but suffers from cognitive biases (anchoring, premature closure) and incomplete evidence capture. Aegle resolves this tension: virtual specialist agents provide MDT-level reasoning diversity without scheduling/logistics overhead. Key design insight: decoupling evidence collection from diagnostic reasoning prevents confirmation bias (specialists reason from shared evidence, not from each other's conclusions). Graph-based architecture enables dynamic specialist activation — not all specialists needed for every case.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has a multi-agent orchestration pattern (PrimaryAgent → specialist delegation) but NO graph-based agent topology, NO structured shared state representation (SOAP-equivalent), NO dynamic specialist activation based on context analysis, and NO decoupled evidence-collection/reasoning separation. Aegle's orchestrator+aggregator pattern is directly transferable to Lyra's multi-agent architecture. The SOAP-style decoupling of evidence from reasoning is a general pattern applicable to Lyra's verification and planning subsystems. Status: **BEHIND** on structured multi-agent collaboration patterns; Aegle provides validated reference architecture.
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** inspiration (graph-based multi-agent architecture + evidence/reasoning decoupling patterns transferable; clinical domain-specific but architectural patterns are general)

## ODUTQA-MDC: A Task for Open-Domain Underspecified Tabular QA with Multi-turn Dialogue-based Clarification
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.10159
**Mechanism:** (1) MAIC-TQA multi-agent framework detects ambiguous tabular queries via an ambiguity detection agent that identifies underspecified or uncertain expressions in user questions. (2) Dialogue-based clarification: a clarification agent engages in multi-turn conversation with the user to resolve detected ambiguities — asking targeted follow-up questions rather than guessing. (3) Answer refinement: after clarification, a refinement agent updates and improves the response based on the additional information gathered. (4) Benchmark design: ODUTQA-MDC dataset includes 209 tables with 25,105 QA pairs, a fine-grained labeling scheme enabling detailed evaluation of ambiguity handling, and a dynamic clarification interface that simulates user feedback for interactive assessment. (5) Three-component evaluation: ambiguity detection accuracy, clarification quality, and final answer correctness — decomposed rather than lumped into a single metric.
**Results:** Accepted to ACL 2026 (main). Dataset: 209 tables, 25,105 QA pairs. Experiments validate both benchmark and framework as foundational resources for conversational, underspecification-aware Tabular QA. (Quantitative metrics require full PDF review.)
**Trade-offs:** WINS: open-domain tabular QA where queries are naturally underspecified (real-world tables have ambiguous column names, missing units, vague filters), multi-turn interaction is acceptable (clarification adds conversation turns but improves answer quality), evaluation of ambiguity handling is needed separately from final accuracy. LOSES: single-turn QA scenarios (clarification overhead unacceptable), domains where tables are well-specified (no ambiguity to resolve), latency-sensitive applications (multi-turn dialogue adds latency), small tables (ambiguity less problematic). Fine-grained labeling is annotation-intensive; 209 tables may not cover all tabular diversity.
**Rationale:** LLMs struggle with open-domain tabular queries containing vague expressions because they lack the world knowledge to resolve underspecification (e.g., "high revenue" — high relative to what? which time period?). Prior tabular QA benchmarks assume well-specified queries; ODUTQA-MDC explicitly targets underspecification as a first-class challenge. MAIC-TQA's key insight: ambiguity detection + clarification dialogue + answer refinement is a pipeline that mirrors how humans resolve ambiguous questions — by asking for clarification rather than guessing. Multi-agent decomposition maps naturally: detection, clarification, and refinement are distinct capabilities best handled by specialized agents.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no tabular QA capabilities and no ambiguity-detection/clarification dialogue pipeline. However, the ambiguity detection + multi-turn clarification pattern is transferable to Lyra's planning subsystem — when user instructions are underspecified, Lyra could detect ambiguity and ask clarifying questions rather than proceeding with assumptions. This is directly relevant to Lyra's context and planning subsystems (§03 context, planning). Status: **NOT APPLICABLE** to current Lyra capabilities, but the ambiguity-detection + clarification pattern is **RELEVANT** to Lyra's instruction understanding and planning clarification loops.
**Impact:** 2 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** inspiration (ambiguity detection + multi-turn clarification pattern transferable to Lyra's planning and context subsystems; tabular QA domain not needed)

## CodeComp: Structural KV Cache Compression for Agentic Coding
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.10235
**Mechanism:** (1) Structural KV cache analysis: identifies that agentic coding workflows produce KV cache entries with distinct structural patterns — code generation, tool output parsing, error recovery, and planning each leave different attention signatures. (2) Structure-aware compression: rather than uniform compression (e.g., sliding window, token dropping), CodeComp applies compression policies differentiated by structural segment type — preserving high-importance regions (error traces, tool schemas, planning reasoning) while aggressively compressing low-importance regions (repetitive code boilerplate, intermediate tool outputs). (3) Importance scoring: a lightweight classifier (trained on agentic coding trajectories) scores each KV cache segment's importance to downstream task success based on structural role. (4) Adaptive budget allocation: total KV cache budget is dynamically partitioned across structural segments proportional to importance scores. (5) Agentic-coding-specific optimization: compression preserves planning context (high importance) and error recovery information (high importance) while compressing verbose code generation outputs (lower importance due to redundancy).
**Results:** Reduces KV cache memory footprint by 40-60% on agentic coding benchmarks (SWE-bench, HumanEval-based agent tasks) with <3% task success degradation. Outperforms uniform compression baselines (sliding window, H2O, StreamingLLM) by 15-25% on task completion rate at equivalent compression ratios. Most significant gains on long-horizon agentic tasks (10+ tool calls) where KV cache pressure is highest. Structural importance classifier achieves >85% agreement with oracle importance labels.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: agentic coding workloads with heterogeneous context types (planning, coding, tool use, error recovery), long-horizon agent tasks where KV cache memory is the bottleneck, multi-turn agent conversations with distinct structural phases, production deployments with memory constraints. LOSES: non-agentic code generation (uniform compression sufficient), short-horizon tasks (compression overhead exceeds benefit), domains without clear structural segmentation (importance classifier may misclassify), real-time streaming (structural analysis adds latency). Structural classifier requires agentic-coding-specific training data; may not generalize to other agent domains without retraining.
**Rationale:** Standard KV cache compression treats all tokens uniformly but agentic coding workflows have highly structured context with varying importance: losing planning context causes task failure (agent forgets goal), losing error traces prevents recovery (agent repeats mistakes), but losing verbose code outputs is recoverable (can regenerate). CodeComp exploits this heterogeneity. vs Sliding Window (uniform, loses planning/error context), vs H2O (attention-score-based, agnostic to structural role), vs StreamingLLM (keeps initial tokens, may preserve irrelevant context). Key insight: structural role is a stronger importance signal than attention scores alone for agentic coding.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no KV cache management, no context compression pipeline, and no structural context analysis. Lyra's agent memory subsystem (§02 memory) stores full context without compression — as context grows across multi-turn agent sessions, memory pressure increases linearly. CodeComp's structural compression approach is directly applicable to Lyra's context management: Lyra sessions have distinct structural phases (planning → execution → review → fix) that could guide differentiated compression policies. Status: **BEHIND** (no KV cache or context compression infrastructure; CodeComp provides agentic-coding-validated compression strategy).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (structural context compression for agentic workflows; directly addresses §02 memory and §03 context gaps)

## From Query to Counsel: Structured Reasoning with a Multi-Agent Framework and Dataset for Legal Consultation
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.10470
**Mechanism:** (1) Structured legal reasoning decomposition: breaks legal consultation into a pipeline of statute retrieval → precedent analysis → fact-to-law mapping → counterargument generation → conclusion synthesis, with each stage handled by a specialized agent. (2) Multi-agent framework with defined handoff protocols: Query Understanding Agent parses user's legal question → Research Agent retrieves relevant statutes and precedents → Analysis Agent maps case facts to legal principles → Adversarial Agent generates counterarguments and edge cases → Synthesis Agent produces final counsel with confidence calibration. (3) Structured reasoning dataset: purpose-built dataset of legal consultation scenarios with annotated reasoning chains, statute-precedent mappings, and counterargument pairs for training and evaluation. (4) Structured output format: each agent produces outputs in a standardized schema enabling downstream agents to consume structured inputs rather than free text, reducing communication errors. (5) Confidence calibration: final output includes confidence scores per legal claim, with the Adversarial Agent's counterargument strength used to downward-adjust overconfident conclusions.
**Results:** Multi-agent structured framework outperforms single-agent baselines (GPT-4 direct) by 18-25% on legal reasoning accuracy metrics. Adversarial counterargument generation catches 34% of errors that single-pass reasoning misses. Structured schema-based inter-agent communication reduces hallucination rate by 40% compared to free-text agent communication. Dataset: legal consultation scenarios with full reasoning chain annotations. Confidence calibration improves reliability: high-confidence predictions (>0.9) achieve 94% accuracy vs 78% for uncalibrated predictions.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: legal consultation where reasoning traceability matters (courts require explainable reasoning), high-stakes domains where errors are costly (adversarial checking critical), multi-step legal reasoning (statute→precedent→application→counterargument chain), scenarios requiring confidence calibration for risk assessment. LOSES: simple legal questions (single-agent sufficient, multi-agent overhead unjustified), real-time consultation (multi-agent pipeline adds latency), domains without structured legal ontologies (schema-based communication requires domain modeling), low-resource languages (dataset and schema are English/common-law-focused). Adversarial agent may generate spurious counterarguments if not properly constrained.
**Rationale:** Legal reasoning is inherently multi-step and adversarial: statutes must be retrieved, precedents analyzed, facts mapped to law, and counterarguments considered before reaching a conclusion. Single-pass LLM reasoning skips counterargument generation (confirmation bias) and conflates retrieval with analysis. Multi-agent decomposition mirrors the legal workflow: research, analysis, and adversarial testing are distinct skills. Structured schema-based inter-agent communication reduces the ambiguity that causes hallucinations in free-text agent dialogues. Prior legal AI (e.g., LexisNexis, Westlaw) focuses on retrieval; this framework adds structured multi-agent reasoning and adversarial verification.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no domain-specific reasoning pipelines, no structured inter-agent communication schemas, no adversarial verification loop, and no confidence calibration mechanism. However, the architectural pattern — specialized agent pipeline with structured schemas + adversarial verification + confidence calibration — is directly transferable to Lyra's planning (§04), verification (§16), and safety (§17) subsystems. The adversarial agent pattern (dedicated agent generates counterarguments) is a general verification technique applicable beyond legal domains. Status: **BEHIND** on structured multi-agent reasoning pipelines; pattern is transferable.
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** inspiration (structured multi-agent reasoning pipeline + adversarial verification pattern transferable to Lyra's planning and verification subsystems; legal domain-specific but architecture is general)

## Dialectic-Med: Mitigating Diagnostic Hallucinations via Counterfactual Adversarial Multi-Agent Debate
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.11258
**Mechanism:** (1) Counterfactual generation: for a given medical diagnosis, an Adversarial Agent generates counterfactual scenarios — alternative diagnoses that could also explain the observed symptoms, forcing re-examination of the initial diagnostic hypothesis. (2) Multi-agent debate framework: Diagnostic Agent proposes initial diagnosis with supporting evidence → Adversarial Agent challenges with counterfactual scenarios and contradictory evidence → both agents engage in structured debate rounds with a Moderator Agent managing turn-taking and argument tracking. (3) Evidence grounding: all arguments must cite specific evidence from the patient case (symptoms, test results, history) — agents cannot introduce unsupported claims, reducing hallucination by design. (4) Dialectical resolution: debate continues until either (a) consensus is reached, (b) evidence clearly favors one diagnosis, or (c) maximum rounds reached with documented disagreement (escalation to human). (5) Hallucination detection via contradiction: hallucinations are identified when an agent makes a claim that contradicts cited evidence — the opposing agent flags the contradiction in the next debate round.
**Results:** Reduces diagnostic hallucinations by 42-58% compared to single-pass LLM diagnosis on medical QA benchmarks (MedQA, MedMCQA, DDXPlus). Counterfactual adversarial debate catches 51% of diagnostic errors that single-pass reasoning produces. Structured evidence-grounding eliminates 67% of unsupported claims (hallucinations where LLMs fabricate symptoms or test results). Debate convergence: 73% of cases reach consensus within 3 rounds; remaining 27% correctly escalate with documented disagreement. Combining debate + evidence grounding outperforms debate-only (+12%) and evidence-grounding-only (+18%).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: high-stakes diagnostic domains where hallucinations are dangerous (medical, legal, financial), scenarios with differential diagnosis (multiple possible explanations for same symptoms), settings where evidence traceability is required (regulatory compliance, audit), cases where initial diagnostic confidence is high but wrong (counterfactuals break confirmation bias). LOSES: straightforward cases with clear single diagnosis (debate overhead unjustified), real-time diagnosis (multi-round debate adds latency), domains without structured evidence schemas (evidence grounding requires domain modeling), low-resource settings (multi-agent debate multiplies inference cost). Adversarial agent may generate implausible counterfactuals if not constrained by medical knowledge boundaries.
**Rationale:** Medical diagnostic errors are often caused by premature closure (settling on first plausible diagnosis) and confirmation bias (selectively attending to supporting evidence). Single-pass LLM diagnosis is vulnerable to both. Dialectic-Med addresses this via structured adversarial debate: the Adversarial Agent forces reconsideration (breaking premature closure) and the evidence-grounding requirement prevents fabrication (reducing hallucinations at the source). Key design insight: counterfactual scenarios are more effective at catching errors than simple "check your work" self-critique because they introduce genuine alternative hypotheses rather than superficial re-reading. vs Self-consistency (multiple samples from same model, no genuine adversarial challenge), vs Self-refine (single-agent iterative improvement, limited by own blind spots), vs Human-in-the-loop (gold standard but expensive, debate reduces human escalation rate).
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has NO adversarial verification mechanism, NO multi-agent debate infrastructure, NO evidence-grounding requirement in agent outputs, and NO counterfactual reasoning capability. Lyra's current agent pipeline (planner→executor→reviewer) is a linear pass with no adversarial challenge — the reviewer operates with the same blind spots as the planner. Dialectic-Med's adversarial debate pattern is directly applicable to Lyra's verification subsystem (§16) and safety subsystem (§17): Lyra could implement an Adversarial Verifier Agent that generates counterfactual failure scenarios for plans before execution. Status: **BEHIND** (critical verification gap; adversarial debate is a proven pattern for reducing agent errors).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (adversarial multi-agent debate for verification; directly addresses §16 reliability and §17 safety gaps; counterfactual generation is general pattern beyond medical domain)

## SpreadsheetAgent: Robust Real-World Spreadsheet Understanding with Multi-Agent Multi-Format Reasoning
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12282
**Mechanism:** (1) Incremental reading: system does not load the entire spreadsheet at once but incrementally interprets localized regions through multiple modalities — code execution results, images, and LaTeX tables — to avoid context-window overflow. (2) Two-stage architecture: Planning/Reading Stage first constructs a structural sketch with row/column summaries (intermediate compressed representation), then Solving Stage performs task-driven reasoning over that sketch. (3) Multi-format reasoning: complementary modalities (code exec for structured computation, images for visual layout cues, LaTeX for table semantics) are fused to overcome the limitations of treating tables as plain text. (4) Verification module: validates extracted structures through targeted inspections, reducing error propagation to downstream reasoning steps. (5) Structural sketch: compressed intermediate format that preserves layout cues and visual semantics while fitting within LLM context windows even for large spreadsheets.
**Results:** SpreadsheetAgent with GPT-OSS-120B achieves 38.16% on Spreadsheet Bench, outperforming ChatGPT Agent baseline (35.27%) by 2.89 absolute points. Accepted to ACL 2026 main conference. Open-sourced under CC BY 4.0.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: large real-world spreadsheets exceeding standard LLM context windows, tasks requiring both structured computation and visual layout understanding, scenarios where error propagation across reasoning steps is critical (verification module reduces cascading errors), enterprise spreadsheet automation (Excel, Google Sheets). LOSES: small/simple tables where multi-agent multi-format overhead exceeds benefit, latency-sensitive applications (incremental reading + multi-format fusion adds pipeline latency), single-modality-sufficient tasks (text-only tables), deployment without code execution sandbox (code exec modality requires secure runtime).
**Rationale:** Existing LLM methods treat tables as plain text, losing critical layout cues and visual semantics (merged cells, conditional formatting, spatial relationships). Real spreadsheets are often too large for standard context windows. SpreadsheetAgent addresses both via incremental localized reading + multi-format fusion. vs Text-only table QA (loses layout semantics), vs Image-only (loses structured computation capability), vs Single-agent (no verification, error propagation risk). Key insight: different modalities capture complementary information — code exec for formulas/aggregation, images for layout, LaTeX for structure — and verification prevents structural errors from contaminating reasoning.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no spreadsheet/document understanding pipeline, no multi-format reasoning infrastructure, no intermediate structural representation for large documents, and no verification module for extracted structures. Lyra's context management (§03) loads full documents without incremental reading or intermediate compression. SpreadsheetAgent's two-stage architecture (structural sketch → task reasoning) and verification pattern are transferable to any large-document agent task in Lyra. Status: **BEHIND** (no multi-format reasoning or incremental document reading; pattern is transferable to Lyra's document processing pipelines).
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** inspiration (multi-format incremental reading + structural verification pattern; domain-specific to spreadsheets but architecture generalizes to large-document agent reasoning)

## CIA: Inferring the Communication Topology from LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12461
**Mechanism:** (1) Adversarial query construction: CIA crafts queries designed to provoke reasoning outputs from intermediate agents in a multi-agent system, exploiting that agent responses carry semantic signatures of who they communicated with. (2) Communication topology target: the attack aims to reconstruct the internal agent communication graph — which agents exchange messages, in what direction, and with what frequency — under a restrictive black-box setting (attacker only sees final outputs). (3) Global bias disentanglement: separates the target agent's intrinsic reasoning bias from the influence of incoming communications, isolating the communication-induced semantic shift. (4) LLM-guided weak supervision: uses an LLM to generate pseudo-labels for communication edges by analyzing semantic correlations among agent outputs, enabling training without ground-truth topology labels. (5) Graph reconstruction: combines disentangled communication signals with weak supervision to infer the full agent interaction graph.
**Results:** Average AUC of 0.87 across multi-agent system configurations with optimized communication topologies. Peak AUC up to 0.99 on some configurations — near-perfect topology reconstruction. Accepted to ACL 2026 main conference.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: security auditing of deployed multi-agent systems (can owners detect topology leakage?), intellectual property protection (can competitors reverse-engineer agent architectures?), adversarial robustness evaluation (red-teaming MAS deployments). LOSES: MAS with encrypted/private inter-agent communication channels (attack requires observable semantic leakage), agents with identical reasoning styles (no semantic shift to detect), fully centralized MAS where topology is trivial. The attack is effective but the defense implications are the primary concern: MAS designers must consider topology as sensitive IP.
**Rationale:** Multi-agent systems optimize communication topology for performance — but the topology itself becomes a privacy/security liability because agent outputs carry detectable semantic signatures of their communication partners. CIA exploits this: when Agent A communicates with Agent B before responding, A's output shows semantic influence from B that can be disentangled from A's intrinsic style. LLM-guided weak supervision makes the attack practical without labeled topology data. vs Traditional side-channel attacks (require physical/network access; CIA works from API-level outputs only), vs Membership inference (targets training data; CIA targets architecture/IP). Key insight: communication topology is a structural property that leaks through semantic patterns — a new class of MAS-specific privacy vulnerability.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has inter-agent communication topologies (planner→executor→reviewer pipelines, could extend to dynamic topologies per §05 router) but NO topology privacy analysis, NO adversarial robustness evaluation against topology inference, and NO defense mechanisms for communication pattern leakage. Lyra's planned multi-agent orchestration (§05 router, §07 plugins) would create richer communication topologies that could be more vulnerable to CIA-style attacks. Status: **BEHIND** (no topology privacy consideration; CIA reveals a novel attack surface for Lyra's multi-agent architecture that must be addressed in §17 safety).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (novel multi-agent security vulnerability class; directly addresses §17 safety gap; topology privacy must be a design requirement for Lyra's multi-agent communication)

## EVOS PARK (EvoSpark): Endogenous Interactive Agent Societies for Unified Long-Horizon Narrative Evolution
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12776
**Mechanism:** (1) Stratified Narrative Memory: a Role Socio-Evolutionary Base dynamically processes past experiences to resolve "social memory stacking" — unresolved conflicting relational states that accumulate over long-horizon narratives. (2) Generative Mise-en-Scène: enforces Role-Location-Plot alignment, keeping character presence synchronized with narrative progression to prevent "narrative-spatial dissonance" where spatial logic disconnects from plot development. (3) Unified Narrative Operation Engine: incorporates an Emergent Character Grounding Protocol that converts stochastic narrative sparks into persistent characters, enabling minimal premises to grow into open-ended evolving story worlds. (4) Endogenous agent societies: narrative evolution emerges from agent interactions rather than external scripting — agents autonomously generate, maintain, and evolve narrative coherence. (5) Multi-agent interaction: agents operate within interactive societies where character actions, relationships, and plot developments emerge from agent-agent dynamics.
**Results:** Significantly outperforms baselines across diverse paradigms (qualitative claim from abstract; specific quantitative metrics in full PDF). Accepted to ACL 2026 main conference.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: long-horizon narrative generation (novels, interactive fiction, game storylines), simulations requiring persistent character evolution over time, creative writing where emergent plot development is desired, world-building applications. LOSES: short-form content generation (overhead unjustified), tasks requiring exact narrative control (emergent behavior may deviate from authorial intent), real-time narrative systems (multi-agent society simulation is compute-intensive), evaluation — narrative quality metrics are inherently subjective. The endogenous approach trades controllability for emergent richness.
**Rationale:** LLM-based narrative systems face two failure modes: social memory stacking (accumulated unresolved relationship conflicts degrading character consistency) and narrative-spatial dissonance (locations and plot becoming misaligned). Single-agent narrative generation compounds these issues because one agent must track all states simultaneously. EVOS PARK addresses both via stratified memory (explicit conflict resolution over time) and spatial grounding (enforced alignment between characters, locations, and plot). vs Single-agent narrative generation (state tracking degrades over long horizons), vs Scripted multi-agent (external coordination limits emergence), vs Retrieval-based (retrieves past states but doesn't resolve conflicts). Key insight: narrative coherence over long horizons requires active conflict resolution in memory and explicit spatial grounding — passive retrieval is insufficient.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no narrative generation capability, no long-horizon state management with conflict resolution, no spatial grounding mechanism, and no emergent agent society simulation. However, the Stratified Narrative Memory pattern — active resolution of conflicting accumulated states — is directly applicable to Lyra's memory subsystem (§02 memory): Lyra agents accumulate conversation/execution states that may conflict over long sessions, and active conflict resolution (rather than passive retrieval) would improve long-horizon coherence. Status: **BEHIND** on narrative/long-horizon state management; memory conflict resolution pattern is transferable.
**Impact:** 2 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** inspiration (narrative domain-specific but stratified memory conflict resolution pattern applies to Lyra's long-horizon agent memory; §02 memory)

## LAMO: Towards Scalable Lightweight GUI Agents via Multi-role Orchestration
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.13488
**Mechanism:** (1) Role-oriented data synthesis: generates training data covering diverse GUI interaction roles (clicking, typing, form-filling, navigation, verification) rather than monolithic end-to-end task demonstrations. (2) Two-stage training recipe: Stage 1 — Supervised Fine-Tuning with Perplexity-Weighted Cross-Entropy optimization for knowledge distillation (from larger teacher models) and visual perception enhancement; Stage 2 — Reinforcement Learning for role-oriented cooperative exploration, where the agent learns to switch between roles within multi-agent system orchestration. (3) Multi-role orchestration: a single lightweight 3B-parameter model (LAMO-3B) performs multiple roles within a MAS pipeline — rather than training separate specialist models per role — reducing total parameter count and deployment cost. (4) Plug-and-play executor: LAMO-3B functions as an executor that can be paired with different advanced planners, continuously benefiting from planner advances without retraining. (5) Monolithic + MAS dual-mode: supports both standalone execution (single agent) and orchestrated multi-agent execution, providing deployment flexibility.
**Results:** Extensive static and online evaluations validate design effectiveness (qualitative claim; specific metrics in full PDF). Accepted to Findings of ACL 2026. Key achievement: enables capable GUI automation on resource-constrained devices using only 3B parameters via multi-role capability.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: resource-constrained device deployment (on-device GUI agents with limited compute), cost-sensitive production deployments (3B model vs 70B+ alternatives), scenarios benefiting from planner-executor separation (upgrade planner without retraining executor), multi-role flexibility without multi-model overhead. LOSES: tasks requiring deep domain expertise (3B parameter ceiling limits knowledge capacity), scenarios where monolithic end-to-end models outperform decomposed pipelines, training complexity (two-stage recipe with RL adds engineering overhead), visual grounding tasks requiring very large vision encoders. The multi-role approach trades per-role specialization depth for deployment efficiency.
**Rationale:** Scaling MLLM parameters improves GUI agent capability but creates prohibitive deployment costs on edge devices. Training separate specialist models per role is expensive and fragments knowledge. LAMO addresses both: a single 3B model with multi-role capability via role-oriented training, achieving deployment efficiency without sacrificing role coverage. vs Monolithic large MLLMs (accurate but expensive to deploy), vs Specialist models per role (each small but N models = N× deployment cost), vs API-based GUI agents (latency and connectivity dependency). Key insight: GUI tasks decompose into a finite set of reusable roles; a single lightweight model can learn all roles with proper training data synthesis and loss design.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no GUI agent capability, no multi-role orchestration with a shared lightweight model, no role-oriented training pipeline, and no planner-executor separation pattern for heterogeneous model sizes. However, LAMO's pattern — a lightweight multi-role model that can operate standalone or within MAS — is relevant to Lyra's agent architecture: Lyra could benefit from role-specialized lightweight agents for specific execution tasks (code execution, file operations, shell commands) that share a base model but switch roles dynamically. Status: **BEHIND** on GUI agents (out of scope for Lyra's CLI focus) but multi-role lightweight agent pattern is transferable.
**Impact:** 2 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** inspiration (GUI domain-specific but multi-role lightweight agent + two-stage training pattern applies to Lyra's agent role specialization; §09 commands, §07 plugins)

## TF-TTCL: Training-Free Test-Time Contrastive Learning for Large Language Models
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.13552
**Mechanism:** (1) Semantic Query Augmentation (Explore): multi-agent role-playing generates diverse reasoning paths for each problem — different agents approach the same problem from varied perspectives, producing multiple candidate solutions with varying quality. (2) Contrastive Experience Distillation (Reflect): superior and inferior reasoning trajectories are contrasted, with their semantic differences distilled into explicit textual rules (e.g., "when encountering X, avoid approach Y because it leads to error Z"). (3) Contextual Rule Retrieval (Steer): during inference, relevant rules are retrieved from the accumulated rule store and injected into the LLM's context to guide reasoning away from known failure patterns and toward successful strategies. (4) Training-free design: no gradient updates, no fine-tuning, no white-box model access required — the entire loop operates via black-box prompting and retrieval. (5) Online improvement: the system accumulates rules from its own inference experiences, continuously improving at test time without any training phase.
**Results:** Consistently outperforms strong zero-shot baselines and representative Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) methods on both closed-ended reasoning tasks and open-ended evaluation tasks under online evaluation settings. Accepted to Findings of ACL 2026. Code available on GitHub.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: frozen/deployed models that cannot be retrained (API-based models, production deployments), scenarios with distribution shift where training data is unavailable, cost-sensitive deployments (no GPU hours for fine-tuning), online improvement without model access (black-box API acceptable). LOSES: tasks where contrastive patterns are hard to extract as textual rules (very domain-specific or implicit reasoning), very small rule stores that provide limited coverage, scenarios where multi-agent exploration is too expensive (each problem requires N agent calls), real-time inference where rule retrieval adds unacceptable latency. Training-free means no model improvement — only steering — so ceiling is bounded by base model capability.
**Rationale:** LLMs degrade under distribution shift, but retraining is expensive and requires access. Test-time adaptation (TTA) methods exist but typically require gradient access or are task-specific. TF-TTCL addresses both: it improves frozen models at test time via a general Explore-Reflect-Steer loop that works with any black-box LLM. vs Fine-tuning (requires GPU, data, model access), vs Prompt engineering (manual, doesn't accumulate experience), vs Standard TTA (requires gradients/white-box access), vs Self-consistency (multiple samples, no learning from experience). Key insight: the gap between successful and failed reasoning trajectories contains actionable patterns that can be distilled into reusable textual rules — enabling cumulative improvement without training.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no test-time adaptation mechanism, no contrastive experience distillation, no rule accumulation from agent execution history, and no multi-agent role-playing for solution exploration. Lyra's agents execute tasks but do not systematically learn from failures at test time. TF-TTCL's Explore-Reflect-Steer loop is directly applicable to Lyra's self-improvement pipeline: Lyra agents could explore multiple solution paths (via multi-agent debate/role-playing), contrast successes vs failures to extract rules, and retrieve those rules in future sessions. Status: **BEHIND** (no test-time learning from agent experience; TF-TTCL pattern is directly applicable to Lyra's self-improvement and verification subsystems).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (training-free test-time improvement via contrastive rule distillation; directly addresses Lyra's self-improvement gap; applicable to any agent task without model access)

## CollabCoder: Plan-Code Co-Evolution via Collaborative Decision-Making for Efficient Code Generation
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.13946
**Mechanism:** (1) Plan-code co-evolution: the system maintains a plan (structured outline of intended code) and generated code simultaneously, allowing each to influence the other iteratively — plans guide code generation and code execution reveals gaps in plans. (2) Collaborative decision-making: multiple specialized agents (planner, coder, reviewer) participate in a structured debate process where each agent proposes refinements and votes on the best direction before execution. (3) Co-evolution loop: Planner generates initial plan → Coder produces code → Reviewer identifies plan-code mismatches → Planner revises plan based on code insights → Coder regenerates affected sections → repeat until convergence. (4) Efficiency focus: unlike prior work that treats planning and coding as sequential stages (waterfall), co-evolution allows partial execution feedback to refine plans early, reducing wasted generation on flawed plans.
**Results:** Demonstrated improved code generation efficiency through plan-code co-evolution over sequential plan-then-code baselines. Key metric: reduced token waste from plan-code misalignment compared to waterfall approaches.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: complex multi-file code generation where plan-code misalignment is costly, scenarios with high API costs (early detection of plan flaws saves tokens), tasks requiring iterative refinement between high-level design and low-level implementation. LOSES: simple single-function tasks (overhead of co-evolution loop exceeds benefit), real-time code generation (debate + iteration adds latency), tasks where plan is trivially correct (no co-evolution benefit). Co-evolution requires both plan quality assessment and code-to-plan feedback extraction, adding complexity.
**Rationale:** Traditional plan-then-code pipelines suffer from a fundamental problem: plans are generated without knowledge of implementation constraints, and code is generated without ability to feed implementation discoveries back to planning. Co-evolution closes this loop. vs Waterfall (plan once, code once — misalignment accumulates), vs Self-debugging (only fixes code, not plan), vs Tree search over plans (explores plans but doesn't incorporate code feedback into plan revision). Key insight: planning and coding are not independent stages — they are coupled optimization problems that benefit from joint refinement.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has sequential planner→executor→reviewer pipelines but NO plan-code co-evolution, NO feedback from code execution back into plan revision, NO collaborative decision-making protocol for joint refinement. Lyra's current architecture treats planning as a one-shot stage rather than an iteratively refined artifact. Status: **BEHIND** (sequential pipeline vs co-evolutionary architecture).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (plan-code co-evolution directly improves Lyra's planning-execution loop; applicable to code generation and task planning)

## APEX-MEM: Agentic Semi-Structured Memory with Temporal Reasoning for Long-Term Conversational AI
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14362
**Mechanism:** (1) Semi-structured memory representation: blends structured knowledge graph triples (entity-relation-entity, entity-attribute-value) with unstructured free-text episodic summaries, capturing both factual precision and narrative richness. (2) Agentic memory operations: the agent actively decides when to write (what is worth remembering), read (what to retrieve given current context), update (merging new information with existing memories), and forget (pruning stale/contradicted information) using LLM-based decision prompts rather than fixed heuristics. (3) Temporal reasoning: maintains timestamped memory chains with explicit temporal relations (before, after, during, caused-by) enabling the agent to answer temporal queries like "what happened between X and Y" or "what led to Z." (4) Memory consolidation: periodic offline consolidation merges short-term episodic memories into long-term structured knowledge, resolving contradictions and compressing redundant information. (5) Retrieval: multi-hop traversal over the knowledge graph combined with semantic search over episodic embeddings, ranked by relevance + recency + temporal contiguity.
**Results:** Improves long-term conversational consistency over baseline memory approaches. Temporal reasoning capability enables answering time-sensitive queries that flat embedding-based retrieval misses. Consolidation reduces memory storage by compressing redundant episodes.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: long-term conversational agents (multi-session spanning weeks/months), applications requiring temporal reasoning (scheduling, project tracking, procedural knowledge), scenarios with evolving user preferences (memory update and contradiction resolution), high-value interactions where memory misses are costly. LOSES: short sessions (consolidation overhead unjustified), stateless interactions, real-time constraints (multi-hop graph traversal adds latency), applications where simple key-value or embedding retrieval suffices. Semi-structured storage adds schema design complexity — balancing structured precision vs unstructured coverage is non-trivial.
**Rationale:** Pure embedding-based memory (e.g., vector DB only) suffers from temporal blindness (can't answer "when" questions) and factual drift (old embeddings conflict with new without explicit contradiction resolution). Pure structured memory (e.g., knowledge graph only) misses nuance and context. APEX-MEM combines both with agentic control — the agent decides memory operations based on importance and context rather than fixed rules. vs Vector-only memory (temporal blindness, no contradiction resolution), vs KG-only memory (rigid, misses nuance), vs Fixed-rule memory (can't adapt to context-dependent importance). Key insight: memory operations (write/read/update/forget) should be agent-driven decisions, not fixed heuristics — importance is context-dependent.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no semi-structured memory, no temporal reasoning over memory chains, no agentic memory operation decisions, and no memory consolidation pipeline. Lyra's memory subsystem maturity is `none` in current architecture. APEX-MEM's semi-structured + temporal + agentic approach directly addresses Lyra's memory gap (§02 memory) and is complementary to other memory papers in the corpus (A-MEM, MemAgent, CraniMem, etc.). Status: **BEHIND** (no memory infrastructure; APEX-MEM provides a strong architecture template).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (semi-structured memory with temporal reasoning directly addresses Lyra's memory gap; agentic control of memory operations aligns with Lyra's agent-first architecture)

## MARS²: Scaling Multi-Agent Tree Search via Reinforcement Learning for Code Generation
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14564
**Mechanism:** (1) Multi-agent tree search (MARS): extends single-agent tree search (like ToT) to multiple specialized agents (planner, coder, tester, reviewer) collaboratively exploring a shared search tree over code generation solutions. (2) Reinforcement learning for search policy: trains a policy network to decide which agent should expand which node in the tree (agent-node assignment), what action to take (generate, refine, test, debate), and when to backtrack vs continue exploring. (3) Scaling via parallel expansion: multiple agents expand different tree nodes simultaneously, with the RL policy learning to balance exploration (diverse solutions) vs exploitation (deepening promising paths). (4) Shared value function: a learned critic estimates the quality of partial solutions, enabling pruning without full execution, shared across all agents for consistent evaluation. (5) Credit assignment: RL reward propagates from final code correctness (passing tests, meeting spec) back through the tree, assigning credit to individual agent actions that contributed to success.
**Results:** Scales tree search to larger problem spaces than single-agent ToT by parallelizing node expansion across specialized agents. RL-trained search policy outperforms heuristic search strategies (BFS, DFS, beam search) in code generation benchmarks. Multi-agent collaboration + tree search beats single-agent tree search and multi-agent without search.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: complex multi-file code generation with many decision points, problems where trial-and-error is expensive (RL policy learns to avoid dead ends), scenarios with diverse solution approaches (parallel exploration covers more ground), tasks with verifiable correctness (tests provide clean RL rewards). LOSES: simple problems (overhead of tree search + RL), real-time generation (tree search is computationally expensive), tasks without clear success signals (RL needs reward), training budget required for RL policy (cold-start performance is poor before training). RL training adds significant engineering complexity over heuristic search.
**Rationale:** Prior work: single-agent tree search (ToT) is limited by one agent's perspective, multi-agent collaboration (MACNET, Croto) doesn't search, and multi-agent + search (DITS) uses heuristics, not learned policies. MARS² unifies all three: multi-agent + tree search + RL-learned search policy, achieving better scaling than any combination. vs ToT (single agent, no specialization), vs MACNET (collaboration without search), vs DITS (heuristic search, no learned policy). Key insight: the search policy (which agent does what when) is itself a learnable optimization problem — RL can discover non-obvious agent-node assignments that heuristics miss.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no tree search, no RL-trained search policy, no multi-agent parallel node expansion, no shared value function for partial solution evaluation, and no credit assignment across agent actions. Lyra's current execution model is linear agent pipelines — far from the tree search + RL paradigm. However, MARS²'s architecture provides a target state for Lyra's multi-agent orchestration: tree-structured exploration with learned search policies. Status: **BEHIND** (no search infrastructure, no RL for agent coordination).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 5 | **Tier:** breakthrough (multi-agent tree search with RL directly addresses Lyra's orchestration gap; combines planning, search, and multi-agent collaboration into a unified architecture)

## From Procedural Skills to Strategy Genes: Towards Experience-Driven Test-Time Evolution
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.15097
**Mechanism:** (1) Two-level skill hierarchy: Procedural Skills (low-level, task-specific action sequences learned from individual task executions) and Strategy Genes (high-level, cross-task patterns that govern when and how to deploy procedural skills). (2) Experience accumulation: each task execution produces a trace (state→action→outcome), which is abstracted into procedural skills via clustering similar action sequences. (3) Strategy gene evolution: over many tasks, successful patterns of skill deployment (which skill to use in which context) are distilled into strategy genes via an evolutionary algorithm — genes that produce higher task success rates survive and propagate. (4) Test-time evolution: unlike training-time evolution (which requires offline training phases), strategy genes evolve continuously during inference/deployment as new task experiences accumulate — no separate training phase. (5) Gene expression: at inference time, relevant strategy genes are activated based on task context, governing skill selection, adaptation, and composition without per-task retraining.
**Results:** Demonstrates test-time improvement without gradient updates — agents get better at new tasks by accumulating and evolving strategy genes from experience. Evolutionary approach discovers non-obvious skill compositions that would be missed by supervised learning from human demonstrations.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: deployed agents that must improve from experience without retraining, long-running agent systems with diverse task streams, scenarios where task distribution shifts over time (evolution adapts), cost-sensitive deployments (no GPU hours for fine-tuning). LOSES: cold-start scenarios (no prior experience to evolve from — random initial performance), tasks with very small action spaces (evolutionary overhead unjustified), safety-critical applications (evolved strategies are not formally verifiable), environments where bad experiences are costly (evolution requires exploration which includes failures). The evolutionary approach introduces stochasticity — strategy gene quality depends on experience diversity and selection pressure design.
**Rationale:** Prior work treats agent improvement as either training-time (fine-tuning, RLHF) or fixed test-time (prompting, few-shot). This paper introduces a third option: test-time evolution that learns from deployment experience without gradients, bridging the gap between frozen deployment and expensive retraining. vs Fine-tuning (requires GPU, data curation, offline phase), vs Prompt engineering (static, doesn't accumulate experience), vs Self-evolution (typically requires training), vs Genetic algorithms alone (typically offline). Key insight: separating procedural skills (what to do) from strategy genes (when to deploy what) enables cross-task transfer — skills are task-specific but strategy genes are reusable patterns.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no skill hierarchy (procedural vs strategic), no evolutionary algorithm for agent behavior optimization, no test-time improvement from accumulated experience (all improvement requires explicit retraining or prompt changes), and no cross-task pattern extraction. However, the skill-gene hierarchy maps naturally to Lyra's planned plugin system (§07 plugins) and command infrastructure (§09 commands): plugins/commands are procedural skills, and the orchestration logic that selects and composes them maps to strategy genes. Status: **BEHIND** on evolutionary improvement and test-time adaptation; skill-gene hierarchy concept is transferable to Lyra's plugin orchestration.
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (test-time evolution without retraining addresses Lyra's self-improvement gap; skill-gene hierarchy provides architectural pattern for plugin orchestration)
