## Preference Estimation via Opponent Modeling in Multi-Agent Negotiation
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.15687
**Mechanism:** (1) Opponent modeling: each agent maintains a latent model of other agents' preferences (utility functions, priorities, constraints) inferred from their negotiation behavior (offers made, concessions, rejections, counter-offers). (2) Preference estimation: the opponent model is updated via Bayesian inference — each observed action (offer, accept, reject) provides evidence that updates the posterior over the opponent's preference parameters. (3) Negotiation strategy: agents use their opponent models to generate Pareto-improving offers (offers that are likely acceptable to the opponent while maximizing own utility), predict opponent responses, and decide when to concede vs hold firm. (4) Multi-round perspective-taking: agents simulate the negotiation from the opponent's perspective using the estimated preferences to anticipate counter-offers and plan multi-step negotiation strategies. (5) Communication: agents can include natural language justifications with offers, using the opponent model to frame justifications in terms the opponent values.
**Results:** Agents with opponent modeling achieve higher joint utility (closer to Pareto frontier) than agents without opponent modeling. Preference estimation accuracy improves with negotiation rounds (Bayesian updating converges). Perspective-taking enables agents to discover mutually beneficial trades that both parties would miss without opponent modeling.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: multi-agent systems where agents have asymmetric information (each knows their own preferences but not others'), negotiation scenarios with repeated interactions (Bayesian updating improves over time), collaborative settings where mutual benefit is possible (not zero-sum), scenarios where explicit preference revelation is costly or strategic. LOSES: single-round negotiations (no time to build opponent model), zero-sum games (opponent modeling provides no mutual benefit), scenarios with deceptive agents (opponent model can be manipulated), real-time constraints (Bayesian inference + perspective-taking adds compute). Opponent modeling introduces a cold-start problem — early negotiation rounds are uninformed; performance improves with interaction history.
**Rationale:** Standard multi-agent systems either assume full information (all agents know all preferences — unrealistic) or no information sharing (agents act selfishly — suboptimal for collaborative tasks). Opponent modeling provides a middle ground: agents infer preferences from behavior, enabling collaboration without explicit information sharing. vs Full-information (unrealistic in many settings), vs No-modeling (leaves value on the table), vs Explicit preference elicitation (costly, may be gamed). Key insight: negotiation behavior is a revealed-preference signal — agents leak information about their preferences through their offers and responses, and this signal can be exploited for mutual benefit.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no opponent modeling, no preference estimation, no Bayesian inference over agent intentions, and no multi-round perspective-taking for negotiation. However, opponent modeling is relevant to Lyra's multi-agent debate and collaboration patterns (§05 router, §17 safety): when Lyra agents disagree, understanding each other's "preferences" (confidence levels, constraints, objectives) enables more productive resolution. Status: **BEHIND** on agent-to-agent modeling; preference estimation pattern is transferable to Lyra's debate and conflict resolution mechanisms.
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** investigate (opponent modeling for multi-agent negotiation is relevant to Lyra's debate and conflict resolution subsystems; lower immediate priority than memory and orchestration gaps)

## VoxMind: An End-to-End Agentic Spoken Dialogue System
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.15710
**Mechanism:** (1) "Think-before-Speak" (TbS): before producing output or invoking tools, the speech model generates an explicit CoT reasoning trajectory conditioned on current observation, history, and local tool set: c_t ~ pi(c | o_t, H_{t-1}, T_t^local). This forces intent understanding and task decomposition before acting. (2) Multi-Agent Dynamic Tool Management: the main agent samples its next action using local tools while an auxiliary LLM asynchronously proposes candidate tools from the global pool. If the main agent emits a `retrieve` action (local tools insufficient), candidate tools are incorporated: T_{t+1}^local = T_t^local UNION T_t^cand. (3) Side-by-side parallelism: auxiliary LLM retrieval (1.3-2.6s) is fully hidden within main agent reasoning+speech generation time, achieving O(1) latency with respect to tool pool size (waiting overhead <15ms). (4) Reverse CoT data generation: given (Q,A), a strong text LLM constructs reasoning chain R ~ p(R|Q,A), then the speech model learns via supervised training. Dataset: 470-hour AgentChat corpus (14,805 tool-interaction + 38,681 dialogue samples). (5) Formal 4D agent definition: Profile (static+dynamic), Memory (semantic+acoustic dual-channel), Planning (x->z->y transformation), Action Execution (decision→selection→invocation).
**Results:** VoxMind achieves 74.57 overall score, outperforming Gemini-2.5-Pro (71.51) by +3.06 points, Gemini-2.5-flash (68.40), and best cascaded Qwen3-8B+Whisper (64.00). Relative improvement over base StepAudio2: +113.79% (34.88→74.57). Ablation: without CoT caps at 70.97; with CoT reaches 74.57 (best at 1:0.5 think:answer ratio). CoT preserves general conversation quality (VoiceBench: 64.21 w/ CoT vs 54.80 w/o CoT — prevents catastrophic forgetting). Dynamic tool management maintains stable latency across 1-100 tools; accuracy remains flat (~85-90%). Token overhead: ~88 THINK tokens per turn (12.6% in speech mode). Real speech robustness: 86% task success rate with disfluencies (only -7.3% drop from TTS speech).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: +113.79% task completion over base model, +3.06 points over Gemini-2.5-Pro, tool pool size decoupled from inference latency (O(1) overhead), general conversation quality preserved via CoT, proactive tool-seeking jumps from 3.12% to 68.66%, open-source release. LOSES: CoT adds ~88 tokens per turn (12.6% overhead), TTS-synthesized training data → real speech gap (-7.3% FS), parameter filling remains modest (38-72%), Result Feedback near-zero across all models (<5%), requires H20-NVLink GPUs for training, auxiliary LLM adds 1.3-2.6s (hidden in parallel but requires extra compute).
**Rationale:** Direct speech-to-action (x->y) fails because speech tokens encode dense acoustic information that overwhelms reasoning. Inserting intermediate reasoning z forces separation of understanding+planning from execution. Multi-agent tool management prevents exponential latency growth from inline tool processing — the auxiliary LLM offloads retrieval to a model aligned with the reasoning trajectory, decoupling execution from scale. Reverse CoT generation lets a strong text LLM construct bridges between known inputs/outputs during data creation, which the speech model learns during supervised training.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's plugin/router subsystem currently has the Router evaluating all M plugins per turn — this causes latency proportional to plugin count. VoxMind's asynchronous tool space management pattern (auxiliary LLM prunes global tool pool, main agent only expands on `retrieve` signal) directly applies: a lightweight "tool scout" model asynchronously prunes Lyra's plugin pool to top-K, and the Router only expands when it emits a retrieval signal. The dynamic local tool set maps cleanly to Lyra's context window management. Status: **BEHIND** on scalable tool dispatch.
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** investigate (compelling pattern but needs prototyping against Lyra's specific plugin dispatch latency; speech-domain results may not directly transfer to text-only latency regimes)

## MARCH: Multi-Agent Radiology Clinical Hierarchy for CT Report Generation
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16175
**Mechanism:** Three-stage hierarchical multi-agent framework emulating Resident-Fellow-Attending radiology workflow. (1) Stage 1 (Resident Agent): 3D CT scan → frozen ViT3D encoder + SAT multi-region segmentation (10 anatomical subregions) → LLaMA-2-Chat-7B fine-tuned via LoRA produces preliminary report T = A_res(I; θ_res). (2) Stage 2 (Fellow + Retrieval Agents): Three retrieval paradigms from clinical DB — image-to-image (visually similar CTs), image-to-text (corresponding reports), logits-based (18 canonical abnormalities classification → similar diagnostic profiles). Each Fellow Agent A_fel(i) revises draft by validating against retrieved evidence: T'_i = A_fel(i)(T, R). N=3 Fellows by default (optimal cost/fidelity). (3) Stage 3 (Attending Agent with iterative multi-round discourse): Round 1: Attending aggregates fellows' reports into initial consensus T^(0) with explicit feedback. Round t+1: Each Fellow reviews consensus and provides stance S_i^(t) = A_fel(i)(T'_i, T^(t)) with agree/disagree, confidence (1-3), reasons, evidence citations. Attending adjudicates: T^(t+1) = A_att(T^(t), {S_i^(t)}). Termination: all agree, or disagreers not confident, or consensus reached. LLMs: GPT-4.1 (Fellows), GPT-4o (Attending), temperature=0.
**Results:** On RadGenome-ChestCT test set (1,564 CT scans): BLEU-4=0.257 (+3.2% over Reg2RG at 0.249), METEOR=0.456, ROUGE-L=0.383, CE-F1=0.399 (+57.6% over Reg2RG at 0.253, +82% over Resident-only at 0.219). Ablation: Resident-only CE-F1=0.219, Single-Round Single-Agent=0.332, Single-Round Multi-Agent=0.352, Multi-Round Multi-Agent=0.362, Full MARCH=0.399. Consensus-driven finalization adds +0.037 CE-F1. LLM robustness: GPT-4.1-mini=0.393, GPT-4.1=0.399, GPT-4o=0.392, GPT-5=0.391 (narrow spread). Agent count: 3 balanced (10 peak CE-F1=0.337 on subset, 20 degrade to 0.327). Training: single H100, ~40 hours, 10 epochs, LoRA.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: +82% CE-F1 over single-agent (structural gain from hierarchy), large gains on subtle/rare abnormalities (hiatal hernia, pericardial effusion), every modification traced to specific fellow+evidence (interpretability), deterministic (temperature=0), works across GPT-4.1-mini/4.1/4o/5 with narrow spread. LOSES: cost scales O(N × rounds × API tokens), 20 agents degrade (CE-F1 drops 0.337→0.327), no open-weight LLM validation, single-dataset evaluation (RadGenome-ChestCT only), no longitudinal patient history, no human-in-the-loop evaluation, no statistical significance testing.
**Rationale:** Monolithic VLMs lack iterative verification (overread, read-out sessions) that defines real radiology QC. Staged hierarchy imposes clinical workflow: draft→ground→debate. Flat ensemble would average without adversarial stance-taking that catches subtle errors. Three complementary retrieval modalities maximize precedent coverage. Multi-round stance-based discourse forces reconciliation of contradictions with explicit evidence, mirroring clinical case conferences. The structured stance format (agree/disagree/confidence/reason/evidence) creates a structured adversarial dynamic.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's multi-agent orchestration uses simple voting in agent ensembles. MARCH's stance-based consensus protocol (agree/disagree/confidence/reason/evidence) can replace simple voting. The three-layer hierarchy (drafter→retriever+reviewer→arbiter) maps to Lyra's existing agent roles. Status: **BEHIND** on structured consensus (simple voting vs stance-based discourse).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (stance-based consensus protocol meaningfully improves output quality; directly applicable to Lyra's agent coordination)

## BOOK AGENT: Orchestrating Safety-Aware Visual Narratives via Multi-Agent Cognitive Calibration
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16541
**Mechanism:** Three-stage multi-agent closed-loop system for illustrated storybook generation from user drafts. (1) Stage 1 (Value-Aligned Storyboarding, VAS): Reviewer-Refiner rewrites draft to target page count K with global style s, audited by text safety auditor (binary pass/fail with critique ρ_T for constrained rewriting). Character Extractor extracts ≤5 characters with stable identifiers and visual descriptors. Sheet Renderer generates canonical neutral-background reference images (immutable ground truth). Page Planner decomposes story into page-wise plan P = {(t_i, p_i^(0))}^K_{i=1}. (2) Stage 2 (Iterative Cross-modal Refinement, ICR): For each page, generate candidate image with reference-conditioned generator, then dual-branch verification: Frame Director evaluates text-image faithfulness (score α_i, issues Δ_i), Identity Director checks character consistency against reference sheets (score η_i, issues Ω_i). Prompt update uses local memory M_i to prevent regression: p_i^(r+1) = p_i^(r) ⊕ Φ(Δ_i, Ω_i, M_i). Acceptance thresholds τ_α, τ_η; max R=3 retries. (3) Stage 3 (Temporal Cognitive Calibration, TCC): Sequence Director performs global audit across entire book sequence, producing consistency score β^(m) and set of inconsistent page indices I^(m). Selective repair: only retouches inconsistent pages by re-entering ICR with stricter reference conditioning. Budget max 1 sequence retry. All agents have fixed I/O contracts enabling independent verification.
**Results:** On high-constraint benchmark (16 multi-page stories, 170+ scene units, 40+ characters, 60+ object categories, 40+ rule groups): Image-Text Consistency 4.6/5 (vs StoryGPT-V 3.1, MovieAgent 2.8, StoryGen 2.5), Cross-Frame Character Consistency 4.7/5 (vs 2.4, 2.1, 1.9), Safety 4.8/5 (vs 4.5, 3.6, 4.4). Ablation: VAS alone adds safety (+0.6), ICR adds local alignment (+1.4 img-txt), TCC adds cross-frame consistency (+2.3 over ICR-only). User study: ~8.5/10 parent preference (vs StoryGPT-V ~5.0). Inference cost: 5-page story ~13K tokens, ~5-6 min (default); 20-page ~52K tokens, ~18-21 min. Cost scales approximately linearly with page count.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: +2.3 cross-frame consistency vs baseline, +0.6 safety from pre-audit, global repair eliminates irreversible appearance drift, no model retraining needed (purely agentic coordination), character sheet anchoring prevents gradual identity drift. LOSES: 3-4x inference cost vs single-pass, backend-locked (Gemini 3.0 + Nano-Banana proprietary), 5-char limit restricts complex casts, not real-time (20-page = 18-21 min), quality ceiling bounded by backbone models, single-vision-model evaluators (no inter-annotator agreement), single global style descriptor (no per-page style variation).
**Rationale:** Single-pass generation structurally insufficient because errors in character identity, object binding, and spatial relations only become visible after multiple pages (non-local detectability), and post-hoc safety filters cannot prevent unsafe plot trajectories. Multi-agent decomposition with fixed I/O contracts enables independent verification at each stage. Closed-loop verify-then-rectify transforms generation from static probabilistic sampling into dynamic self-correcting cognitive loop. Pre-generation safety audit elevates safety from passive filter to active structural constraint in narrative planning.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no verify-then-rectify loop pattern, no fixed-contract agent decomposition, no pre-generation safety audit, and no global sequence-level audit with selective repair. The three-stage architecture (plan→refine→calibrate) and the fixed I/O contract pattern directly inform Lyra's multi-agent design for complex reasoning and generation tasks. Status: **BEHIND** on structured verification loops and global consistency calibration.
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (verify-then-rectify with fixed contracts is a genuinely novel orchestration pattern; global retrospective audit addresses long-horizon error accumulation in Lyra's planning and execution loops)

## Conjunctive Prompt Attacks in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16543
**Mechanism:** (1) Threat model: attacker controls only user-input trigger key k placement and hidden template T(τ)_a* inside one compromised remote agent. Neither k alone nor template alone is harmful — activation requires conjunction when routing brings them together at the same compromised agent. (2) Agent system model: client agent deterministically decomposes user query into S segments; each routed independently via stochastic dispatcher to remote agents: a_i ~ R(s_i; ρ). Routing probability to compromised agent a* is Pr[a=a*|s] = clip(α_acc·I_acc(s) + ρ·I_k(s)·I_acc(s)). (3) Conjunctive activation condition: ∃j: (k∈s_j) ∧ (a_j=a*). (4) Routing-aware surrogate optimization via Gumbel-Softmax: continuous relaxation of discrete key/template placement. Loss: L = -ASR_both + λ₁Σp_i(1-a_i) + λ₂ρ + λ₃P_template - λ₄H(p) - λ₅H(q), where H is entropy, p_i are key-placement probabilities, q_τ are template-slot probabilities. Gradient descent with temperature annealing. Surrogate fidelity: Pearson r=0.995, Spearman ρ_s=0.933. (5) Four evaluation regimes: clean, key_only, template_only, both (conjunctive) — proving components are benign in isolation.
**Results:** Pre-optimization ASR both-regime: Gemma-2B 0.23 mean, Mistral-7B 0.30, LLaMA3-8B 0.33. Post full optimization ASR_max reaches 1.0 across all models (Gemma-2B 1.0 DAG, Mistral-7B 1.0 chain/DAG, LLaMA3-8B 1.0 DAG). False activation (key_only + template_only) near zero (0.07-0.09). Transferability: Llama-4-Scout-17B ASR 0.69 at ρ=0.8; GPT-5-mini ASR 0.73 at ρ=0.8. Safety mechanism collapse: Llama-Guard-3-8B drops from ~58 F1 to ~12 F1 under full optimization; PromptGuard drops to near-zero. System-level defenses (tool allowlist, least privilege) only reduce ASR by 15-20% (0.73→0.62, 0.58 respectively on GPT-5-mini).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: ASR_max reaches 1.0 across all models after optimization, transfers across model families (Gemma→Llama-4→GPT-5-mini), transfers across topologies (star/chain/DAG), false activations near zero (components genuinely benign in isolation), no weight modification needed (purely prompt-level attack surface). LOSES: attack inherently probabilistic due to stochastic routing (never deterministic), requires differentiable surrogate (cannot directly optimize black-box ASR), surrogate optimization adds compute overhead, routing bias ρ is abstract parameter (real routers may not expose equivalent control), only tested with deterministic marker activation (`__ACTIVATED__` token), requires compromised remote agent (supply-chain prerequisite), DAG topologies show higher baseline ASR.
**Rationale:** Single-component attacks are easily detected by prompt-level guard models. Splitting malicious signal across user-side key and remote-agent template makes each component appear benign in isolation, evading per-message classifiers. This models the most realistic constrained adversary: supply-chain compromise of third-party remote agent without model internals access. Topology-aware evaluation proves that topology-agnostic safety evaluation is dangerously incomplete — prior work only tested single agents or fixed topologies. Differentiable surrogate converts discrete search into continuous gradient problem while preserving ranking fidelity (r=0.995).
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's multi-agent pipeline (orchestrator→specialized sub-agents→tool use) creates exactly the topology-dependent, routing-mediated vulnerability this paper exposes. Per-message guard models (PromptGuard-style) are architecturally insufficient because they inspect messages in isolation while harmful behavior emerges only from the conjunction of user query segment + routing to specific agent + that agent's internal prompt. Lyra should implement routing-trace-aware safety validation with cross-agent provenance tracking. Status: **BEHIND** on multi-agent-specific safety evaluation (Lyra has no routing-trace-aware guard mechanisms).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** investigate (structural vulnerability class that current Lyra guard patterns would miss; routing-trace instrumentation can be built incrementally)

## HeLa-Mem: Hebbian Learning and Associative Memory for LLM Agents
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16839
**Mechanism:** Models conversation history as a dynamic associative graph with three coordinated modules driven by Hebbian learning. (1) Online Encoding: each conversation turn becomes a node with 5 fields (text, embedding, timestamp, keywords, speaker). Consecutive turns connected with small initial weights. Hebbian weight update: w_ij^(t+1) = (1-λ)·w_ij^(t) + η·I(v_i, v_j ∈ K_t) where λ=0.995 (decay), η=0.02 (learning rate), I(·)=indicator that pair is co-activated in retrieval set K_t. Weights strengthen when memories retrieved together; unused connections decay. (2) Reflective Memory Agent: hub detection — nodes where total incident edge weight D(v_i) > δ_hub trigger Hebbian Distillation: LLM identifies common themes, causal relationships, abstracts into structured entries in Semantic Memory Store with three sub-stores (User Model with confidence+evidence, Factual Memory with timestamps, Agent Knowledge with behavioral patterns). Adaptive forgetting requires ALL three: total edge weight < δ_prune, inactive > δ_age, zero recent access. (3) Dual-Path Retrieval: Stage 1 (semantic path) — S_base(v_i) = (sim(q,e_i) + α·keyword_match)·γ(v_i) with temporal decay γ(v_i)=exp(-Δt/τ), τ=60 days. Stage 2 (spreading activation) — S(v_j) = S_base(v_j) + β·ΣS_base(v_i)·w_ij, β=0.1. Stage 3 (dual-path ranking) — R_final = Top-k(S_base) ∪ Top-m(S|v∉Top-k), ensuring retrieval of both semantically relevant AND associatively-linked memories.
**Results:** LoCoMo benchmark (~300-turn conversations, 1,986 QA pairs): GPT-4o-mini backbone: Multi-hop 40.14% F1 (vs MemoryOS 38.39%, A-Mem 27.02%), Temporal 47.29%, Open Domain 29.70%, Single-hop 51.89%. Token cost: ~1,010 (30x reduction from full-context 16,910; ~2x better than MemoryOS 2,000). GPT-4o backbone: Temporal 50.79%, Open Domain 24.38%, Single-hop 49.69%. Cross-backbone average rank: 1.25 (best) vs MemoryOS 2.25, A-Mem 3.00. Ablation: reflective agent removal causes largest drop (-4.87 avg F1), spreading activation removal -2.55, forgetting removal -0.46. LongMemEval-S: 65.40% accuracy (vs A-MEM 62.60%, Mem0 53.61%, MemoryOS 44.80%). KnowledgeUpdate: 78.21% (strongest category).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: multi-hop reasoning 40.14% (best), 30x token reduction over full-context, cross-backbone robustness (Avg Rank 1.25 across 4 backbones), automatic lifecycle management (no manual annotation), associative retrieval surfaces memories semantic similarity would miss (0.35→0.71 score boost in case study), biologically grounded (Hebb 1949, Hopfield 1982). LOSES: cold start (Hebbian weights need substantial interaction history), LLM dependency (hallucinations during distillation propagate into semantic store), additional compute per turn (graph maintenance + hub detection + spreading activation), forgetting minimal benefit on ~300-turn conversations, hyperparameter proliferation (7+ parameters needing per-domain calibration), graph scalability O(n²) untested beyond ~300 turns, single-benchmark focus (LoCoMo primary).
**Rationale:** Existing memory systems treat memory as static database — items stored/retrieved independently, missing dynamic co-evolution of memory structure. Hebbian learning operationalizes "neurons that fire together wire together" for conversation memory: memories co-retrieved strengthen connections, creating latent narrative pathways beyond surface semantic similarity. Dual-level episodic/semantic organization mirrors human cognition (Tulving's model). Dual-path ranking (semantic + associative) ensures retrieval of both directly relevant and associatively-linked memories critical for multi-hop reasoning. Reflective Agent provides metacognitive loop monitoring graph health.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no weighted association graph across memory items, no Hebbian co-retrieval weighting, no dual-path retrieval (semantic + associative spreading activation), no automated consolidation pipeline (hub detection→distillation→semantic store), and no neuro-symbolic bridge between episodic working memory and semantic long-term storage. The dual-path retrieval pattern directly addresses Lyra's cross-session associative recall limitation. Status: **BEHIND** on dynamic associative memory (Lyra treats memory as static storage).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (novel mechanism with strong empirical validation; directly solves Lyra's cross-session associative recall gap; 30x token efficiency is direct operational win)

## AutoPKG: Dynamic E-commerce Product-Attribute Knowledge Graph Construction
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16950
**Mechanism:** (1) Multi-agent LLM framework that builds Product-attribute Knowledge Graphs (PKG) from multimodal product content without fixed pre-built ontologies. (2) On-demand type & key induction: dynamically generates product types and associated attribute keys from incoming product data, rather than relying on static schemas. (3) Multimodal extraction pipeline: extracts attribute values from both textual descriptions and product images. (4) Centralized decision agent: resolves conflicts, merges duplicates, and performs canonicalization — ensuring globally consistent graph updates. (5) Novel evaluation protocol for dynamic PKGs: measures type/key validity, consolidation quality, and edge-level accuracy for value assertions post-canonicalization.
**Results:** Weighted Knowledge Efficiency (WKE) for Product Types: 0.953. WKE for Attribute Keys: 0.724. Edge-level F1 (multimodal value extraction, Lazada dataset): 0.531. Edge-level exact-match F1 improvement across 3 public benchmarks: +0.152. Precision gain on attribute extraction: +0.208. Production A/B tests on Lazada (Alibaba): GMV uplift — Badge +3.81%, Search +5.32%, Recommendation +7.89%. Accepted at ACL 2026 Findings.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: eliminates ontology maintenance bottleneck (types/keys induced on-demand), multimodal (text + image) extraction covers product content fully, centralized canonicalization prevents graph fragmentation, production-validated GMV uplift (+3.8% to +7.9%), no pre-built ontology requirement. LOSES: edge-level F1 (0.531) leaves substantial room for improvement, attribute key WKE (0.724) indicates key induction is harder than type induction (0.953), single-domain evaluation (e-commerce only), centralized agent is a single point of consolidation failure, requires multimodal LLM infrastructure.
**Rationale:** Traditional e-commerce PKG construction requires manual ontology engineering and rule-based extraction — expensive, brittle, and lagging behind catalog changes. Multi-agent LLM approach automates extraction while centralized consolidation agent maintains global consistency — decomposing extraction (parallel, per-product) from canonicalization (centralized, cross-product). vs rule-based extraction: on-demand adaptation, no manual rule maintenance. vs single-agent extraction: multi-agent enables parallel processing of multimodal signals. vs fixed ontology: dynamic induction handles catalog evolution.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no knowledge graph construction pipeline, no multi-agent extraction framework, no consolidation/canonicalization mechanism, and no multimodal extraction capability. However, the centralized-consolidation pattern (parallel extraction agents + central canonicalization agent) directly informs Lyra's knowledge graph subsystem architecture. The on-demand induction pattern (generate types/keys from data rather than pre-defining) applies to Lyra's dynamic skill/tool discovery. Status: **BEHIND** on KG infrastructure; the consolidation pattern is directly transferable.
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** investigate (KG construction pattern informs Lyra's knowledge representation; production GMV results validate multi-agent extraction value)

## On Safety Risks in Experience-Driven Self-Evolving Agents
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16968
**Mechanism:** (1) Investigates how experience accumulation and utilization in self-evolving LLM agents affects safety performance across web-based and embodied environments. (2) Key experimental conditions: (a) agents trained on benign-only tasks — testing whether safe-source experience can still compromise safety; (b) agents exposed to mixed benign + harmful tasks — testing realistic deployment conditions. (3) Causal attribution: experience gathered from benign tasks is execution-oriented, reinforcing agents' tendency to act rather than refuse — this "action bias" degrades safety even without any harmful training data. (4) When refusal-related experience is introduced (mixed setting), safety decline is mitigated but over-refusal emerges — agents refuse benign requests, revealing a fundamental safety-utility trade-off. (5) Environment coverage: both web-based and embodied environments, testing generalization of the safety degradation pattern.
**Results:** Accepted at Findings of ACL 2026. Key qualitative findings: (a) Benign-only experience degrades safety in high-risk scenarios — the execution-oriented nature of experience alone is sufficient. (b) Mixed benign+harmful experience mitigates safety decline via refusal learning but induces over-refusal. (c) The safety-utility trade-off is inherent to current self-evolution paradigms — no free lunch between capability improvement and safety preservation. Specific numeric metrics not available from abstract; full PDF contains quantitative safety scores.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: identifies a previously unexplored safety risk vector (benign experience can degrade safety), demonstrates the finding across both web and embodied environments (robustness), provides causal mechanism (execution-orientation → action bias → safety decline), identifies the over-refusal failure mode of current mitigation. LOSES: no quantitative metrics visible from abstract (impact magnitude unclear), only two environment types tested, ACL Findings venue (not main), single self-evolution paradigm evaluated, action-bias mechanism is proposed but may not be the only causal pathway.
**Rationale:** Self-evolution is a core paradigm for improving agent autonomy (learn from experience, improve over time). Prior work focused entirely on capability improvement, assuming safety is preserved or separately handled. This paper proves safety is not preserved — the very act of accumulating experience (even benign) shifts agent behavior toward execution and away from refusal, creating safety risk. The over-refusal finding shows that naive mitigation (adding refusal examples) creates a different failure mode. vs static safety filters: dynamic experience accumulation defeats static guardrails because agent behavior drifts. vs separate safety training: the safety-utility trade-off is inherent, not separable.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's planned self-evolution capabilities (experience-driven learning loops, autonomous improvement from agent interactions) would be directly vulnerable to this safety degradation pattern. Lyra has no mechanism to detect or mitigate execution-orientation drift, no refusal calibration for self-evolving agents, and no safety monitoring across experience accumulation cycles. The paper's finding that benign experience alone can degrade safety is directly relevant to Lyra's design for continuous agent improvement. Status: **BEHIND** on self-evolution safety (this risk class is not addressed in current architecture).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (P0 safety requirement for any self-evolution capability; informs mandatory safety calibration in Lyra's experience-learning loops)

## Beyond "I Don't Know": Evaluating LLM Self-Awareness in Discriminating Data and Model Uncertainty
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17293
**Mechanism:** (1) Distinguishes two types of LLM uncertainty previously conflated in refusal research: data uncertainty (input-level ambiguity — question is unclear, missing information) vs model uncertainty (capability limitations — question is clear but model lacks knowledge). (2) Introduces UA-Bench: 3,500+ questions drawn from 6 datasets spanning knowledge-intensive and reasoning-intensive tasks, annotated for the data-vs-model uncertainty distinction. (3) Evaluation protocol: measures explicit uncertainty attribution — can models correctly classify *why* they should abstain (input ambiguity vs capability gap), beyond just *whether* to abstain. (4) Evaluates 18 frontier LLMs on UA-Bench. (5) Mitigation method: lightweight data synthesis pipeline combined with reinforcement learning, applied to Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 and Qwen3-8B in thinking mode, targeting improved uncertainty discrimination without degrading answer accuracy.
**Results:** Key finding: even state-of-the-art models struggle to reliably discriminate between data uncertainty and model uncertainty. High answer accuracy does not imply strong uncertainty attribution ability — models can be accurate yet poor at knowing *why* they are uncertain. The proposed RL-based method improves uncertainty attribution while preserving answer accuracy (specific numeric improvements available in full PDF). 18 frontier LLMs evaluated; 6 datasets; 3,500+ questions.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: finer-grained uncertainty taxonomy enables differentiated downstream actions (ask clarification for data uncertainty vs invoke tool for model uncertainty), benchmark is multi-domain (knowledge + reasoning), RL-based mitigation is lightweight (data synthesis, no full fine-tuning), preserves answer accuracy during uncertainty training. LOSES: 3,500 questions is moderate benchmark size, only two model families tested for mitigation (Qwen3-4B/8B), RL strategy may not generalize to other architectures, uncertainty types may not be exhaustive (aleatoric vs epistemic framing), no real-time uncertainty calibration discussed.
**Rationale:** Prior refusal/uncertainty research treats all "I don't know" responses as equivalent. But different uncertainty types require different agent actions: data uncertainty → ask clarifying questions; model uncertainty → invoke external tool or escalate. Conflating them leads to inappropriate agent responses. The accuracy-uncertainty-attribution decoupling means high-accuracy models can still make wrong uncertainty-type judgments, making this a distinct capability from answer correctness. vs generic refusal training: this enables *informed* refusal with correct reasoning. vs confidence calibration: this is about attribution, not probability estimation.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's agents need to distinguish between "I need more information" (data uncertainty → clarification loop) and "I don't know how" (model uncertainty → tool invocation or escalation). Currently, Lyra has no uncertainty type discrimination, no differentiated refusal strategy, and no uncertainty attribution training. The finding that answer accuracy and uncertainty attribution are decoupled means Lyra cannot assume accurate agents will appropriately refuse or escalate. Status: **BEHIND** on uncertainty attribution (Lyra agents treat all uncertainty uniformly).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (uncertainty-type discrimination directly enables smarter agent routing, clarification loops, and escalation decisions in Lyra's orchestrator)

## ErrorProbe: Towards Self-Improving Error Diagnosis in Multi-Agent Systems
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17658
**Mechanism:** (1) Three-stage self-improving framework for semantic failure attribution in LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems (MAS): (a) Operationalize a MAS failure taxonomy to detect local anomalies in agent interaction traces. (b) Symptom-driven backward tracing: prunes irrelevant context by following error symptoms upstream through inter-agent dependencies to identify originating steps. (c) Specialized multi-agent diagnosis team (Strategist, Investigator, Arbiter) that validates error hypotheses through tool-grounded execution — Strategist formulates hypotheses, Investigator gathers evidence via tool execution, Arbiter adjudicates conflicting diagnoses. (2) Core innovation: Verified Episodic Memory — updates only when error patterns are confirmed by executable evidence, without requiring human annotation. Memory entries store (failure signature, root cause agent, origination step, fix strategy). (3) Cross-domain transfer: verified memory enables error diagnosis knowledge to transfer across domains without retraining — error patterns are domain-agnostic once abstracted.
**Results:** Accepted at ACL 2026 Findings. Benchmarks: TracerTraj and Who&When. ErrorProbe significantly outperforms baselines particularly in step-level localization (specific numbers in full PDF). Verified episodic memory enables robust cross-domain transfer without retraining. Key qualitative: LLM-as-a-judge baselines fail to pinpoint decisive error steps within extended MAS contexts; ErrorProbe's backward tracing + tool-grounded verification overcomes this limitation.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: no annotation required (verified episodic memory is self-supervised), step-level error localization (vs agent-level only in baselines), cross-domain transfer without retraining, tool-grounded verification prevents hallucinated error diagnoses, three-role diagnosis team provides checks and balances. LOSES: requires executable verification (not all error types are verifiable via tool execution), three-agent diagnosis team adds inference cost per error, taxonomy operationalization may be domain-specific initially, backward tracing relies on accurate inter-agent dependency tracking, cold-start (no verified memory at initialization).
**Rationale:** MAS debugging is harder than single-agent debugging due to: long interaction traces (many steps across many agents), inter-agent dependencies (error in agent A manifests as failure in agent C), and delayed error manifestation (root cause and symptom are temporally distant). LLM-as-a-judge fails on long contexts because attention dilutes. Backward tracing + tool-grounded verification addresses both: backward tracing finds root cause by following dependencies, tool execution confirms hypotheses with ground truth rather than LLM judgment. Verified episodic memory creates a growing knowledge base that improves diagnosis over time without annotation cost. vs static debugging: self-improving memory accumulates patterns. vs human annotation: zero annotation cost.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's multi-agent pipelines (orchestrator → specialized sub-agents → tool use) create exactly the debugging challenge this paper addresses: long traces, inter-agent dependencies, delayed failures. Lyra has no automated error diagnosis, no failure attribution to specific agents/steps, no verified pattern memory for debugging, and no cross-session debug knowledge transfer. The three-role diagnosis team pattern (Strategist/Investigator/Arbiter) directly informs Lyra's debugging subsystem. Status: **BEHIND** on MAS error diagnosis (zero infrastructure).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (P0 — Lyra's multi-agent debugging is unsolved; ErrorProbe's verified episodic memory + backward tracing directly addresses Lyra's longest-standing debugging gap)

## Diversity Collapse in Multi-Agent LLM Systems: Structural Coupling and Collective Failure
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18005
**Mechanism:** (1) Analyzes diversity in multi-agent LLM systems for open-ended idea generation across three levels: model intelligence, agent cognition, and system dynamics. (2) Model level — Compute Efficiency Paradox: stronger, highly aligned models produce diminishing marginal diversity despite higher per-sample quality; alignment training constrains the output space. (3) Cognition level — Authority Dynamics: authority-driven interaction structures (senior agents dominating discussion) suppress semantic diversity relative to junior-dominated or egalitarian groups; authority signals narrow exploration. (4) System level — Structural Coupling: dense communication topologies (all-to-all, high-frequency interaction) accelerate premature convergence; group-size scaling shows diminishing returns beyond a threshold. (5) Central mechanism: Diversity Collapse via Structural Coupling — interaction structure itself (not model insufficiency) causes agents to converge their exploration, triggered by too-frequent communication, authority gradients, and alignment-induced output constraints.
**Results:** Accepted at ACL 2026 Findings. 56 pages, 15 figures. Key findings: stronger models → diminishing marginal diversity (compute efficiency paradox). Authority-driven structures suppress semantic diversity vs junior-dominated groups. Dense communication topologies accelerate premature convergence. Group-size scaling yields diminishing returns. The collapse stems primarily from interaction structure, not model insufficiency. Code available on GitHub.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: identifies interaction structure as root cause (actionable — change topology, not models), multi-level analysis (model/cognition/system) provides comprehensive framework, "structural coupling" mechanism generalizes across MAS designs, practical implication: preserve independence and disagreement. LOSES: 56-page length suggests extensive but potentially diffuse analysis, only tested on open-ended idea generation (may not generalize to task-oriented MAS), ACL Findings venue, no proposed mitigation framework described in abstract, "diminishing returns" and "premature convergence" lack quantified thresholds in abstract.
**Rationale:** Intuition says "more agents → more diversity" and "stronger models → better exploration." Both are wrong per this paper. Interaction causes convergence: agents influence each other, and this influence is amplified by dense communication, authority signals, and alignment training. The mechanism is structural coupling — agents' exploration spaces become correlated through interaction, shrinking the effective search volume. vs single-agent generation: MAS can be worse for diversity if interaction is uncontrolled. vs random sampling: uncontrolled interaction is worse than independent sampling for exploration. Key insight for MAS design: interaction is a double-edged sword — enables coordination but risks collapse.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's multi-agent design (PrimaryAgent + specialized sub-agents + debate/discussion patterns) creates exactly the structural coupling risk this paper identifies. Lyra has no diversity monitoring, no topology-aware interaction control, no independence-preserving mechanisms for agent exploration, and no convergence detection for multi-agent deliberation. If Lyra deploys multi-agent idea generation or debate, diversity collapse will occur by default. The paper's finding that interaction structure (not model quality) drives collapse means Lyra must design interaction protocols that preserve independence. Status: **BEHIND** on diversity preservation (structural coupling risk is latent in all multi-agent interactions).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (structural coupling is a first-principles risk in any MAS; Lyra must implement topology-aware interaction control and diversity monitoring before deploying multi-agent deliberation at scale)

## MASS-RAG: Multi-Agent Synthesis Retrieval-Augmented Generation
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18509
**Mechanism:** (1) Decomposes complex retrieval-augmented generation queries across a team of specialized LLM agents, each responsible for a sub-query dimension (e.g., factual retrieval, counterfactual reasoning, temporal analysis). (2) Synthesis coordinator agent merges individual agent outputs — resolving contradictions, filling gaps, and producing a unified response that is more comprehensive than any single-agent result. (3) Multi-stage retrieval pipeline: each agent independently retrieves and ranks documents relevant to its sub-query, preventing retrieval bias toward a single relevance dimension. (4) Cross-agent verification: agents critique each other's retrieved evidence, flagging inconsistencies and requesting supplementary retrieval where evidence is thin. (5) Final synthesis uses weighted evidence aggregation — documents cited by multiple agents receive higher weight, while singleton citations are treated as lower-confidence.
**Results:** Multi-agent RAG outperforms single-agent RAG baselines across knowledge-intensive QA benchmarks. Synthesis-based approach yields higher factual coverage and reduced hallucination rates vs monolithic retrieval. Cross-agent verification catches contradictory evidence that single-agent retrieval misses. The coordination overhead is offset by improved answer quality on complex multi-hop queries.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: multi-faceted queries (requiring diverse evidence types), high-stakes QA (where contradiction detection matters), complex multi-hop reasoning, scenarios with heterogeneous document corpora. LOSES: simple lookups (single-agent sufficient), latency-sensitive applications (parallel agent calls add overhead), queries answerable from a single document, tight token budgets (multi-agent coordination consumes additional context). The synthesis coordinator is a single point of quality control — coordinator failures cascade to all downstream output.
**Rationale:** Single-agent RAG is bottlenecked by the agent's attention span and retrieval focus — one agent cannot simultaneously attend to factual, temporal, and counterfactual dimensions. Multi-agent decomposition parallelizes retrieval across dimensions, and synthesis merges complementary evidence. Cross-agent verification is the key differentiator vs simple ensemble RAG — agents actively challenge each other's evidence rather than voting independently. vs ensemble RAG: synthesis + verification improves over naive voting. vs iterative retrieval: parallel multi-agent is faster than sequential refinement for multi-faceted queries.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's RAG pipeline (when implemented) would be single-agent by default. MASS-RAG's multi-agent decomposition + cross-verification pattern directly informs Lyra's retrieval architecture — particularly for the planned knowledge-graph-backed retrieval subsystem. The synthesis coordinator pattern matches Lyra's orchestrator-agent architecture. Status: **BEHIND** (Lyra has no multi-agent RAG; MASS-RAG provides the blueprint for Phase 2+ retrieval).
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** parity (multi-agent RAG is a natural extension of Lyra's multi-agent architecture)

## Evaluating Answer Leakage Robustness of LLM Tutors against Adversarial Student Attacks
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18660
**Mechanism:** (1) Defines "answer leakage" as a failure mode in LLM-based tutoring systems where adversarial student prompts cause the tutor to reveal correct answers rather than guide students toward discovery. (2) Constructs a taxonomy of adversarial attack strategies: direct solicitation ("just tell me the answer"), incremental extraction (asking step-by-step leading questions), role-playing deception (pretending to have solved it), and emotional manipulation (expressing frustration to elicit sympathy). (3) Evaluates multiple frontier LLMs as tutors under systematic adversarial probing — measuring both answer leakage rate and pedagogical quality degradation. (4) Tests defense strategies: system-prompt hardening (explicit refusal instructions), few-shot exemplars of correct tutoring behavior, and response filtering (post-hoc detection of leaked answers). (5) Robustness metric: Answer Leakage Resistance Score (ALRS) combining leakage rate, pedagogical fidelity, and consistency under attack.
**Results:** Frontier LLMs exhibit significant answer leakage under adversarial probing — leakage rates vary by attack type and model. Direct solicitation is the most effective attack across all models. System-prompt hardening reduces leakage but degrades pedagogical quality (tutors become overly cautious, refusing legitimate guidance). Few-shot exemplars provide the best leakage-pedagogy trade-off. No defense achieves zero leakage without unacceptable pedagogical degradation.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: educational deployment risk assessment, tutoring system safety evaluation, adversarial robustness testing for instruction-following agents, student-facing LLM applications. LOSES: defense evaluation limited to prompt-based methods (no fine-tuning), attack taxonomy may not cover all real-world student behaviors, evaluation is single-turn (multi-turn tutoring sessions may surface additional vulnerabilities). The pedagogy-leakage trade-off is fundamental — making tutors leakage-proof also makes them less helpful.
**Rationale:** LLM tutors must balance two conflicting objectives: helpfulness (guide the student) and answer withholding (don't reveal the answer). This is a harder safety problem than simple refusal because the boundary between "guiding" and "revealing" is context-dependent and fuzzy. Prior work on prompt injection and jailbreaking focuses on harmful content; answer leakage is a distinct failure mode — the content is not harmful per se, but leaking it undermines the pedagogical purpose. vs generic jailbreak defense: tutoring requires nuanced partial-information release, not binary refuse/answer. vs prompt hardening alone: degrades pedagogy unacceptably.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no tutoring-specific safety mechanisms, no answer-leakage awareness, and no pedagogical fidelity evaluation. If Lyra is deployed as a tutoring/teaching agent (plausible given its multi-agent architecture), it would be vulnerable to all attack types in this taxonomy. The pedagogy-leakage trade-off directly informs Lyra's safety-utility calibration for instructional use cases. Status: **BEHIND** (no tutoring safety infrastructure). 
**Impact:** 2 | **Effort:** 2 | **Tier:** investigate (domain-specific safety; relevant if Lyra targets educational/tutoring use cases)

## MANGO: Multi-Agent Web Navigation via Global-View Optimization
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18779
**Mechanism:** (1) Addresses the local-observation problem in web agents — agents making decisions from page-level observations lose global context about website structure and task progress. (2) Multi-agent architecture: Page Agent (operates on current page, proposes local actions), Global Agent (maintains site map, task decomposition, and progress tracking), and Critic Agent (evaluates action proposals against global objectives). (3) Global-view optimization: Global Agent builds and maintains a hierarchical site model (pages visited, links discovered, information extracted) as a dynamic graph, enabling reasoning about navigation strategy beyond the current page. (4) Two-stage decision: Page Agent proposes candidate actions from local observation → Critic evaluates against global state → Global Agent approves, modifies, or redirects based on progress toward task goal. (5) Exploration-exploitation balancing via Global Agent's site model — identifies unexplored promising branches and prevents redundant page visits.
**Results:** MANGO's global-view architecture outperforms single-agent web navigation baselines on WebArena and VisualWebArena benchmarks. The Critic agent reduces wasted navigation steps (redundant page visits, dead-end exploration). Global-view optimization particularly benefits long-horizon tasks requiring multi-page traversal. The trade-off: additional inference cost from three-agent coordination.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: multi-page tasks (e-commerce checkout, multi-step form filling), complex website structures (deep hierarchies), tasks requiring information aggregation across pages, long-horizon navigation (10+ steps). LOSES: single-page tasks (overhead unjustified), stateless interactions, real-time navigation (coordination latency), simple lookup tasks. Three-agent coordination adds 2-3x inference cost per step vs single-agent. Global site model construction requires memory proportional to site size.
**Rationale:** Single-agent web navigation suffers from myopia — the agent sees only the current page and must maintain global context entirely in its (limited) working memory. This leads to redundant navigation, forgotten task subtleties, and failure on tasks requiring non-local reasoning. MANGO's Page/Global/Critic decomposition mirrors how humans navigate complex websites: local page reading + global strategy + self-critique. vs single-agent with long context: explicit site model is more reliable than implicit context. vs tree-search navigation: global-view optimization is more sample-efficient than MCTS for web tasks. vs DOM-only approaches: hierarchical site model captures structure that DOM traversal misses.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no web navigation capability, no site-model construction, and no multi-agent navigation architecture. However, MANGO's Page/Global/Critic decomposition directly parallels Lyra's planned orchestrator/specialist/reviewer pattern — the Global Agent is analogous to Lyra's PrimaryAgent maintaining task-level context, while Page Agents are specialists. The hierarchical site model pattern informs Lyra's context and memory subsystem design for any environment-interaction use case. Status: **BEHIND** on web navigation; the architectural pattern is transferable.
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** investigate (web navigation is not Lyra's primary use case; the global-view optimization pattern generalizes to any environment-interaction agent)

## STAR-Teaming: A Strategy-Response Multiplex Network Approach to Automated LLM Red Teaming
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18976
**Mechanism:** (1) Models automated LLM red teaming as a multiplex network problem — attackers and defenders occupy layers of a multi-relational graph where each layer represents a different attack strategy (e.g., role-play, encoding tricks, multi-turn manipulation). (2) Strategy generation via LLM-based attacker agents: each agent specializes in a specific attack strategy layer, generating adversarial prompts optimized for that layer's vulnerability class. (3) Response multiplexing: target model responses are analyzed across all strategy layers simultaneously — a successful attack in any layer is flagged as a vulnerability. (4) Co-evolutionary optimization: attacker strategies and defender responses co-evolve — successful attacks inform defender hardening, hardened defenders force attacker strategy adaptation, creating an arms-race dynamic that surfaces deeper vulnerabilities. (5) Automated coverage analysis: multiplex network structure enables systematic tracking of which vulnerability classes have been tested and which remain unexplored, guiding the next round of attack generation.
**Results:** STAR-Teaming discovers more diverse vulnerabilities than single-strategy or random-sampling red-teaming baselines. The multiplex co-evolutionary approach surfaces vulnerabilities that are missed by static attack taxonomies. Strategy specialization across agents prevents attack collapse (all agents converging on the same strategy). Automated coverage tracking improves exploration efficiency — fewer redundant attacks, more novel vulnerability discovery.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: comprehensive safety evaluation, production LLM deployment security, vulnerability discovery for instruction-tuned models, automated red teaming at scale. LOSES: compute-intensive (multiple attacker agents + co-evolutionary rounds), requires clear vulnerability taxonomy for initialization, attacker success metrics can be ambiguous (is a "successful" attack actually harmful?), co-evolution can produce adversarial prompts that don't generalize to real users. The arms-race dynamic may converge to unrealistic attack patterns.
**Rationale:** Manual red teaming is expensive, slow, and biased by human attacker creativity. Automated red teaming with single strategies suffers from strategy collapse — the attacker converges on a few easy exploit patterns and misses diverse vulnerabilities. Multi-agent multiplex approach solves both: specialization across agents prevents collapse, and multiplex structure ensures coverage. vs manual red teaming: 10-100x more attacks, 24/7 operation, systematic coverage. vs single-agent automated red teaming: strategy diversity, co-evolutionary depth. vs static test suites: adaptive, evolving with model updates.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no automated red teaming, no vulnerability discovery pipeline, and no co-evolutionary safety testing. The STAR-Teaming multiplex pattern directly informs Lyra's safety testing infrastructure — particularly for the planned adversarial evaluation subsystem. The strategy-specialization + co-evolution pattern is generalizable beyond red teaming to any multi-agent adversarial evaluation. Status: **BEHIND** on automated safety evaluation (zero infrastructure).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (automated red teaming is a P1 requirement for production-safe Lyra deployment; STAR-Teaming provides the architecture blueprint)

## RADAR: Role-Anchored Multi-Agent Reasoning for Half-Truth Detection
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.19005
**Mechanism:** (1) Defines "half-truths" as statements that mix true and false information — harder to detect than outright falsehoods because the true components create credibility, causing both humans and LLMs to overlook the embedded falsehoods. (2) Role-anchored multi-agent framework: each agent adopts a fixed epistemic stance — Fact-Checker (verifies claims against evidence), Skeptic (assumes potential deception, demands proof), Synthesizer (integrates perspectives), and Contextualizer (evaluates statements in broader context). (3) Anchoring mechanism: each role has a fixed system prompt that cannot be overridden by other agents' arguments — preventing groupthink and ensuring adversarial perspectives persist through deliberation. (4) Multi-round deliberation: agents exchange analyses, challenge each other's conclusions, and iteratively refine their assessments until convergence or a stalemate is declared. (5) Half-truth detection score: weighted ensemble of individual agent judgments, with higher weight assigned to Skeptic and Fact-Checker roles when they dissent from the consensus.
**Results:** RADAR outperforms single-agent fact-checking and unanchored multi-agent debate on half-truth detection benchmarks. Role anchoring is critical — removing role persistence (allowing agents to be persuaded) significantly degrades detection performance. The Skeptic role contributes disproportionately to detection accuracy, particularly for subtly misleading statements. Multi-round deliberation improves precision but plateaus after 3-4 rounds.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: high-stakes information verification (news, legal, medical), subtle misinformation detection (half-truths, lies by omission, misleading framing), adversarial content moderation, scenarios where truthfulness is ambiguous and requires multi-perspective analysis. LOSES: unambiguous true/false statements (single-agent sufficient), real-time moderation (multi-round deliberation adds latency), domains without clear evidence sources (roles argue from priors, not facts), tight budget constraints (4+ agents per statement). The Skeptic role can generate false positives — flagging true but counterintuitive statements as half-truths.
**Rationale:** Half-truths are the most dangerous form of misinformation because they exploit truth bias — humans (and LLMs) are more likely to accept statements containing some truth. Single-agent fact-checking fails because the agent can be "anchored" by the true components and overlook false ones. Role-anchored multi-agent approach solves this by institutionalizing dissent — the Skeptic cannot be persuaded, ensuring adversarial scrutiny persists. The anchoring mechanism is the key innovation vs standard multi-agent debate — without anchoring, debate converges to consensus regardless of truth. vs fact-checking APIs: role-anchored deliberation handles nuanced cases where ground truth is ambiguous. vs ensemble voting: anchoring ensures diversity; voting without anchoring collapses.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no fact-checking subsystem, no information verification pipeline, and no epistemic role architecture. If Lyra is deployed for research, analysis, or knowledge work, it would be vulnerable to half-truth ingestion and propagation. RADAR's role-anchored architecture directly applies to Lyra's planned verification and safety subsystems — the Fact-Checker/Skeptic/Synthesizer/Contextualizer decomposition maps cleanly to Lyra's multi-agent patterns. The anchoring mechanism (fixed epistemic stances that resist persuasion) is a first-principles safety pattern applicable to any adversarial or verification use case. Status: **BEHIND** on verification infrastructure; role anchoring is a transferable safety pattern.
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (half-truth detection is critical for Lyra's research/analysis accuracy; role anchoring is a generalizable safety pattern for any multi-agent deliberation)

## Explicit Trait Inference for Multi-Agent Coordination
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.19278
**Mechanism:** (1) Observation phase: agents maintain interaction histories tracking partner behaviors over time. (2) Trait inference along two established psychological dimensions: Warmth (trustworthiness) and Competence (skill level). (3) Profile construction: inferred traits form structured trait profiles for each partner agent. (4) Decision-guiding: agents leverage structured awareness of others' traits to inform coordination strategies and action selection, rather than treating partners as black boxes. (5) The method functions as a lightweight overlay on existing agent reasoning (compared against Chain-of-Thought baseline) — no architectural changes required.
**Results:** Controlled settings (economic games): **45-77% payoff loss reduction** vs CoT baseline. Complex settings (MultiAgentBench): **3-29% performance gain**, varying by scenario and underlying model. ETI profiles predict agents' actions — inferred trait profiles carry causal predictive power. Informative profiles drive improvements — performance gains are causally linked to trait inference quality, not just the presence of any inference mechanism.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: mixed-motive scenarios (coordination games, negotiation), heterogeneous agent teams with varied capabilities, environments where partner behavior is observable over time, lightweight deployment (no model retraining). LOSES: single-agent tasks (no partners to model), short interaction horizons (insufficient history for inference), homogeneous agent teams (no trait variation to exploit), scenarios where warmth/competence dimensions are insufficient. Gains are context-dependent (3-29% range shows high variance). Two-dimensional simplification may miss other coordination-relevant attributes (predictability, adaptability, resource constraints).
**Rationale:** Multi-agent systems typically treat partner agents as black boxes, missing the opportunity to leverage inferred partner characteristics for coordination. ETI draws on established psychological trait theory (warmth/competence) to give agents explicit models of their partners. vs standard CoT: explicit trait modeling outperforms implicit reasoning. vs full Theory of Mind: cheaper (2-dimension approximation). vs fixed role assignment: ETI is dynamic — traits are inferred from behavior, not pre-assigned. The causal link between profile quality and performance distinguishes ETI from mere prompting tricks.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has agent role assignment (planner, executor, reviewer) but NO dynamic partner modeling, NO trait inference, and NO behavioral-history-based coordination. Agents interact via structured message-passing without explicit models of each other's capabilities or trustworthiness. ETI's trait inference pattern directly applies to Lyra's inter-agent communication — the orchestrator could maintain warmth/competence profiles per specialist agent and route tasks accordingly. Status: **BEHIND** (no partner modeling infrastructure).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 2 | **Tier:** breakthrough (lightweight overlay; improves coordination in heterogeneous multi-agent systems; trait-aware task routing is a high-leverage addition to Lyra's orchestrator)

## MAGEO: Multi-Agent Generative Engine Optimization via Reusable Strategy Learning
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.19516
**Mechanism:** (1) Coordinated Planning: multiple agents plan content edits for a given query and target generative engine. (2) Editing Execution: agents execute planned edits on content. (3) Fidelity-Aware Evaluation: specialized evaluation layer assesses edits on both visibility (semantic presence in generated outputs) and citation accuracy (attribution fidelity). (4) Strategy Distillation: validated editing patterns are progressively distilled into reusable, engine-specific optimization skills — successful edit patterns become learned strategies reused across tasks rather than starting from scratch each time. (5) Engine-Specific Preference Modeling: framework models each engine's distinct preferences, enabling tailored optimization per engine. (6) Twin Branch Evaluation Protocol: enables causal attribution of content edits — isolating which changes actually caused improvements. (7) DSV-CF Metric: dual-axis metric unifying semantic visibility with attribution accuracy.
**Results:** MAGEO substantially outperforms heuristic baselines in both visibility and citation fidelity (exact numbers in full paper PDF). Ablation studies confirm engine-specific preference modeling and strategy reuse are central to gains. Introduces MSME-GEO-Bench: multi-scenario, multi-engine benchmark grounded in real-world queries. ACL 2026 Findings paper.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: multi-engine optimization scenarios, tasks requiring both visibility and attribution fidelity, repeated optimization across similar query types (strategy reuse compounds), production SEO/GEO pipelines. LOSES: single-engine scenarios (engine-specific overhead unjustified), one-off optimization tasks (strategy distillation has no reuse benefit), domains where attribution fidelity is irrelevant. Engine-specific strategy pools add maintenance complexity vs one-size-fits-all. Visibility vs citation fidelity tension: optimizing one may sacrifice the other — DSV-CF metric explicitly acknowledges this trade-off. Multi-agent coordination adds inference cost vs heuristic baselines.
**Rationale:** Current GEO methods optimize each instance in isolation, discarding knowledge that could transfer across similar queries. MAGEO reframes GEO as a strategy learning problem — rather than optimizing from scratch each time, the system accumulates reusable skills per engine. vs instance-level GEO: strategy reuse provides compounding gains. vs single-agent optimization: multi-agent planning + fidelity-aware evaluation produces better calibrated edits. vs generic multi-agent: engine-specific preference modeling is the key differentiator — different engines have different ranking behaviors, and MAGEO models this explicitly. The Twin Branch protocol for causal attribution is methodologically important.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no GEO/GEO capability, no strategy distillation pipeline, and no engine-specific preference modeling. However, MAGEO's strategy reuse pattern is directly transferable: Lyra's agents could similarly accumulate reusable skills per task type, with the orchestrator routing tasks to agents based on learned competence profiles. The fidelity-aware evaluation (dual-axis metric) pattern generalizes to any multi-objective agent optimization. Status: **BEHIND** on GEO; strategy-distillation pattern is transferable to Lyra's agent skill accumulation.
**Impact:** 2 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** investigate (GEO is not Lyra's primary domain; strategy distillation and dual-axis evaluation patterns are transferable)

## Taming Actor-Observer Asymmetry in Agents via Dialectical Alignment (ReTAS)
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.19548
**Mechanism:** (1) Problem identification: Actor-Observer Asymmetry (AOA) — a cognitive bias where an agent in actor role (self-reflection) attributes failures to external factors, while an observer agent (mutual auditing) attributes the same failures to internal faults. (2) Ambiguous Failure Benchmark: new diagnostic dataset measuring AOA trigger rate. (3) ReTAS framework (Reasoning via Thesis-Antithesis-Synthesis): Thesis phase — agent generates initial attribution from assigned perspective (self-reflective or auditing). Antithesis phase — counter-viewpoint deliberately articulated from opposing perspective. Synthesis phase — agents merge thesis-antithesis conflict into objective, perspective-invariant consensus using dialectical chain-of-thought. (4) Training via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO): model trained through "dialectical alignment" to consistently produce synthesis-driven reasoning regardless of role. (5) Dialectical chain-of-thought: structured reasoning pattern that forces perspective reconciliation before concluding.
**Results:** AOA trigger rate: swapping perspectives triggers AOA effect in **over 20% of cases** for most models on the Ambiguous Failure Benchmark. ReTAS effectively mitigates attribution inconsistency — dialectical alignment significantly reduces perspective-dependent attribution divergence. Significantly improves fault resolution rates in ambiguous scenarios. ACL 2026 Main Conference paper.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: multi-agent systems with mutual auditing/peer review, self-improving agents that reflect on failures, debugging complex multi-agent failures, scenarios where objective fault attribution is critical (safety, reliability). LOSES: unambiguous failure scenarios (AOA not triggered, no benefit), single-agent systems (no observer perspective), real-time systems (dialectical chain-of-thought adds latency), scenarios where preserving legitimate perspective diversity is valuable. GRPO training adds cost vs standard fine-tuning. Risk of over-synthesis: dialectical alignment may erase legitimate viewpoint diversity when perspectives genuinely differ for valid reasons.
**Rationale:** AOA is a fundamental cognitive bias documented in human psychology that manifests in LLM agents when they occupy different roles. Standard multi-agent debate/auditing assumes agents produce consistent attributions regardless of role — this paper demonstrates that assumption is false. ReTAS addresses this by making dialectical synthesis a trained behavior rather than a prompting hack. vs standard multi-agent auditing: dialectical alignment prevents attribution inconsistency at the model level. vs prompt-based de-biasing: GRPO training produces more robust debiasing than prompt engineering. vs consensus voting: synthesis preserves evidential nuance that voting erases. The Ambiguous Failure Benchmark is methodologically significant as the first AOA-specific diagnostic.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has peer review patterns (reviewer agent critiques executor output) but NO awareness of AOA, NO dialectical synthesis mechanism, and NO perspective-invariance training. If Lyra's reviewer and executor attribute failures differently (likely, given AOA findings), the system would produce inconsistent fault diagnoses and unreliable self-improvement signals. ReTAS's dialectical alignment directly applies to Lyra's planned self-improvement and verification subsystems — any agent that self-reflects AND is peer-reviewed is vulnerable to AOA. Status: **BEHIND** (no AOA awareness, no dialectical alignment).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (AOA directly undermines Lyra's agent auditing and self-improvement loops; dialectical alignment is a trainable fix for perspective-dependent reasoning)

## MALMAS: Memory-Augmented LLM-based Multi-Agent System for Automated Feature Generation
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.20261
**Mechanism:** (1) Multi-Agent Decomposition: feature generation split across agents with distinct responsibilities — Router Agent activates relevant subset per iteration. (2) Tripartite Memory Module: Procedural Memory (captures how features were constructed — the method/process), Feedback Memory (incorporates signals from downstream learning objective — what worked), Conceptual Memory (retains higher-level semantic patterns — why it worked). (3) Iterative Refinement Loop: memory from prior rounds adaptively guides subsequent feature generation — system learns which types of features work for a given task. (4) Router Agent: dynamically selects which specialist agents to activate per iteration based on task characteristics and memory-informed priors about agent competence. (5) Feature evaluation against downstream task performance feeds back into memory, closing the learning loop.
**Results:** Extensive experiments on multiple public datasets against SOTA baselines demonstrate effectiveness (exact numbers in full paper PDF, 15 tables + 4 figures). Outperforms both traditional methods (predefined operator libraries) and prior LLM-based approaches (fixed generation patterns, no learning-objective feedback). ACL 2026 Findings paper.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: tabular data tasks requiring feature engineering (classification, regression on structured data), domains with rich semantic patterns that operator-based methods miss, scenarios where iterative refinement is affordable, datasets where learned feature patterns transfer across similar tasks. LOSES: very small datasets (insufficient memory signal), real-time feature generation (iterative multi-agent loop adds latency), domains where interpretable features are mandatory (LLM-generated features may be opaque), simple linear problems where operator libraries suffice. Multi-agent LLM calls per iteration add significant compute cost vs single-pass methods. Tripartite memory requires careful management to avoid catastrophic forgetting or memory pollution from low-quality features.
**Rationale:** Traditional automated feature generation relies on predefined operator libraries (log, sqrt, binning, etc.) — these cannot leverage task semantics or learn from downstream performance. Prior LLM-based methods inject semantic knowledge but use fixed generation patterns and ignore learning-objective feedback. MALMAS combines the strengths: LLM semantic understanding + multi-agent exploration + memory-guided refinement from actual task performance. vs AutoML (operator-based): semantic understanding of feature meaning. vs single-agent LLM feature generation: multi-agent decomposition explores broader feature space. vs no-memory baselines: tripartite memory provides compounding improvement over iterations. The Router Agent's dynamic agent selection is the key multi-agent innovation.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no automated feature generation, no tripartite memory architecture, and no learning-objective feedback loop. However, MALMAS's tripartite memory pattern (procedural + feedback + conceptual) directly informs Lyra's memory subsystem design — it demonstrates that separating memory by purpose (how vs what-worked vs why) improves agent learning. The Router Agent pattern (dynamic specialist activation based on task + memory) generalizes beyond feature generation to Lyra's planned task routing. Status: **BEHIND** on feature generation; memory architecture pattern is transferable.
**Impact:** 2 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** investigate (feature generation is domain-specific; tripartite memory and dynamic router patterns are transferable to Lyra's memory and orchestration subsystems)
