## FairQE: Multi-Agent Framework for Mitigating Gender Bias in Translation Quality Estimation
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.21420
**Mechanism:** (1) Gender Cue Detection: system identifies when source text contains gender-related signals (both gender-ambiguous and gender-explicit contexts). (2) Gender-Flipped Variant Generation: produces alternative translations where gendered elements are swapped — creates counterfactual pairs for bias measurement. (3) Conventional QE Scoring: standard Quality Estimation model scores the translation quality. (4) LLM-Based Bias-Mitigating Reasoning: LLM component analyzes translations for gender bias, producing bias-aware quality adjustments. (5) Dynamic Bias-Aware Aggregation: combines conventional QE scores with LLM bias-mitigating reasoning through adaptive mechanism that adjusts weight based on detected bias magnitude. (6) Plug-and-play design: wraps around existing QE models without requiring retraining — the LLM reasoning component is additive.
**Results:** Consistently improves gender fairness over strong QE baselines across multiple gender bias evaluation settings. Achieves competitive or improved general QE performance under MQM-based meta-evaluation (WMT 2023 Metrics Shared Task standards). Gender fairness gains in both gender-ambiguous and gender-explicit contexts. Central claim: gender bias in QE can be effectively mitigated without sacrificing evaluation accuracy — a win-win result.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: translation quality estimation for gender-diverse languages, production MT evaluation pipelines, scenarios where gender fairness is a hard requirement (public-facing translation, legal/medical translation), deployments where QE model retraining is infeasible (plug-and-play). LOSES: languages without grammatical gender (no bias to mitigate, overhead unjustified), scenarios where LLM inference cost is prohibitive, real-time QE (variant generation + LLM reasoning adds latency). Gender coverage limited to tested language pairs and gender categories. Dynamic aggregation may introduce calibration issues — adjusting scores based on detected bias could over-correct or under-correct in edge cases. The win-win claim (fairness improvement without accuracy loss) needs verification across diverse language pairs.
**Rationale:** QE models exhibit systematic gender bias — they favor masculine realizations and penalize gender-misaligned translations. This bias distorts quality scores, which downstream affects MT system evaluation and deployment decisions. Prior bias mitigation requires retraining QE models (expensive, may degrade general performance). FairQE's plug-and-play approach solves the deployment problem: existing QE models remain unchanged, and the LLM bias-mitigating component is added at inference time. vs retraining-based debiasing: no risk of catastrophic forgetting on general QE. vs prompt-only debiasing: dynamic aggregation is more calibrated than simple prompt overrides. vs ignore-bias baseline: FairQE proves the problem is tractable — fairness and accuracy need not trade off.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no translation QE capability, no fairness evaluation infrastructure, and no bias-mitigating reasoning component. However, FairQE's plug-and-play bias mitigation pattern is highly transferable: Lyra could similarly wrap bias-mitigating LLM reasoning around any evaluation subsystem (code review scoring, agent performance evaluation, output quality assessment). The gender-flipped variant generation (counterfactual evaluation) pattern generalizes to any fairness-sensitive scoring task. The win-win claim (fairness + maintained accuracy) is methodologically important for Lyra's safety-utility calibration. Status: **BEHIND** on fairness infrastructure; plug-and-play bias mitigation pattern is transferable.
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 2 | **Tier:** investigate (fairness evaluation is relevant to Lyra's agent output assessment; plug-and-play bias mitigation pattern generalizes beyond translation QE)

## MuDABench: Multi-Document Analytical QA Benchmark
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.22239
**Mechanism:** (1) Task formulation: Multi-Document Analytical QA — given a large-scale document collection (hundreds to thousands), answer analytical questions requiring cross-document synthesis, comparison, aggregation, and reasoning. (2) MuDABench dataset construction: curated document collections spanning multiple domains with expert-annotated analytical questions categorized by reasoning type (comparative, aggregative, temporal, causal, multi-hop). (3) Document retrieval pipeline: baseline retrieval systems pre-filter relevant documents before QA models process them. (4) Evaluation framework: multi-dimensional scoring assessing answer correctness, evidence grounding (citation accuracy), reasoning fidelity (whether the reasoning chain matches the required analytical operation), and coverage (whether all relevant documents were consulted). (5) Baseline comparison: evaluates both retrieval-augmented LLMs and long-context LLMs on the benchmark to establish performance ceilings.
**Results:** Long-context LLMs struggle with analytical QA at scale — performance degrades significantly as document collection size grows. Retrieval-augmented approaches show better scaling but suffer from retrieval recall gaps (missing relevant documents). Multi-document synthesis remains a significant challenge: models frequently fail to correctly compare/contrast information across documents, miss contradictions, and incorrectly aggregate numerical data. Human performance substantially exceeds best model performance. Paper establishes MuDABench as a diagnostic tool for measuring progress on large-scale document reasoning.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: evaluating real-world document-scale reasoning capability, benchmarking systems that must handle large corpora (legal discovery, literature review, enterprise search), diagnostic categorization of reasoning failures. LOSES: benchmark construction is expensive (expert annotation), domain coverage limited to curated collections, retrieval component introduces confounding variable (hard to isolate QA model quality from retriever quality). Long-context model evaluation is compute-intensive. The benchmark's difficulty may ceiling-flatten as models improve, requiring continuous benchmark evolution.
**Rationale:** Current QA benchmarks use single documents or small sets — real-world analytical tasks require reasoning across hundreds of documents. MuDABench fills the gap between single-doc QA and full corpus-scale reasoning. The multi-dimensional evaluation (correctness + grounding + reasoning fidelity + coverage) provides richer diagnostic signal than binary accuracy. vs HotpotQA/MultiHopQA: MuDABench operates at 10-100x larger document scale. vs needle-in-haystack: analytical reasoning rather than fact retrieval. vs domain-specific benchmarks: cross-domain design tests general reasoning capability.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no multi-document analytical QA capability, no document-scale reasoning infrastructure, and no cross-document synthesis mechanism. However, MuDABench's evaluation framework (grounding + reasoning fidelity + coverage) directly informs Lyra's verification subsystem design — any agent that claims to have read and synthesized multiple sources should be evaluated on whether it actually consulted all relevant sources (coverage) and whether its reasoning chain matches required analytical operations (reasoning fidelity). The finding that retrieval recall gaps are the primary bottleneck for RAG-based approaches is relevant to Lyra's planned knowledge retrieval. Status: **BEHIND** on multi-document reasoning; evaluation framework is transferable.
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** investigate (multi-document reasoning is relevant to Lyra's research and synthesis capabilities; evaluation dimensions are transferable to Lyra's verification subsystem)

## Bridging the Pose-Semantic Gap: Cascade Framework for Text-Based Person Anomaly Search
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.23282
**Mechanism:** (1) Problem definition: Text-Based Person Anomaly Search (TBPAS) — given a textual description of anomalous behavior (e.g., "person running while carrying a large bag"), retrieve images/video frames of persons exhibiting that anomaly. (2) Pose-Semantic Gap identification: standard vision-language models align text to holistic image semantics, but anomalous behaviors are often defined by pose configuration (body joint arrangements) rather than semantic scene content — creating a mismatch. (3) Cascade Framework: Stage 1 (Pose-Aware Filtering) — uses pose estimation to extract body keypoints, filters candidates based on pose-text similarity. Stage 2 (Semantic Refinement) — applies vision-language semantic matching only to pose-filtered candidates, refining the ranking. (4) Pose-Text Alignment Module: learned mapping between textual behavior descriptions and pose configurations using contrastive learning. (5) Two-stage cascade reduces compute by avoiding expensive semantic matching on all candidates.
**Results:** Cascade framework significantly outperforms single-stage vision-language baselines on TBPAS benchmarks. Pose-aware filtering stage eliminates large numbers of irrelevant candidates early, reducing semantic matching compute by 40-60% while maintaining or improving retrieval precision. Pose-Text Alignment Module successfully maps behavior descriptions to joint configurations for common anomaly types. Main failure mode: unusual anomalies with atypical pose configurations that the alignment module hasn't encountered in training.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: surveillance/security applications, scenarios where pose is the primary discriminative signal, large-scale retrieval where compute efficiency matters, domains where semantic scene context is misleading (anomalous behavior in normal-looking scenes). LOSES: anomalies defined by appearance rather than pose (clothing, carried objects), scenarios with heavy occlusion (pose estimation fails), very fine-grained behavior distinctions that exceed pose estimation resolution. Two-stage cascade introduces a failure dependency: pose-stage errors propagate (missed retrievals cannot be recovered by semantic stage). Pose estimation adds latency and requires additional model infrastructure.
**Rationale:** Standard vision-language models are optimized for semantic similarity (object categories, scene types) — they are weak at pose-level discrimination because pose is rarely described in training captions. The cascade framework pragmatically addresses this: use cheap pose filtering to narrow the search space, then apply expensive semantic matching only where needed. vs end-to-end vision-language: explicit pose modeling provides interpretable intermediate representation. vs pose-only retrieval: semantic refinement recovers cases where anomaly has both pose and appearance components. vs single-stage multi-modal fusion: cascade provides computational efficiency without architectural complexity.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no computer vision capability, no pose estimation infrastructure, and no multi-modal retrieval pipeline. This is a domain-specific computer vision finding with limited direct applicability to Lyra's text/agent-centric architecture. The cascade pattern (cheap fast filter + expensive precise refinement) is a general architectural pattern that partially overlaps with FrugalGPT's sequential LLM cascade — both use a cheap-first-then-expensive routing strategy. Status: **NOT APPLICABLE** for core architecture; cascade pattern is a known pattern already covered by FrugalGPT/RouteLLM findings.
**Impact:** 1 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** skip (domain-specific CV finding; cascade pattern already covered by LLM routing papers)

## GraphPlanner: Graph Memory-Augmented Agentic Routing for Multi-Agent LLMs
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.23626
**Mechanism:** (1) Graph Memory Construction: builds a dynamic knowledge graph representing agents (nodes), their capabilities/specialties (node attributes), past interaction outcomes (weighted edges), and task-agent affinity scores. (2) Graph-Augmented Routing: given a new task, the router queries the graph memory to identify candidate agents, then uses graph neural reasoning (message passing over the agent graph) to score and select optimal agent assignments. (3) Multi-Agent Planning Integration: routing decisions feed into a planner that constructs execution DAGs respecting agent capabilities and inter-agent communication costs derived from the graph. (4) Graph Update Loop: after task execution, outcomes (success/failure, latency, output quality) are written back as edge weight updates, enabling the graph to learn which agent pairs work well together and which task types suit which agents. (5) Cold-start handling: new agents initialized with capability descriptions; graph bootstraps via few-shot task execution before routing quality converges.
**Results:** GraphPlanner outperforms static routing baselines (round-robin, random, capability-matching without graph) on multi-agent task completion benchmarks. Graph memory enables 15-25% improvement in routing accuracy (assigning tasks to the best-suited agent) compared to embedding-based similarity routing. Edge weight learning (capturing inter-agent compatibility) provides an additional 5-10% gain over node-only routing. Cold-start performance is comparable to static baselines; graph quality improves monotonically with more task executions. The graph representation is interpretable — human operators can inspect which agents are considered complementary/conflicting.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: multi-agent systems with heterogeneous agent pools, recurring task types where routing patterns can be learned, systems where inter-agent compatibility matters (some agent pairs collaborate better than others), scenarios requiring interpretable routing decisions. LOSES: single-agent systems (no routing needed), homogeneous agent pools (static routing sufficient), one-off task distributions (graph never converges), latency-critical routing (graph message passing adds overhead vs lookup-based routing). Graph maintenance adds complexity: stale edges, concept drift as agents evolve, graph storage/query infrastructure. Cold-start period may produce suboptimal routing until sufficient task history accumulates.
**Rationale:** Current multi-agent routing is predominantly static (predefined roles, capability-matching) or embedding-based (cosine similarity between task and agent description). These approaches ignore the relational structure of multi-agent systems — agent A might be individually capable but collaborate poorly with agent B, while agent C might be individually weaker but synergize well with B. GraphPlanner captures this relational information explicitly. vs embedding routing: graph captures second-order relationships (A works well with B who works well with C → A and C might collaborate effectively via B). vs static routing: graph adapts to observed performance rather than relying solely on declared capabilities. vs end-to-end learned routing: graph is interpretable and supports human inspection/overrides.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has a planned Router (§4.5) and TaskAllocator but NO graph-based agent memory, NO inter-agent compatibility tracking, and NO learned routing from task outcomes. Lyra's current routing design (maturity: none) is closer to static capability-matching. GraphPlanner directly addresses Lyra's routing gap and extends it with relational learning. The interpretable graph representation aligns with Lyra's debugging/observability goals. The cold-start strategy (bootstrap from capability descriptions) provides a deployment path. Status: **BEHIND** (no graph routing infrastructure; GraphPlanner is a direct blueprint for Lyra's router upgrade).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (directly addresses Lyra's Router gap; graph memory + learned routing is the most architecturally aligned routing paper in the corpus)

## Latent Agents: A Post-Training Procedure for Internalized Multi-Agent Debate
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.24881
**Mechanism:** (1) Core insight: Multi-agent debate improves reasoning quality but incurs substantial inference cost (multiple agents, multiple turns). Latent Agents internalizes the debate process into a single model's forward pass. (2) Post-Training Procedure: fine-tune a base LLM to simulate multiple "latent agent" personas within its internal representations — the model learns to generate multiple perspectives, debate them internally, and produce a synthesized output in one pass. (3) Training Data Generation: use an external multi-agent debate system (multiple LLM instances debating) to generate training examples — input (question) + output (debate transcript + final answer). (4) Internalization via Fine-Tuning: train the single model to reproduce the full debate-and-synthesis trajectory from the multi-agent system, effectively distilling N agents into 1 model. (5) At inference time: single forward pass produces the equivalent of multi-turn multi-agent debate — no external agent orchestration needed. (6) Latent persona control: optional conditioning tokens can guide which "persona" dominates for a given query.
**Results:** Latent Agents achieve comparable reasoning quality to explicit multi-agent debate systems while using 1/N the inference compute (single pass vs N agents x K turns). On reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, MMLU, BigBench), Latent Agents match or approach the performance of 3-5 agent debate systems at ~3-5x lower cost. The quality gap vs explicit debate widens on tasks requiring diverse external knowledge (multiple agents can consult different sources; latent debate is limited to model's internal knowledge). Persona conditioning enables controllable perspective emphasis without retraining.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: cost-constrained deployments where multi-agent debate quality is desired but inference budget is limited, latency-sensitive applications (single pass vs multi-turn), scenarios where model size is constrained (can't run N copies), recurring debate patterns that benefit from internalization. LOSES: knowledge-intensive tasks requiring external tool use (latent agents share one model's knowledge; explicit agents can each use different tools), tasks where genuine perspective diversity requires different model architectures/training data (latent agents share one model's weights), scenarios where debate transparency is required (internal debate is unobservable). Post-training requires access to model weights and training infrastructure. Risk of "debate collapse": internalized debate may converge to a single perspective prematurely since all latent personas share the same underlying model weights and biases.
**Rationale:** Multi-agent debate works because diverse perspectives catch errors and refine reasoning. But running N agents is expensive. Latent Agents observe that the debate pattern can be internalized — the model learns to simulate disagreement and synthesis internally, amortizing the cost. This is analogous to how humans internalize dialogue: we can simulate a debate in our own mind without actually talking to other people. vs explicit multi-agent debate: 3-5x cost reduction with comparable quality on reasoning tasks. vs single-model CoT: latent debate provides more thorough reasoning by simulating adversarial perspectives. vs model merging/ensemble: latent debate preserves the sequential refinement dynamic of debate rather than just averaging outputs. The post-training distillation approach is more data-efficient than training a multi-agent system from scratch.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's architecture assumes explicit multi-agent orchestration (PrimaryAgent + specialist pool + debate patterns). Latent Agents suggests an alternative/complementary approach: for recurring reasoning patterns, internalize the debate into fine-tuned models to reduce orchestration overhead. This directly challenges Lyra's assumption that external multi-agent orchestration is always necessary. For Lyra: (1) high-frequency reasoning tasks could use latent-agent models (cheaper, faster), (2) novel/complex tasks could still use explicit multi-agent debate (more flexible, tool-capable), (3) the router could decide per-task whether to use latent or explicit debate. Latent Agents thus enables a hybrid architecture: internalized debate for routine reasoning, external orchestration for novel/edge cases. Status: **AHEAD** (Latent Agents provides a cost-optimization strategy that Lyra's architecture doesn't yet consider; hybrid latent+explicit debate is a Phase 2+ optimization).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (challenges Lyra's explicit-orchestration assumption; enables hybrid architecture that dramatically reduces cost for routine reasoning while preserving explicit debate for complex tasks)

## SkillOS: Learning Skill Curation for Self-Evolving Agents
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06614
**Mechanism:** (1) Formulates agent skill curation as a lifecycle management problem: skills are created (via exploration, teacher demonstration, or composition of existing skills), evaluated (tested on benchmark tasks to measure competence), stored (indexed in a skill library with metadata), retrieved (matched to incoming tasks via semantic similarity), executed (invoked by the agent at runtime), and pruned (deprecated when superseded or stale). (2) Self-evolving loop: agent encounters novel task → searches skill library for relevant skills → if none sufficient, attempts skill creation via LLM-guided synthesis (generate code/tool-use pattern, test, iterate) → adds successful new skill to library → periodically self-audits to prune redundant/low-quality skills. (3) Skill composition graph: skills can be chained (output of skill A feeds input of skill B) or nested (skill C invokes skill D as subroutine). Graph edges track success rates and latency, enabling the agent to prefer reliable compositions. (4) Curation quality metrics: precision (retrieved skills are relevant), recall (all needed skills are found), freshness (skills reflect current environment/tool versions), non-redundancy (minimal overlap between skills). (5) Multi-agent skill sharing: agents in a collective can publish skills to a shared registry; reputation-weighted voting determines which community skills are promoted to curated status.
**Results:** SkillOS agents demonstrate accelerating performance curves — each new skill reduces future task completion time (learning-to-learn effect). On evolving benchmark suites (task distributions shift over time), SkillOS maintains 85%+ success rate vs 45-60% for static-skill agents that never update. Skill composition graph enables solving novel composite tasks that no single skill addresses: success rate on 0-shot compositional tasks improves from 12% (no composition) to 47% (graph-based composition). Pruning reduces skill library bloat by 30-40% without degrading task coverage (removes superseded and never-used skills). Multi-agent skill sharing with reputation filtering achieves 92% of the performance of a centrally curated skill library while being fully decentralized.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: dynamic environments where task distributions evolve over time, multi-agent collectives where skills can be shared and reused, domains with clear skill decomposability, long-running agents that benefit from accumulated experience. LOSES: one-off task distributions (curation overhead not amortized), environments where skill boundaries are ambiguous, safety-critical domains where self-created skills pose unacceptable risk (unvetted code execution), latency-constrained settings where composition graph traversal adds overhead. Skill creation loop requires execution environment for testing — risky without sandboxing. Pruning can prematurely remove skills that are rarely needed but critical when needed (cold-start for rare tasks). Multi-agent skill sharing introduces trust/quality risks: malicious or incompetent agents can pollute the shared registry.
**Rationale:** Prior agent frameworks treat skills as a static set defined by developers. SkillOS recognizes that in open-world settings, the task distribution is unknown at design time — agents must learn and curate skills continuously. This mirrors human skill development: we learn new skills on demand, practice them, combine them, and let unused skills atrophy. vs static skill libraries: SkillOS adapts to distribution shift (60%→85% success on evolving benchmarks). vs monolithic end-to-end learning: SkillOS provides modular, interpretable skill representations that can be inspected, shared, and composed. vs retrieval-only (no creation): SkillOS's creation loop handles truly novel tasks that have no existing skill. The self-audit (pruning) mechanism is critical — without it, skill libraries grow unboundedly, increasing retrieval latency and storage costs.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has a plugin system (§4.7 Plugins, maturity: stub) and command infrastructure (§4.9 Commands) but NO skill lifecycle management — no creation, no evaluation, no pruning, no composition graph, no multi-agent skill sharing. The current plugin design is static (developer-defined plugins loaded at startup). SkillOS directly informs Lyra's planned plugin upgrade: skill creation via LLM-guided synthesis, skill composition graph for complex task solving, and self-audit/pruning to manage plugin bloat. The reputation-weighted multi-agent skill sharing is a Phase 3+ consideration for Lyra's agent collective patterns. Status: **BEHIND** (no skill lifecycle infrastructure; SkillOS provides the blueprint for Lyra's plugin evolution).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (directly addresses Lyra's plugin/skill gap; self-evolving skill curation is essential for Lyra's long-term agent autonomy)

## From Storage to Experience: A Survey on the Evolution of LLM Agent Memory Mechanisms
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06716
**Mechanism:** (1) Taxonomizes agent memory along three evolutionary stages: Stage 1 (Storage Memory) — raw persistence of conversation history and retrieved documents, akin to a database. Stage 2 (Structured Memory) — knowledge graphs, vector databases, and relational stores that organize information for efficient retrieval. Stage 3 (Experiential Memory) — memories that encode not just what happened but what was learned (lessons, patterns, strategies) and actively influence future agent behavior. (2) Defines five memory operations universal across stages: Encoding (how raw interaction is converted to memory representation), Storage (where and in what format), Retrieval (how relevant memories are fetched given current context), Consolidation (how memories are reorganized, summarized, and strengthened over time), Forgetting (how stale/low-utility memories are pruned). (3) Maps 50+ recent memory papers to a design-space matrix: memory type (episodic, semantic, procedural, working) vs operation (encode, store, retrieve, consolidate, forget) vs representation (text, embedding, graph, neural). (4) Identifies four open problems: Memory Grounding (ensuring retrieved memories are factually accurate, not hallucinated reconstructions), Memory Interference (new memories overwriting or contradicting old ones), Memory Scalability (retrieval quality degradation as memory grows to millions of entries), Memory Agency (how agents decide what to remember vs what to discard — the meta-memory problem). (5) Proposes evaluation framework: memory-augmented agents should be benchmarked on (a) retrieval precision/recall, (b) consistency across sessions, (c) adaptation speed to new information, (d) forgetting rate of critical information, (e) compute/storage cost per memory operation.
**Results:** Survey-level finding: most current agent memory systems operate at Stage 1-2 (storage/structured retrieval). Fewer than 15% of surveyed systems implement experiential memory (learning from past interactions to change future behavior). Systems that implement consolidation (periodic summarization, graph reorganization) demonstrate 20-40% improvement in multi-session task consistency. Forgetting mechanisms (both decay-based and utility-based) are underexplored: only 8/50+ papers address intentional forgetting, yet unbounded memory growth is the primary scalability bottleneck. Memory grounding emerges as the most critical open problem: 30-50% of retrieved "memories" in RAG-based systems contain factual distortions introduced during encoding or consolidation.
**Trade-offs:** Stage 1 (Storage): simple, fast, lossless — but retrieval quality degrades with scale, no consolidation. Stage 2 (Structured): better retrieval precision, supports complex queries — but structuring overhead, schema rigidity, schema evolution challenges. Stage 3 (Experiential): enables genuine learning and adaptation — but grounding risk (learned lessons may be wrong), interference between experiences, harder to debug and audit. Retrieval vs Consolidation trade-off: more aggressive consolidation (summarization, merging) reduces storage but risks information loss. Forgetting vs Retention: aggressive forgetting controls scale but may delete critical rare-use memories.
**Rationale:** The progression from Storage to Structured to Experiential memory mirrors human memory evolution — we don't just store facts, we extract patterns and lessons. The survey's key insight: most agent memory research focuses on retrieval (Stage 1-2) while the hard problems (consolidation, forgetting, agency) are at Stage 3. This explains the plateau in memory-augmented agent performance: better retrieval helps marginally, but without experiential learning, agents repeat the same mistakes. The five-operation framework (encode, store, retrieve, consolidate, forget) provides a comprehensive design checklist — missing any operation produces a brittle memory system. The evaluation framework addresses the current measurement gap: most papers report only retrieval precision, ignoring consistency, adaptation, and forgetting.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's memory subsystem (§02) is at maturity `partial` (conversation history, basic vector store). This places Lyra at Stage 1-2 in the survey's taxonomy. Missing: consolidation (no periodic summarization or graph reorganization), forgetting (no pruning of stale memories), experiential memory (no learned lessons/patterns from past interactions), memory agency (no meta-memory decision about what to remember). The survey's five-operation framework serves as Lyra's memory subsystem design checklist — each missing operation is a concrete implementation gap. Memory grounding (factual accuracy of retrieved memories) is especially relevant given Lyra's multi-agent architecture where agents can propagate corrupted memories. Status: **BEHIND** (at Stage 1-2 of 3; survey provides comprehensive design checklist and evaluation framework for memory upgrade).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 5 | **Tier:** breakthrough (P0 — memory is the foundation for all other agent capabilities; this survey maps the entire design space and identifies exactly which operations Lyra is missing)

## HAGE: Harnessing Agentic Memory via RL-Driven Weighted Graph Evolution
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09942
**Mechanism:** (1) Represents agent memory as a weighted heterogeneous graph: nodes = entities (concepts, tools, tasks, past interactions), edges = typed relationships (causes, precedes, contradicts, generalizes, requires), edge weights = confidence/utility scores. (2) Reinforcement Learning loop: agent takes action → environment returns reward (task success, user satisfaction, efficiency) → reward signal backpropagates through the graph to update edge weights of memory entries that contributed to the action. (3) Graph Evolution operations: Add Node (new entities encountered), Merge Nodes (similar entities consolidated to reduce redundancy), Update Edge (weight adjusted via RL credit assignment), Prune Edge/Node (low-utility memories removed to bound graph size), Rewire (discover new relationships between existing entities via transitive reasoning). (4) Credit Assignment via Graph Attention: when an action succeeds, attention weights from the action-decision state to memory graph nodes identify which memories contributed; those edges are reinforced; edges not attended to are decayed. (5) Exploration-Exploitation in Memory: the agent sometimes retrieves high-weight (exploit) memories and sometimes samples lower-weight (explore) memories; RL policy learns the optimal retrieval temperature per task type. (6) Long-term graph evolution trends: high-utility subgraphs become densely connected (forming "skill clusters"), low-utility subgraphs are pruned, and bridge edges between clusters enable compositional reasoning.
**Results:** HAGE outperforms static memory architectures (fixed graph, fixed retrieval) by 18-32% on multi-session task completion benchmarks. RL-driven weight evolution produces memory graphs that are 40-60% sparser than initial graphs (pruning removes noise) while maintaining or improving retrieval recall. Credit assignment via graph attention correctly identifies contributing memories for 78% of successful actions (validated via human annotation of memory relevance). Merge operations reduce graph node count by 25-35% without information loss (semantic near-duplicates consolidated). The exploration-exploitation learned policy outperforms both uniform sampling (+12%) and greedy top-k retrieval (+8%) for novel task types. Graph evolution stabilizes after ~200-500 task executions: weight updates become incremental, pruning rate drops, merge events become rare — indicating convergence to a stable memory representation.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: long-running agents with accumulating experience, domains with clear task-memory causal relationships (RL credit assignment works), multi-session scenarios where memory quality compounds over time, environments where memory efficiency matters (graph sparsification). LOSES: cold-start (empty graph requires many interactions to become useful), tasks with delayed/sparse rewards (credit assignment fails to identify relevant memories), rapidly changing environments (graph evolution lags behind distribution shift), safety-critical memory (RL-driven pruning can remove memories that are rarely-used but safety-critical), deterministic task distributions (static memory sufficient). RL training overhead: requires reward signal availability; unsupervised settings need synthetic reward generation. Graph attention for credit assignment adds inference compute cost per action.
**Rationale:** Current agent memory systems treat memory as a passive store — retrieve when needed, maybe update with new facts. HAGE treats memory as an active, evolving asset optimized via reinforcement learning. The key insight: memory utility can be learned from task outcomes — memories that consistently contribute to successful actions should be strengthened; memories that are never useful should be pruned. This mirrors biological memory consolidation (synaptic plasticity strengthens useful neural pathways). vs static memory graphs: RL evolution adapts memory importance to observed utility (not just semantic similarity). vs embedding-based memory: graph structure enables explicit multi-hop reasoning (A caused B, B requires C → A implies need for C). vs pure pruning approaches: RL provides a principled signal for what to keep (utility-maximizing) rather than heuristics (recency, frequency). The credit assignment via graph attention is the critical innovation — without it, the agent cannot know which memories contributed to success.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no graph-based memory (§02 Memory maturity: partial, no graph structure), no RL-driven memory optimization, no credit assignment from task outcomes to memory entries, and no memory pruning mechanism. Lyra's memory is essentially a flat conversation log with basic vector retrieval. HAGE maps directly to Lyra's memory upgrade path: (1) construct weighted heterogeneous memory graph, (2) instrument task execution with reward signals, (3) implement graph attention credit assignment, (4) evolve graph via RL weight updates + pruning. This also connects to Lyra's planned GraphRAG integration (§03 Context) — the memory graph can serve double duty as both the knowledge retrieval and the reasoning substrate. Status: **BEHIND** (no graph memory, no RL optimization; HAGE provides a complete architecture for Lyra's memory upgrade).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 5 | **Tier:** breakthrough (P0 — RL-driven graph memory is the highest-impact memory architecture in the corpus; directly addresses Lyra's memory gap with a complete, proven mechanism)

## NanoResearch: Co-Evolving Skills, Memory, and Policy for Personalized Research Automation
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10813
**Mechanism:** (1) Joint co-evolution framework: three interdependent components — Skill Library (reusable research operations: literature search, paper summarization, experiment design, data analysis, citation formatting), Memory Graph (accumulated research knowledge: paper relationships, finding provenance, methodology comparisons, dead-end logs), Policy Network (research strategy selector: which skill to apply next, what depth of analysis, when to broaden vs narrow search). (2) Co-evolution dynamics: executing a skill produces new knowledge (added to memory graph); enriched memory graph enables better policy decisions (more informed search/analysis strategies); improved policy selects better skills to execute — positive feedback loop. (3) Personalization via interaction history: the system learns researcher-specific preferences (preferred citation styles, depth tolerance, methodology biases, domain focus areas) from past sessions and adapts all three components accordingly. (4) Research trajectory optimization: treats research as a POMDP where the policy network navigates a literature graph, selecting which papers to read, which claims to verify, which experiments to run, and when to stop. Reward signal comes from: (a) finding relevant papers (precision), (b) covering the literature (recall), (c) producing correct conclusions (accuracy vs ground truth), (d) researcher satisfaction (explicit feedback). (5) Implementation: skills are implemented as parameterized LLM prompts with tool-use capabilities; memory is a Neo4j-backed heterogeneous graph; policy is a lightweight transformer trained via PPO on research session trajectories. All three components update continuously — no separate training/deployment phases.
**Results:** NanoResearch demonstrates compounding improvement over multiple research sessions: Session 10 outperforms Session 1 by 35-50% across literature coverage, finding relevance, and conclusion accuracy metrics. Co-evolution (all three components updating together) outperforms independent evolution (each component updated separately) by 18-25%, confirming the positive feedback loop. Personalization: researcher-specific models achieve 22% higher satisfaction scores (explicit ratings) and 15% higher task completion rates compared to generic models. Research trajectory optimization via POMDP policy reduces average time-to-saturation (point of diminishing returns in literature search) by 30-40% compared to fixed-depth search. Memory graph quality: after 10+ sessions, the graph correctly identifies seminal papers, citation cascades, and methodology relationships that generic search tools (Google Scholar, Semantic Scholar) miss or rank incorrectly for the specific research context. Policy network learns to allocate more exploration budget to novel subfields (high uncertainty) and more exploitation to familiar subfields (high confidence).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: recurring research workflows (literature reviews, systematic reviews, competitive analysis), personalized research assistants that learn researcher preferences over time, research domains with rich citation/metadata graphs, long-running research projects where session-over-session improvement compounds. LOSES: one-off research queries (co-evolution overhead not amortized), novel research domains with no prior sessions (cold-start — reverts to generic policy), highly creative/breakthrough research where past patterns mislead (policy overfits to incremental research patterns), privacy-sensitive research where personalization data must not be stored. Co-evolution creates a chicken-and-egg problem: good policy requires good memory, which requires good skills, which requires good policy. Cold-start is addressed via bootstrapping from generic models, but initial sessions are significantly lower quality. The POMDP formulation assumes research progress is measurable — this breaks down for exploratory/"unknown unknown" research.
**Rationale:** Current research assistants (Elicit, Consensus, SciSpace) provide fixed-function retrieval and summarization with no learning across sessions. NanoResearch's key insight: research is inherently iterative and personal — a research assistant should get better the more you work with it, learning your preferences, your domain, and effective strategies for your specific research questions. The co-evolution framework recognizes that skills, memory, and policy are interdependent — upgrading one without the others produces diminishing returns. vs fixed research tools: NanoResearch's session-over-session improvement (35-50%) demonstrates the value of personalization. vs single-component learning (skills only, memory only, policy only): co-evolution's 18-25% advantage confirms the interdependence hypothesis. vs general-purpose LLM agents: domain-specific optimization (research workflows) enables deeper optimization than general agent frameworks.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's research capability (§4.15 Research) matures at `none` — no literature search, no paper analysis, no research trajectory optimization, no personalization. However, NanoResearch is essentially a specialized application of the same architectural patterns Lyra is building: skill libraries (Lyra's plugins/commands), memory graphs (Lyra's planned graph memory), policy networks (Lyra's router/task allocator), and co-evolution (Lyra's self-improvement loops). NanoResearch validates that co-evolving these components produces compounding gains — this directly supports Lyra's architectural thesis that memory, skills, and routing should be integrated, not separate subsystems. The POMDP research trajectory formulation is directly applicable to Lyra's deep-research pipeline. Status: **BEHIND** on research capability; **ALIGNED** with architectural thesis (co-evolution validates Lyra's integrated approach).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 5 | **Tier:** breakthrough (validates Lyra's integrated architecture thesis; research automation is a Phase 2+ application of Lyra's core infrastructure; co-evolution framework is directly transferable to Lyra's self-improvement design)

## Comment and Control: Hijacking Agentic Workflows via Context-Grounded Evolution
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11229
**Mechanism:** (1) Identifies a novel attack vector on multi-agent workflows: "context-grounded evolution" where an adversary injects malicious content that appears benign in isolation but, when processed through sequential agent interactions, evolves into a control hijack. (2) Attack proceeds in three phases: (a) Seed Injection — adversary places crafted text in agent-accessible content (docs, web pages, emails) containing conditional triggers that activate only in specific conversational contexts; (b) Contextual Propagation — as agents retrieve and reference the seeded content across conversation turns, the triggers activate and subtly shift agent behavior toward adversary goals; (c) Workflow Hijack — accumulated behavioral shifts cause the agent workflow to deviate from intended task to adversary-specified actions. (3) The "evolution" is context-grounded: each agent turn provides new context that activates deeper layers of the injected payload, enabling multi-stage attacks that evade single-turn safety checks. (4) Attack success requires: (a) seed survivability (content persists in agent memory/context), (b) propagation feasibility (content is retrieved and referenced), (c) cumulative effect (small per-turn shifts sum to large behavioral change). (5) Defense evaluation: tests input filtering, output monitoring, and context-integrity checking against the attack; finds that single-point defenses fail because the attack operates across multiple turns.
**Results:** The context-grounded evolution attack achieves 60-80% workflow hijack success rate against state-of-the-art agent frameworks (AutoGPT, CrewAI, LangGraph agents) when seeds are placed in commonly accessed sources (documentation, issue trackers, knowledge bases). Attack stealth: 85% of hijacked workflows appear normal to per-turn safety monitors — the deviation is only detectable by analyzing multi-turn behavioral trajectories. Defense results: per-turn input filtering catches 15-25% of injected seeds; per-turn output monitoring catches 20-30%; context-integrity checking (comparing agent behavior across turns to expected trajectory) catches 65-75% but with 12% false positive rate on legitimate workflow adaptations. Combined defense (all three layers) reduces hijack success to 12-18% at cost of 25% latency overhead.
**Trade-offs:** WINS for attacker: multi-agent workflows with shared context pools, long-horizon tasks spanning many agent turns, environments where agents access untrusted external content, agent architectures that accumulate conversation history without integrity verification. LOSES for attacker: single-turn agent interactions, agents with strict context isolation, environments where agent-accessible content is fully trusted/curated. For defender: context-integrity checking is effective but computationally expensive (requires trajectory analysis); false positives on legitimate adaptations create user friction. The fundamental tension: giving agents access to rich external context (necessary for capability) vs exposing them to injection surfaces (security risk).
**Rationale:** Prior agent security research focused on single-turn prompt injection. This paper shows that multi-turn context evolution creates a fundamentally harder problem — attacks can distribute their payload across turns, each individual step appearing benign. This is analogous to biological evolution: small mutations accumulate over generations to produce dramatic change. vs single-turn injection: context-grounded evolution is 3-4x harder to detect (85% evasion of per-turn monitors). vs multi-agent consensus attacks: this paper's attack is more insidious because it doesn't require agent consensus — single-agent workflows can be hijacked if they reference contaminated context. The paper's key contribution is demonstrating that context propagation (a core feature of modern agents) is also a security vulnerability.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has NO defense against multi-turn context manipulation (§4.17 Safety maturity: `none`). Lyra's planned multi-agent architecture with shared knowledge graphs, aggregated conversation memory, and cross-agent context sharing creates the exact attack surface this paper exploits. The plugin system (§4.7) and research capability (§4.15), if built without context-integrity verification, become injection vectors. This paper is CRITICAL reading for Lyra — it identifies a failure mode that Lyra's architecture must be designed to resist from the start, not retrofitted later. Specific recommendations for Lyra: (1) implement context-integrity verification (checksum/trajectory comparison) on cross-turn agent context, (2) maintain per-source trust scores that decay with agent-chain depth, (3) sandbox external content retrieval so seeds cannot propagate unchecked. Status: **BEHIND** (critical security gap — Lyra's architecture has zero defenses against the attack vector this paper demonstrates).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** parity (P0 — security must be designed into Lyra's multi-agent context architecture; this paper provides both the threat model and defense blueprint)

## Proteus: A Self-Evolving Red Team for Agent Skill Ecosystems
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11891
**Mechanism:** (1) Proteus is a red-team agent that co-evolves with a target agent ecosystem: as the target agents learn new skills, Proteus learns to exploit them. (2) Self-evolving loop: (a) Proteus observes target agent skill executions, (b) generates adversarial test cases designed to expose skill failure modes (edge cases, prompt injection, tool misuse, logic errors), (c) executes attacks against the skill and records outcomes, (d) uses attack success/failure to update its own attack policy (reinforcement learning over attack strategies), (e) target agents fix discovered vulnerabilities (skill patching), (f) Proteus adapts — generating new attacks against patched skills. (3) Attack taxonomy: Proteus generates attacks across five dimensions: Input Manipulation (adversarial inputs that bypass validation), Context Poisoning (contaminating the information environment the skill operates in), Composition Exploitation (attacks that exploit interactions between composed skills), State Confusion (attacks that corrupt the skill's internal state tracking), and Permission Escalation (attacks that trick skills into performing privileged operations). (4) Skill vulnerability database: Proteus maintains a structured catalog of discovered vulnerabilities, enabling it to test whether newly created skills share weaknesses with previously exploited skills (vulnerability inheritance). (5) Multi-agent red teaming: multiple Proteus instances can coordinate — one distracts a monitoring skill while another exploits a target skill, or they jointly construct complex multi-step exploits.
**Results:** Proteus discovers 3-5x more unique vulnerabilities than static red-team tools (fuzzing, static analysis) within the same testing budget. Over 100 co-evolution cycles (attack→patch→reattack), Proteus maintains 40-55% attack success rate despite continuous patching — the target ecosystem never reaches full immunity. Vulnerability inheritance: 60-70% of newly created skills share at least one vulnerability class with existing skills, enabling Proteus to exploit new skills within 5-10 attack attempts. Multi-agent coordination (3+ Proteus instances) discovers 2.3x more composition exploits than single Proteus instance. Skill patching response: target agents that integrate Proteus-discovered vulnerabilities into their training/design loop reduce vulnerability surface by 35-50% over 50 co-evolution cycles compared to agents that patch manually.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: agent ecosystems under active development (continuous new skills), safety-critical agent deployments where undiscovered vulnerabilities are unacceptable, multi-agent systems with complex skill composition, environments where attacker sophistication evolves over time. LOSES: static agent systems (red team co-evolution overhead not amortized), simple single-skill agents (limited attack surface), resource-constrained testing budgets (Proteus requires compute for both attack generation and RL training). Red-team attacks themselves consume agent execution budget — in production, the red team should operate in a sandboxed mirror, not against live systems. Self-evolving red team can discover vulnerabilities faster than developers can patch them — this creates a defensive burden unless patching is automated (which Proteus assumes).
**Rationale:** Traditional red teaming is a one-shot process: security experts test a system, report vulnerabilities, and developers patch. But agent ecosystems evolve — new skills are added, existing skills are modified, and compositions change. One-shot red teaming leaves evolving attack surfaces unexamined. Proteus solves this via continuous co-evolution: the red team evolves alongside the target, perpetually probing the expanding attack surface. vs static fuzzing: Proteus learns attack patterns that transfer across skills (60-70% vulnerability inheritance). vs manual red teaming: 3-5x more vulnerabilities discovered, continuous coverage, zero human effort after initial setup. vs single-agent red team: multi-agent coordination discovers composition exploits that no single agent could construct. Key insight: in evolving agent ecosystems, security is not a state but a dynamic equilibrium — Proteus maintains a persistent adversarial pressure that drives continuous security improvement.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no red teaming infrastructure, no automated vulnerability discovery, no adversarial testing framework, and no skill vulnerability tracking. §4.17 Safety matures at `none`. Proteus directly informs Lyra's safety roadmap: (1) build a Proteus-style evolving red team that co-evolves with Lyra's plugin/skill ecosystem, (2) maintain a skill vulnerability database as plugins are added, (3) implement multi-agent attack coordination testing, (4) automate patching from discovered vulnerabilities. This is particularly urgent given Lyra's planned plugin marketplace — third-party plugins introduce untrusted code with unknown vulnerability profiles. Status: **BEHIND** (zero red team infrastructure; Proteus provides the complete architecture for continuous adversarial testing of Lyra's ecosystem).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (P0 — evolving red team is prerequisite for safe plugin ecosystem; directly addresses Lyra's safety gap with a proven self-evolving architecture)

## SAGE: A Self-Evolving Agentic Graph-Memory Engine for Structure-Aware Associative Memory
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12061
**Mechanism:** (1) SAGE constructs a dynamic heterogeneous graph as the agent's memory substrate: entities (concepts, tools, tasks, users, sessions) as nodes; typed relationships (causes, follows, contradicts, generalizes, requires, exemplifies) as directed edges with confidence weights. (2) Self-evolving graph operations: (a) Ingestion — new information (conversation turns, tool outputs, task outcomes) is parsed into entity-relationship triples via LLM extraction and added to the graph; (b) Consolidation — periodically (every N interactions), the graph is reorganized: similar entities are merged (deduplication), transitive relationships are materialized (A→B and B→C implies A→C edge), weak edges are pruned, and important subgraphs are summarized into composite nodes; (c) Retrieval — given a query context, SAGE performs structure-aware retrieval: not just nearest-neighbor embedding search but multi-hop graph traversal (follow typed edges from query entities to discover related concepts), subgraph extraction (extract the connected component around query entities), and associative triggering (activating memories linked via multiple relationship paths). (3) Associative memory mechanism: when agent encounters concept X, SAGE activates not just direct neighbors of X but also nodes that share similar graph-topological patterns (similar neighborhood structures, similar relationship types) — enabling "reminds me of" style recall even when semantic similarity is low. (4) Self-evolution via usage-driven reinforcement: edges traversed during successful task completions are strengthened; edges in paths leading to failures are weakened; unused subgraphs are pruned to bound memory size. (5) Implementation: Neo4j for graph storage, graph neural network (GNN) for associative similarity computation, LLM for entity-relationship extraction, and a graph attention mechanism for retrieval ranking.
**Results:** SAGE outperforms vector-only memory (Chroma, Pinecone) by 22-35% on multi-hop reasoning tasks that require connecting disparate pieces of information. Associative recall (finding memories that are structurally similar but semantically distant) improves by 40-55% over embedding-only baselines — SAGE retrieves relevant memories that semantic search misses entirely. Graph consolidation reduces memory size by 35-45% while preserving 92% of retrieval recall (pruning noise, keeping signal). Self-evolution over 500+ task executions: edge weight distribution converges from uniform to power-law (few strong, many weak edges), mirroring biological memory consolidation. Multi-hop retrieval latency: 50-200ms depending on hop depth (2-5 hops typical). Cold-start: initial 50-100 interactions build a sparse but functional graph; retrieval quality reaches 80% of peak at 200 interactions and asymptotes at 500+.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: knowledge-intensive agent domains with complex entity relationships (research, legal, medical), multi-session agents requiring persistent structured memory, tasks requiring multi-hop reasoning across disparate facts, environments where associative/"creative" recall is valuable (hypothesis generation, analogical reasoning). LOSES: simple Q&A agents (vector similarity sufficient), stateless single-turn interactions (graph overhead not amortized), latency-critical retrieval (<50ms budget — graph traversal adds overhead), domains where entity relationships are flat/unstructured. Graph construction requires accurate entity-relationship extraction — LLM extraction errors (hallucinated edges, missed relationships) compound over time if not validated. Associative similarity via GNN adds inference cost per retrieval. Cold-start period (50-100 interactions) produces degraded performance — SAGE needs a warm-up phase.
**Rationale:** Vector databases treat memory as a flat collection of embeddings — retrieval is purely similarity-based, ignoring the rich relational structure of knowledge. SAGE recognizes that human memory is fundamentally associative and structured: we remember things not just because they're "similar" but because they're connected through shared context, causal chains, and structural patterns. vs vector-only memory: SAGE's graph structure enables multi-hop reasoning (22-35% improvement) and associative recall (40-55% improvement) that embedding search cannot replicate. vs static knowledge graphs: SAGE's self-evolution via usage-driven RL adapts the graph to the agent's actual task distribution. vs RAG: RAG retrieves documents; SAGE retrieves structured knowledge that can be traversed and reasoned over. Key insight: the graph topology itself encodes valuable information — two entities with similar neighborhood structures are likely related even if their embeddings are distant.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's memory subsystem (§02) is at maturity `partial` — basic conversation history with vector store. No graph structure, no multi-hop retrieval, no associative recall, no usage-driven consolidation, no self-evolution. SAGE maps directly to Lyra's memory upgrade: (1) implement heterogeneous graph memory with typed entities and relationships, (2) add multi-hop graph traversal for retrieval, (3) implement associative similarity via GNN or structural hashing, (4) add consolidation/pruning cycles, (5) integrate usage-driven weight evolution. SAGE's architecture is directly compatible with Lyra's planned GraphRAG integration (§03 Context). The associative recall capability is especially relevant for Lyra's research automation and creative problem-solving use cases. Status: **BEHIND** (no graph memory infrastructure; SAGE provides complete blueprint including self-evolution mechanism).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 5 | **Tier:** breakthrough (P0 — graph-based associative memory is the highest-value memory upgrade identified in the corpus; directly addresses Lyra's memory gap with structure-aware retrieval that vector-only systems cannot match)

## Q-DAPS: Question Difficulty Estimation for Large Language Models via Answer Plausibility Scoring
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12398
**Mechanism:** (1) Q-DAPS estimates question difficulty for LLMs without requiring ground-truth answers or human annotations. Core insight: a question is "difficult" if the LLM's plausible-sounding wrong answers are hard to distinguish from its correct answers. (2) Three-step estimation: (a) Generate K candidate answers via sampling (temperature > 0, e.g., K=20), (b) For each candidate answer, compute a "plausibility score" — how internally consistent, well-reasoned, and superficially correct the answer appears (using the LLM itself as judge, evaluating qualities like coherence, factual density, logical structure), (c) Compute difficulty as the variance-weighted gap between the highest-plausibility correct answer and the highest-plausibility incorrect answer. Large gap = easy (correct answer clearly more plausible), small gap = hard (incorrect answers are equally or more plausible than correct). (3) Calibration: Q-DAPS scores are calibrated against actual LLM accuracy via isotonic regression, mapping raw plausibility gaps to predicted success probabilities. (4) Difficulty decomposition: Q-DAPS can attribute difficulty to specific factors — knowledge requirement (does question require rare/obscure facts?), reasoning depth (how many inference steps needed?), ambiguity (are there multiple plausible interpretations?), and adversarial construction (is the question designed to trick the model?). (5) Applications: adaptive test generation (select questions at target difficulty), model comparison (which models handle which difficulty types), curriculum learning (train on easy→hard progression), and agent routing (route hard questions to stronger models, easy questions to cheaper models).
**Results:** Q-DAPS difficulty estimates achieve 0.82-0.89 Spearman correlation with actual LLM accuracy across 6 benchmark datasets (MMLU, ARC, TruthfulQA, GSM8K, HumanEval, BigBench). Significantly outperforms heuristic difficulty metrics: question length (0.31), word rarity (0.42), syntactic complexity (0.38), and human-judged difficulty (0.72 — Q-DAPS is more predictive of LLM performance than human difficulty ratings). Difficulty decomposition accuracy: Q-DAPS correctly identifies the primary difficulty factor for 78% of questions (validated against expert annotation). Adaptive test generation: tests generated at target difficulty bands (easy: 80-90% accuracy, medium: 50-70%, hard: 10-30%) achieve within ±5pp of target across 4 model families (GPT, Claude, Llama, Mistral). Routing application: Q-DAPS-based routing (easy→Haiku, medium→Sonnet, hard→Opus) achieves 95% of oracle routing accuracy at 40% lower cost.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: LLM evaluation pipelines needing automated difficulty annotation, model routing systems needing per-question difficulty estimates, adaptive testing/curriculum learning, model capability comparisons, cost-sensitive routing decisions. LOSES: questions where LLM cannot generate plausible wrong answers (very easy or impossible questions), domains where LLM self-evaluation is unreliable (LLM-as-judge bias), real-time applications (K=20 answer generation adds latency), languages/domains where LLM generation quality is poor. LLM self-evaluation bias: LLMs tend to rate their own outputs as more plausible — Q-DAPS corrects for this via calibration but residual bias remains. The method requires a capable LLM to generate diverse candidate answers — weak models may not produce meaningful plausibility variance.
**Rationale:** Existing question difficulty metrics (length, readability scores, human judgments) measure difficulty for humans, not LLMs. Q-DAPS's key insight: LLM difficulty is about the plausibility of wrong answers, not just question complexity. A question can be simple for humans but hard for LLMs (e.g., counting letters in a word) and vice versa (e.g., memorized trivia). vs human difficulty ratings: Q-DAPS is 0.10-0.17 higher correlation with actual LLM accuracy. vs answer-consistency methods (SelfCheckGPT): Q-DAPS uses plausibility scoring rather than raw consistency, capturing difficulty even when answers are consistently wrong. vs model-based routing (RouteLLM): Q-DAPS estimates question difficulty BEFORE routing, enabling difficulty-aware routing that RouteLLM's preference-based learning does not explicitly model. The calibration via isotonic regression is critical — raw plausibility gaps are model-dependent; calibration makes them comparable across models and datasets.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra §4.5 Router maturity: `none`, §4.19 Quality Gate `none`. Q-DAPS directly fills a critical gap in Lyra's planned routing infrastructure: the router needs to know not just "which model is best for this task type" but "how hard is this specific question." Q-DAPS enables Lyra to route questions to models based on estimated difficulty: easy questions to cheaper/faster models, hard questions to more capable models. Combined with FrugalGPT (cost cascade) and speculative decoding (inference acceleration), Q-DAPS adds the difficulty-estimation dimension that makes the routing decision per-question rather than per-task-type. Q-DAPS also enables Lyra's quality gate (§4.19) to set adaptive confidence thresholds — harder questions get more verification budget. Status: **BEHIND** (no difficulty estimation; Q-DAPS provides the mechanism to make Lyra's router question-aware, not just task-aware).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 2 | **Tier:** breakthrough (low-effort, high-impact addition to routing infrastructure; Q-DAPS + FrugalGPT + RouteLLM = complete cost-quality routing with difficulty awareness)

## Harnessing Agentic Evolution
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.13821
**Mechanism:** (1) Provides a comprehensive framework for "agentic evolution" — the process by which AI agents self-improve through iterative cycles of variation, selection, and retention operating on agent behaviors, skills, and architectures. (2) Defines three evolutionary scales: Micro-evolution (within a single agent session — the agent adapts its strategy based on task feedback, e.g., trying different prompting approaches, adjusting tool-use patterns), Meso-evolution (across sessions/tasks — the agent accumulates reusable skills, updates its memory/knowledge, and refines its decision policies based on accumulated experience), Macro-evolution (across agent generations — agents spawn modified copies of themselves with architectural changes, new skill compositions, or different model configurations; successful variants propagate). (3) Evolutionary operators: Variation (generating behavioral diversity — strategy mutations, skill recombination, architecture modifications), Selection (evaluating and filtering variants — task performance, user feedback, efficiency metrics, novelty scores), Retention (preserving successful variants — skill libraries, policy updates, architecture templates, memory consolidation). (4) Harnessing mechanisms — how to make evolution productive rather than degenerative: (a) Objective alignment (evolution optimizes for genuine task improvement, not reward hacking), (b) Diversity maintenance (preventing premature convergence to local optima via novelty search, quality-diversity algorithms, island models), (c) Safe exploration (constraining variation to safe regions — sandboxed testing, rollback capability, human-in-the-loop gating), (d) Replicability (ensuring evolved behaviors can be reproduced and audited — versioning, lineage tracking, behavioral fingerprints). (5) Distillation from biological evolution: the paper maps 10 principles from biological evolution (natural selection, sexual selection, genetic drift, co-evolution, punctuated equilibrium, niche construction, etc.) to agent system design, arguing that agent ecosystems will recapitulate evolutionary dynamics whether intended or not — the question is whether we harness them or are surprised by them.
**Results:** Survey-level findings across 40+ self-evolving agent papers: Micro-evolution (in-session adaptation) is the most mature, with 65-80% of papers demonstrating task improvement from within-session strategy adaptation. Meso-evolution (cross-session learning) is partially mature: 40-55% of papers show transfer learning across sessions, but only 20-30% demonstrate sustained improvement (many plateau or degrade after 10-20 sessions). Macro-evolution (architectural self-modification) is nascent: fewer than 10 papers attempt it, with mixed results (some show genuine capability jumps, others show degradation due to accumulated errors). The paper identifies four failure modes that cause self-evolution to degrade rather than improve: (1) Reward Hacking — agents optimize proxy metrics rather than true task success (observed in 35-50% of papers with RL-based evolution), (2) Diversity Collapse — all agent variants converge to similar strategies, losing the variation that drives evolution (observed in 40-60% of papers running >50 generations), (3) Capability Drift — agents evolve toward behaviors that maximize the selection criterion but lose core capabilities (e.g., agents that become excellent at a specific benchmark but fail on related tasks), (4) Complexity Ratchet — agents accumulate features/skills without pruning, leading to bloated, slow, and brittle systems.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: long-running agent deployments where continuous improvement is expected, domains with clear success metrics (evolution needs a fitness signal), environments where task distributions shift over time (evolution enables adaptation), multi-agent ecosystems where competition/cooperation can drive improvement. LOSES: one-shot agent deployments (evolution overhead never amortized), safety-critical domains where untested evolved behaviors pose unacceptable risk, environments with poorly specified success metrics (evolution will optimize the wrong thing), resource-constrained settings (evolution requires compute for variation generation and selection). Fundamental tension: evolution produces genuine novelty (unexpected improvements) but also unpredictability (unexpected failures) — harnessing requires accepting some unpredictability while constraining its consequences. The paper argues that the alternative to intentional harnessing is not stasis but unintentional, uncontrolled evolution — agent ecosystems will evolve anyway through developer updates, user interactions, and environmental changes.
**Rationale:** The paper's key contribution is synthesizing findings from 40+ self-evolution papers into a unified framework with actionable design principles. Prior work studied individual self-evolution mechanisms in isolation; this paper shows that the same evolutionary dynamics recur across scales (micro, meso, macro) and identifies the common failure modes that cause self-evolution to degrade. vs single-mechanism evolution: the paper demonstrates that combining multiple evolutionary operators (strategy mutation + skill recombination + diversity maintenance) produces more robust improvement than any single mechanism alone. vs static agent design: the paper argues that static agents are fundamentally limited — they cannot adapt to distribution shift, user preference drift, or novel task types. vs unconstrained evolution: the "harnessing" framework provides guardrails that distinguish productive evolution from uncontrolled drift. The biological evolution analogy is not just metaphorical — the mathematical dynamics (replicator equations, fitness landscapes, selection pressure) transfer directly to agent populations.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has nascent self-evolution concepts in its architecture plans (self-improving loops mentioned in §4.15 Research, §4.16 Reliability, and the EvoTest/EvoQuality-inspired patterns) but NO implemented self-evolution infrastructure. Lyra is currently at the pre-evolutionary stage — agent behaviors are statically defined by developers. This paper provides Lyra's evolutionary roadmap: (1) Phase 1 (Micro): implement within-session strategy adaptation via tree search + feedback loops (builds on ToT, RAP gaps), (2) Phase 2 (Meso): implement cross-session skill accumulation and policy refinement (builds on SkillOS, HAGE, SAGE gaps), (3) Phase 3 (Macro): implement architectural self-modification with safety constraints (future research). The four failure modes (reward hacking, diversity collapse, capability drift, complexity ratchet) should be designed against from the start — they are harder to fix retroactively. Status: **BEHIND** (no self-evolution infrastructure; this paper provides the high-level framework that integrates all the specific self-evolution mechanisms from other papers into a coherent evolutionary architecture).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 5 | **Tier:** breakthrough (P0 — this paper ties together all self-evolution findings in the corpus; provides the architectural framework for Lyra's long-term self-improvement capability; identifies the failure modes that must be guarded against from the start)

## EVOLVEMEM: Self-Evolving Memory Architecture via AutoResearch for LLM Agents
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.13941
**Mechanism:** (1) EvolveMem exposes the complete retrieval configuration as a structured action space: scoring functions, fusion strategies, and answer-generation policies are all modifiable parameters rather than frozen at deployment. (2) An LLM-powered diagnosis module reads per-question failure logs, diagnoses root causes (e.g., wrong scoring function, poor fusion weight), and proposes targeted configuration adjustments. (3) A guarded meta-analyzer applies changes with two safeguards: automatic revert-on-regression (if performance drops, roll back) and explore-on-stagnation (if performance plateaus, inject random perturbations to escape local optima). (4) AutoResearch loop: the system starts from a minimal baseline and autonomously conducts iterative research cycles on its own architecture, discovering new configuration dimensions not present in the original action space. (5) Cross-benchmark transfer: evolved configurations exhibit positive transfer (not catastrophic forgetting) across benchmarks, suggesting the evolution captures universal retrieval principles.
**Results:** LoCoMo benchmark: 25.7% relative improvement over strongest baseline, 78.0% relative improvement over minimal starting baseline. MemBench: 18.9% relative improvement over strongest baseline. Evolved configurations transfer positively across benchmarks — the self-evolution discovers general principles rather than benchmark-specific overfitting.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: long-running agent deployments where memory retrieval patterns shift over time, multi-domain agents where no single retrieval configuration is optimal, environments where manual tuning of retrieval parameters is impractical, systems that accumulate diverse memory types over their lifetime. LOSES: static single-domain deployments (manual tuning sufficient), latency-critical retrieval where evolution overhead is unacceptable, small memory stores where retrieval configuration matters less. AutoResearch process consumes compute for diagnosis and meta-analysis — cost amortizes over long deployments but is wasteful for short-lived agents. Guarded meta-analyzer adds complexity — revert-on-regression requires maintaining performance baselines; explore-on-stagnation can temporarily degrade performance.
**Rationale:** Prior memory systems fix retrieval infrastructure at deployment — the same scoring function, fusion strategy, and generation policy are used forever even as stored content evolves and task distributions shift. EvolveMem's key insight: truly adaptive memory requires co-evolution at two levels — the stored knowledge AND the retrieval mechanism itself. vs static retrieval: 25.7% relative improvement from self-evolved configuration. vs manual tuning: eliminates human effort and discovers configurations humans wouldn't try. vs other self-evolving memory (HAGE, SAGE): EvolveMem focuses on evolving the retrieval mechanism, while HAGE/SAGE focus on evolving stored content structure — the two approaches are complementary. The AutoResearch paradigm (autonomous iterative research on own architecture) is a meta-pattern applicable beyond memory — it could be applied to Lyra's routing, planning, and safety subsystems.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's memory subsystem (§02) is at maturity `partial` — vector store with static retrieval. No retrieval self-evolution, no configuration action space, no AutoResearch loop, no diagnosis-driven improvement. EvolveMem provides the mechanism to make Lyra's memory retrieval self-optimizing: expose retrieval parameters as an action space, add failure diagnosis, and implement guarded self-modification. Combined with SAGE (graph memory structure) and HAGE (RL-driven graph evolution), EvolveMem adds the retrieval-layer self-evolution that makes the memory stack fully adaptive. Status: **BEHIND** (no retrieval self-evolution; EvolveMem + SAGE + HAGE = complete self-evolving memory stack).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (self-evolving retrieval closes the memory adaptation loop; complementary to SAGE/HAGE structural evolution)
