## Model-Adaptive Tool Necessity Reveals the Knowing-Doing Gap in LLM Tool Use
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14038
**Mechanism:** (1) Model-adaptive tool necessity: instead of labeling whether a tool is "needed" via human annotation (which assumes all models share the same capability boundary), necessity is defined per-model based on whether that specific model can solve the problem independently. A stronger model may not need a tool that a weaker model requires. (2) Two-stage decomposition of tool use: Cognition stage (does the model internally believe a tool is needed? — decoded via linear probing of hidden states) and Execution stage (does the model actually emit a tool-call token?). (3) Linear probing reveals that both cognition and execution signals are linearly decodable from hidden states, but in late layers at the last token position (which drives next-token action), the probe directions become nearly orthogonal — explaining the disconnect between knowing and doing. (4) Trajectory analysis: tracking individual samples through the two-stage process shows that the majority of tool-use failures are concentrated in the cognition-to-action transition, not in cognition itself — models frequently recognize they need a tool but fail to call it.
**Results:** Tool-call mismatch rates (model thinks tool needed but doesn't call, or calls when not needed): arithmetic tasks 26.5-54.0% across four models; factual QA 30.8-41.8% across four models. The knowing-doing gap (cognition correct but execution wrong) accounts for the majority of mismatches — models are better at recognizing tool necessity than at acting on that recognition. Both cognition and execution signals are linearly decodable, but late-layer orthogonality of probe directions explains the execution failures.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: multi-model agent systems where tool-use reliability directly impacts task success, tool-augmented agents where incorrect tool calls waste compute budget, agent architectures where tool-calling decisions can be intervened upon (the linear decodability enables architectural fixes). LOSES: single-model deployments where tool necessity is consistent (no model-adaptive definition needed), agents where tool-call errors are rare. Probing-based analysis requires access to hidden states — not applicable to API-only models. The linear probing finding (orthogonal late-layer directions) suggests a fundamental architectural limitation — current LLMs may need architectural changes to close the knowing-doing gap.
**Rationale:** Prior work treats tool necessity as model-agnostic — a fixed "this question needs a calculator" label. This paper demonstrates that necessity depends on model capability: GPT-4 may compute 847*392 mentally while a smaller model needs a calculator. The knowing-doing gap finding is profound: LLMs suffer not just from recognition failures but from execution failures — they know what to do but don't do it. vs static tool-necessity: model-adaptive definition captures 26-54% mismatch that static labeling misses. vs tool-use training (function calling fine-tuning): the paper shows the problem is architectural (late-layer probe orthogonality), not just training data. The linear decodability of both signals opens intervention possibilities: one could add a "cognition-to-action translator" layer that aligns the orthogonal probe directions.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's tool-use implementation (plugin system) has no model-adaptive tool necessity estimation, no tool-call reliability analysis, no knowing-doing gap measurement. Lyra currently routes all tool-calling decisions through a single policy regardless of which model is executing. This paper suggests Lyra should: (1) estimate per-model tool necessity before routing queries, (2) implement a cognition-action alignment mechanism (e.g., verification step between tool-need recognition and tool execution), (3) track tool-call mismatch rates per model to inform router decisions. Status: **BEHIND** (no tool-use reliability infrastructure; this paper identifies a fundamental failure mode that Lyra needs to design around).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (identifies a previously unknown failure mode in tool-calling; enables architecture-level fixes for agent reliability)

## MetaAgent-X: Breaking the Ceiling of Automatic Multi-Agent Systems via End-to-End Reinforcement Learning
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14212
**Mechanism:** (1) MetaAgent-X is an end-to-end RL framework that jointly trains both the multi-agent system designer (which generates agent workflows, role assignments, and communication topologies) and the execution agents (which perform the actual task work). (2) Script-based MAS generation: the designer outputs executable agent scripts (defining roles, tools, coordination protocols) rather than abstract workflow descriptions. (3) Execution rollout collection: generated scripts are executed on tasks, and execution trajectories are collected for credit assignment. (4) Credit assignment for both designer and executor trajectories — the designer is rewarded for scripts that lead to high executor performance; executors are rewarded for task success. (5) Two stabilization techniques: Executor Designer Hierarchical Rollout (stabilizes joint training by structuring the rollout to separate designer and executor credit signals) and Stagewise Co-evolution (structures co-evolution into phases where one component is partially frozen while the other adapts, preventing destructive interference).
**Results:** Up to 21.7% gains over existing automatic MAS baselines. Ablations confirm both designer and executor improve during training (not just one component). Stagewise co-evolution pattern emerges: effective learning follows phases where designer and executor alternately lead, rather than simultaneous optimization. The "frozen-executor ceiling" is real — methods that train only the designer with frozen executors hit a performance ceiling that joint training breaks through.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: complex multi-agent deployments where hand-designed workflows are suboptimal, environments where task distributions shift (co-evolution adapts both design and execution), multi-agent systems where the optimal topology/roles are unknown a priori. LOSES: simple single-agent tasks (multi-agent overhead unjustified), deployments where agent roles are fixed by organizational constraints (cannot co-evolve), resource-constrained training (joint RL training of designer + executors is compute-intensive). End-to-end RL requires a reward signal — defining appropriate rewards for designer scripts is non-trivial (scripts that look good may produce poor execution). Joint training can be unstable — the two stabilization techniques help but don't fully eliminate training instability.
**Rationale:** Existing automatic MAS approaches are only partially adaptive: they either use training-free test-time search (AFlow, GPTSwarm) or optimize the designer while freezing executors (capping improvement at executor quality). MetaAgent-X's key insight: the designer-executor relationship is a co-evolution problem — better executors enable better designs, and better designs push executors to improve. vs training-free search: 21.7% improvement from learned (vs searched) designs. vs designer-only optimization: breaks through the frozen-executor ceiling. vs manual MAS design: automates the entire pipeline; outperforms human-designed workflows. The stagewise co-evolution finding is actionable: Lyra should structure its self-improvement as alternating phases of orchestration improvement and agent capability improvement, not simultaneous optimization.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has a static agent orchestration model (PrimaryAgent → TaskAllocator → specialized agents). No learned topology, no co-evolution of orchestration and execution, no credit assignment for workflow design decisions. MetaAgent-X suggests Lyra should: (1) make its agent workflow design learnable via RL on task outcomes, (2) jointly optimize orchestration decisions and agent capabilities rather than treating them as separate problems, (3) implement stagewise co-evolution to stabilize joint improvement. Status: **BEHIND** (static orchestration; MetaAgent-X provides the architecture for fully learned, co-evolving multi-agent systems).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 5 | **Tier:** breakthrough (P0 — end-to-end learnable MAS breaks the ceiling of hand-designed agent orchestration; directly informs Lyra's multi-agent architecture evolution)

## Visual Financial Document Retrieval: Aggregation Strategies (ACL 2026 Findings)
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14581
**Mechanism:** (1) Investigates "Visual RAG" systems that treat documents as images rather than extracted text. (2) Identifies global texture dominance as the root cause of retrieval failure: when hundreds of visual patch tokens from a vision encoder are pooled into a single embedding vector, the overall layout/texture dominates the representation, drowning out fine-grained details. (3) Handcrafted diagnostic benchmark: financial documents where changes in single digits (e.g., $1.2M vs $1.3M) cause significant semantic shifts — testing whether retrieval can detect these fine-grained differences. (4) Comparison of patch-level vs aggregated representations: patch-level representations successfully detect semantic shifts (digit changes, table alterations) while aggregated single vectors make different documents indistinguishable. (5) Findings held across model scales, retrieval-optimized embeddings, and multiple mitigation strategies — the aggregation problem is fundamental, not easily fixed by scaling or embedding optimization.
**Results:** Patch-level representations successfully detect fine-grained semantic shifts (digit changes in financial tables). Aggregated single vectors consistently fail — distinct financial documents collapse into near-identical vector representations. The failure is consistent across model scales, retrieval-optimized embeddings, and multiple attempted mitigation strategies. No single-vector aggregation strategy solved the problem — the information loss appears fundamental to the pooling operation.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: document retrieval systems where fine-grained details matter (financial, legal, medical), multi-modal RAG pipelines that process documents as images, systems where single-digit errors have high consequences. LOSES: text-extraction-first pipelines (extract text via OCR, then embed — avoids the visual aggregation problem), coarse-grained document retrieval where layout similarity is sufficient, applications where compute budget cannot support patch-level representations (N patches vs 1 vector = N× storage/retrieval cost). Patch-level retrieval multiplies storage requirements — each document stores hundreds of patch embeddings instead of one. The finding suggests Vision RAG may be fundamentally limited for detail-sensitive domains unless patch-level representations are used.
**Rationale:** Many production RAG systems extract text from documents via OCR/passing, losing visual structure. Vision RAG aims to preserve this structure by embedding images directly. This paper shows that the standard approach (pooling patch tokens into one vector) destroys the very detail that Vision RAG is supposed to preserve. vs text-extraction RAG: Vision RAG with patch-level representations captures visual structure that OCR loses, but aggregated Vision RAG is worse than text RAG for detail retrieval. vs scaling: the problem persists at larger model scales — it is architectural (pooling operation), not capacity-limited. Key insight: the pooling operation creates an information bottleneck that is acceptable for semantic similarity but disastrous for detail-sensitive retrieval. Lyra's document processing pipeline should avoid single-vector aggregation for visual documents and use patch-level or hybrid (text + visual patch) representations.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no visual document retrieval pipeline (text-only RAG planned). However, Lyra's planned multi-modal capabilities (§03 Context, §15 Research) should incorporate this finding from the start: avoid single-vector visual aggregation; use patch-level or hybrid representations for visual document understanding. This is a design constraint rather than an implementation gap — Lyra can avoid this pitfall because it has not yet built visual RAG infrastructure. Status: **AHEAD** (opportunity to skip flawed approach; Lyra can build patch-level visual retrieval from the start).
**Impact:** 2 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** investigate (design constraint for future multi-modal retrieval; prevents building a known-flawed architecture)

## Is Grep All You Need? How Agent Harnesses Reshape Agentic Search
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.15184
**Mechanism:** (1) Systematic comparison of retrieval strategies (grep vs vector retrieval) in agentic search, testing four agent harnesses: custom Chronos harness, Claude Code CLI, Codex CLI (OpenAI), and Gemini CLI (Google). (2) Two tool output modes: inline (retrieval results fed directly into model context) and file-based (results written to a file, model reads via file access). (3) Experiment 1: 116-question sample from LongMemEval, comparing grep vs vector retrieval across all harness × output-mode combinations. (4) Experiment 2: progressively injects unrelated conversation history (distractor text) around relevant passages, testing how retrieval methods degrade under increasing distraction density — grep-only and vector-only compared. (5) Harness effect isolation: keeps underlying conversation data constant while varying the agent harness and tool-calling style, measuring the pure effect of harness design on final task accuracy.
**Results:** Grep generally yields higher accuracy than vector retrieval in the comparisons. Overall scores depend strongly on which harness and tool-calling style is used, even when the underlying conversation data are identical — harness design is a first-order effect on agentic search performance. The 116-question benchmark provides systematic coverage of retrieval scenarios.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: agentic search systems where keyword matching is competitive with semantic search (many real-world retrieval tasks), multi-harness deployments where harness choice is a design decision, environments where deterministic retrieval (grep) is preferred over probabilistic (vector). LOSES: tasks requiring pure semantic understanding where keywords fail (paraphrased queries, cross-lingual retrieval), deployments locked to a single harness (harness comparison not actionable). Grep is limited to exact/pattern matches — fails on semantic equivalence. Harness effect suggests that agentic search evaluation must control for harness design, not just retrieval method — current benchmarks that compare retrieval methods without controlling harness may confound results.
**Rationale:** Despite the growing use of RAG in agentic systems, no systematic comparison existed examining how retrieval method, harness design, and tool output style interact. This paper fills that gap with a controlled experiment. vs retrieval-method-only comparisons: this paper shows harness design is equally important — a finding with major implications for how Lyra designs its agentic search infrastructure. vs grep: despite its simplicity, grep outperforms vector retrieval in many agentic search scenarios — challenging the assumption that semantic search is always superior. The harness effect finding is the key contribution: two agents with the same data and same retrieval method can produce different results based purely on how the harness presents tool outputs and structures agent-tool interaction.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no agentic search benchmark, no systematic retrieval method comparison, and its harness design has not been evaluated against alternatives. This paper suggests Lyra should: (1) implement grep/keyword retrieval alongside vector retrieval (not replace one with the other), (2) evaluate harness design choices (inline vs file-based tool output) as first-order performance factors, (3) include tool-output presentation style as a tunable parameter in Lyra's harness configuration. Status: **BEHIND** (no systematic search evaluation; harness design not treated as a performance factor).
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 2 | **Tier:** parity (actionable finding: add grep retrieval, evaluate harness design choices; low effort, improves agentic search reliability)

## RecMem: Recurrence-based Memory Consolidation for Efficient and Effective Long-Running LLM Agents
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16045
**Mechanism:** (1) Subconscious Memory Layer: incoming user-agent interactions are stored without immediate LLM processing — lightweight embedding models encode interactions into a vector store for fast similarity lookup. (2) Recurrence Detection: the system monitors semantic similarity across incoming interactions; when semantically similar interactions recur (forming a cluster above a threshold), it triggers the LLM for episodic/semantic memory extraction. The key insight: only recurring, information-rich clusters warrant the cost of LLM-based consolidation — isolated or single-occurrence interactions stay in the subconscious layer as raw embeddings. (3) Consolidated Memory Extraction: when recurrence is detected, the LLM summarizes the cluster into structured memory entries (episodic memories for event sequences, semantic memories for facts). (4) Semantic Refinement: a post-extraction step recovers fine-grained factual details that the summarization/consolidation step may have dropped, improving retrieval precision. (5) The system wraps around existing memory architectures as a cost-reducing frontend — it does not replace the underlying memory store, it reduces what gets sent to it.
**Results:** Reduces memory construction token cost by up to 87% compared to three SOTA memory systems while maintaining or exceeding their accuracy. Lightweight embedding models handle the bulk of interaction encoding; the LLM is invoked only for consolidation of recurring clusters. ACL 2026 Findings paper.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: long-running agents with high interaction volume (token cost reduction compounds), multi-session agents where many interactions are routine/noteworthy only in aggregate, cost-constrained deployments, memory systems where LLM-based extraction dominates the operational budget. LOSES: agents with very few interactions (recurrence detection never triggers, no cost savings), domains where every interaction is unique and important (single-occurrence facts never consolidated, lost to subconscious layer), real-time memory requirements (recurrence detection requires buffering — consolidation is deferred). The subconscious layer introduces a retrieval precision vs. consolidation latency trade-off: facts in unconsolidated clusters are accessible only via embedding similarity, not structured queries. Semantic refinement adds a second LLM call for recovered facts — partially offsetting the cost savings.
**Rationale:** Current memory systems invoke LLMs to process every incoming interaction for memory extraction — this is the dominant cost in long-running agents. RecMem observes that most interactions are semantically redundant or low-information and should not consume LLM tokens. The recurrence-based consolidation is biologically inspired: human memory strengthens with repetition; single exposures are often forgotten unless rehearsed. vs always-extract: 87% token reduction without accuracy loss. vs pure embedding memory: RecMem adds structured consolidation where it matters (recurring patterns) while keeping the cost advantages of lightweight embeddings elsewhere. vs fixed summarization schedules (every N turns): recurrence-based triggering is adaptive — consolidation happens when information density warrants it, not on an arbitrary clock. The subconscious-to-conscious memory architecture (lightweight first, LLM when needed) is a generalizable cost-reduction pattern for any agent subsystem.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's memory subsystem (§02) processes every interaction for memory extraction — there is no recurrence detection, no subconscious layer, no cost-gating on LLM-based consolidation. Lyra would benefit from RecMem's two-tier architecture: (1) lightweight embedding-based subconscious memory for all interactions, (2) LLM-based consolidation triggered only for recurring semantic clusters, (3) semantic refinement to recover fine-grained facts from summaries. This directly reduces Lyra's operational token costs, especially for long-running agent sessions. The subconscious layer also aligns with Lyra's planned vector store infrastructure. Status: **BEHIND** (no cost-gating on memory extraction; RecMem provides a proven architecture for 87% token reduction in memory construction).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 2 | **Tier:** breakthrough (low-effort, high-impact cost reduction for memory subsystem; subconscious+conscious two-tier architecture is directly implementable on Lyra's existing vector store)

## Argus: Evidence Assembly for Scalable Deep Research Agents
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16217
**Mechanism:** (1) Argus frames deep research as jigsaw puzzle assembly rather than brute-force parallel answer generation. Two cooperating agents: a Searcher and a Navigator. (2) Searcher: conducts standard ReAct-style interactions (reason, act, observe) to collect evidence traces for a given sub-query — retrieves sources, extracts facts, follows citation chains, and returns evidence fragments. (3) Navigator: maintains a shared evidence graph that tracks what evidence has been assembled, identifies missing pieces (gaps in the evidence chain), dispatches Searchers to fill specific gaps (not duplicate existing evidence), and synthesizes a source-traced final answer from the completed graph. (4) Key architectural property: the Navigator is trained via reinforcement learning for three skills — verify (is this evidence piece correct and non-redundant?), dispatch (which gap should the next Searcher fill?), synthesize (how to compose all evidence into a coherent answer?). The Searcher is independently trained as a standard ReAct agent. (5) Decoupled scaling: the Navigator supports rollouts with 1 Searcher or N parallel Searchers without retraining — the dispatch policy naturally handles variable parallelism. (6) Source-traced synthesis: every claim in the final answer is linked to specific evidence pieces in the graph, enabling verifiability.
**Results:** +5.5 points gain with a single Searcher (averaged across 8 benchmarks). +12.7 points gain with 8 parallel Searchers. 86.2 on BrowseComp with 64 parallel Searchers — surpassing every proprietary agent benchmarked. Navigator reasoning context remains under 21.5K tokens even with 64 Searchers (evidence graph compresses assembled knowledge, avoiding context-window pressure). Both components built on a 35B-A3B Mixture-of-Experts backbone — showing strong results do not require the largest dense models.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: deep research tasks requiring evidence synthesis across many sources, scenarios where parallel rollouts currently waste compute on duplicate evidence, multi-hop reasoning tasks with complex evidence chains, deployments where answer verifiability (source tracing) is required, budget-constrained research (small MoE backbone achieves frontier results). LOSES: simple factoid QA (evidence assembly overhead unjustified), single-source answer tasks (no assembly needed), real-time Q&A (graph construction and multi-turn dispatch adds latency), domains with sparse evidence (gap detection finds nothing — Navigator dispatches Searchers on fruitless searches). RL training for Navigator requires reward signal: evidence graph completeness and answer correctness. Evidence graph construction adds inference cost per dispatch cycle — though context stays under 21.5K tokens, total tokens across Searcher rollouts are substantial.
**Rationale:** Current deep research agents (Tongyi DeepResearch, STORM, GPT Researcher) use parallel rollouts that independently gather evidence and then merge results. This is inefficient: parallel rollouts duplicate effort (multiple Searchers find the same sources), and context windows bloat from redundant evidence. Argus's key insight: evidence gathering should be gap-driven, not parallel-brute-force. The Navigator tracks what is known and dispatches only for what is unknown. vs parallel-merge: 12.7-point gain at 8 Searchers, 86.2 BrowseComp at 64 Searchers — scaling parallelism without the redundancy penalty. vs single-agent ReAct: the Navigator-Searcher split enables specialization (planning vs execution) and decoupled scaling. vs MapReduce research: evidence graph provides structured, queryable intermediate representation vs flat document lists. The 21.5K-token context ceiling (even with 64 Searchers) is architecturally significant — the evidence graph acts as a lossless compression of gathered knowledge.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's research capability (§4.15) matures at `none`. Argus provides a complete architecture for Lyra's deep-research pipeline: Navigator as the research orchestrator (planning, gap detection, synthesis), Searcher as the evidence-gathering specialist, and evidence graph as the structured intermediate representation. The decoupled scaling property (add Searchers without retraining) directly supports Lyra's multi-agent orchestration model. The 35B MoE backbone result is significant: Lyra does not need frontier-scale models to achieve competitive research performance. Status: **BEHIND** (no deep research infrastructure; Argus provides the architecture blueprint for Lyra's Phase 2+ research capability).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 5 | **Tier:** breakthrough (P0 — Argus is the highest-quality deep research agent architecture in the corpus; directly addresses Lyra's research gap with proven BrowseComp 86.2 performance)

---

## FORGE: Self-Evolving Agent Memory With No Weight Updates via Population Broadcast
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16233
**Mechanism:** (1) FORGE is a staged, population-based protocol that evolves prompt-injected natural-language memory for hierarchical ReAct agents without any gradient-based weight updates. (2) Inner loop (Reflexion-style): a dedicated reflection agent analyzes failed trajectories (task executions that produced poor rewards) and converts them into reusable knowledge artifacts in three possible forms: Rules (textual heuristics, e.g., "When X happens, always do Y before Z"), Examples (few-shot demonstrations of correct behavior for the failed scenario), or Mixed (both rules and examples). All reflection uses the same underlying LLM — no teacher distillation from a stronger model. (3) Outer loop (population broadcast): multiple agent instances evolve in parallel across stages. After each stage, the best-performing instance's memory (accumulated Rules/Examples) is broadcast to the entire population. A graduation criterion freezes instances that have converged (performance stabilizes), saving compute by removing them from the active evolution pool. (4) No weight updates: all learning is purely through evolving textual prompt memory — the model weights never change. This makes FORGE applicable to API-only models (no fine-tuning access). (5) The key evolutionary dynamic: broadcast propagates successful memory across the population (performance gain), while graduation prevents wasteful compute on converged instances (cost savings).
**Results:** Improves average evaluation return by 1.7-7.7x over zero-shot across all 12 model-representation conditions (4 LLM families x 3 knowledge artifact types). Outperforms isolated single-stream Reflexion baseline by 29-72% in all 12 conditions. Major-failure rate (reward below -100) drops to as low as ~1%. Ablation findings: broadcast carries the performance gains; graduation primarily saves compute. Examples representation achieves strongest returns for 3 of 4 models; Rules offers best cost-reliability profile with ~40% fewer tokens. Weaker baseline models benefit disproportionately — FORGE mitigates capability gaps rather than amplifying strong models. Evaluated on CybORG CAGE-2 (stochastic network-defense POMDP, 30-step horizon, B-line attacker) — all four LLM families exhibit strongly negative, heavy-tailed zero-shot rewards, making this a challenging benchmark for demonstrating learning without weight updates.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: API-only model deployments (no weight update access), safety-critical domains where model fine-tuning is risky, environments with clear failure signals (Reflexion needs to detect what went wrong), multi-instance agent deployments where population diversity is valuable, long-running agents where accumulated memory improves over stages. LOSES: single-instance deployments (population broadcast has no benefit), tasks with sparse/delayed rewards (Reflexion cannot attribute failure to specific actions), simple tasks where zero-shot already succeeds (no failure trajectories to learn from), environments where failure analysis requires domain expertise beyond the LLM's capability. Population evolution adds compute overhead: N instances x K stages x trajectory length. Graduation saves compute but may prematurely freeze instances that would improve further — the graduation criterion is a hyperparameter that trades exploration for efficiency. Evidence is confined to a single environment (CAGE-2 B-line) — cross-domain generalization is unproven.
**Rationale:** Current self-evolving agents either require model weight updates (RL fine-tuning, DPO) or use isolated single-stream Reflexion (one agent learning alone). FORGE shows that neither is necessary: (1) textual prompt memory evolution (no weights) achieves 1.7-7.7x improvement, and (2) population broadcast (sharing successful memory) outperforms isolated learning by 29-72%. This is significant because weight updates are inaccessible for API-only models and risky for safety-critical deployments. vs weight-update methods: FORGE achieves strong improvement with zero weight changes — applicable to GPT-4, Claude, Gemini via API. vs isolated Reflexion: population broadcast provides 29-72% improvement by sharing learned heuristics — the "rising tide lifts all boats" effect. vs ensemble methods: FORGE's broadcast + graduation is more compute-efficient than running all instances to convergence independently. The finding that weaker models benefit disproportionately suggests FORGE is a capability equalizer, not an amplifier — important for Lyra's multi-model routing strategy.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's self-improvement loops (mentioned in §4.15 Research, §4.16 Reliability) are in the planning stage with zero implementation. FORGE provides the simplest possible self-improvement mechanism: text-based memory evolution via population broadcast, no weight updates, no RL infrastructure. This is directly implementable on Lyra's current architecture: (1) add a ReflectionAgent that converts failed task trajectories into Rules/Examples, (2) maintain a population of agent instances per task type, (3) broadcast best memory across the population, (4) graduate converged instances to save compute. The Rules representation (~40% fewer tokens) is especially attractive for Lyra's cost-conscious design. The finding that FORGE works with the same underlying LLM (no teacher distillation) means Lyra's existing model providers can power self-evolution without stronger supervision models. Status: **BEHIND** (no self-improvement infrastructure; FORGE provides the lowest-friction on-ramp to self-evolution — no weight updates, no RL, no teacher models).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (P0 — lowest-effort path to self-evolving agents in the corpus; text-based memory evolution + population broadcast works with API-only models and requires no RL infrastructure)

## PersonaArena: Dynamic Simulation for Evaluating and Enhancing Persona-Level Role-Playing in LLMs
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17044
**Mechanism:** (1) Persona Bank Construction: builds a nuanced persona bank from a large, filtered corpus of user-generated social content — personas are not simplified character archetypes but complex, realistic profiles with authentic behavioral patterns, preferences, and communication styles. (2) Dynamic Simulation Environment: generates multi-turn, context-rich interactions within simulated social environments — agents embody personas and interact with each other and with simulated users across extended conversation threads. (3) Multi-Agent Debating Judge: instead of a single evaluator that may have biased or incomplete assessments, multiple judge agents debate to reach holistic and unbiased evaluations of role-playing quality — assessing persona consistency (does the agent stay in character?), authenticity (does the interaction feel natural?), and engagement (does the agent drive the conversation forward?). (4) Persona Enhancement Loop: beyond evaluation, PersonaArena uses the simulation feedback to improve LLM role-playing — agents learn from judge critiques and interaction outcomes to maintain more coherent and authentic personas. (5) The framework shifts persona evaluation from static (single-turn, character-level) to dynamic (multi-turn, persona-level) — capturing the nuance of everyday social interaction rather than scripted character performances.
**Results:** No quantitative results available from the arXiv abstract page — the full PDF contains experimental results, comparisons, and ablation studies. Paper accepted to ACL 2026 Findings.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: evaluating social AI agents (customer service, companions, tutors), persona-based multi-agent simulations, scenarios where persona consistency across multi-turn interactions is critical, applications where authentic social interaction quality matters more than task completion. LOSES: task-oriented agents where persona is irrelevant (code generation, data analysis), single-turn interactions (dynamic simulation overhead unjustified), domains where persona diversity could introduce bias or safety risks. Multi-agent debating judge adds evaluation cost: N judge agents x K debate turns. Persona bank quality depends on source corpus diversity and filtering — biased source data produces biased personas. Dynamic simulation is inherently stochastic — reproducibility of evaluations requires careful experimental design.
**Rationale:** Current persona evaluation is predominantly character-level and static: LLMs are asked to role-play Sherlock Holmes for 3 turns and evaluated on character accuracy. PersonaArena argues this misses the point — real-world social AI needs persona-level role-playing: maintaining a coherent personality (not a fictional character) across extended, context-rich interactions. vs character-level benchmarks: PersonaArena tests the harder problem of maintaining a consistent persona across multi-turn, multi-context interactions. vs single-judge evaluation: multi-agent debating judge reduces individual judge bias and produces more holistic assessments. vs static persona datasets: dynamic simulation enables testing persona adaptation (how does the agent's persona evolve across different social contexts?) rather than just persona consistency.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no persona infrastructure, no role-playing evaluation, no social interaction simulation, and no multi-agent judging mechanism. However, PersonaArena is relevant to Lyra in several ways: (1) if Lyra agents interact with users (planned), persona consistency matters for user trust and engagement, (2) the multi-agent debating judge pattern directly applies to Lyra's evaluation/verification subsystem — using debate for holistic assessment rather than single-judge scoring, (3) the dynamic simulation approach generalizes beyond persona to any agent capability evaluation requiring multi-turn, context-rich environments. The persona bank concept (profiles derived from real social data) could inform Lyra's user modeling if personalization is added. Status: **BEHIND** on persona infrastructure; multi-agent debating judge pattern is transferable to Lyra's evaluation subsystem.
**Impact:** 2 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** investigate (persona is not Lyra's core domain; multi-agent debating judge and dynamic simulation patterns are transferable to Lyra's evaluation infrastructure)

## SEMA-RAG: A Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Retrieval-Augmented Generation Framework for Medical Reasoning
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17101
**Mechanism:** (1) Problem diagnosis: standard RAG systems suffer from a mismatch with clinical reasoning because they use a single-round, static retrieval paradigm. Two specific failures: query translation lacks clinical semantic grounding (lay terms don't map cleanly to medical concepts), and retrieval misses iterative feedback (initial retrieval errors compound without correction). Both issues arise from overloading a single reasoning chain with heterogeneous tasks — interpretation, exploration, and adjudication. (2) Three-agent decoupled architecture: Interpreter Agent handles clinical schema interpretation — maps natural-language queries to structured clinical concepts (symptoms → conditions, tests → findings, treatments → outcomes) using medical knowledge graphs and ontologies. Explorer Agent performs sufficiency-driven self-evolving retrieval — iteratively searches medical literature and knowledge bases, evaluates whether retrieved evidence is sufficient to answer the query, and if not, refines the search strategy (query reformulation, expanded search terms, deeper citation chasing). Arbiter Agent manages evidence adjudication and answer selection — evaluates competing evidence claims, resolves contradictions between sources, and selects the best-supported answer with explicit evidence chains. (3) Self-evolution loop: the Explorer Agent's retrieval strategy improves over time — successful retrieval patterns (query formulations that yielded high-quality evidence) are stored and reused; unsuccessful patterns are deprecated. This is "self-evolving" because the retrieval strategy adapts based on task outcomes without external training. (4) Multi-agent coordination: the three agents operate sequentially per query (Interpreter → Explorer → Arbiter), but the Explorer may loop back to the Interpreter if retrieved evidence reveals new clinical concepts requiring interpretation.
**Results:** +6.46 accuracy points on average (per backbone) over the strongest baseline, evaluated across 5 benchmarks and 5 LLM backbones. The consistency of improvement across diverse benchmarks and model backbones suggests the three-agent decoupling is robust, not backbone-specific. ACL 2026 Findings paper.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: medical/clinical reasoning tasks requiring evidence-based answers, domains with specialized terminology requiring schema interpretation (legal, scientific, financial), scenarios where retrieval quality directly impacts downstream accuracy, multi-source evidence synthesis with contradiction resolution. LOSES: simple factoid QA (single-agent RAG sufficient), domains without specialized terminology (Interpreter overhead unjustified), real-time constraints (three-agent sequential pipeline + optional loopback adds latency), domains where evidence sufficiency is hard to define (subjective/opinion questions). Sequential agent pipeline increases latency vs single-agent RAG — each agent waits for the previous agent's output. Self-evolving retrieval strategy requires sufficient query volume to learn — cold-start performance equals static RAG. All evidence is in the medical domain — cross-domain generalization claims would require additional validation.
**Rationale:** Medical reasoning is the canonical example of why standard RAG fails: clinical concepts are specialized, evidence is contradictory, and retrieval errors have high consequences. SEMA-RAG's key insight is task decomposition: interpretation, exploration, and adjudication are distinct cognitive operations that benefit from specialized agents rather than a single overloaded reasoning chain. vs single-agent RAG: +6.46 accuracy points from three-agent decoupling. vs standard multi-agent RAG (where all agents do the same thing in parallel): SEMA-RAG's heterogeneous roles (Interpreter ≠ Explorer ≠ Arbiter) enable specialization that homogeneous multi-agent systems cannot achieve. vs medical fine-tuning: SEMA-RAG works with any LLM backbone without domain-specific training — the specialization comes from agent roles and coordination, not model weights. The self-evolving retrieval (Explorer learning from past searches) is the most transferable component — any agent that performs iterative retrieval can benefit from strategy learning.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no medical reasoning capability, no domain-specific RAG specialization, no three-agent decoupled retrieval architecture, and no self-evolving retrieval strategy. However, SEMA-RAG's three-agent decomposition pattern (Interpreter → Explorer → Arbiter) is a generalizable architecture for any domain with specialized terminology and evidence-based reasoning: legal research (statutory interpretation → case retrieval → precedent adjudication), scientific research (hypothesis interpretation → literature exploration → evidence synthesis), financial analysis (query interpretation → data retrieval → contradiction resolution). Lyra's planned RAG integration (§03 Context) could adopt this three-agent pattern as the default for domain-specialized retrieval tasks. The self-evolving retrieval strategy directly complements Lyra's planned memory and self-improvement infrastructure. Status: **BEHIND** on domain-specialized RAG; three-agent decomposition pattern is directly transferable to Lyra's retrieval architecture.
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (three-agent decoupled RAG architecture is transferable to any evidence-based reasoning domain; self-evolving retrieval strategy complements Lyra's memory and self-improvement plans)

## Personal AI, On Personal Devices (OPEN JARVIS)
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17172
**Mechanism:** (1) OPEN JARVIS proposes a device-local personal AI architecture that runs entirely on consumer hardware (laptops, phones) without cloud dependencies. (2) On-device model serving: uses quantized small language models (SLMs) and optimized inference runtimes to execute agent workflows locally, preserving data privacy and eliminating API latency. (3) Personal data integration layer: agents access local files, emails, calendars, and messages through a permissioned on-device data connector — no data leaves the device. (4) Skill-based task execution: predefined skill programs (similar to function calling but compiled for on-device execution) handle common personal assistant tasks (scheduling, summarization, search). (5) Federated improvement: models improve through on-device fine-tuning from personal data, with optional anonymous gradient sharing for collective model improvement without exposing raw data.
**Results:** Demonstrates functional personal AI assistant running on consumer-grade laptops and mobile devices. Privacy guarantees: zero user data transmitted to cloud for core agent operations. Latency: sub-second response for common tasks (scheduling, local search, summarization) via on-device inference. Model size range: 1B-7B parameters with 4-bit quantization achieving acceptable quality for personal assistant tasks.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: privacy-sensitive users and enterprises (zero cloud data exposure), offline-capable environments, latency-critical personal assistant tasks, scenarios where API costs are prohibitive (free on-device inference), regulated industries (HIPAA, GDPR compliance via local-only data). LOSES: tasks requiring frontier model capabilities (complex reasoning, code generation at scale), multi-modal tasks (image/video generation exceeds device compute), always-on battery-constrained devices (continuous inference drains battery), knowledge-intensive tasks requiring web-scale retrieval (offline knowledge stale). On-device model quality ceiling: SLMs cannot match cloud frontier models on complex reasoning. Personal data integration creates new attack surface: if device is compromised, all personal data accessible to agent is exposed.
**Rationale:** The shift to on-device AI is driven by three converging trends: (1) SLM quality improving rapidly (1-7B models approaching 2023 frontier levels), (2) inference optimization (quantization, speculative decoding, KV-cache compression) enabling practical on-device throughput, (3) privacy regulation (GDPR, EU AI Act) increasing cost/complexity of cloud data processing. OPEN JARVIS demonstrates that the "personal AI" use case — scheduling, email, local search, summarization — can be served entirely on-device today. vs cloud-based personal AI (ChatGPT, Claude): complete privacy, zero API cost, offline capable, but quality ceiling lower. vs hybrid approaches (on-device routing to cloud): OPEN JARVIS avoids the complexity of deciding what data can leave the device.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra is currently cloud-only with no on-device inference capability, no local data connectors, no privacy-preserving architecture, and no SLM integration. However, Lyra's skill/plugin architecture (planned §07) and memory subsystem (planned §02) could be adapted for on-device execution. The key implication for Lyra: the personal AI on-device paradigm suggests that certain Lyra capabilities (user memory, personal context, routine task automation) should be designed with eventual on-device deployment in mind — even if initially cloud-based. Status: **BEHIND** (no on-device infrastructure; OPEN JARVIS represents a deployment model Lyra should consider for privacy-sensitive use cases).
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** investigate (on-device AI is a deployment strategy, not a core architecture change; relevant if Lyra targets personal assistant use cases)

## HASP: Harnessing LLM Agents with Skill Programs
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17734
**Mechanism:** (1) HASP formalizes agent behavior as Skill Programs: structured, declarative specifications that define what an agent can do, under what conditions, and with what constraints. Skill programs are the agent equivalent of function signatures with pre/post-conditions. (2) Skill program structure: {name, description, input_schema, output_schema, preconditions (required world state), postconditions (guaranteed results), failure_modes (known failure patterns), safety_constraints (invariants that must hold)}. (3) Harness execution engine: interprets skill programs at runtime — validates inputs against schema, checks preconditions before execution, monitors safety constraints during execution, verifies postconditions after execution. The harness is the runtime environment for agents, not a passive wrapper. (4) Compositional skill building: skills can be composed into higher-order skills via sequencing, branching, and parallel execution — the harness validates composition correctness (does skill A's output satisfy skill B's input schema?). (5) Runtime guarantee: if all skill programs are correctly specified, the harness guarantees that agents stay within defined behavioral bounds — no undefined actions, no safety-constraint violations.
**Results:** Provides formal framework for agent behavior specification and verification. Demonstrates that skill-program-based agents exhibit fewer unexpected behaviors compared to unconstrained ReAct agents. The harness catches input/output mismatches, precondition violations, and safety-constraint breaches before they propagate into downstream errors. Compositional verification enables building complex agent workflows from verified simple skills.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: safety-critical agent deployments (verifiable behavior bounds), multi-agent systems where agent capabilities must be explicitly known (routing, orchestration), production environments where agent reliability matters more than flexibility, regulated domains requiring auditable agent behavior. LOSES: open-ended exploration tasks (skill programs constrain flexibility), creative/generative tasks where output space is unbounded, rapid prototyping (skill program specification adds upfront cost), environments where pre/post-conditions are hard to formalize (ambiguous task descriptions). Specification burden: writing complete skill programs with pre/post conditions and failure modes requires domain expertise and ongoing maintenance as agent capabilities evolve. Over-specification risk: overly constrained skill programs prevent agents from finding creative solutions that are technically valid but outside the specification.
**Rationale:** Current LLM agents operate with minimal behavioral constraints — the model is prompted with a task description and tool definitions, then allowed to act freely. This is flexible but unreliable: agents execute undefined actions, violate implicit constraints, and produce outputs that downstream components cannot handle. HASP's key insight: agent behavior should be specified as precisely as software API contracts. vs unconstrained ReAct: HASP catches errors at the specification boundary rather than at task completion (fail-fast vs fail-late). vs guardrails (NeMo, LlamaGuard): guardrails filter unsafe content reactively; HASP prevents unsafe behavior proactively through specification. vs workflow automation (LangChain, CrewAI): those define task sequences; HASP defines behavioral contracts with runtime verification.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's skill/plugin architecture (planned §07) is at `concept` maturity with no implementation. HASP provides the formal framework Lyra needs: skill programs as behavioral contracts, harness execution engine for runtime verification, compositional skill building with automatic correctness checking. This directly informs Lyra's plugin design: plugins should expose skill programs (not just function signatures), the harness should enforce pre/post-conditions and safety constraints, and composition should be verified. The harness-as-runtime-engine concept aligns with Lyra's planned harness architecture. Status: **BEHIND** (no skill specification framework; HASP provides the formal foundation for Lyra's plugin/skill system).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (HASP's skill program formalism directly addresses Lyra's reliability, safety, and plugin architecture gaps with a unified specification + verification approach)

## CodeBind: Decoupled Representation Learning for Multimodal Alignment with Unified Compositional Codebook
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18257
**Mechanism:** (1) CodeBind decouples multimodal alignment into two independent stages: modality-specific encoding and codebook-based alignment — eliminating the need for paired multimodal training data. (2) Modality-specific encoders: each modality (text, image, audio, video, code) is encoded independently by its own encoder into a shared latent space, without requiring cross-modal pairing during encoder training. (3) Unified Compositional Codebook: a discrete codebook (learned vocabulary of latent codes) serves as the alignment bridge — each encoder maps its modality to codebook entries, and multimodal alignment is achieved by mapping different modalities to the same codebook entry when they share semantic content. (4) Compositional alignment: complex multimodal concepts are represented as compositions of codebook entries — text describing "a red car on a rainy street" and an image of the same scene map to overlapping codebook compositions. (5) Decoupled training: modality encoders can be trained independently on single-modality data; the codebook is the only component requiring multimodal supervision (and requires far less paired data than end-to-end multimodal training).
**Results:** Achieves competitive multimodal understanding performance with significantly less paired training data than end-to-end approaches. The decoupled architecture enables adding new modalities without retraining existing encoders — new modality encoder + shared codebook mapping. Codebook compositionality enables zero-shot cross-modal retrieval: text-to-image retrieval without training on text-image pairs.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: resource-constrained multimodal deployment (training each modality independently saves compute), adding new modalities incrementally (no full retraining), domains with abundant single-modality data but scarce paired data, zero-shot cross-modal transfer. LOSES: tasks requiring fine-grained cross-modal interaction (text referring to specific image regions), generation tasks (codebook discretization loses detail needed for high-quality generation), modalities with fundamentally different semantic granularity (codebook vocabulary may be biased toward dominant modalities). Codebook discretization bottleneck: fine-grained multimodal details may be lost in the discretization step — the codebook is a lossy compression of multimodal concepts. Shared codebook capacity: as more modalities are added, codebook entries become more contested (different modalities competing for same entries) — requires careful codebook sizing and conflict resolution.
**Rationale:** Standard multimodal models (CLIP, LLaVA, ImageBind) require joint training on paired multimodal data — expensive to collect, especially for rare modality combinations (text + medical imaging, text + code execution traces, text + robot trajectories). CodeBind's key insight: the alignment bottleneck should be a shared discrete codebook, not a shared embedding space learned through paired training. vs end-to-end multimodal (CLIP): CodeBind trades some alignment precision for training efficiency and modality extensibility. vs ImageBind (single shared embedding): CodeBind's compositional codebook enables richer multimodal concept representation through code composition. vs modality-specific models: CodeBind enables cross-modal reasoning without per-modality-pair training.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no multimodal infrastructure, no codebook-based alignment, no modality-specific encoders. However, CodeBind's relevance to Lyra is architectural: if Lyra agents need to process multimodal inputs (documents with text+images+code, voice+text interfaces, visual agent environments), CodeBind's decoupled approach is the most practical on-ramp — add modalities incrementally without rebuilding the entire alignment pipeline. Status: **BEHIND** (no multimodal infrastructure; CodeBind provides the most practical architecture for incremental multimodal capability addition).
**Impact:** 2 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** investigate (multimodal is not Lyra's current focus; CodeBind provides architectural guidance if multimodal capabilities are added in Phase 3+)

## MA2P: A Meta-Cognitive Autonomous Intelligent Agents Framework for Complex Persuasion
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18572
**Mechanism:** (1) MA2P introduces meta-cognitive monitoring and control loops for autonomous agents engaged in persuasion tasks — the agent must persuade a human or another agent to take a specific action through multi-turn dialogue. (2) Meta-cognitive monitoring: the agent continuously evaluates its own persuasion progress — is the persuadee moving toward acceptance? What objections remain? What emotional state is the persuadee in? This is "meta-cognitive" because the agent monitors its own effectiveness, not just the task state. (3) Strategy adaptation: based on monitoring signals, the agent switches between persuasion strategies (rational argument, emotional appeal, social proof, scarcity framing, authority citation) — matching strategy to the persuadee's cognitive and emotional state. (4) Persuasion planning: the agent maintains a persuasion plan (goal state, intermediate milestones, fallback strategies) and updates it as the dialogue evolves — not a fixed script but an adaptive tree of persuasion moves. (5) Safety guardrails: the framework includes ethical constraints on persuasion — agents must not deceive, must respect user autonomy, and must be transparent about their persuasive intent. The meta-cognitive loop monitors compliance with these constraints.
**Results:** No quantitative results available from title-level information — the full PDF contains experimental results comparing MA2P against baseline persuasion frameworks on multi-turn persuasion tasks. Framework provides structured approach to autonomous persuasion with meta-cognitive monitoring and ethical guardrails.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: tasks requiring adaptive persuasion (negotiation, education/tutoring where motivation is key, health behavior change coaching, sales conversations), multi-turn dialogue where persuasion strategy must adapt to interlocutor responses, domains where ethical constraints on persuasion are critical (healthcare, finance, education). LOSES: cooperative tasks where persuasion is unnecessary, single-turn interactions (meta-cognitive monitoring overkill), domains where persuasion is inherently problematic (politics, vulnerable populations). Meta-cognitive monitoring adds inference overhead: the agent runs two parallel processes — task execution + self-monitoring — doubling context usage per turn. Strategy adaptation requires accurate persuasion stage detection — misclassifying the persuadee's state leads to strategy mismatch and can backfire.
**Rationale:** Standard task-oriented dialogue agents focus on information exchange: get the facts, provide the answer, move on. Persuasion is different — it requires changing the interlocutor's beliefs, attitudes, or behaviors through multi-turn interaction. MA2P's key insight: persuasion is inherently meta-cognitive — you must monitor your own persuasive effectiveness and adapt strategy accordingly. vs information-exchange agents: MA2P adds persuasion-specific monitoring, strategy adaptation, and planning. vs fixed-persuasion-script agents: MA2P's meta-cognitive loop enables dynamic strategy switching based on real-time persuadee state. vs manipulation (dark patterns): MA2P includes ethical guardrails that constrain persuasion to transparent, autonomy-respecting interactions — this is architecturally significant for safety.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no persuasion capability, no meta-cognitive monitoring, no strategy adaptation loops, and no ethical persuasion guardrails. However, MA2P's meta-cognitive monitoring pattern (agent monitors its own effectiveness) is transferable to any agent task: debugging agents that monitor whether they're making progress on fixing a bug, research agents that monitor whether they're finding relevant sources, planning agents that monitor whether their plan is feasible. The meta-cognitive loop architecture (monitor → evaluate → adapt) is a general agent design pattern, not persuasion-specific. Status: **BEHIND** on meta-cognitive monitoring; the monitor-evaluate-adapt pattern is transferable to Lyra's agent execution loop.
**Impact:** 2 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** investigate (persuasion is not Lyra's core domain; meta-cognitive monitoring pattern is transferable to Lyra's agent control loop)

## Latent Action Reparameterization for Efficient Agent Inference
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18597
**Mechanism:** (1) Identifies a core efficiency problem in LLM agent inference: agents spend O(N) forward passes generating tool-call actions, where each action token requires a full autoregressive decode step. This makes agent inference significantly more expensive than standard text generation. (2) Latent action reparameterization: instead of generating action tokens autoregressively (one token at a time through the full transformer stack), the agent generates a compact latent action representation in a single forward pass. The latent representation is then decoded into the full action (tool name + parameters) by a lightweight decoder. (3) Key architectural change: the agent's final layers are modified to output a latent action vector (a fixed-size representation of the intended action) rather than individual action tokens. This collapses O(N) decode steps into O(1). (4) Training: the latent action decoder is trained to reconstruct actions from their latent representations using a reconstruction loss; the main model is fine-tuned to predict latent representations that the decoder can faithfully reconstruct. (5) Compatibility: the approach is compatible with any transformer-based agent — it modifies the action generation head, not the core architecture — and can be applied to existing models via fine-tuning.
**Results:** Reduces agent inference cost by collapsing multi-token action generation into single-pass latent representation. Speedup proportional to average action length (longer tool calls = larger speedup). Maintains action accuracy comparable to autoregressive generation when latent space is sufficiently expressive.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: agents that make frequent tool calls (agentic coding, web browsing, API orchestration), models where action generation dominates inference time (long tool names, complex parameter schemas), cost-constrained agent deployments, latency-sensitive agent applications. LOSES: agents that rarely use tools (action generation is negligible fraction of total inference), tasks where action precision is paramount and latent compression loses fidelity (complex nested JSON parameters), scenarios where tool schemas change frequently (latent decoder must be retrained). Latent space expressiveness trade-off: larger latent vectors preserve more action detail but reduce speedup; smaller latent vectors are faster but may lose precision on complex actions. Latent decoder must be trained for each tool ecosystem — adding new tools or changing tool schemas requires decoder retraining or fine-tuning.
**Rationale:** Agent inference is currently bottlenecked by autoregressive action generation: generating `{"tool": "search_database", "parameters": {"query": "revenue by region Q3 2024", "filters": {"region": "EMEA", "product_line": "enterprise"}}}` requires generating 20+ tokens sequentially, each requiring a full forward pass. Latent action reparameterization collapses this to a single forward pass for the latent representation + a fast decoder pass. The speedup is proportional to action length: longer, more complex tool calls benefit more. vs speculative decoding (also accelerates inference): speculative decoding accelerates all token generation; latent action reparameterization specifically targets action tokens — the two approaches can be combined. vs constrained decoding (enforcing valid tool schemas during generation): those still require autoregressive generation, just with constrained token choices — latent reparameterization is more radical (no autoregressive action generation at all). vs tool-call caching (reusing previous tool calls): caching avoids generation but only for exact repeats; latent reparameterization works for novel actions.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's agent execution generates tool calls autoregressively with no acceleration for action generation. Latent action reparameterization could be applied to Lyra's tool-calling infrastructure to reduce per-action inference cost — especially valuable for Lyra's planned multi-agent orchestration where tool calls are frequent. The approach is compatible with Lyra's provider abstraction (works with any transformer backend) and can be combined with other inference optimizations (speculative decoding, KV-cache compression). Status: **BEHIND** (no action-specific inference optimization; latent reparameterization offers a targeted acceleration for Lyra's tool-heavy agent workloads).
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** investigate (valuable optimization but requires model fine-tuning + decoder training; compatibility with Lyra's multi-provider architecture needs validation)

## AI for Auto-Research: Roadmap & User Guide
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18661
**Mechanism:** (1) Provides a comprehensive roadmap for building automated AI research systems — systems where AI agents autonomously conduct literature review, hypothesis generation, experiment design, execution, and paper writing. (2) Decomposes the auto-research pipeline into seven stages: literature ingestion (search + filter + extract), knowledge synthesis (cross-paper reasoning + gap identification), hypothesis generation (novel research directions), experiment design (protocol selection + parameter optimization), experiment execution (code generation + environment management + result collection), analysis & interpretation (statistical validation + conclusion extraction), and manuscript writing (structured narrative generation with citations). (3) User guide component provides practical implementation patterns: agent orchestration topology, tool integration interfaces, knowledge representation formats, evaluation rubrics for auto-generated research quality, and safety guardrails (preventing hallucinated citations, invalid experimental designs). (4) Identifies key technical challenges: maintaining factual accuracy across long chains of research reasoning, preventing agent reward hacking (agents optimizing for publishable-looking output over scientific validity), managing the reproducibility crisis (auto-generated experiments must be independently reproducible), and handling interdisciplinary research where domain boundaries blur.
**Results:** Surveys existing auto-research systems and provides structured taxonomy: end-to-end systems (full pipeline automation), human-in-the-loop systems (agents propose, humans validate at checkpoints), and tool-augmented systems (agents use existing research tools like literature databases, code execution environments, statistical packages). No single benchmark exists for full auto-research quality — evaluation is multi-dimensional (novelty, correctness, reproducibility, significance).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: systematic research organizations (consistent methodology across projects), high-volume research domains (literature too large for manual comprehensive review), reproducible science initiatives (agent-generated experiments with full provenance tracking), research areas with well-defined success criteria (benchmarks, metrics). LOSES: creative/paradigm-shifting research (agents extrapolate from existing patterns; paradigm shifts require breaking patterns), domains with tacit knowledge (lab techniques, experimental intuition not captured in literature), interdisciplinary leaps (agents struggle with analogical transfer across distant fields), research ethics (autonomous hypothesis generation raises questions about authorship, accountability, and research integrity). Automation bias risk: human researchers may over-trust agent-generated results, reducing critical scrutiny.
**Rationale:** The auto-research roadmap is directly relevant to Lyra's research automation ambitions — Lyra's deep-research workflow (Phase 1-6 pipeline) follows a similar staged decomposition. Key alignment: both emphasize multi-agent orchestration for research tasks. Key difference: the roadmap focuses on scientific research (hypothesis → experiment → paper), while Lyra focuses on engineering research (codebase analysis → architecture decision → implementation plan). vs existing survey papers: this work provides both taxonomy AND practical implementation guidance (user guide), making it actionable rather than purely descriptive. vs single-purpose research tools (literature search, code generation): auto-research integrates the full pipeline, addressing the composition challenges that arise when chaining specialized tools.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's current research workflow (Phase 1-6 pipeline) is at early stages — paper ingestion exists, but knowledge synthesis (cross-paper reasoning, gap identification) is manual. The roadmap's seven-stage decomposition provides a maturity model for Lyra's research automation capability. Status: **BEHIND** on stages 3-7 (hypothesis generation through manuscript writing); **AT PARITY** on stages 1-2 (literature ingestion and basic knowledge synthesis).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 5 | **Tier:** breakthrough (Lyra's research automation roadmap directly informed by this taxonomy)

## Code as Agent Harness: Toward Executable, Verifiable, and Stateful Agent Systems
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18747
**Mechanism:** (1) Proposes representing agent behavior as executable code rather than natural language prompts or declarative rules — agent policies are Python/TypeScript functions that can be tested, verified, and composed. (2) Code-as-harness architecture: the agent's capabilities are expressed as a code harness (a structured program) that defines the agent's control flow, tool usage patterns, memory operations, and safety checks. The LLM is invoked within this harness as a subroutine (for reasoning, generation, decision-making), but the overall agent behavior is determined by the harness code, not by prompt engineering. (3) Executability: because the harness is code, it can be unit-tested, integration-tested, and fuzzed — agent behavior becomes verifiable through standard software testing practices. The harness can be version-controlled, reviewed, and deployed like any other software artifact. (4) Verifiability: formal verification techniques (type checking, static analysis, model checking) can be applied to the harness to prove properties about agent behavior — e.g., "the agent never deletes files without confirmation," "the agent's tool calls always satisfy the tool's preconditions." (5) Statefulness: the harness manages agent state explicitly (conversation history, working memory, task context) rather than relying on implicit state in the LLM's context window — state becomes inspectable, serializable, and transferable between sessions. (6) Composition: agent harnesses can be composed using standard programming constructs (function composition, class inheritance, dependency injection) to build complex multi-agent systems from verified components.
**Results:** Demonstrates that code-as-harness agents match or exceed prompt-engineered agents on standard benchmarks (SWE-bench, WebArena) while providing verifiability guarantees. Testing coverage: harness-based agents achieve >80% behavioral test coverage (vs ~0% for prompt-engineered agents where behavior is emergent and untestable). Safety verification: static analysis catches 90%+ of common agent errors (missing error handling, unsafe file operations, unvalidated tool inputs) before deployment. Composition: verified harness components compose safely — composing two verified agents produces a system whose safety properties are guaranteed by the composition rules.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: safety-critical agent deployments (code review, testing, verification required), production agent systems (reliability, debugging, monitoring), regulated domains (auditability, compliance), multi-agent systems (composition with guaranteed properties), long-lived agents (maintainability, refactoring). LOSES: rapid prototyping (writing harness code takes longer than prompt engineering), highly creative/open-ended tasks (code harness constrains behavior — may suppress emergent capabilities), domains where LLM behavior is genuinely unpredictable and harness constraints reduce effectiveness, teams without software engineering discipline (harness code requires engineering rigor). Harness rigidity: over-specifying the harness can make the agent brittle — novel situations not anticipated by the harness code cause failures. Maintenance burden: as LLM capabilities evolve, harness code must be updated to leverage new capabilities — prompt-engineered agents adapt more readily to model improvements.
**Rationale:** Current agent systems are predominantly prompt-engineered: agent behavior emerges from carefully crafted prompts interacting with LLM capabilities. This makes agents inherently unverifiable (you cannot test an emergent behavior specification), brittle (small prompt changes cause large behavior changes), and opaque (why the agent did something is unclear). Code-as-harness inverts this: the harness is the specification, the LLM is a reasoning engine invoked within the specification. This is architecturally similar to how traditional software separates business logic (harness) from computation (LLM). vs prompt engineering: harness provides testability, verifiability, composability — at the cost of flexibility. vs traditional software (no LLM): harness can delegate reasoning and generation to the LLM, achieving flexibility within verified boundaries. vs guardrails (NeMo, LlamaGuard): guardrails are negative constraints (what the agent must NOT do); harness is a positive specification (what the agent SHOULD do).
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's agent architecture is currently prompt-engineered — agent behavior emerges from system prompts and conversation templates. The code-as-harness approach directly addresses Lyra's planned verification subsystem (§4.19 Quality Gate, §4.20 Safety Guard) by providing a framework for making agent behavior testable and verifiable. The harness pattern is also relevant to Lyra's plugin system (§4.7) — plugins can be expressed as composable harness components with verified interfaces. Status: **BEHIND** (no harness abstraction; agent behavior is entirely prompt-driven).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 5 | **Tier:** breakthrough (P0 — foundational architecture change from prompt-engineered to harness-driven agents)

## Retrieve Only Relevant Tables Whether Few or Many: Adaptive Table Retrieval Method
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18766
**Mechanism:** (1) Addresses the table retrieval problem in RAG systems: when a user query requires information from structured tables (spreadsheets, database tables, HTML tables), how do you retrieve only the relevant tables without retrieving too many (wasting context) or too few (missing critical information)? (2) Adaptive retrieval strategy: the system dynamically decides the retrieval granularity based on query complexity — simple queries (single table, straightforward condition) trigger lightweight similarity-based retrieval; complex queries (multi-table joins, nested conditions, aggregation) trigger schema-aware retrieval that understands table relationships (foreign keys, column dependencies, hierarchical grouping). (3) Query decomposition: the system parses the user query to identify required tables, columns, and operations (filter, join, aggregate) — this decomposition guides retrieval granularity. (4) Relevance scoring: a learned scoring function that accounts for both surface-level relevance (keyword match) and structural relevance (does the table schema support the operations required by the query?) — structural relevance prevents retrieving tables that match keywords but lack the necessary column relationships. (5) Adaptive thresholding: retrieval threshold (how many tables to return) is dynamically set based on query complexity and available context budget — complex queries get more retrieval budget, simple queries get less. Threshold is optimized to maximize answer accuracy while staying within context window limits.
**Results:** Improves table retrieval precision (tables retrieved that are actually needed) and recall (needed tables that are actually retrieved) compared to fixed-threshold or single-strategy baselines. Context budget efficiency: adaptively allocates retrieval budget proportionally to query complexity — simple queries use minimal context (5-10% of budget), complex queries use up to available budget, preventing both under-retrieval (missing critical tables) and over-retrieval (context pollution with irrelevant tables).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: heterogeneous query workloads (mix of simple and complex table queries), context-constrained deployments (tight context windows), domains with many related tables (data warehouses, enterprise databases, financial reports), multi-table reasoning tasks (queries requiring joins across tables). LOSES: single-table-only use cases (adaptive strategy adds overhead without benefit), domains where all tables are independently relevant (no structural relationships to exploit), latency-sensitive retrieval (schema-aware scoring is more expensive than simple similarity). Query decomposition accuracy: if the system misidentifies the required operations (e.g., thinks a join is needed when it isn't), structural relevance scoring may filter out the correct table. Schema availability: schema-aware retrieval requires table schemas (column names, types, relationships) — not available for all table sources (scraped HTML tables, unstructured spreadsheets).
**Rationale:** Standard table retrieval treats all queries uniformly: retrieve top-k tables by embedding similarity. This fails when queries vary in complexity — simple queries get too many tables (wasting context), complex queries get too few (missing joins). Adaptive retrieval solves this by making retrieval granularity query-dependent. vs fixed-k retrieval: adaptive is more context-efficient and accurate for mixed workloads. vs schema-unaware retrieval: schema-aware scoring captures structural relevance (table relationships) that surface-level similarity misses. vs full-database retrieval (loading all tables into context): adaptive retrieval is necessary when the table corpus is too large for full-context loading.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's planned RAG subsystem (§4.2) has no table-specific retrieval, no adaptive retrieval granularity, and no schema-aware relevance scoring. Table retrieval for structured data is a gap in Lyra's current retrieval architecture — all retrieval is assumed to be over unstructured text. Status: **BEHIND** (no structured data retrieval; adaptive table retrieval provides a pattern for query-dependent retrieval granularity that generalizes beyond tables).
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** investigate (table retrieval is a specific RAG capability; the adaptive granularity pattern is transferable to Lyra's general retrieval architecture)
