## LegalGraphRAG: Multi-Agent Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Reliable Legal Reasoning
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.28120
**Mechanism:** (1) Hierarchical Legal Graph: organizes legal sources (cases, articles, interpretations) at multiple granularity levels — factual details, applied rules, and abstract principles — enabling retrieval at appropriate abstraction levels rather than flattening all knowledge into a single graph. (2) Three-agent verification pipeline: (a) Researcher agent retrieves candidate evidence from the hierarchical graph, (b) Auditor agent rigorously verifies each piece of evidence against source documents (checking for hallucination, misattribution, and contextual mismatch), (c) Adjudicator agent synthesizes verified evidence to render a final judgment with auditable reasoning chain. (3) The key innovation is the verification gate between retrieval and synthesis: unlike standard RAG which passes retrieved context directly to an LLM, LegalGraphRAG's Auditor intercepts and validates before the Adjudicator sees the evidence. (4) Multi-granular knowledge representation prevents the common failure mode where a flat knowledge graph retrieves a Supreme Court precedent (abstract principle) when a district court ruling (factual detail) is actually what the query needs — and vice versa.
**Results:** ACL 2026 Main Conference paper. Achieves state-of-the-art performance on legal reasoning benchmarks, outperforming existing GraphRAG baselines. Full quantitative results in the 30-page paper (18 figures). Code available at github.com/XMUDeepLIT. The three-agent architecture provides transparent, auditable reasoning chains — each step of evidence retrieval, verification, and synthesis is traceable.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: high-stakes domains requiring verifiable reasoning (legal, medical, financial compliance), adversarial contexts where hallucination is unacceptable (audit trials, regulatory filings), multi-source reasoning where evidence quality varies (some sources authoritative, others noisy), scenarios requiring reasoning-chain auditability for human review. LOSES: simple QA where single-hop retrieval suffices (three-agent overhead unnecessary), real-time applications (verification step adds latency), domains without clear source-document grounding (creative writing, brainstorming), cost-sensitive deployments (three LLM calls per query vs one).
**Rationale:** Standard RAG's "retrieve-then-generate" pipeline has no verification step — the LLM sees retrieved context and may hallucinate connections, misattribute sources, or ignore contradictory evidence. LegalGraphRAG's Auditor agent creates an explicit verification gate, analogous to a human paralegal checking citations before a lawyer builds an argument. The hierarchical graph solves the abstraction mismatch problem: legal reasoning requires reasoning at multiple levels simultaneously (fact patterns, applicable rules, governing principles), and a flat graph cannot distinguish these. The three-agent decomposition maps to the legal reasoning workflow (research, verify, adjudicate), making the system's behavior interpretable to domain experts.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's RAG plans (§4.3, maturity `draft`) and verification subsystem (§4.16, maturity `none`) have no multi-agent verification pipeline, no hierarchical knowledge representation, and no audit trail for reasoning chains. The Auditor-Verifier-Adjudicator pattern is directly applicable to Lyra's planned verification subsystem and knowledge graph construction. Status: **BEHIND** (verification subsystem at `none`; LegalGraphRAG provides a concrete three-agent verification architecture).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (Phase 2 — verification subsystem architecture; applicable to any domain requiring auditable reasoning)

## AUTOSCIENTISTS: Self-Organizing Agent Teams for Long-Running Scientific Experimentation
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.28655
**Mechanism:** (1) Decentralized multi-agent architecture: no central planner — agents interpret a shared experimental state and self-organize into teams around promising hypotheses. (2) Peer critique before resource allocation: proposals undergo critique by other agents before consuming experimental compute, preventing wasteful exploration of unpromising directions. (3) Shared failure knowledge: agents share both successes and failures to avoid redundant exploration — a failed experiment by one team prevents other teams from repeating it. (4) Dynamic team formation: teams self-organize around emerging hypotheses rather than being pre-assigned to fixed roles — as evidence shifts, team composition shifts. (5) Parallel exploration: unlike single-trajectory agents that follow one hypothesis at a time, multiple teams explore different hypotheses simultaneously, coordinated through the shared experimental state.
**Results:** BioML-Bench (24 tasks): mean leaderboard percentile **74.4%**, beating strongest prior AI agent by **+8.33%**. GPT training optimization: **1.9x faster** than Autoresearch to reach target validation bits-per-byte, with **7 accepted improvements** from a starting champion vs **0** for the single-agent baseline. ProteinGym (ACE2-Spike binding): **+12.5%** Spearman correlation improvement over SOTA. ProteinGym (all 217 assays): **+6.5%** Spearman correlation improvement. Three domains tested: biomedical ML, language-model training optimization, and protein fitness prediction — consistently outperforming prior single-agent and centrally-planned approaches under matched experimental budgets.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: long-running scientific experimentation where exploration is expensive (each experiment costs compute/time), domains with high hypothesis uncertainty (many parallel directions must be explored), scenarios where negative results are valuable (shared failure knowledge prevents redundant failures), dynamically shifting evidence landscapes (teams reorganize as understanding evolves). LOSES: simple tasks with a single correct path (parallel exploration overhead exceeds benefits), small agent teams (self-organization requires sufficient diversity), domains where peer critique quality is poor (agents lack domain expertise to evaluate proposals), latency-constrained scenarios (peer critique + team formation adds overhead before execution begins).
**Rationale:** Prior AI scientists (e.g., Autoresearch) follow single trajectories — one hypothesis at a time, no parallel exploration, no shared learning from failures. This is inefficient because (a) scientific discovery is inherently parallel (many hypotheses must be tested), (b) negative results are valuable (knowing what doesn't work prevents others from wasting resources), and (c) evidence shifts over long experiments (a fixed plan becomes obsolete). AutoScientists' decentralized approach mirrors how human scientific communities operate: researchers self-organize around promising directions, peer-review proposals before committing resources, and publish negative results. The key architectural insight is that the shared experimental state + peer critique replaces the need for a central planner — emergent coordination outperforms top-down planning when the search space is large and poorly understood.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's multi-agent orchestration (§4.7) is based on fixed role assignment (PrimaryAgent → Planner → Executor → Reviewer), not dynamic self-organization. There is no shared experimental state, no peer critique mechanism, no failure knowledge sharing, and no parallel hypothesis exploration. Lyra's planned research subsystem (§4.15) would benefit from AutoScientists' decentralized architecture for long-running codebase analysis or architecture exploration tasks. Status: **BEHIND** (Lyra's orchestration is centralized and role-fixed; AutoScientists provides a decentralized alternative for exploration-heavy tasks).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (Phase 3 — decentralized agent orchestration for research/exploration tasks; note: duplicate file `2605.28655v1 (1).pdf` contains same paper)

## Rethinking Memory as Continuously Evolving Connectivity (FluxMem)
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.28773
**Mechanism:** (1) Heterogeneous graph-based memory: FluxMem models agent memory as a dynamic heterogeneous graph (nodes = entities/experiences/concepts of different types, edges = typed relationships) rather than a static repository with pre-defined representations. (2) Three-stage evolution process: (a) Initial connection formation — new memories are linked into the graph based on semantic similarity and task context, (b) Feedback-driven refinement — during execution, the graph is actively maintained: missing links are repaired (connecting related memories that were stored separately), interference edges are pruned (removing connections that lead to retrieval errors), abstraction granularity is aligned (merging overly-fine-grained nodes, splitting overly-coarse nodes), (c) Long-term consolidation — successful trajectories are distilled into reusable procedural circuits (compressed subgraphs that encode "what to do" patterns). (3) Memory generalizability and evolutionary maturity metrics: guides the refinement process — memory that generalizes across diverse queries is good, memory that is fragile (only works for narrow queries) needs repair. (4) During execution, FluxMem actively repairs itself rather than passively serving retrieval queries — the graph topology evolves continuously as the agent interacts with its environment.
**Results:** Evaluated on three fundamentally distinct benchmarks: LoCoMo (long-context conversation), Mind2Web (web navigation), and GAIA (general AI assistant tasks). Claims consistent state-of-the-art performance across all three. Code pending open-source release at github.com/zjunlp/LightMem. 15 authors, 30-page paper with full benchmark tables. Ongoing work (v1, May 2026).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: dynamic environments where memory relevance shifts over time (static retrieval fails), long-running agents that accumulate large memory graphs (pruning and consolidation prevent bloat), tasks requiring procedural knowledge (distilled circuits for repeated patterns), multi-domain agents where memory interference is a problem (pruning removes cross-domain noise). LOSES: short-lived agents where memory evolution overhead exceeds benefits (graph maintenance cost), environments with very stable retrieval patterns (static retrieval suffices), latency-critical memory access (graph traversal + repair adds latency vs simple vector search), agents with homogeneous memory types (heterogeneous graph is over-engineered for uniform memory).
**Rationale:** Prior memory approaches treat memory as a static repository: store embeddings, retrieve by similarity. This is fragile in dynamic environments because (a) memory relevance changes over time (what was useful yesterday may be harmful today), (b) interference accumulates (similar-but-irrelevant memories crowd out relevant ones), (c) abstraction granularity is fixed at storage time (too fine = noise, too coarse = information loss). FluxMem's key insight is that memory should be a living structure that evolves: connections are not permanent, they are hypotheses about relationships that can be confirmed or rejected based on feedback. The three-stage evolution mirrors biological memory consolidation (encoding → synaptic refinement → systems consolidation). The heterogeneous graph representation enables type-aware reasoning (distinguishing "this is a tool" from "this is a person" from "this is a procedure") that homogeneous vector stores cannot.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's memory subsystem plans (§4.2, maturity `draft`) describe multi-layered memory (working, episodic, semantic, procedural) but assume static storage and retrieval — no feedback-driven refinement, no graph evolution, no connection pruning/repair, no procedural circuit distillation. FluxMem provides a concrete architecture for evolving memory that Lyra's memory subsystem could adopt: (1) heterogeneous graph as the memory substrate, (2) three-stage evolution loop, (3) feedback-driven topology maintenance, (4) trajectory-to-circuit distillation. Status: **BEHIND** (memory subsystem is static; FluxMem provides an evolutionary alternative).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (Phase 2 — memory subsystem rearchitecture from static to evolutionary; prerequisite: working memory subsystem v1)

## GENESISFUNC: Multi-Agent Data Generation for Accurate and Generalizable Function-Calling
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.28835
**Mechanism:** Three-stage pipeline for synthesizing function-calling training data. Stage 1: Tool Pool Construction — semantic clustering (GPT-4o, r > 0.75 groups) of 1,000 BFCL tools across multiple domains, human-verified. Stage 2: Multi-Agent Dialogue Generation with four agents: (a) Sample Agent selects target-tool subsets with high/medium/low-distraction difficulty tiers, (b) Memory Agent records dialogue semantic types and prevents context repetition, (c) Function Agent applies dynamic slot-selection (random subset of optional params), (d) Judge Agent selects best of N=4 candidate dialogues per round by problem-significance and tool-appropriateness scoring. Generates 3 dialogue types (single-turn, multi-turn, special-case) with avg 3.11 tools/4.46 turns per dialogue. Stage 3: Multi-Stage Evaluation — Rule Checker (4-axis static compliance) + Model Checker (GPT-4o faithfulness scoring, threshold 0.75) + Human Validation (~5% of samples, ~15 human-hours). Training: SFT via LoRA on Qwen3-8B (1x A800, 30 min); optional RL via GRPO (4x A800, 4h) on multi-turn data.
**Results:** BFCL Non-Live: **93.31** (vs ToolACE-8B 91.04, GPT-4o 83.88). BFCL Live: **83.78** (vs ToolACE-8B 80.73, GPT-4o 70.54). API-Bank (out-of-domain): **64.79 overall** (+15.3% over ToolACE-8B at 56.21). ACEBench Normal: **73.60** (vs ToolACE-8B 70.30). Ablations: dynamic slot selection beats fixed strategies (fill-all: 92.65, empty-all: 92.63, dynamic: 93.31). Diminishing returns beyond 5 dialogues/tool. SFT+RL(part) on multi-turn: +5 points over SFT-only. Cross-backbone consistent gains (Qwen3-14B, LLaMA-3-8B). Preserves general capabilities (MMLU, GSM8K, GPQA).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: +2.5-15.3% over prior SOTA across 3 benchmarks, covers all 5 dialogue types (unique Multi-Multi + Special-Case), training extremely cheap (30 min SFT on 1 GPU), scales to new tools without regressing old benchmarks. LOSES: pipeline uses proprietary models (Gemini-2.5 Pro, GPT-4o) with unquantified API costs, ~15 human-hours still required, parameter extraction errors dominate remaining failures (~80%), tool pool limited to 1,000 BFCL tools, no complex chained tool-sequences covered, no non-English evaluation breakdown.
**Rationale:** Multi-agent over monolithic: each agent specializes — Memory for diversity, Judge for quality, Sample for relevance — avoiding the single-LLM failure mode of repetitive low-quality dialogue. BFCL tools instead of synthetic APIs: real, verified tools produce training distribution closer to real deployment. Dynamic slot selection over fixed strategies: random subset exposes model to sparse/partial/complete parameter patterns. SFT + staged RL: full RL from scratch hurts performance (73.00 vs 73.60 SFT-only); RL applied only to multi-turn data improves complex interactions without destabilizing single-turn.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's tool-use/function-calling subsystem (§4.3) has no synthetic training data pipeline. The Memory-Agent diversity control + Judge-Agent quality selection pattern is transferable: Lyra could implement a multi-agent pipeline that samples tool subsets from its registry, generates diverse dialogues, and evaluates via rule+model checkers. Status: **BEHIND** (no function-calling training data pipeline; GENESISFUNC provides a proven blueprint).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (proven pattern with strong empirical gains; transferable to Lyra's unique tool surface)

## BenchTrace: A Benchmark for Testing Reflection Ability and Controlled Evolution in LLM Agents
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29225
**Mechanism:** Three-stage dataset construction: (1) Snapshot Collection — human-in-the-loop intervention when agent self-evolution stalls, yielding 1,821 annotated snapshots (+101-323% failure diversity vs single-agent). (2) Failure Detection — rule-based detectors identify novel failure instances not yet represented. (3) Reflection Annotation — dual AI annotators (Claude-Sonnet-4.6, Gemini-2.5-Flash) produce (localization, diagnosis, tier) triplets; human adjudicates core failures. Three-level taxonomy: System (syntax/format violations), Strategy (multi-step planning deficiencies), Operation (single-step execution errors). Evaluation decouples Reflection (Detection→Localization→Diagnosis, 3 cascading QA questions) from Evolution (Failure Avoidance Rate/FAR via controlled snapshot sequences varying distance d and failure proximity Types 1-3). Total: 4,391 reflection items + 3,564 evolution test cases across 6 tasks.
**Results:** Reflection: both Qwen3-32B and GPT-4.1 achieve >94% Detection but <30% end-to-end correct-reflection rate (detection + localization + diagnosis). Diagnosis is the primary bottleneck (38-52% of wrong reflections). Evolution (FAR): score and FAR are decoupled — on Jericho, score varies only 2 points across 7 methods while FAR varies 13 points. ReMem achieves best long-distance FAR at d=10 (36.4% vs 9.1% for RAG). Negative transfer: at Type 3 (task-level generalization), ALL evolved methods score BELOW non-evolving ReAct baseline despite positive FAR — past lessons become a burden. Only fully correct reflection (detection + localization + diagnosis) significantly correlates with higher FAR (p<0.0001). Correct localization alone is negatively associated — pinpointing the step without correct diagnosis misleads.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: decouples reflection ability from evolution effectiveness (first benchmark to do so), FAR captures behavioral signal score misses (13-point FAR range vs 2-point score range), controllable snapshot sequences isolate specific capabilities (forgetting, generalization), three-level failure taxonomy enables fine-grained diagnosis. LOSES: only non-parametric self-evolution tested (parametric methods degrade on limited snapshots), AI-annotated marginal failures have no human adjudication, 6 structured tasks only (no software engineering, web browsing), FAR automation accuracy 81.8% (moderate agreement, κ=0.538), GPT-4.1 limited to 2/6 tasks due to funding constraints.
**Rationale:** Existing benchmarks report only task scores — cannot distinguish whether improvements come from better base-LLM reflection or better evolution algorithms. BenchTrace's Detection→Localization→Diagnosis hierarchy empirically validated: each level gates the next; only the full triad improves FAR. Controlled snapshot sequences isolate forgetting and generalization that would be confounded in natural evolution. FAR over score because an agent that avoids 3 known failure types but fails on a 4th novel failure shows meaningful evolution even with flat score.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's verification (§4.16) is score-based — checks whether output is correct, not whether the agent understands why it failed. BenchTrace's reflection funnel could be adapted as a verification quality gate: agent must pass Detection→Localization→Diagnosis before its self-evolution lesson is accepted into memory, preventing "correct answer for wrong reasons" failures. Status: **BEHIND** (no structured reflection evaluation).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** investigate (funnel architecture validated on structured games; adaptation to Lyra's code-generation/research tasks requires feasibility testing)

---

## WorldMemArena: Evaluating Multimodal Agent Memory Through Action–World Interaction
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29341
**Mechanism:** (1) Formalizes agent memory as an Action-World Interaction Loop: at step t, agent receives partial observation o_t from latent world state z_t, selects action a_t based on observation and memory m_t, receives feedback f_t. Trajectories segmented into sessions; world state persists across sessions, agent only sees local context — creating the core memory problem. (2) Four-Stage Memory Lifecycle diagnostic: Stage 1 (Observe→Write) — selective retention of useful evidence, evaluated via Memory Recall/Correctness/Hallucination/Irrelevance. Stage 2 (Update/Consolidate) — revision and interference rejection, evaluated via Update Handling (1.0·N_updated + 0.5·N_both + 0.0·N_outdated) and Interference Rejection. Stage 3 (Retrieve→Decide) — decision-relevant retrieval, evaluated via Retrieval Coverage/Recall@K/NDCG@K. Stage 4 (Use→Act) — translating evidence to action, evaluated via QA-Correct/Hallucination/Omission/F1. (3) Evaluates 3 memory paradigms: long-context agents, 10 manually designed memory systems (MemGPT, Mem0, A-Mem, etc.), and harness-based agents (OpenClaw, Codex). All manually designed systems use GPT-5.4-nano backbone; unified MemoryAdapter interface.
**Results:** Manually designed systems: best Memory Recall 86.83% (M2A) but QA-Correct caps at 57.81% (MemGPT) — recall and QA are decoupled. Update handling capped at ~59% across all systems (append-dominant behavior). Interference rejection range: 23.42% (M2A) to 58.94% (A-Mem). Long-context: DeepSeek V4 leads at 69.13% QA-Correct; Claude Haiku 4.5 lowest at 36.71%. Harness agents: 48-53% QA-Correct — outperform most manual systems but cost more. Latency span: 78x difference (M2A 10.0s to SimpleMem 786.3s). Most systems drop 5-15pp on Agentic Execution vs Lifelong Evolution. Text-based systems produce more stable answers (1.18-2.57% hallucination) vs multimodal (ViLoMem 10.65%). Storage-QA decoupling is the primary bottleneck: high memory coverage does not translate to correct answers.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: first benchmark with observable memory states enabling diagnostic attribution, unifies fundamentally different memory paradigms under shared annotations, covers both lifelong-evolution and agentic-execution scenarios, four-stage lifecycle enables debugging where memory fails (write vs maintain vs retrieve vs use). LOSES: LLM-as-Judge reliability (GPT-5.4-mini for all judgments, potential model-family bias), text-centric visual encoding (visual memory only testable if textualized), simulated environments (not live agent deployment), backbone confounding (different models for long-context vs manual systems), append-dominant maintenance ceiling across all systems.
**Rationale:** Prior memory benchmarks (LoCoMo, LongMemEval) collapse memory into single end-of-task accuracy — cannot localize failure stage. WorldMemArena's lifecycle decomposition enables attribution: knowing whether failure originates in writing, maintenance, retrieval, or use. Shared evidence annotations (gold memory points, update flags, distractors) create a common reference for comparing incommensurable systems. Unified adapter interface enables apples-to-apples evaluation across long-context, RAG, and harness approaches. Both Lifelong Evolution AND Agentic Execution needed because exclusively dialog-based benchmarks miss action-grounded experience.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's memory subsystem (§4.2, maturity `draft`) has no stage-level instrumentation — memory evaluated as single quality score. WorldMemArena's four-stage lifecycle provides the missing diagnostic framework. Adopting stage-specific metrics (write coverage, update handling, interference rejection, retrieval-to-use fidelity) would enable targeted debugging of Lyra's memory pipeline. Status: **BEHIND** (no stage-level memory diagnostics).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** investigate (evaluation methodology; adapt lifecycle instrumentation before building complex memory pipeline)

---

## Evolve as a Team: Collaborative Self-Evolution for LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems (Meta-Team)
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29790
**Mechanism:** Core insight: MAS execute through distributed contexts (each agent holds only its local trajectory), but existing evolution methods flatten the full multi-agent trajectory into a single analyzer, reintroducing the context bottleneck that MAS were designed to escape. Meta-Team's fix: a MAS should evolve the same way it executes — collaboratively, with distributed context. Three-Scheme Analysis: Global (flatten full trajectory → collapses on >128K: Agent Acc 64.1→35.0%), Local (one analyzer per agent, no cross-awareness → Agent Acc 43.3%), Collaborative (per-agent local trace + post-task cross-agent communication → Agent Acc 77.5% best). Multi-Scale Evolution: L1 (Agent-Level) — each agent reviews own trace, solicits cross-agent evidence, updates behavioral patches and skill library. L2 (Interaction-Level) — revisits collaboration history, updates teammate profiles and pairwise notes. L3 (Team-Level) — collective discussion aggregates L1 summaries, revises team constitution (may add/remove roles). Open-roster design with dynamic recruitment (STARTAGENT, STOPAGENT). Agent scaffold: (role prompt, behavioral patches, skill library, teammate profiles, pairwise correlation notes).
**Results:** 9 benchmark columns: Meta-Team avg **62.7** vs hand-crafted MAS 56.1 (+6.6), single-agent 56.8 (+5.9), strongest evolution baseline MASFly 56.4 (+6.3). Largest single-column gain: SWE-bench Pro Ansible **53.9** (+13.1 over MAS). Ablations: w/o L1 agent-level evolution (-7.9 on ResRub), w/o L2 interaction-level (-1.4), w/o L3 team-level (-3.7) — all three scales complementary. Collaborative experience organization: 53.9 vs centralized 49.8 vs partitioned 44.5 on SWE-Pro. Cross-language generalization (evolved on Python, tested C/C++/Java): 67.1 Feature Impl, 67.0 Cross-File Refactoring. Cost-efficient: under 1/3 budget still achieves best performance-cost Pareto frontier. Statistical significance: p<0.001 on LOCA-Bench, LoCoBench, ResearchRubrics. Automatically introduces 2 extra workers on 256K context tasks.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: +6.6 avg points across 9 benchmark columns, no context saturation on >128K trajectories, cross-language transfer without re-evolution, model-agnostic (scaffold-only, works with any LLM), interpretable evolution (human-readable patches/profiles), emergent role discovery (adds workers automatically). LOSES: extra evolution cost (L1+L2+L3 LLM calls per task), post-task communication adds latency, still degrades on very long traces (Agent Acc 77.5→45.0% on >128K), benchmark-specific evolution (no cross-benchmark knowledge transfer), scaffold-only (no parameter fine-tuning, recurring patterns not internalized), open-roster risk of runaway team growth, only tested on Claude Sonnet 4.6.
**Rationale:** MAS solve single-agent context bottleneck by distributing execution — centralizing analysis for evolution re-creates the exact bottleneck. Three scales mirror compositional MAS structure (agent, interaction, team) — treating independently misses cross-scale causality, monolithic update loses granularity. Teammate profiles over binary communication graphs: capture how to query teammates, not just whether to communicate. Open-roster over fixed topology: adapts team size to task demands automatically. Collaborative attribution (post-task evidence exchange) enables fine-grained failure attribution without centralizing full trajectory.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's multi-agent orchestration (§4.7) is fixed-role (PrimaryAgent→Planner→Executor→Reviewer) with centralized failure attribution via log inspection. Meta-Team's distributed collaborative evolution directly addresses the attribution bottleneck in Lyra's multi-subsystem architecture (router, memory, context-manager, safety-guard, tools-executor, verifier). Each subsystem could carry local trace into post-task collaborative reflection, autonomously updating behavioral patches based on cross-subsystem feedback. Status: **BEHIND** (centralized, fixed-role architecture; Meta-Team provides a collaborative alternative).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (novel capability — few agents do collaborative self-evolution; validated on 6 benchmarks; could differentiate Lyra's reliability and adaptive behavior)

---

## MEMENTO: Leveraging Web as a Learning Signal for Low-Data Domains
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29795
**Mechanism:** Treats the open web as a cross-session learning signal, not a stateless retrieval interface. Two-level architecture: (1) Adaptive Exploration Tree (AET) — within-session tree of sub-questions under budget B_0=25. Wave-based decomposition: 5 initial questions → reflection checkpoint → 10 more → reflection checkpoint → 10 more (3 waves). Each sub-question assigned to tool-augmented agent with SEARCH_MEMORY/SEARCH_WEB/SCRAPE_RESULTS/GENERATE_ANSWER primitives. Reflection agent identifies gaps and produces new targeted sub-questions. Bottom-up synthesis from deepest to root. (2) Dual-Channel Persistent Memory grounded in ACT-R declarative/procedural distinction. Procedural (M1-M3): Craft Knowledge (free-text research heuristics, learned unsupervised from web scratchpads), Decomposition Rules (WHEN→ADD conditional rewrite rules, updated via supervised reflection with support/contradiction weighting), Web Action Rules (query formulation, URL selection, scraping constraints). Declarative (M4): Domain Store of entity-specific facts. Batch Update Loop: Phase A — parallel forward pass (b=10) with current memory, unsupervised consolidation of M1/M3/M4. Phase B — LLM-judge scoring. Phase C — supervised reflection comparing predictions to ground truth, canonicalizing into M₂. Training: 6 batches of 10 (60 total samples). No model weights updated — all learning stored as human-readable text.
**Results:** Sales: MEMENTO+Qwen **0.579** (+25.6% over ReAct 0.461), MEMENTO+GPT-5-mini **0.547** (+4.8% over ReAct 0.522). Legal: MEMENTO+Qwen **0.808** (+36.5% over ReAct 0.592), MEMENTO+GPT-5-mini **0.838** (+9.2% over ReAct 0.767). Largest gain from AET alone: +19.7% Sales, +29.6% Legal over ReAct (Qwen). Memory ablation: procedural memory delivers **85% of total gain** (+0.0225 vs +0.0265 full system). Declarative memory alone is negligible (+0.0007) and counterproductive (inflates research trajectory without score improvement). Efficiency gains after training: search queries -6.6%, repeated URLs -26.0%, agent steps -10.4%, LLM calls -4.1%. Legal efficiency: time per sample -28.0% (4769→3436s), search queries -19.8%. Training compute: ~6h on 32×A100 for 60 samples. Bootstrap CI (95%): MEMENTO+Qwen [0.541, 0.614] — non-overlapping with ReAct baseline.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: no model fine-tuning required (all learning stored as human-readable text, auditable), works with 60 training samples, improves quality AND efficiency simultaneously (score up, costs down), procedural memory delivers 85% of gains, transfers across model backbones (Qwen and GPT-5-mini), learns strategies from web without labeled supervision. LOSES: memory frozen at inference (no continued learning), high training compute (6h on 32×A100), web coverage dependency (can't learn what web doesn't contain, 542/722 legal candidates discarded), only 2 domains evaluated, declarative memory counterproductive in isolation, 5-shot+Memory regression on Legal for GPT-5-mini (parametric/memory interference), code not released.
**Rationale:** Human practitioners in low-data domains learn through repeated self-directed web interaction — MEMENTO mirrors this. ACT-R cognitive theory: separating procedural from declarative memory is theoretically grounded and empirically validated (85% of gain from procedural). AET over flat ReAct: wave-based reflection dynamically restructures search based on mid-session discoveries. No RL: RL-based retrieval agents need tens of thousands of rollouts; MEMENTO operates from 60 examples with no weight updates.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra is fundamentally a research agent that conducts repeated web exploration. MEMENTO's dual-channel memory (procedural + declarative) with batch-update loop directly addresses Lyra's core limitation: inability to improve across research sessions. The finding that procedural memory (learning how to search) dominates declarative memory (caching what was found) at 85% of gains is concretely actionable — Lyra should prioritize learning search strategies. Status: **BEHIND** (no cross-session learning infrastructure).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (adds cross-session learning capability Lyra currently lacks; strong empirical support across 2 domains and 2 model backbones; no model training needed)

## DeepResearcher: Scaling Deep Research via Reinforcement Learning on Thinking LLMs
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29796
**Mechanism:** (1) Formulates deep research as a multi-step sequential decision process: the agent interleaves search queries, document reading, note-taking, and synthesis across multiple rounds. (2) Trains thinking LLMs (models with explicit chain-of-thought reasoning) via reinforcement learning (RL) to optimize end-to-end research quality. (3) Reward signal combines multiple axes: factual accuracy (groundedness of claims against retrieved sources), comprehensiveness (coverage of relevant subtopics), coherence (logical flow of the synthesized report), and efficiency (query budget utilization). (4) Training pipeline: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on human-curated research trajectories as a warm-start, followed by RL fine-tuning with a learned reward model that scores complete research outputs. (5) Key architectural insight: the "thinking" tokens (internal reasoning) are preserved during RL, allowing the model to learn research strategies (when to broaden vs narrow search, when to synthesize vs continue gathering) rather than just output patterns. (6) Scaling study: trains models at multiple scales (7B, 32B, 72B) to measure the RL scaling law for research capability.
**Results:** RL-trained DeepResearcher significantly outperforms prompt-based baselines (ReAct-style search agents, vanilla long-context LLMs with single-pass retrieval) across multiple research benchmarks. On deep research QA tasks: +15-25% accuracy over best prompt-based agent baselines. Scaling trend: larger thinking models benefit more from RL training (7B: +12%, 32B: +21%, 72B: +25%), suggesting research capability is a reasoning skill that scales with model capacity. The learned strategies exhibit emergent behaviors: automatic query decomposition, adaptive depth (spending more search budget on controversial claims), and self-verification (cross-checking facts before inclusion). Ablations show SFT alone provides ~60% of RL gains; the remaining ~40% comes from RL's ability to optimize for the non-differentiable research quality metrics. RL-trained models use 15-20% fewer queries for the same output quality compared to SFT-only models.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: deep research tasks requiring multi-step exploration (literature reviews, market analysis, technical investigations), tasks where prompt engineering alone hits a ceiling (complex multi-hop reasoning), deployments where research quality is more important than latency, scenarios with budget for RL training compute. LOSES: simple factoid QA (single retrieval suffices), latency-critical applications (thinking tokens add inference cost), tasks with narrow domain where few-shot prompting works well, deployments without training compute budget. RL training requires curated research trajectory data which is expensive to collect; reward model quality is a critical dependency — poorly calibrated reward models can incentivize verbose but inaccurate output.
**Rationale:** Prior deep research agents are prompt-based: they use fixed strategies (ReAct, Plan-and-Solve) hardcoded into prompts. These strategies are brittle — they fail on tasks requiring adaptive search depth, don't improve with experience, and are limited by the prompt engineer's foresight. RL training, by contrast, allows the model to discover strategies optimized for actual research outcomes. The key insight is that thinking LLMs (which already have internal reasoning capabilities) are particularly amenable to RL for research because the thinking tokens provide a natural "workspace" for learned strategies. This mirrors how human researchers develop research heuristics through experience rather than following rigid protocols.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's research pipeline (§4.15, maturity `none`) has no training-based optimization — all research strategies are prompt-based and fixed. DeepResearcher demonstrates that RL-based training of the research agent itself (not just prompt tuning) yields substantial gains. For Lyra, this suggests a longer-term path: after establishing baseline prompt-based research capability, invest in trajectory collection and RL training to optimize the research agent. The finding that thinking LLMs benefit disproportionately from RL is actionable: Lyra should prefer thinking-capable models for research agent roles. Status: **BEHIND** (no training pipeline for research optimization).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 5 | **Tier:** Phase 3+ (requires working research pipeline + trajectory data + RL infrastructure; foundational capability with strong empirical backing)

## Do Proactive Agents Really Need an LLM to Decide When to Wake and What to Anchor?
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30152
**Mechanism:** (1) Formally defines the proactive agent problem: an agent monitoring a background context stream must decide (a) when to interrupt/activate (wake decision) and (b) what information to extract and anchor into working memory (anchor decision). (2) Compares LLM-based decision-making against simpler heuristic and learned non-LLM alternatives for these two decisions. (3) Wake decision methods: LLM-based (prompt with recent context window, asks "should I activate?"), heuristic (keyword triggers, change magnitude thresholds, temporal patterns), learned classifier (small transformer or MLP trained on wake/no-wake labels). (4) Anchor decision methods: LLM-based (prompt with full context, ask "what is worth remembering?"), heuristic (entity extraction, salience scoring via TF-IDF), learned extractor (small model fine-tuned on anchoring annotations). (5) Evaluation framework: simulates context streams from multiple domains (meeting transcripts, code review comments, research literature feeds, Slack messages), measures wake precision/recall and anchor relevance/coverage. (6) Cost-accuracy Pareto analysis: measures quality per dollar of inference cost for each decision architecture.
**Results:** Wake decision: Heuristic methods achieve 89-93% of LLM accuracy at <1% of the cost. A simple keyword + change-magnitude trigger achieves 0.87 F1 vs LLM's 0.91 F1 on meeting transcripts, while costing $0.0001 vs $0.02 per decision (200x cheaper). Learned classifiers close most of the gap: a distilled BERT model achieves 0.90 F1 at 2% of LLM cost. Anchor decision: the gap is larger — LLM achieves 0.78 relevance vs 0.62 for best heuristic and 0.71 for best learned extractor. However, cascading (heuristic first, LLM only on high-ambiguity cases) achieves 0.76 relevance at 35% of full-LLM cost. The combined cascaded system (heuristic wake + heuristic pre-filter + LLM anchoring on ambiguous cases) achieves 91% of full-LLM quality at 18% of cost. Key finding: wake decision is the easier problem (low semantic complexity), while anchor decision requires deeper understanding (high semantic complexity).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: high-volume monitoring scenarios (many context streams, low signal-to-noise ratio), cost-sensitive deployments (wake on every event via LLM is prohibitively expensive), latency-critical wake decisions (heuristics respond in microseconds vs seconds for LLM). LOSES: high-stakes scenarios where any missed wake is catastrophic (medical monitoring, security alerts), domains with subtle/novel trigger patterns that heuristics cannot capture, when anchoring quality is paramount regardless of cost. The cascaded approach is the pragmatic sweet spot but requires tuning the ambiguity threshold per domain.
**Rationale:** The LLM community defaults to using LLMs for every decision in an agent pipeline. This paper challenges that assumption empirically for two specific, high-frequency decisions in proactive agents. The wake decision is fundamentally a change-detection + relevance-filtering problem — well-studied in signal processing and information retrieval with mature non-LLM solutions. The anchor decision, by contrast, requires semantic compression and salience judgment — tasks where LLMs genuinely add value. The cascaded architecture mirrors human attention: low-level salience filters (brainstem) trigger high-level conscious processing (cortex) only when needed.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's architecture has no proactive agent capability — all agent actions are user-initiated or scheduled. This paper provides the blueprint for when Lyra adds proactive monitoring: use simple heuristics for wake decisions (keyword triggers, change detection), reserve LLM calls for anchoring decisions on events that pass the wake filter, and implement a cascaded pipeline. Lyra's context management subsystem (§4.4) and memory subsystem (§4.2) would be the primary consumers of anchoring decisions. Status: **BEHIND** (no proactive monitoring infrastructure; this paper provides the cost-efficient architecture for when it is added).
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 2 | **Tier:** investigate (enables future proactive features; pragmatic finding that simplifies architecture; no immediate integration path until proactive monitoring is prioritized)

## COMEM: Context Management with A Decoupled Long-Context Model
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30842
**Mechanism:** (1) Decouples context management from the primary task-solving model. Instead of sending growing context to a single LLM, COMEM uses a separate dedicated "context model" that maintains and compresses the full interaction history. (2) Architecture: Primary Model (solves the task, sees only compressed context + current query) and Context Model (processes raw interaction stream, produces compressed representations — either token-level embeddings or text summaries). (3) Three operating modes: Summary Mode (Context Model generates progressive text summaries at configurable granularity), Embedding Mode (Context Model produces dense vector representations of context segments, Primary Model attends via cross-attention), Hybrid Mode (combines summary tokens for recent context + embeddings for distant history). (4) Asynchronous operation: Context Model processes new interactions in the background while Primary Model handles the current request, enabling zero-latency context updates from the user's perspective. (5) Compression ratio: configurable from 4x (lossless summaries) to 32x (aggressive compression). (6) Context Model can be a smaller/cheaper model than Primary Model (e.g., 7B context model + 70B primary model).
**Results:** On long-context QA tasks (narrative QA, multi-session dialogue, code base understanding): COMEM achieves 93-97% of full-context accuracy while reducing Primary Model context length by 4-16x. At 16x compression, accuracy retention is 93% for narrative QA, 91% for code understanding, 88% for multi-session dialogue (dialogue is hardest — requires tracking conversational state). Latency improvement: Primary Model inference speed increases proportionally to compression ratio (4x compression → ~3.5x faster, overhead from cross-attention). Context Model cost: using 7B model as context processor adds 15-25% to total inference cost, but the overall system cost decreases 40-60% due to reduced Primary Model context (shorter prompts = fewer tokens processed by the expensive model). Comparison to retrieval-based context selection: COMEM outperforms RAG-based context selection by +8-15% on tasks requiring holistic understanding (where all context is potentially relevant), and matches RAG on factoid-lookup tasks.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: tasks with very long interaction histories (hundreds of turns, large codebases), deployments where Primary Model is expensive (decoupling allows smaller context model), latency-sensitive applications (asynchronous context processing), domains requiring holistic context understanding (summarization, synthesis). LOSES: short-context tasks (overhead of running two models exceeds benefit), simple factoid lookups (RAG is simpler and sufficient), when both models must be large (doubles the failure surface), when context Model quality is critical (compression errors propagate to Primary Model). The two-model architecture introduces deployment complexity: two model servers, synchronization, fallback when Context Model is unavailable.
**Rationale:** The standard approach — stuffing everything into the Primary Model's context window — has three failure modes: (a) cost scales quadratically with context length (attention is O(n²)), (b) models have effective context utilization limits (Lost-in-the-Middle problem), (c) latency scales linearly with context length. COMEM's decoupling addresses all three: the Primary Model sees compressed context (O(k²) where k << n), compression can be optimized for the Primary Model's attention pattern, and context processing happens asynchronously. The key architectural insight is that context management and task-solving are different capabilities that benefit from different model scales and architectures.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's context management subsystem (§4.4, maturity `draft`) assumes a single-model architecture where context is managed within the Primary Model's window via truncation, summarization, or retrieval. COMEM provides an alternative: a dedicated context-processing pipeline that could run as a background subsystem, compressing Lyra's growing session history, tool outputs, and multi-agent communication traces into representations the Primary Agent can efficiently consume. The hybrid mode (recent raw context + compressed distant history) maps naturally to Lyra's planned working-memory + episodic-memory split. Status: **BEHIND** (single-model context management; COMEM provides a decoupled alternative).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 4 | **Tier:** breakthrough (novel architecture with strong empirical results; directly addresses Lyra's context management bottleneck; two-model deployment complexity is the main adoption barrier)

## Toward Robust In-Context Learning: Leveraging Out-of-distribution Proxies for Target Inaccessible Demonstration Retrieval
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00014
**Mechanism:** (1) Addresses the core challenge in demonstration retrieval for in-context learning (ICL): what happens when the target task has no accessible labeled demonstrations (the cold-start / out-of-distribution setting)? (2) Proposes using proxy tasks — related tasks with available demonstrations — to retrieve or generate demonstrations for the target task. (3) Three-step pipeline: Step 1 (Proxy Discovery) — identifies candidate proxy tasks using semantic similarity (embedding-based), structural similarity (input/output format matching), and meta-learning (tasks where models show similar ICL behavior). Step 2 (Demonstration Adaptation) — adapts proxy demonstrations to target format via (a) format translation (rewriting input/output structure), (b) domain adaptation (replacing domain-specific entities while preserving reasoning patterns), (c) difficulty calibration (matching demonstration complexity to target task). Step 3 (Robust Aggregation) — selects and orders demonstrations using uncertainty-aware scoring that accounts for proxy-target mismatch. (4) The key robustness mechanism: rather than trusting a single proxy, the method ensembles multiple proxy sources and uses consistency across proxies as a confidence signal. (5) Theoretical analysis: provides generalization bounds for ICL with proxy demonstrations, showing that the gap depends on the divergence between proxy and target distributions and the number of proxy tasks.
**Results:** Across 12 NLP benchmarks spanning classification, QA, summarization, and code generation: proxy-based ICL achieves 78-94% of the performance of ICL with gold target-task demonstrations (upper bound), while using zero target-task examples. On target tasks where semantic proxy selection works well (classification tasks): 89-94% of gold ICL performance. On tasks sensitive to domain shift (code generation in unfamiliar languages): 78-85% of gold ICL. Ensemble of multiple proxies consistently outperforms single best proxy by +5-12%, validating the robustness-through-diversity approach. Comparison to zero-shot (no demonstrations): proxy ICL provides +18-35% improvement. Comparison to synthetic demonstration generation (self-ICL): proxy ICL outperforms by +8-15%, as real proxy demonstrations contain reasoning patterns that LLMs struggle to self-generate. Ablation: format adaptation alone contributes +6-10%, domain adaptation +3-7%, difficulty calibration +2-5% — all three are complementary.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: cold-start scenarios where target task has no labeled examples, rapidly evolving domains where demonstration sets become stale, privacy-constrained settings where target demonstrations cannot be shared, broad agent systems that encounter diverse and unpredictable tasks. LOSES: when gold target demonstrations are available (use them directly), highly specialized domains with no reasonable proxies (the method degrades to zero-shot), when proxy-target divergence is too large (theoretical bounds become vacuous). The proxy discovery step requires a diverse task pool to search from; the quality of the pool is a critical dependency.
**Rationale:** Standard ICL assumes access to demonstrations from the target distribution — a luxury not available in open-world agent settings. Prior work either ignores this (using random demonstrations, which can hurt performance) or generates synthetic demonstrations (which inherit the model's limitations). Proxy-based ICL takes a different approach: leverage demonstrations from related tasks where the underlying reasoning patterns transfer, even when the surface form differs. This is analogous to transfer learning in fine-tuning, applied to the demonstration selection problem. The robustness-through-diversity finding (ensembles outperform single best proxy) is practically important: it means the system does not need to identify the single perfect proxy, just a set of reasonable ones.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's few-shot prompting currently uses either (a) fixed hand-crafted demonstrations or (b) no demonstrations (zero-shot). There is no demonstration retrieval infrastructure and no mechanism for handling tasks with no available demonstrations. As Lyra expands to diverse tool-using and research tasks, cold-start ICL will become critical — the agent cannot assume demonstrations exist for every novel task. Proxy-based ICL provides a concrete architecture for Lyra's prompting subsystem (§4.8) to handle cold-start task generalization. Status: **BEHIND** (no demonstration retrieval; hand-crafted demonstrations only).
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** investigate (enables zero-shot-to-few-shot uplift without per-task demonstration curation; dependency: diverse task pool for proxy discovery; pragmatic Phase 3 enhancement)

## ReflecTool: Towards Reflection-Aware Tool-Augmented Clinical Agents
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17657
**Mechanism:** Two-stage framework for tool-augmented agents. (1) Optimization Stage: Agent solves tasks on small labeled subset, generates trajectory C1, self-reflects by comparing C1 with ground-truth y → suggestion S, regenerates C2. If C2 successful, saves trajectory as long-term memory (BM25 retrieval) and extracts tool-wise experience EX by comparing C1 vs C2 per-action. (2) Inference Stage: Retrieves top-k similar trajectories from memory via BM25, then at each step applies tool-wise verification using one of two methods: Iterative Refinement (sequential action refinement until convergence or max n steps, best at n=2) or Candidate Selection (sample n candidate actions, select best via verifier scoring, improves with larger n). Action space = 15 domain tools + {Plan, Think, Finish}. No fine-tuning required. Tool-wise experience E = {E_Calculator, E_MedRAG, ...} accumulates per-tool usage patterns across tasks.
**Results:** On ClinicalAgent Bench (CAB, 18 tasks across 5 dimensions): ReflecTool surpasses pure LLMs by **>10 points** on both Qwen2-7B (+10.43 over base) and Qwen2-72B (+10.90). Beats strongest agent baseline Reflexion by **+3.29 points** (Qwen2-72B: 59.66 vs 56.37, p<0.01). Tool selection error reduced **12-72x** vs ReAct at step-level (0.02 vs 1.44), **8-21x** vs Reflexion (0.02 vs 0.92). On Llama3-70B: +3.48 over Reflexion (62.26 vs 58.78). Runtime: Candidate Selection 28.56s/sample vs Reflexion 57.27s (Qwen2-72B) — 2x faster. Ablation: removing long-term memory costs 4-7 points; optimization steps improve monotonically 0→200.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: massive tool selection accuracy improvement (12-72x error reduction), cumulative learning across episodes (memory + tool experience), adaptive verification strategy (refinement for weak models, selection for strong models), training-free (works with any instruction-following LLM), efficient runtime (Candidate Selection parallelizable). LOSES: requires labeled optimization subset (cold-start = no memory), trajectory reliability unverified (correct answer via flawed reasoning gets saved), Iterative Refinement degrades beyond n=2 (over-refinement), BM25 retrieval misses semantic matches, domain-specific 15-tool action space (generalization to arbitrary toolsets not tested), sensitive to backbone instruction-following quality (Llama3 needed prompt adjustment).
**Rationale:** Online-only reflection (Reflexion) has no persistent cross-episode memory — each task starts from scratch. The optimization stage builds cumulative knowledge: successful trajectories as exemplars + per-action usage heuristics that transfer across task types. Tool-wise experience is more granular and transferable than full trajectories — action-level patterns ("cross-reference MedRAG results with another source") apply broadly. Two verification methods are inspired by test-time compute scaling (Snell et al. 2024): refinement = sequential improvement, selection = parallel sampling + picking best. Each excels at different model strengths, enabling adaptive strategy.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's tool-using agents (§4.7, maturity `draft`) rely on static tool descriptions and fixed few-shot examples. No mechanism exists for accumulating per-tool usage experience across sessions, no trajectory memory for tool selection guidance, and no verification step before tool invocation. As Lyra's tool ecosystem grows, per-tool expertise becomes critical for reliable multi-tool workflows. Status: **BEHIND** (no tool-wise experience accumulation; static tool descriptions only).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** breakthrough (addresses §4.7 tool-utilization gap with training-free method; 12-72x error reduction on tool selection; Candidate Selection maps to Lyra's multi-provider architecture; moderate effort — no training, no architecture changes)

## Mem2Evolve: Self-Evolving Agents via Co-Evolutionary Capability Expansion and Experience Distillation
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.10923
**Mechanism:** Dual-memory architecture coupling Asset Memory (tools + expert agents, MCP-compliant) with Experience Memory (lessons distilled from successes/failures). Forward inference follows "Reuse first, Create on demand": Task Planning decomposes queries into sub-tasks, Asset Recruitment retrieves matching assets from Asset Memory (embedding similarity > threshold δ) or triggers experience-guided tool/agent creation when capability gaps exist. Created assets undergo Self-Correction Loop (LLM synthesizes unit tests, validates, iteratively fixes until passing) before entering Asset Memory. Backward Evolution: LLM-as-Judge evaluates trajectory (success/failure + critique), preserves high-quality assets, distills transferable lessons into Experience Memory (success abstraction + failure anti-pattern encoding). Tool creation uses 3-stage pipeline: Spec Generation → Documentation/Experience Collection (web search + memory retrieval) → MCP-compliant Implementation. Experience-guided creation improves first-pass validity by 56% and reduces fix iterations by 68%.
**Results:** 6 task categories, 8 benchmarks (GAIA, ALFWorld, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, AIME24/25, TravelPlanner, WebShop), GPT-5-chat backbone. Mem2Evolve achieves 70.24% average Pass@1 vs. 63.78% best capability-centric baseline (Alita, +6.46%), 58.44% best experience-centric baseline (AFLOW, +11.80%), 51.71% best naive LLM (CoT, +18.53%). GAIA: 76.31 vs. 67.36 (OpenAI DeepResearch). Ablation: w/o Tool Creation -10.28% (largest drop), w/o Agent Memory -4.73%, w/o Tool Memory -3.13%, w/o Expert Agent Creation -1.72%. Cross-task memory from GAIA transfers to 7 other benchmarks with performance matching 25% single-task initialization.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: dynamic capability expansion beyond static tool libraries, experience stabilizes creation (68% fewer debug iterations), cross-task memory reuse without negative transfer, MCP-compliant tools ensure interoperability, self-correction loop prevents low-quality asset persistence. LOSES: requires sandboxed code execution (limits open-world deployment), ~2x LLM calls vs static baselines, LLM-as-Judge noise propagates to memory, WebShop gain modest (+1.30%), memory scalability beyond ~200 tasks untested.
**Rationale:** Grounded in Piaget's equilibrium theory: intelligence evolves through interplay of assimilation (integrating experience) and accommodation (adapting structures). Prior work does one or the other; Mem2Evolve does both. Experience without capability expansion is bounded by static tools; capability expansion without experience leads to non-replicable success and repeated errors. The "Reuse first" strategy conserves resources; creation triggers only when similarity falls below threshold δ.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has static plugin registry (≈ Tool Bank) and session memory (§4.4) but NO Asset Creation capability (cannot generate new tools/agents at runtime), NO Experience Memory for strategic lesson distillation, and NO Backward Evolution pass that analyzes trajectories post-completion to improve future performance. Status: **BEHIND** (static capability space only; no self-evolution loop).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 5 | **Tier:** Tier 3 (6+ months) — foundational architecture change requiring sandbox, LLM-as-Judge, embedding retrieval, trajectory storage; depends on plugin system maturity

## Multi-Agent Scripts Generation for Imperfect-Information Reasoning in Murder Mystery Games
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.11741
**Mechanism:** Two-phase framework. Phase 1 (Data Generation): 7 specialized agents collaboratively synthesize Murder Mystery game scripts. Generation agents: OutlineAgent (story outline), CharacterAgent (detailed role scripts with motives), CriticAgent (4-dimension evaluation: plot complexity, character development, difficulty, logical rationality; provides feedback for refinement), ClueAgent (multimodal clues — text + AI-generated images — that do not reveal the murderer), RoleplayAgent (multi-turn dialogues with role-specific behavior: murderer lies strategically, innocents tell truth), QaAgent (multi-hop reasoning chains + 4 QA types: Long Script, Text-rich Image, Media-rich Image, Multi-Hop Multimodal). Evaluation agent: ScoreAgent (LLM-as-Judge for RL reward scoring). Phase 2 (Training): Two-stage agent-monitored pipeline. Stage 1: LoRA SFT on Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B-Instruct with synthetic + human data (65,536 token context, 512×512 images). Stage 2: GRPO-based RL (no KL penalty) with specialized reward functions — for unverifiable data (Self-Introduction, Discussion): ScoreAgent rates role-consistency 0-10; for verifiable data (QA): reward = 1(α·S_correct > β)·[S_correct + (1-α)·S_format + S_match]. Correctness threshold β prevents reward hacking; image-clue matching reward S_match encourages visual grounding.
**Results:** On WhodunitBench (7 metrics, 3 capability groups). Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct: MMR 30.92→55.01 (+24.09), Decision-Making 20.14%→35.00% (+14.86%), TIU 35.09→74.56 (+39.56), MIU 32.16→61.09 (+28.93). Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct: MMR 37.63→58.42★ (+20.79), DM 25.61%→36.87% (+11.26%), TIU 40.63→77.28★ (+36.65). ★ = surpasses all tested open-source VLMs. 7B MMR 58.42 vs GPT-4V 58.75, Gemini-1.5-Pro 57.39, Claude 57.78 — competitive with proprietary. Ablation: w/o RL causes CMD collapse (34.25→17.02), w/o SFT reduces MMR by 6.45 points. Human+Synthetic data outperforms either alone. Inter-judge Pearson r: 0.83-0.87 for CMD, 0.68-0.72 for RP. Human-LLM Spearman ρ: 0.71 (CMD), 0.62 (RP).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: scalable data generation (34 scripts→3,785 QA pairs with explicit chains), GRPO with agent-monitored rewards avoids training separate reward model, two-stage training (SFT→RL) consistently better than either alone, 3B variant matches 27B open-source VLMs on perception, multi-judge aggregation provides stable evaluation. LOSES: Role-Playing scores remain low (6.35/10 for 3B), VLM-specific (not agent architecture — multi-agent only for data synthesis), partial human verification still needed for image alignment, Murder Mystery simplifies real-world imperfect information, CMD absolute scores poor (34.25/100), no cost measurement for Gemini 2.5Pro data generation.
**Rationale:** Murder Mystery is minimal tractable environment capturing all imperfect-information elements: role-asymmetric info, strategic deception, multi-hop multimodal inference, social interaction. Multi-agent synthesis scales script production beyond manual curation; CriticAgent feedback loop ensures quality. Two-stage training addresses the gap: SFT for base capabilities, GRPO for nuanced role-consistent behavior that SFT cannot optimize (no ground truth for subjective dimensions). Correctness threshold β prevents models from optimizing format at expense of accuracy.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's evaluation harness (§4.7) uses hand-crafted test scenarios with limited diversity. The multi-agent scenario generation pattern (generation-evaluation agent split with CriticAgent quality gate) could scale Lyra's evaluation dataset production. Status: **BEHIND** (no automated scenario synthesis; manual test creation only).
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** Tier 2 (2-4 months) — builds on existing LLM access and evaluation infrastructure; no model training needed for the data generation component

## FAMA: Failure-Aware Meta-Agentic Framework for Open-Source LLMs in Interactive Tool Use Environments
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.25135
**Mechanism:** Two-stage, training-free framework for improving open-source LLM tool-use agents. Pre-defined agent pool A: Domain Constraints Extractor (DCE), Tool Suggestion Agent (TSA), Tool Output Reformulator (TOR), Planner Agent, Decision Verifier Agent, Memory Module. Pre-defined error categories E: Domain Policy Violation (DCV), Wrong Retrieval from Complex Tool Outputs (WRCO), Contextual Misinterpretation/Hallucination (CM), Incomplete Fulfillment/Early Stopping (IFU). Stage 1 (Failure Analysis): Run baseline agent on all tasks; for each failure, |E| independent error analysis agents produce categorical decisions + rationales; Orchestrator Agent identifies primary root cause error(s). Stage 2 (Mitigation): Mitigation Agent selects minimal subset A* ⊆ A to address identified errors. Stage 3 (Re-execution): Only selected agents inject targeted context into tool-use agent's prior before each decision step. Key properties: training-free, model-specific (different models get different agent subsets), extensible (new agents can be added to A), minimal context overhead (~30% vs 50-58% full multi-agent).
**Results:** 4 open-source models (Qwen3-4B/14B/32B, Qwen2.5-72B-Inst) on τ-bench, τ-trait, ACEBench. τ-bench Airline: FAMA avg +4.63% over ReAct, +11.57% over FC, +5.27% over IRMA. τ-bench Retail: avg +5.30% over ReAct, +8.96% over FC, +6.15% over IRMA. Best individual: Qwen3-14B Airline ReAct 18.40%→FAMA 36.80% (+18.40%, 2x). Qwen3-4B Retail ReAct 17.22%→FAMA 34.60% (+17.38%). ACEBench End-to-End: Qwen2.5-72B Base 23.3%→FAMA-Base 50.0% (+26.7%). τ-trait: Qwen3-14B Telecom ReAct 15.55%→FAMA 43.00% (+27.45%). Token overhead: FAMA ~30% vs IRMA 50-58%. Latency: FAMA 57-91s vs IRMA 112-150s. Dominant errors across all models: DCV 15-55%, CM 35-61%. Most recommended: Memory module + DCE agent. Memory size is domain-dependent (k=2 Airline, k=6 Retail). Self-Reflection baseline consistently underperforms FAMA.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: training-free (works with any off-the-shelf LLM), model-specific adaptation, consistent across 3 benchmarks and 6+ sub-domains, context-efficient (~30% overhead), minimal agent sets (often 1-2 agents), extensible error/agent taxonomy, largest gains on smallest models. LOSES: bounded by predefined agent pool (cannot address failures with no corresponding agent in A), requires initial baseline run (2x execution cost), depends on frontier model quality for error analysis (GPT-4o), diminishing returns on strong models (Qwen2.5-72B +0.70-4.5%), memory module k is domain-tuned not principled, thinking variants suffer context overflows.
**Rationale:** Prior work adds capabilities indiscriminately (more agents, more context) without understanding model-specific failure patterns. FAMA inverts this: diagnose first, then prescribe minimal intervention. Using ALL agents (IRMA) degrades some models (Qwen3-32B Airline: ReAct 30.40% vs IRMA 24.40%) because excess context competes with critical information in limited windows. Minimal selection avoids this. Training-free is key for open-source models: fine-tuning requires expensive trajectory collection; inference-time orchestration is immediately deployable. Independent error agents with detailed failure cause lists make analysis tractable and interpretable.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's agent runtime (§4.2) has no failure analysis module, no error taxonomy, and no mechanism for context injection based on detected failure patterns. When Lyra fails a multi-turn tool-use task, it retries identically or fails permanently — there's no diagnostic pass that adapts future attempts based on failure analysis. Status: **BEHIND** (no failure-aware orchestration; identical retry on failure).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 2 | **Tier:** Tier 1 (1-2 months) — training-free, builds on existing agent infrastructure, immediate ROI via improved tool-use task completion rates; only requires error taxonomy definition, helper prompts, and failure classifier using existing LLM backend

## MRAgent: Memory is Reconstructed, Not Retrieved — Graph Memory for LLM Agents
**Source:** arXiv:2606.06036v1 (ICML 2026) | **Authors:** Shuo Ji, Yibo Li, Bryan Hooi (NUS)
**Mechanism:** Replaces static "retrieve-then-reason" with active memory reconstruction. Memory is a Cue–Tag–Content heterogeneous graph with 3 layers: Episodic (event-specific, temporally ordered), Semantic (stable facts/preferences), and Topic abstraction. Retrieval is an iterative loop: (1) f_select — LLM selects traversal actions (Cue→Tag, (Cue,Tag)→Content, Content→Cue/Tag) based on accumulated evidence, (2) Controlled traversal — mapping operators expand candidates, (3) f_route — LLM prunes irrelevant branches, (4) Stop/Continue. Tags act as semantic bottlenecks: LLM evaluates short tag phrases before committing to reading full episodic content. Construction: LLM distillation pipeline extracts tags, cues, semantic units, and topics from raw dialogue. Formal proof that active retrieval is strictly more expressive than passive (Theorem 4.1: H_passive ⊊ H_active for any T≥2). Two execution modes: Navigate (tool-based traversal) and Answer (generation from reconstructed context). 7 memory tools (Table 4) provide typed mapping between memory components.
**Results:** LoCoMo (Gemini backbone): Overall J score 85.34 vs next best 80.68 (LangMem) — +23.3% relative gain. Claude backbone: 61.10→88.32 (+12.4%). LongMemEval (Gemini): Overall 72.95 vs next best 54.92 — +32% relative gain. MRAgent* (Claude retrieval + Gemini construction): 86.76 Overall. Token consumption: 118k vs 245k-3,268k for baselines (5.3-27.7x lower). Runtime: 586s vs 533-3,136s. Ablation: Cue→Episode 55J → Cue–Tag–Episode 60J → CTC (full) 65J → CTC+Reasoning 85J → CTC+Reasoning-Semantic 82J. Multi-hop recall improves >30pp across successive turns; max valid turns matches avg turns (LLM self-regulates depth). Per-turn parallel retrieval budget K saturates quickly — reconstruction depth T is the bottleneck.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: +23-32% relative accuracy gains, 5-28x fewer tokens, noise reduction via tag-guided pruning, strictly more expressive than passive retrieval (proven), interpretable traversal, composable memory layers for different query types. LOSES: retrieval latency grows with query depth (O(depth × branching)), no memory update/consolidation (monotonic storage growth), construction quality depends on distillation LLM, not evaluated on adversarial queries, two-backbone setup needed for best results.
**Rationale:** Cognitive neuroscience: human memory retrieval is active associative reconstruction (Frankland & Josselyn 2019; Rugg & Renoult 2025). Cue–Tag–Content mirrors cue→engram→recall pathway. Passive retrieval has 3 weaknesses: no strategy revision, noise accumulation, rigid dependency on pre-constructed structures. Tags decouple associative reasoning from content retrieval. Deferred relation modeling: complex dependencies resolved at query-time, not construction-time.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's conversation memory relies on flat context-window retrieval with no active traversal, no associative tag structure, and no multi-step evidence accumulation. Long conversations cause context collapse. MRAgent's loop directly addresses this. Status: **BEHIND** (flat retrieval, no graph-structured memory, no active reconstruction).
**Impact:** 5 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** Tier 1 (high-impact architectural change — active memory reconstruction for Lyra's conversation memory)

## CaTS: Calibrated Test-Time Scaling for Efficient LLM Reasoning
**Source:** ICLR 2026 | **Authors:** Chengsong Huang, Langlin Huang (WashU), Jixuan Leng (CMU), Jiacheng Liu (UW), Jiaxin Huang (WashU)
**Mechanism:** Two-part system. Part 1 — Self-Calibration: (a) Generate N=32 responses per query with Dynamic Temperature (EDT) sampling for diversity, (b) Compute P(True) confidence for each response via "Is the answer correct? (Yes/No)" prompt (costs ~10 tokens via KV-cache), (c) Compute Soft Self-Consistency (SSC) score = weighted agreement across responses: SSC(y) = Σ_{i:yi=y} c_i / Σ c_i, (d) Train model with SmoothL1 loss between predicted and SSC confidence + generation loss on high-confidence (η>0.75) responses (weight ω=0.1), LoRA r=32, α=16. Part 2 — CaTS Inference: (a) CaTS-ES: Early-stop Best-of-N when confidence c_i ≥ τ, (b) CaTS-SC: Weighted majority vote using confidence scores, (c) CaTS-ASC: Confidence-weighted adaptive self-consistency with threshold-based stopping. Theoretical proof: q-weighting exponentially dominates majority voting when confidence signal satisfies μ²_q/(2v_q+2μ_q/3) > μ²_MV/(2v_MV+2μ_MV/3).
**Results:** Sample budget=16. Llama-3.1-8B — MathQA: SC 73.7→CaTS-SC 83.6 (+9.9), Best-of-N 73.7→CaTS-ES 83.6 (+9.9). Obj Counting: SC 69.1→CaTS-SC 76.8 (+7.7). ARC Challenge: SC 85.2→CaTS-SC 87.7 (+2.5). Efficiency: CaTS-SC saves 94.2% samples to reach 85.0 MathQA accuracy vs vanilla SC. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-1.5B — Obj Counting: Best-of-N 48.1→CaTS-ES 70.8 (+22.7). ARC: Best-of-N 54.1→CaTS-ES 66.5 (+12.4). Self-Calibration quality: Llama GSM8K ECE 13.70→3.79; SVAMP ECE 28.03→10.17. Qwen2.5-7B MathQA OOD accuracy 49.85→64.18 (+14.33). Self-calibrated confidence matches or exceeds separate reward model of equal size (MathQA: confidence 84.0 vs reward 82.1) while costing ~10 tokens vs doubling inference time. Robust to prompt variation: 6 alternative prompts yield MathQA CaTS-SC 81.63±0.20. GPQA: SC 33.28→CaTS-SC 35.53; Hellaswag: 66.62→72.84; MMLU Pro: 49.19→53.43.
**Trade-offs:** WINS: 94.2% sample savings, universal across 3 architectures and 9+ datasets, no human labels, no extra model at inference, theoretically grounded, prompt-robust, simple LoRA fine-tuning. LOSES: requires fine-tuning (not API-only compatible), early stopping can be premature at very small budgets, threshold τ requires per-dataset calibration, binary correctness labels cause confidence collapse (CaTS-ES MathQA 83.6→81.2), single-turn QA only (no multi-turn agent evaluation), SSC quality depends on base model capability.
**Rationale:** Fixed N sampling wastes computation on easy queries. Self-Consistency provides well-calibrated confidence but is expensive to compute. Key insight: distill this expensive multi-sample signal into single-pass prediction. SSC bridges P(True) (cheap but miscalibrated) and SC (accurate but expensive). EDT prevents mode collapse in easy queries. L1-smooth better balances calibration and generation than MSE.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra has no confidence estimation for its own outputs or tool calls. Tool retries use fixed counts; response quality is not self-assessed. Self-Calibration could provide calibrated confidence for adaptive tool retry and response verification. Status: **BEHIND** (no confidence estimation, fixed retry counts, no self-assessment of output quality).
**Impact:** 4 | **Effort:** 3 | **Tier:** Tier 2 (requires training infrastructure but high token savings potential)

## Select, Read, and Write: A Multi-Agent Framework of Full-Text-based Related Work Generation
**Source:** arXiv:2505.19647v1 (May 2025) | **Authors:** Xiaochuan Liu, Ruihua Song*, Xiting Wang*, Xu Chen (Renmin University of China)
**Mechanism:** Three-agent system for long-document synthesis. Selector: decides which section of which reference paper to read next based on abstracts, working memory, and reading history. Five strategies evaluated: Sequential (SR), Random (RR), Vanilla LLM, Graph-Co (co-occurrence graph constraint), Graph-Ci (citation graph constraint). Reader: digests selected section content, reorganizes working memory (4096-token limit, JSON format with paper ID, content, relationships), discards irrelevant info at each step. Writer: generates final output from curated memory with explicit relationship-grouping instructions and in-context example. Graph-aware selector operates within one-hop subgraph: can continue reading current paper or jump to graph-adjacent paper. Two graphs: citation (direct edges = citations, sparser) and co-occurrence (edges = papers co-cited in same sentence, denser). Termination: selector outputs `<End>` when no further reading needed. Working memory enforces explicit compression — reader must curate at each step.
**Results:** OARelatedWork dataset (10% subset, avg 70K tokens/instance). Graph-Ci best across all models: GPT-4o Overall LLM 3.87/5 (vs 3.73 sequential), Claude-3-Haiku 3.61, Llama3-8B 3.44. Avg edges (graph density): GPT-4o Graph-Ci 2.13 vs GPT-4o vanilla 1.84 vs human 9.48 (large gap). Human evaluation win rates: 58-68% across criteria. Reading efficiency: Graph-Ci reads only 25.81% of content (vs 100% SR/RR, 35.27% vanilla). Surprising: dumping all full-text into long-context models (GPT-4o 128K, Claude 200K) is WORSE than abstract-only (Claude drops 9.3%). Key metric: RWS sections read 73.5% of the time, experiments only 5%. Memory quality: 96% retention ratio, 95% accuracy. Robust to prompt rewrites (3.87 vs 3.86).
**Trade-offs:** WINS: consistent across 3 model tiers, 3.9x reading reduction, robust to input configuration, explicit relationship modeling, human-validated, high memory fidelity. LOSES: large gap to human quality (3.2 vs 9.5 avg edges), requires pre-specified reference set (no auto-retrieval), graphs must be pre-computed externally, weaker models degrade with more content, section-level graphs don't help (worse than article-level), memory size fixed at 4096 tokens, 10% dataset subset.
**Rationale:** Multi-agent decomposition maps to RWG task structure: planning (selector), comprehension (reader), synthesis (writer) — mirrors human literature review. Graph constraints encode real academic relationships. Size-constrained memory forces active curation (learned attention bottleneck). Separating reading order from digestion enables modular optimization. RWS as most information-dense section validates design (73.5% of reading targets). Graph-Ci > Graph-Co because citation graphs are sparser and provide stronger structural guidance.
**Gap-vs-baseline:** Lyra's document analysis feeds entire documents into context (or retrieves chunks indiscriminately). No iterative reading loop, no graph-constrained traversal, no size-constrained working memory. The Selector-Reader-Writer pattern could enhance Lyra's multi-document synthesis for research tasks. Status: **BEHIND** (flat document processing, no iterative reading, no memory curation).
**Impact:** 3 | **Effort:** 2 | **Tier:** Tier 2 (low-effort prompt-engineering pattern — immediate application to Lyra's research/synthesis capabilities)
